statement: There is no fundamental difference between software design and software architecture; high-level structure and low-level details form one continuous fabric of decisions from the highest to the lowest level.
When a system is built well, changes are simple and rapid, defects are few, and far fewer human resources are required to build and maintain it.
Getting a program to work once is easy; getting the software structured right is hard and demands knowledge, discipline, and dedication most programmers do not invest.
The rules of software architecture are the same across all system types and are independent of every other variable.
Because the building blocks of programs (sequence, selection, iteration) have not changed, the rules for ordering and assembling them are likewise universal and unchanging.
The architectural significance of a design decision is measured by its cost of change: the decisions that are expensive to change are the architectural ones.
A good architecture must meet the needs of its users, developers, and owners not only at one point in time but continuously over time.
Treat an architecture as a hypothesis to be proven by implementation and measurement rather than as a frozen, final artifact.
The only way to go fast in software is to go well; sacrificing structure for short-term speed slows a team down over time.

Boxes on a diagram are only one chosen view of an architecture, not the architecture itself; what to include, exclude, or emphasize is a choice, so a diagram should not be mistaken for the system's true structure.
The goal of software architecture is to minimize the human resources required to build and maintain the required system.

Design quality is measured by the effort required to meet customer needs: if that effort stays low across the system's lifetime the design is good, and if it grows with each release the design is bad.

When systems are thrown together hastily and little thought is given to code cleanliness or design structure, developer productivity declines asymptotically toward zero even as staffing and cost rise.
The belief that messy code can be cleaned up later is false, because market pressure never abates and the cleanup never happens.
Making messes is always slower than staying clean, regardless of the time scale considered.
In a controlled six-day experiment, completing the same task with test-driven development ran about 10% faster than without it, and even the slowest TDD iteration beat the fastest non-TDD iteration.
Rewriting a system from scratch is usually driven by the same overconfidence that produced the original mess and tends to reproduce that mess, so it is rarely the best option.

Every software system delivers two distinct values to stakeholders — behavior (what it does) and structure (architecture, how easily it changes) — and developers are responsible for keeping both high.
Treating implementing requirements and fixing bugs as the entirety of a developer's job is a mistake, because it ignores the second value of software, its structure.
Software is meant to be soft (easy to change), so the difficulty of making a change should be proportional only to the scope of the change and not to its shape.
Development cost grows disproportionately to change size when the shape of the system does not match the shape of the requested changes.
Architectures should be as shape-agnostic as practical, not preferring one shape of change over another.

Ease of change is the greater long-term value: a program that works but cannot be changed becomes useless when requirements change, whereas one that is easy to change can be made to work and kept working.
A system can become practically impossible to change when the cost of a change exceeds its benefit, even though no software is literally impossible to change.
condition: when the cost of change exceeds the benefit of change

statement: Software behavior is urgent but not always important, while architecture is important but never urgent; the damaging mistake is elevating urgent-but-unimportant features above the important architecture.

Because business managers are not equipped to evaluate the importance of architecture, it is the development team's responsibility to assert the importance of architecture over the urgency of features.
Developers are stakeholders in the software and must struggle as equals with other stakeholders to defend the architecture they know the system needs.
If architecture is addressed last, the system becomes ever more costly to develop until change becomes practically impossible for part or all of it.
A programming paradigm dictates which control structures to use and when, and is largely independent of any particular language.

There are three programming paradigms — structured, object-oriented, and functional — and each one removes a capability from the programmer rather than adding one, so further negative paradigms are unlikely.
Structured programming imposes discipline on direct transfer of control, replacing unrestrained goto with if/then/else and do/while constructs.
Object-oriented programming imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control through the disciplined use of polymorphism (function pointers).
Functional programming imposes discipline upon assignment, founded on immutability of values.

The three paradigms map onto the three big architectural concerns: polymorphism is the mechanism for crossing architectural boundaries, functional programming disciplines the location of and access to data, and structured programming is the algorithmic foundation of modules.
All programs can be constructed from just three structures — sequence, selection, and iteration — as proven by Bohm and Jacopini.

Formal mathematical proofs of program correctness proved impractical and were never adopted at scale; few programmers today regard formal proofs as an appropriate way to produce high-quality software.
Software development is like a science rather than mathematics: correctness cannot be proven, only falsified, so we deem a program correct enough once tests fail to prove it incorrect.
Testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence; a program can be proven incorrect by a test but never proven correct by one.
A program that is not provable cannot be deemed correct no matter how many tests are applied to it.
condition: when the program is not decomposable into provable units, e.g. due to unrestrained goto

statement: Structured programming is valuable today because it forces a program to be recursively decomposed into small, falsifiable (testable) units.

Software architects should define modules, components, and services that are easily falsifiable (testable), applying restrictive disciplines analogous to structured programming at the architectural level.
Functional decomposition remains one of the best practices at the architectural level.
Encapsulation is not unique to object-oriented languages, and OO languages actually weakened the strong encapsulation available in C, so OO cannot be defined by strong encapsulation.
Inheritance and polymorphism both predate object-oriented languages; OO did not invent them but made them far more convenient and, for polymorphism, much safer.
Polymorphism is fundamentally an application of pointers to functions; OO's contribution is removing the dangerous manual conventions, which imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control.
Polymorphism lets a program use new implementations as plugins without changing or recompiling the calling code, as long as those implementations honor the agreed interface.
condition: as long as the new implementation honors the agreed interface (e.g. the standard IO functions)

statement: Programs should be device independent, which is why the plugin architecture was invented and has been implemented in almost every operating system since.
Without polymorphism, source code dependencies inexorably follow the flow of control, because every caller must name the module that contains its callee.
Polymorphism enables dependency inversion: by inserting an interface, a source code dependency can be made to point in the direction opposite to the flow of control.

Because OO provides safe and convenient polymorphism, any source code dependency anywhere can be inverted, giving the architect absolute control over the direction of every source code dependency in the system.
Dependencies should be arranged so that the UI and the database depend on the business rules rather than the reverse, making the UI and database plugins to the business rules.
When business rules do not mention the UI or database in source code, those concerns can be compiled and deployed as separate components, achieving independent deployability.
Modules that can be deployed independently can also be developed independently by different teams.

To the architect, OO is the ability — through polymorphism — to gain absolute control over every source code dependency, enabling a plugin architecture in which high-level policy modules are independent of low-level detail modules.
In functional languages variables do not vary: they are initialized but never modified.
Race conditions, deadlocks, and concurrent-update problems all stem from mutable variables, and none of them can occur if no variable is ever mutated.
An architect should care about concurrency and design systems to remain robust in the presence of multiple threads and processors.
Immutability is practicable in real systems only when certain compromises are made, since infinite storage and processor speed are not available.
condition: provided certain compromises are made; trivially practicable only with infinite storage and processor speed

statement: A common and recommended compromise is to segregate an application into immutable, purely functional components and separate mutable components, confining state mutation to the latter.
Mutable state should be protected from concurrent updates and race conditions using transactional memory, which guards in-memory variables the way a database guards records on disk.

Event sourcing stores the transactions rather than the state and derives current state by replaying transactions, which removes mutable state and concurrent-update problems; periodic snapshots bound the replay cost.
condition: given enough storage and processing power for the application's reasonable lifetime

statement: When a data store is never updated or deleted (only appended), applications become CR rather than CRUD and no concurrent-update issues can arise.
Architects should push as much processing as possible into immutable components and drive as much code as possible out of the components that must mutate state.
All software is composed of sequence, selection, iteration, and indirection — nothing more and nothing less.
The SOLID principles govern how to arrange functions and data into classes and how those classes interconnect, and apply to any cohesive grouping of functions and data, not only object-oriented code.
The goal of the SOLID principles is to create mid-level software structures that tolerate change, are easy to understand, and serve as the basis of reusable components.
The Single Responsibility Principle means a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor — not that a module or class should do only one thing.
The SRP directs you to separate code that different actors depend on; cohesion is the force that binds together the code responsible to a single actor.
Placing code that serves different actors in close proximity lets one actor's required change silently break behavior another actor depends on, for example through a shared helper function.
Putting methods responsible to different actors in one source file invites colliding, risky merges, which is a further reason to separate code that supports different actors.
One way to satisfy the SRP is to separate the data from the functions, giving each actor its own class over a shared method-free data structure, optionally unified behind a Facade.
The SRP reappears at higher levels: as the Common Closure Principle among components and as the Axis of Change that creates architectural boundaries.
The Open-Closed Principle states that a software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification, so behavior is extended by adding new code rather than changing existing code.

If simple extensions to the requirements force massive changes to the software, the architecture has failed; a good architecture reduces the amount of changed code toward the barest minimum, ideally zero.
OCP at the architectural level is achieved by separating the things that change for different reasons (SRP) and then organizing the dependencies between them properly (DIP).
To protect component A from changes in component B, arrange the dependency so that B depends on A; point source-code dependencies toward the components you want to protect.
Components should be organized into a hierarchy of protection by level, with the highest-level components (the business rules) the most protected from changes in lower-level components.
Architects separate functionality based on how, why, and when it changes, then arrange the separated parts into a component dependency hierarchy.
Interpose interfaces to invert dependencies that would otherwise point from high-level policy toward low-level detail.
Software entities should not depend on things they do not directly use, and transitive dependencies are a violation of this principle.
Interfaces should hide a component's internals so clients do not acquire transitive dependencies on things they do not directly use.

The Liskov Substitution Principle requires that subtypes be substitutable for their base type, such that any program defined in terms of the base behaves unchanged when a subtype instance is substituted.

The square/rectangle case violates LSP because a Square's coupled dimensions break behavior a Rectangle's independently mutable dimensions guarantee, and defending against it forces the user to test for the actual subtype, proving the types are not substitutable.

The LSP has broadened from a rule guiding inheritance into a general design principle about interfaces and the interchangeability of their implementations, whether language interfaces, shared method signatures, or REST services.
The LSP applies wherever users depend on a well-defined interface and on the substitutability of that interface's implementations.
The LSP should be extended to the architectural level, because a single violation of substitutability can pollute a system's architecture with a significant amount of extra mechanism.
Do not embed concrete identifiers (such as a specific vendor name) into branching code; insulate such variation behind a configuration-driven mechanism rather than special-case if statements.

The Interface Segregation Principle says not to depend on a module that contains more than you need; in statically typed languages, depending on unused operations forces needless recompilation and redeployment.
Segregate fat interfaces into client-specific interfaces so that each user depends only on the operations it actually uses.

Dynamically typed languages avoid the source-code declarations that force recompilation and redeployment, which tends to make their systems more flexible and less tightly coupled than statically typed ones.

The deeper, architectural lesson of the ISP is that depending on something which carries baggage you do not need can cause troubles you did not expect, such as a framework bound to an unused database forcing redeploys or propagating failures.
The Dependency Inversion Principle states that the most flexible systems are those whose source-code dependencies refer only to abstractions, not to concretions.
Apply the DIP only to volatile concrete elements that are under active, frequent change; tolerate dependencies on stable concretions such as String or operating-system and platform facilities.
exception: stable, rarely-changing concretions (e.g. String, OS/platform facilities) are excepted from the don't-depend-on-concretions rule

statement: Interfaces are less volatile than their implementations, and good designers work to keep interfaces stable by adding functionality to implementations without changing the interfaces.

The DIP reduces to concrete coding rules: do not refer to volatile concrete classes (use abstract interfaces), do not derive from them, do not override their concrete functions, and never mention the name of anything concrete and volatile.
Inheritance is the strongest and most rigid of all source-code relationships, so it should be used with great care.
Creating a volatile concrete object should be handled through an Abstract Factory, because object creation otherwise forces a source-code dependency on the concrete type.
DIP violations cannot be entirely eliminated, so they should be gathered into a small number of concrete components (such as main) and kept separate from the rest of the system.

At a dependency-inversion boundary the source-code dependencies cross toward the abstract side while the flow of control crosses in the opposite direction, and this inversion is the basis of what becomes the Dependency Rule.
Components are the units of deployment — the smallest entities (jar, gem, DLL, or binary aggregations) that can be deployed as part of a system.
Well-designed components always retain the ability to be independently deployable and therefore independently developable.
Deciding which classes belong in which component is an important design decision that should be guided by principles rather than made ad hoc based on context.

The Reuse/Release Equivalence Principle holds that the granule of reuse is the granule of release: components cannot be reused unless they are tracked through a release process and given release numbers.
Classes and modules grouped into one component must form a cohesive group that shares an overarching theme or purpose and is releasable together.
A release process must produce appropriate notifications and release documentation so that users can make informed decisions about when and whether to adopt a new release.

The Common Closure Principle says to gather into one component the classes that change for the same reasons and at the same times, and to separate classes that change at different times or for different reasons; it is the SRP restated for components.
For most applications maintainability outweighs reusability, so confining a change to a single component minimizes the work of releasing, revalidating, and redeploying.
condition: for most applications, where maintainability is more important than reusability

statement: Because 100% closure is unattainable, closure must be strategic: design components to be closed against the most common kinds of change you expect or have experienced.

The Common Reuse Principle says not to force the users of a component to depend on things they do not need, and that classes reused together (which depend heavily on each other) belong in the same component.

A using component depends on the whole used component, so any change in the used component can force the user to be recompiled, revalidated, and redeployed even when irrelevant; therefore put only inseparable classes together in a component.
The Common Reuse Principle is the component-level generalization of the Interface Segregation Principle, and both reduce to: do not depend on things you do not need.

The three component-cohesion principles are in tension — REP and CCP are inclusive and enlarge components while CRP is exclusive and shrinks them — and a good architect resolves this tension for the team's current concerns.

The right balance among the cohesion principles shifts with project maturity: develop-ability (CCP) dominates early, and reuse (REP/CRP) grows in importance as other projects begin to draw on the code.
condition: balance varies with project maturity and how the project is developed and used

statement: The Acyclic Dependencies Principle requires that there be no cycles in the component dependency graph.
Cycles in the component dependency graph cause the morning-after syndrome and fuse the involved components into one entangled block that is hard to build, unit-test, and release in any clear order.
Partition the development environment into independently releasable, release-numbered components so teams can adopt new releases on their own schedule and integration happens in small increments.

Continuously monitor the component dependency structure for cycles and break any that appear, either by applying the DIP to invert a dependency through a new interface or by extracting the shared classes into a new component.
The component dependency structure cannot be designed top-down; it is not designed first but evolves as the system grows and changes.
Component dependency diagrams are a map of a system's buildability and maintainability, not a description of its function.

A primary concern when shaping the component dependency graph is isolation of volatility: arrange dependencies so that volatile components cannot affect stable, high-value components such as the business rules.
The Stable Dependencies Principle says to depend in the direction of stability: a component expected to be volatile must not be depended on by a component that is hard to change.
A module designed to be easy to change can be made hard to change merely by another hard-to-change module hanging a dependency on it, without a single line of its own code changing.

Stability is measured by the work required to change a component, not by its frequency of change; a component with many incoming dependencies is stable because every change must be reconciled with all its dependents.

A component's instability can be quantified as I = Fan-out / (Fan-in + Fan-out) in the range [0,1], where I=0 is maximally stable (responsible and independent) and I=1 is maximally unstable (irresponsible and dependent).

The Stable Dependencies Principle in metric form requires that a component's I value be greater than the I values of the components it depends on, so instability decreases in the direction of dependency.

Not all components should be stable: if every component were maximally stable the system would be unchangeable, so deliberately design some components to be unstable and have them depend on the stable ones.
By convention, draw unstable components at the top of a dependency diagram so that any upward-pointing arrow visibly signals a Stable Dependencies (and Acyclic Dependencies) violation.
Abstract components that contain only interfaces and no executable code are highly stable and make ideal dependency targets for less stable components in statically typed languages.
The Stable Abstractions Principle says a component should be as abstract as it is stable.
Place the high-level architecture and policy of a system into stable components (I=0) and confine volatile, frequently-changing software to unstable components (I=1).
Keep stable, high-policy components flexible by making them abstract (interfaces and abstract classes), so that, per the OCP, they can be extended without modification despite their stability.

The Stable Abstractions Principle pairs stability with abstractness: a stable component should be abstract so its stability does not block extension, and an unstable component should be concrete so its instability permits easy change.
The SAP and SDP together form the DIP for components: dependencies run toward stability, stability implies abstraction, so dependencies run in the direction of abstraction.
A component's abstractness can be quantified as A = Na/Nc (abstract classes and interfaces divided by total classes), ranging from 0 (wholly concrete) to 1 (wholly abstract).

Components should lie on or near the Main Sequence, the line from maximally-stable-and-abstract (0,1) to maximally-unstable-and-concrete (1,0), so a component is depended on to the extent it is abstract and depends on others to the extent it is concrete.
Stable concrete components (the Zone of Pain near A=0,I=0) are rigid and hard to change, so volatile software — for example a volatile database schema — should be kept out of that zone.
Maximally abstract components with no dependents (the Zone of Uselessness near A=1,I=1) are useless detritus, typically leftover abstract classes that nobody ever implemented.

Compute each component's distance from the Main Sequence as D = |A + I - 1| (range [0,1]); re-examine and restructure components whose D is far from zero, and track D over time and statistically to catch dependency drift.
Dependency-management metrics are measurements against an arbitrary standard, not absolute truths; they are imperfect aids and should not be treated as gods.
A software architect is and remains a programmer; the notion that architects pull back from code is a lie, because they must keep experiencing the problems they create for the rest of the team.
The architecture of a system is the shape given to it by how it is divided into components, how those components are arranged, and how they communicate.

The primary purpose of architecture is to facilitate the development, deployment, operation, and maintenance of the system — not chiefly to make it work — and the strategy is to leave as many options open as possible for as long as possible.
Architecture has little bearing on whether a system works: many badly-architected systems work fine, and their real troubles appear in deployment, maintenance, and ongoing development.
The ultimate goal of good architecture is to minimize the lifetime cost of the system and maximize programmer productivity.

Team structure shapes architecture, but a component structure driven solely by the development schedule (such as one component per team) is rarely the best architecture for deployment, operation, and maintenance.
A goal of architecture should be to make the system deployable with a single action, and deployment must be considered early rather than after development is complete.

Operational inefficiency can usually be remedied by adding cheap hardware, whereas development, deployment, and maintenance problems consume expensive people, so the cost equation favors optimizing the latter; even so, the architecture should reveal operation by elevating use cases and behaviors to visible, first-class entities.

Maintenance is the most costly aspect of a system, dominated by spelunking (finding where and how to make a change) and the risk of inadvertent defects, and a careful architecture mitigates both by separating components behind stable interfaces.
Keep software soft by leaving as many options open as possible for as long as possible, where the options to leave open are precisely the details that do not matter.

Every software system decomposes into policy (the business rules and procedures, where the true value lives) and details (IO devices, databases, web, frameworks, protocols) that enable communication with the policy but do not affect its behavior.
The architect's goal is to shape the system so that policy is the central, essential element and the details are irrelevant to it, which lets decisions about those details be deferred.

Defer decisions about details such as the database, web server, REST, service frameworks, and dependency injection, because the high-level policy should not depend on them and waiting yields more information to decide well.
condition: when the high-level policy can be developed without committing to the detail

statement: Deferring detail decisions also lets you run experiments — for example trying several databases or web frameworks against working policy — before committing.

A good architect maximizes the number of decisions not yet made, and even when a detail has already been chosen by others, shapes the system so that decision stays deferrable or changeable as long as possible.

Bind code to abstract device or service interfaces rather than directly to IO devices; abstracting IO behind operating-system services (device independence) was an early embodiment of the Open-Closed Principle.

Keep high-level policy agnostic about physical and structural details — for example a disk's cylinder/head/sector layout — using an abstraction such as relative addressing to decouple that decision from the application.

Good architects separate details from policy and decouple the policy from the details so thoroughly that the policy has no knowledge of and no dependency on the details, which lets detail decisions be delayed as long as possible.
A good architecture must support the system's use cases and operation, its maintenance, its development, and its deployment.

The most important thing architecture can do for behavior is to make the system's use cases and intent visible at the top level, so behaviors are first-class, prominently named elements that developers do not have to hunt for.

Leave the operational mode open: a system that depends on a monolithic structure cannot easily move to processes, threads, or services, whereas one whose components stay isolated and do not assume their communication mechanism transitions easily as operational needs change.

Conway's law holds that a system's design mirrors the communication structure of the organization that builds it, so partition the system into well-isolated, independently developable components that can be allocated to teams working independently.
A good architecture makes the system immediately deployable after build rather than relying on dozens of configuration scripts, property-file tweaks, or manually arranged files.

Architects rarely know all the use cases, operational constraints, team structure, or deployment requirements up front, and these change over the life cycle, so use inexpensive principles to partition into isolated components and leave options open despite the uncertainty.

Apply the SRP and CCP to separate things that change for different reasons into decoupled horizontal layers such as the UI, application-specific business rules, application-independent business rules, and the database.

Separate application-specific business rules (such as input-field validation) from application-independent domain business rules (such as interest calculation), because they change at different rates and for different reasons.
Decouple use cases from one another as thin vertical slices cutting through the horizontal layers, so new use cases can be added without interfering with existing ones.
The decoupling done for use cases also serves operations: separated components that do not share an address space can run on separate servers and be replicated where higher throughput is needed.
Strong decoupling of layers and use cases mitigates interference between teams and lets the architecture support any team organization, whether feature, component, or layer teams.

Distinguish true duplication, where every change to one instance forces the same change to the other, from accidental duplication, where two similar sections change at different rates and for different reasons and will eventually diverge.

Resist the knee-jerk elimination of duplication between vertically separated use cases: similar screens, algorithms, or queries are usually accidental duplication, so confirm the duplication is real before unifying, or separating them later will be hard.

Do not pass a database record straight up to the UI just because its structure resembles a screen view; create a separate view model, since that resemblance is almost certainly accidental duplication and a view model keeps the layers decoupled.

Layers and use cases can be decoupled at three modes: source level (manage source dependencies within one address space, a monolith), deployment level (independently deployable units such as jars or DLLs), and service level (independent execution units communicating over the network).
It is hard to know the best decoupling mode early and the optimal mode changes as a project matures, so the decoupling mode should be left open as an option.

Decoupling at the service level by default is expensive in development time and resources and forces coarse-grained boundaries; creating service boundaries where none are needed wastes effort, memory, and cycles.

Prefer to push decoupling to the point where a service could be formed if needed, while keeping components in the same address space as long as possible, so the system can be born a monolith and grow to services (and back) with most source code protected from the change.

Software architecture is the art of drawing boundaries that separate elements and restrict each side from knowing about the other; boundaries drawn early defer decisions and keep them from polluting the core business logic.

Coupling — especially coupling to premature decisions — is what saps the people-power that architecture aims to minimize, and premature decisions are those unrelated to business requirements, such as choices of frameworks, databases, web servers, libraries, and dependency injection.

A premature architectural decision, such as adopting a three-tier distributed design or a full service-oriented tool suite for a system that never needs it, can multiply development effort enormously.
There is nothing intrinsically wrong with structuring a system around services; the error is the premature adoption and enforcement of a service or tool suite before it is actually needed.

Drawing a boundary line between business rules and the database behind a simple data-access interface lets you defer the database choice for a long time, try cheaper options such as a file system, keep tests fast, and still adopt a database trivially later.

Draw boundaries between things that matter and things that do not: the GUI does not matter to the business rules, and the database does not matter to the GUI or the business rules, so a line belongs between each such pair.

The database is a tool the business rules use only indirectly; the business rules need not know the schema, query language, or other database details, only a set of functions to fetch and save data, so put the database behind an interface.

Arrange the dependency so the database depends on the business rules: keep the data-access interface in the business-rules component and the translation/access code in the database component, so the business rules can use any database and the choice can be deferred.

The IO is irrelevant: the real system is the model of data structures and business rules, not the GUI, and the model would run without any interface, so separate the GUI from the business rules with the less-relevant GUI depending on the business rules.
Treat the UI and the database as plugins to the core business rules so each can be replaced with any technology (web, client-server, or console UI; SQL, NoSQL, or file-based database).

Design asymmetric, plugin relationships in which some modules are immune to changes in others, so that, for example, the business rules do not break when a web page format or a database schema changes.
A plugin architecture creates firewalls across which changes cannot propagate.

Draw boundaries along an axis of change, where the components on each side change at different rates and for different reasons; this is the Single Responsibility Principle telling you where to draw the lines.

To draw boundaries, partition the system into core-business-rule components and plugin components, then arrange the source-code arrows to all point in one direction toward the core business, which is an application of the DIP and SAP with dependencies pointing from low-level details to high-level abstractions.
At runtime a boundary crossing is just a function on one side calling a function on the other and passing data; the real work is managing the source-code dependencies that propagate change.

A monolith's boundaries are an invisible-at-deployment but real and valuable source-level segregation of functions within one address space, preserving the ability to develop and assemble components independently.
Component-partitioned architectures rely on dynamic polymorphism (OO) to manage internal dependencies; without it, architects must resort to risky function pointers or abandon partitioning.

When a high-level client must invoke a lower-level service, use dynamic polymorphism to invert the dependency against the flow of control so that all source-code dependencies cross the boundary toward the higher-level component.

Boundary-crossing cost rises with boundary strength: function calls in monoliths and deployment components are fast and can be chatty, local-process crossings are moderately expensive, and service crossings over the network are slow (tens of milliseconds to seconds) with high latency.
Match a boundary's communication style to its mode by carefully limiting chattiness across stronger, higher-latency boundaries such as processes and services.
Threads are not architectural boundaries or units of deployment but a way to organize the schedule and order of execution.

Across local-process and service boundaries, lower-level processes or services should plug into higher-level ones, so a higher-level component's source code must not contain the names, physical addresses, registry keys, or URIs of lower-level ones.
Most non-monolithic systems mix boundary strategies, so a system's boundaries are typically a mixture of fast chatty boundaries and latency-sensitive ones.
A software system is fundamentally a statement of policy — a detailed description of how inputs are transformed into outputs — that decomposes into many smaller statements of policy.

Separate policies and regroup them by how they change: policies that change for the same reasons and at the same times are at the same level and belong in one component, while those that change differently are at different levels and belong in different components.
Level is the distance from the inputs and outputs: the farther a policy is from both, the higher its level, and the policies that manage input and output are the lowest level.

Decouple source-code dependencies from data flow and couple them to level, so that in a good architecture every low-level component depends on the high-level components regardless of which way the data flows.

Higher-level policies far from the IO change less often and for more important reasons, while lower-level policies near the IO change frequently and urgently but for less important reasons, so pointing all dependencies toward the higher levels keeps trivial urgent low-level changes from affecting important high-level policy.
Critical Business Rules are the rules or procedures that make or save the business money and would exist and make money even if executed manually without any computer.
Critical Business Rules and the Critical Business Data they operate on are inextricably bound and should be combined into an object called an Entity.

An Entity must stand alone as pure business rules over critical business data, unsullied by concerns about databases, user interfaces, or frameworks so it is usable in any system, and it requires only that the data and rules be bound in one separate module, not an object-oriented language.

Use cases are application-specific business rules describing how an automated system is used — its inputs, outputs, and processing steps — and make sense only as part of an automated system, unlike Critical Business Rules.
Use cases orchestrate when and how the Entities' Critical Business Rules are invoked, controlling the dance of the Entities.

A use case must not describe the user interface beyond the data flowing in and out, so that from the use case alone you cannot tell whether the application is delivered on the web, a thick client, a console, or as a service.

Entities are higher level than use cases: use cases depend on Entities and Entities do not depend on use cases, because Entities are general and reusable across applications (far from IO) while use cases are application-specific (closer to IO).
A use case should accept simple, dependency-free request data structures and return simple response data structures that know nothing of the web, framework types such as HttpRequest, SQL, or the UI.

Do not let request and response models reference Entity objects even though they share data, because the two change for different reasons; coupling them violates the CCP and SRP and breeds tramp data and conditionals.

Business rules are the reason a software system exists and should remain pristine and unsullied by the UI or database, forming the most independent and reusable code with lesser concerns plugged into them.

A system's architecture — its top-level directory and package structure — should scream its use cases and domain, such as Health Care System, rather than the frameworks it uses, such as Rails or Spring.
Frameworks are tools to be used, not architectures to conform to; if your architecture is based on a framework, it cannot be based on your use cases.
Center a good architecture on use cases so the supporting structures can be described without committing to frameworks, databases, or web servers, treating frameworks as options to be left open.

The web is merely a delivery mechanism and IO device — a detail to be deferred — so the architecture should be as ignorant as possible of delivery, allowing the app to ship as a console, web, thick-client, or service application without fundamental change.
View each framework skeptically: ask how to use it and how to protect yourself from it, and devise a strategy that prevents it from taking over the architecture.

If the architecture is about use cases and frameworks are kept at arm's length, all use cases can be unit-tested without the web server, database, or frameworks, since testability is an attribute of good architecture.
Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters), DCI, and BCE architectures share one objective — separation of concerns via layers with at least a business-rules layer and an interface layer.
A clean architecture produces systems that are independent of frameworks, testable, independent of the UI, independent of the database, and independent of any external agency.

The Dependency Rule is the overriding rule of the Clean Architecture: source-code dependencies must point only inward toward higher-level policies, and nothing in an inner circle may mention the name of anything declared in an outer circle.
Data formats declared in an outer circle, especially those generated by a framework, must not be used by an inner circle.

The Clean Architecture's concentric layers run from Frameworks and Drivers (details such as the database and web) through Interface Adapters (MVC, presenters/views/controllers, with SQL confined here) to Use Cases (application-specific rules) and Entities (enterprise Critical Business Rules), with abstraction and policy increasing inward.

The number of layers is not fixed at four, but the Dependency Rule always applies and the level of abstraction and policy increases as you move inward, with the innermost circle the most general and highest level.

The Entities layer is the least likely to change when something external changes, and no operational change to a particular application — such as page navigation or security — should affect the entity layer.
Confine all SQL and database knowledge to the interface-adapters (database) layer, so no code inward of that circle knows anything about the database.

Cross boundaries against the flow of control using the DIP: when an inner-circle use case must invoke an outer-circle component such as a presenter, have the use case call an output-port interface in the inner circle that the outer component implements.

Only simple, isolated data structures should cross architectural boundaries — never Entity objects or database row structures — and always in the form most convenient for the inner circle, so the Dependency Rule is not violated.

The Humble Object pattern splits behavior into a humble module holding the hard-to-test essence and a separate module holding the easy-to-test behavior, and this split often defines an architectural boundary.

Make the View the humble object that only moves data from the View Model onto the screen without processing it, and have the Presenter do all formatting into the View Model as strings, booleans, and flags.

Place database gateways — polymorphic interfaces with one method per CRUD operation — between use-case interactors and the database, with the gateway implementations in the database layer as the humble objects, so the interactors stay testable by substituting stubs and test-doubles.

There is no true object-relational mapper, because objects are sets of operations with private data while data structures are public data with no behavior; ORMs are really data mappers and belong in the database layer as another humble-object boundary.

Expect the Humble Object pattern at every architectural boundary, with a simple data structure crossing it and the boundary dividing hard-to-test from easy-to-test code, which greatly increases the testability of the whole system.

Full architectural boundaries are expensive — reciprocal polymorphic interfaces, input/output data structures, and independent compile and deploy — so an architect may judge the cost too high yet still reserve a place for one with a partial boundary.

Reserving a place for a future boundary is anticipatory design that the Agile YAGNI principle frowns on, but an architect may still implement a partial boundary when a boundary seems likely to be needed.

One way to build a partial boundary is to do all the work for separable components but keep them compiled and deployed as a single component, avoiding the version-tracking and release overhead of multiple components.

A partial boundary tends to degrade over time: once it becomes clear the separation is not needed, dependencies start crossing the line the wrong way and re-separating the components later becomes a chore.

A one-dimensional boundary uses the Strategy pattern with dependency inversion to hold a place for a future full boundary, but without reciprocal interfaces only developer discipline prevents backchannel dependencies.

The Facade pattern is the simplest partial boundary and sacrifices even dependency inversion, so the client gains a transitive dependency on all the service classes and backchannels become easy to create.
It is a function of the architect to decide where an architectural boundary might one day exist and whether to fully or partially implement it.
Most systems have more than the three obvious components (UI, business rules, database), and architectural boundaries appear along every axis of change.
Define inter-component boundary APIs so they are owned by the upstream, higher-level component: the calling component declares the interface that the called component implements.
Direct source-code dependencies by level rather than by data flow: even when a system's data flow splits into several streams, all dependencies still point toward the highest-level policy component.
Higher-level policy can itself be split from lower-level mechanics, with the lower-level component declaring events up to the higher-level component that manages the more important state.

Architectural boundaries exist everywhere; full boundaries are expensive to build, yet boundaries that are ignored are very expensive to add later — even with comprehensive tests and refactoring discipline.

There is a real tension between YAGNI (do not anticipate abstraction, since over-engineering is often worse than under-engineering) and the high cost of retrofitting a needed boundary, so the architect must guess intelligently where boundaries lie.

Boundary decisions are not one-time: watch the system as it evolves and implement each boundary at the inflection point where the cost of implementing it becomes less than the cost of continuing to ignore it.
Every system has at least one Main component that creates, coordinates, and oversees all the others.

Main is the ultimate detail and lowest-level policy: it is the entry point, depended on by nothing but the operating system, whose job is to create all the factories, strategies, and global facilities and then hand control to the high-level abstract portions of the system.
Inject dependencies through a dependency-injection framework only in the Main component, and once injected let Main distribute those dependencies normally without further use of the framework.

Treat Main as a plugin behind an architectural boundary so a system can have many Main components — one per configuration such as Dev, Test, Production, country, jurisdiction, or customer — which makes configuration much easier to solve.

Using services does not by itself constitute an architecture: architecture is defined by boundaries that separate high-level policy from low-level detail and follow the Dependency Rule, whereas services that merely separate behaviors are expensive function calls and not necessarily architecturally significant.
Services can still be worthwhile for separating functionality across processes and platforms whether or not they obey the Dependency Rule, but that benefit does not make them an architecture.

The decoupling fallacy of services: they are decoupled at the variable level but remain strongly coupled through the data they share, so adding a field to a shared record forces every service that uses it to change and to agree on its interpretation.
Service interfaces are no more formal, rigorous, or better defined than function interfaces, so that supposed benefit of services is largely an illusion.

The fallacy of independent development and deployment: large scalable systems can also be built from monoliths and component-based systems, and because services are coupled by shared data and behavior, their development, deployment, and operation often still require coordination.

A single cross-cutting feature can force changes across every service in a functionally decomposed service architecture, proving the services are coupled and cannot be independently developed, deployed, and maintained.
Cross-cutting concerns afflict every system, service-oriented or not, and functional decompositions are especially vulnerable to new features that cut across all the functional behaviors.

Handle cross-cutting concerns with an object/component design where new features extend abstract base classes via Template Method or Strategy in new components that obey the Dependency Rule, so a feature is added as a new dynamically loaded unit without changing existing components.

Services need not be little monoliths: design each service internally with the SOLID principles and a component structure so new features are added by adding components rather than by redeploying the service, conforming to the Open-Closed Principle.

Architectural boundaries do not fall between services but run through them, dividing each into components, so the components within services — not the services themselves — define the architectural boundaries.

Services are not in themselves architecturally significant; a system's architecture is defined by the boundaries drawn within it and the dependencies that cross them, not by the physical mechanisms by which elements communicate and execute.
Tests are part of the system and participate in its architecture, and from an architectural viewpoint all kinds of tests — TDD, FitNesse, Cucumber, and the rest — are equivalent.
Tests follow the Dependency Rule as the outermost circle: they are detailed and concrete, always depend inward on the code being tested, and nothing in the system depends on them.
Treating tests as outside the design of the system is a catastrophic mistake, because tests not well integrated into the design tend to be fragile and make the system rigid and hard to change.

The Fragile Tests Problem arises when tests are strongly coupled to the system, so a trivial change breaks hundreds or thousands of tests, which then makes developers resist change and renders the system rigid.

The first rule of software design, for testability or any other reason, is do not depend on volatile things; since GUIs are volatile, tests driven through the GUI must be fragile, so design the system and tests to verify business rules without the GUI.

Create a dedicated testing API that lets tests verify all business rules while bypassing security constraints and expensive resources such as databases and forcing the system into particular testable states; it is a superset of the interactors and interface adapters the UI uses.
The purpose of a testing API is to decouple the structure of the tests from the structure of the application, not merely to detach the tests from the UI.

Structural coupling — having a test class for every production class and a test method for every production method — is one of the strongest and most insidious forms of test coupling, making tests fragile and production code rigid.

Hide the application's structure from the tests so production code and tests can evolve independently, since over time tests grow more concrete and specific while production code grows more abstract and general.
If a testing API's superpowers would be dangerous in production, keep the testing API and its dangerous implementation in a separate, independently deployable component.
condition: if the testing API's superpowers would be dangerous in a production system

statement: Software does not wear out, but it can be destroyed from within by unmanaged dependencies on firmware and hardware, which denies it a long useful life.

Firmware is defined not by living in ROM but by what it depends on and how hard it is to change as hardware evolves, so burying SQL in code or spreading platform dependencies throughout the code is also writing firmware.

Intermingling software and firmware is an anti-pattern that resists change, makes changes dangerous and prone to unintended consequences, and forces full regression testing for minor changes, so separate business logic from hardware and platform.
Getting an app merely to work (the App-titude test) is not enough; follow Kent Beck's order — first make it work, then make it right by refactoring for understanding and evolution, then make it fast.

Embedded software is not so special that the architectural principles in this book fail to apply, and clean architecture eliminates the target-hardware bottleneck in which code can be tested only on the target hardware.
Separate the system into layers with the hardware at the bottom so that the inevitable hardware change is not a bigger job than necessary.

Firm up the line between software and firmware with a Hardware Abstraction Layer whose API is tailored to the software's needs and hides how the hardware does its job, for example exposing Indicate_LowBattery() rather than Led_TurnOn(5), or storing name/value pairs without revealing that flash memory is used.

A clean embedded architecture is testable off the target hardware: a good HAL provides the seam or substitution points that enable off-target testing and must not reveal hardware details to its users.

Confine processor access registers and vendor-specific C extensions to very few places entirely within the firmware behind a processor abstraction layer, because any code that knows those registers becomes firmware bound to the silicon.

Prefer standardized headers such as stdint.h over vendor-specific type headers so the software stays processor-independent and portable; all software should be processor-independent even though not all firmware can be.

Treat the operating system as a detail and protect against OS dependencies with an operating-system abstraction layer, so changing the RTOS means writing a new OSAL rather than modifying complex code scattered throughout the system.

An OSAL also lets the valuable application code be tested off-target and off-OS and encourages a common application structure, such as shared message passing instead of each thread hand-crafting its concurrency model.
A layered architecture is built on programming to interfaces: when one module interacts with another through an interface, one service provider can be substituted for another.

Use header files as interface definitions and limit their contents to the function declarations, constants, and struct names callers need, keeping implementation-only data structures, constants, and typedefs out, because that clutter creates unwanted dependencies.
Limit the visibility of implementation details and expect them to change, because the fewer places that know a detail, the fewer places must be tracked down and modified when it changes.

Don't scatter target-identifying conditional-compilation directives (such as #ifdef BOARD_V2) throughout the code, which violates DRY; hide the hardware type under a HAL and use the linker or runtime binding instead of conditional compilation.

The database is a detail — a low-level utility that provides access to data and does not rise to the level of an architectural element — and a good architect does not let such low-level mechanisms pollute the system architecture.
The data model — the structure given to data within the application — is architecturally significant, but the database that stores and retrieves it is not, and the two must be distinguished.

There is nothing architecturally significant about arranging data into rows within tables, so knowledge of the tabular structure should be restricted to the lowest-level utility functions in the outer circles of the architecture.

Passing database rows or tables around the system as objects is an architectural error because it couples the use cases, the business rules, and sometimes even the UI to the relational structure of the data.

Database systems are prevalent largely because rotating disks are slow: they exist to mitigate disk latency with indexes, caches, and query schemes, and they split into document-based file systems and content-based relational databases.

Programmers already read stored data into RAM and reorganize it into lists, trees, hash tables, and similar structures accessed by pointers, which is what they would do if disks vanished, so the database is merely a detail for moving data between disk and RAM.

Data-storage performance is an architectural concern, but it can be entirely encapsulated and separated from the business rules with low-level data-access mechanisms and has nothing to do with the overall architecture.

When a non-engineering requirement such as customer expectation forces a technology like an RDBMS, bolt it onto the side behind a narrow, safe data-access channel while keeping the core data in the form most convenient to the application.
condition: when a non-engineering requirement (such as market or customer expectation) demands the technology

statement: The industry oscillates endlessly between centralizing computing power in servers and distributing it to terminals or browsers, and the web is just one such oscillation that changed nothing architecturally fundamental.
Architects must treat short-term technology oscillations as details to push away from the central core of business rules.
The GUI is a detail, the web is a GUI, and therefore the web is a detail — an IO device — that should be placed behind boundaries that keep it separate from the core business logic.
Decouple the business rules from the UI, because you never know what marketing-driven UI change will be demanded next.

Full device independence from a rich GUI is impractical because the UI-application interaction is chatty in GUI-specific ways, but a boundary can still be abstracted by treating the business logic as use cases that exchange complete input and output data structures, operating the UI as an IO device in a device-independent manner.
Frameworks are not architectures, even though some frameworks try to be.
Framework authors write to solve their own problems, not yours; the overlap with your problems is what makes a framework useful, but the author cannot have your best interests at heart.
Adopting a framework is an asymmetric marriage: you make a huge long-term commitment to it while the framework author makes no commitment to you and wants you coupled as tightly as possible.

Coupling to a framework carries real risks: frameworks often violate the Dependency Rule by asking you to inherit their code into your Entities, you may outgrow the framework, it may evolve unhelpfully, or a better one may appear that you cannot switch to.
Do not marry the framework: use it but keep it at arm's length as a detail in an outer circle, and never let it into the inner circles of the architecture.

If a framework wants your business objects to derive from its base classes, refuse, and instead derive proxies kept in plugin components that integrate the framework while following the Dependency Rule.
Use a framework such as Spring only in the Main component; do not scatter framework annotations like @autowired through your business objects, which should not know about the framework.

Some frameworks, such as a language's standard library, you must marry, but that should still be a conscious decision made with the understanding that you are committed for the life of the application.
When determining the initial architecture, first identify the system's actors and use cases.
Because the system's actors are its primary sources of change under the SRP, partition the system so that a change serving one actor does not affect any other actor.

Structure the build environment into fine-grained components so independent deliverables are possible, while reserving the right to combine them into fewer deliverables and to change that grouping as the system evolves.

In a clean component architecture the using relationships point with the flow of control while the inheritance relationships point against it, applying the Open-Closed Principle so that changes to low-level details do not ripple up to high-level policies.

Separate components along two dimensions — by actor (the Single Responsibility Principle) and by level of policy (the Dependency Rule) — to separate components that change for different reasons and at different rates.

Package by layer (horizontal slicing into web, business logic, and persistence) is a quick way to start but does not scream the business domain and becomes insufficient as the system grows in scale and complexity.
Package by feature (vertical slicing by domain concept) makes the top-level code scream the domain and gathers a use case's code in one place, but it is still suboptimal.

Ports-and-adapters / hexagonal architecture separates domain-focused code (the inside) from technical details such as frameworks and databases (the outside), with the firm rule that the outside depends on the inside and never the reverse.
Name everything on the inside in terms of the ubiquitous domain language, for example Orders rather than OrdersRepository.

A strict layered architecture's acyclic graph can be cheated into a relaxed layered architecture where a controller bypasses the service layer to call a repository directly, which is usually undesirable because it can skip logic such as authorization.

Architectural principles such as web controllers must never access repositories directly require enforcement, and relying on developer discipline and code reviews is fallible while static-analysis enforcement has a longer-than-ideal feedback loop.
Prefer to let the compiler enforce your architecture wherever possible.

Package by component bundles all the responsibilities for a coarse-grained component, including business logic and persistence, behind a clean interface in one package while keeping the UI separate, giving one place to go for a domain area; well-defined components in a monolith are a stepping stone to micro-services.
The different code-organization approaches all unravel if the implementation details are wrong, so a chosen architectural style is undermined by poor implementation.

Overly liberal use of the public access modifier wastes the language's encapsulation facilities and lets code instantiate concrete implementation classes directly in violation of the intended architecture, so restrict access modifiers to let the language help enforce the architecture.
If all types are marked public, packages become a mere organization mechanism rather than a means of encapsulation, and every architectural style collapses to the same thing syntactically.

Apply access modifiers deliberately: make public only the interfaces that have inbound cross-package dependencies, and keep implementation classes package-protected so nothing outside the package can depend on them directly.
In a monolithic application, lean on the compiler to enforce your architectural principles rather than relying on self-discipline and post-compilation tooling.
Module systems such as OSGi and the Java 9 module system let you distinguish public types from published types, exposing only a small subset of a module for external consumption.

You can decouple source-code dependencies by splitting code across separate source trees or build modules — for example domain, web, and persistence — where the web and persistence trees have compile-time dependencies on the domain but the domain knows nothing of them.

Beware the Périphérique anti-pattern: placing all infrastructure code in a single source tree lets infrastructure in one area (such as a web controller) call code in another area (such as a database repository) without passing through the domain, especially if access modifiers are forgotten.

Good design intentions can be destroyed by the implementation strategy, so map the design onto code structures, choose decoupling modes pragmatically given team size, skill, and budget, use the compiler to enforce the style, and watch for coupling in other areas such as data models.

A dependency-normal boundary points its source-code dependencies with the flow of control — as when applications depend on a supervisor — and can still abstract the output device so the applications do not know which device they write to.

A dependency-inverted boundary lets a higher-level component start lower-level ones through a uniform polymorphic entry point with no compile-time dependency on them, so the flow of control runs opposite to the source-code dependencies.

Communicate across an architectural boundary with short, simple, DSL-like command packets, which keeps the two sides cleanly decoupled — as when one unit sent primitive commands like DIAL or MEASURE to another.

Dividing one large binary into independently compilable modules and routing every inter-module call indirectly through a runtime dispatch table makes the modules independently deployable and is, in effect, polymorphic dispatch and a plugin architecture.
Code that nobody understands eventually becomes officially rigid — locked down and forbidden to change — which destroys the value it embodies and demonstrates the worth of clean code.

Failing to isolate device-control and UI logic from the business rules — for example smearing modem bit-level control throughout the code — leaves a system unable to absorb a hardware change without a terrible hack, which is why hardware must be isolated from business rules behind abstract interfaces.
A from-scratch redesign team struggles to ever catch up with a large staff that is actively maintaining and extending the old system.
Forking a code base to handle divergent requirements produces two similar-but-divergent versions that become very hard or impossible to reintegrate later, especially in a fast-changing market.
Failing to recognize an obvious architectural boundary early — such as separating dialing from measurement — can cost a fortune later when the boundary finally has to be introduced.

Two wildly different architectures — a dataflow pipes-and-filters design and a one-task-per-terminal design — can both be equally effective, showing that software architectures can differ greatly yet work well.

Smearing embedded SQL and vendor-specific API calls throughout the code coupled a system so tightly to one database vendor that switching vendors became practically impossible when that product was cancelled, demonstrating that databases are details that must be isolated from the business purpose.
Strongly coupling to a third-party software system is dangerous and should be avoided, because you become trapped when that system is cancelled, degrades, or raises its price.

A service-oriented design can have real architectural boundaries — independently deployable services in their own domains with dependencies running the right way — even when it is not a clean plugin architecture.

Externalizing a state machine into a data file lets you change application flow — adding and rewiring services, even while the system runs — without changing code, which is an application of the Open-Closed Principle.

Pointing dependencies in the traditional flow-of-control direction (GUI to representation to rules to database) rather than toward high-level policy aided a product's eventual demise, confirming the value of directing dependencies toward policy.
Adopting a magical third-party database or framework can turn into a big, slow, intrusive, expensive dependency that impedes progress on every level and proves to be a major practical mistake.

Over-architecture is a real failure mode: too many layers, each with its own communications overhead, reduce team productivity, so an architecture must be flexible enough to fit the size of the problem rather than building for the enterprise when a small tool is all that is needed.
You cannot make a reusable framework until you first make a usable one, because reusable frameworks must be built in concert with several reusing applications.
Sharing a single database across multiple services creates a coupling point that makes it hard to change a shared schema and prevents the services from evolving their codebases independently.
Teams should expose their data and functionality only through service interfaces, with no direct reads of another team's datastore, no shared-memory model, and no backdoors.
Information hiding between modules is what lets parts of a software system be changed independently; exposing a schema to multiple services removes that independence.

For sharing datasets across an organization, a messaging system optimized to retain and hold datasets can be more appropriate than a database optimized to publish them, because consumers tend to take a subset of the data and maintain their own independent copy.

Turning a set of largely independent applications into a web of highly connected synchronous services raises the probability of system-wide failure, because one important but flaky service can have far-reaching effects and in the worst case halt the whole system.

Adding an asynchronous publish-subscribe messaging layer lets new applications be plugged into the architecture without disturbing the existing web of synchronous interactions that drive the frontend.
Events decouple systems, which lets different parts of a company operate independently of one another and makes it easier to plug new systems into the real-time stream of events.

Traditional messaging systems have no notion of history or retention, which limits their value, because business operations still need historical data such as account history, customer lists, or analytics.

HTTP-fronted data services make ad hoc lookups simple but make moving data around hard: to extract a dataset a consumer must run a query and then periodically poll the service for changes, which burdens the service operators.

A replayable log such as Kafka acts as a middle ground between a messaging system and a database: it decouples services like a messaging system while also providing a fault-tolerant, scalable, central source of truth any application can fall back to.

Microservices should not share their databases with one another (the Integration Database antipattern), because a database's rich, widely shared API makes it hard to determine how one application affects others through data couplings, contention, or load.
The data that services share ("data on the outside") is the most tightly coupled data of all, and the more services an ecosystem has, the more tightly coupled that shared data becomes.

To reduce coupling on shared data, move the data into your own application where you control it; data movement gives an application a level of operability and control that is unachievable with a direct runtime dependency on another service.
A replayable log is a suitable place to hold shared data precisely because you cannot query it: it is purely about storing data and pushing it somewhere new, which keeps shared data loosely coupled.

Adopting streaming is a change in mindset rather than just an RPC replacement: it means rethinking the business as an evolving stream of data and services as functions that transform those streams into something new.
Unlike a traditional database query, a stream processing query computes continuously: every time an input arrives it is recomputed and a new result is emitted only if the query's value has changed.

A stateful streaming computation such as a windowed count must persist its running state so that, if the stream processor crashes and restarts, the computation resumes from its previous position and the result stays accurate.
condition: the computation is stateful (e.g. an aggregation or windowed count)

statement: Kafka Streams and KSQL manage stream processing state internally and back that state up to Kafka via a changelog topic.

A streaming layer can be fault-tolerant and elastically scalable by running as a cluster across nodes: if one node exits another takes over its work, and adding nodes automatically reroutes work and required state to the new resources.

Making a message-at-a-time network call per event is a poor design for a high-throughput event stream; instead stream processors should write and read state from local storage for speed and back it up to Kafka to inherit Kafka's durability guarantees.

A broker is separate infrastructure that broadcasts messages to interested programs and stores them as long as needed, which makes it well suited to streaming or fire-and-forget messaging but adds little value to request-response interactions that need neither broadcast nor storage.
exception: the interaction is request-response, where there is no need for broadcast or storage

statement: Kafka's home ground is event-based communication, where events are business facts that have value to more than one service and are worth keeping around.

An ESB or messaging layer controlled by a central team that dictates schemas, message flows, validation, and transformation constrains an organization and makes it hard for individual services to evolve at their own pace; teams should avoid recreating these ESB problems on top of Kafka.
The core mantra of event-driven services is to centralize an immutable stream of facts while decentralizing the freedom to act, adapt, and change.
Kafka and KSQL are optimized for continual computation rather than batch processing; Kafka is about real-time processing first and long-term storage second.

Kafka's scalability comes largely from simplicity: its underlying abstraction is a partitioned log of append-only files spread over many machines, which encourages sequential access patterns that flow with the grain of the hardware.
Kafka ingests data at roughly network speed, but replication overhead typically divides effective throughput by about three, so a three-node 10 GbE cluster ingests around 1 GB/s in practice.

At the heart of Kafka is a partitioned, replayable log: messages are appended sequentially to a file, and a consumer reads by seeking to the position of its last-read message, scanning sequentially, and periodically recording its new position.
A log-structured store makes both reads and writes sequential operations, which are sympathetic to the underlying media (leveraging prefetch, caching, and natural batching) and therefore efficient.
When reading messages, the Kafka server uses zero-copy: data is copied directly from the disk buffer to the network buffer without being imported into the JVM.

Traditional brokers rely on in-memory index structures (hash tables or B-trees) whose maintenance cost significantly limits retention, whereas Kafka's log is O(1) for reading or writing to a partition, so whether the data is on disk or cached in memory matters far less.

Because Kafka is log-structured, a consumer that stops reading for a long time and builds a large backlog does not significantly slow the infrastructure, unlike traditional brokers that tend to slow down as they fill up.

In Kafka each log is a replica of a partition held on a different machine; one partition can be replicated several times for high availability, with each replica being a separate log holding the same data.

A producer's partitioner decides each message's partition: it spreads messages round-robin across available partitions when no key is given, or hashes the message key to choose the partition when a key is provided, so that messages with the same key always land in the same partition and are strongly ordered.
condition: a partitioning key is supplied for hash-based routing

statement: Kafka provides ordering guarantees only within a partition, so messages that require relative ordering must be routed to the same partition by giving them the same partitioning key (for example, partitioning customer-update messages by CustomerId).
When global ordering across all messages is required, use a single-partition topic; this limits throughput to that of a single machine, which is typically sufficient for such use cases.
condition: global (not just per-key) ordering is required

statement: Kafka scales by partitioning data over all available machines so reads and writes spread across the cluster; scaling is done by adding machines and rebalancing, and consumption is parallelized by spreading a topic's partitions over consumers in a consumer group.
Producers should enable retries so that messages not successfully sent because of a network glitch, long garbage-collection pause, or failure are retried automatically.
To preserve ordering while retries are enabled, configure the producer to send only one batch at a time per destination machine, so that retried batches cannot reorder events when failures occur.
condition: producer retries are enabled and ordering must be preserved

statement: Kafka provides durability through replication: messages are written to a configurable number of machines, and a replication factor of three allows two machines to be lost without losing data.
For sensitive service-based datasets, configure three replicas per partition, configure the producer to wait for replication to complete before proceeding, and enable producer retries.
condition: the dataset is sensitive (e.g. service-based application data)

statement: Synchronous flushing of data to disk should be used sparingly because it significantly reduces throughput, especially in highly concurrent environments; when it is used, increase the producer batch size so each disk flush is more effective.
exception: highly sensitive use cases that genuinely require synchronous disk flushing
