statement: A single Kafka cluster shared by many services is multitenant and risks inadvertent denial-of-service and contention; Kafka quotas mitigate this by allocating bandwidth to specific services to enforce SLAs and aggressively throttle greedy services, applied per instance or per load-balanced group.
Event-driven services should always run in a highly available configuration because running a second instance both load-balances and provides high availability essentially for free.
exception: there is genuinely no requirement for high availability

statement: Kafka assigns whole partitions to consumers, and a single partition can only ever be assigned to one service instance in a consumer group; this invariant guarantees ordering is preserved even as services fail and restart.
Because Kafka releases are always backward-compatible with the previous version, a service can be upgraded to a new version through rolling restarts without taking the system offline.

By default Kafka topics are retention-based (messages kept for a configurable time), while compacted topics manage keyed datasets by retaining only the most recent event for each key and also support deletes.
Log compaction is an asynchronous process, so a compacted topic may still contain some superseded messages that are waiting to be compacted away.
Compacted topics slow a dataset's growth in a data-specific way by removing superseded events per key (rather than by age), and the resulting smaller datasets are easier to move between machines.

Loading a table from a compacted topic is faster and more efficient than loading from a regular topic, because the stream processor does not have to load the whole versioned history, only the latest value per key.
condition: the source data is held in a compacted topic

statement: Kafka can serve as a long-term storage layer holding hundreds of terabytes in retention-based or compacted topics, but it remains a commit log with no broad query functionality, not a database.

The latest-versioned pattern combines a regular topic (good for audit and Event Sourcing) with a compacted topic (smaller footprint), linking them with a Kafka Streams job to get the benefits of both at the cost of additional storage.

Kafka offers enterprise-grade security: client authentication via Kerberos or TLS client certificates, a Unix-like permissions system for authorization, encrypted network communication for untrusted networks, and optional authentication between Kafka and ZooKeeper.
Most business systems need strong ordering guarantees, because processing updates out of order can overwrite a newer value with an older, out-of-date one.
exception: many analytics use cases, where strong ordering is often not required

statement: To break the synchronous ties between independently operated services, use asynchronicity together with a message broker as an intermediary; an alternative is to give each individual service a significantly higher SLA than the system as a whole.
As the number of independent services grows, the web of synchronous interactions grows with it and previously benign availability issues begin to trigger far more widespread outages.
The imperative programming model, where services are commanded to do work, is not a good fit for estates in which services are operated independently.

In a publish-subscribe broker the logic for routing messages is defined by the receivers rather than the senders (receiver-driven routing), so each receiver retains control over its participation and the system becomes pluggable.

When events are used purely for notification, the producing service has no knowledge that any consuming service exists; it just raises an event recording what it did, and each consumer decides whether to react, which flips the burden of responsibility to the receiver and reduces coupling.

Functional couplings between services are optional, but core data couplings are essential: an application cannot work around not having the data it needs, so large organizations have an unavoidable base level of essential data coupling.

Event-carried state transfer uses the event stream to replicate a dataset from its source service to a consuming service, where it can be queried locally; replicating data locally is advantageous much like caching because it makes data access faster.

Querying by event-carried state transfer gives better isolation and autonomy (data stays local and under the service's control), faster data access (especially when combining data from several services or spanning geographies), and offline availability for disconnected environments.

The REST/RPC approach has advantages of simplicity (fewer moving parts and no state to manage), singleton state (a value changed in one place is immediately visible to all, important for use cases needing synchronicity such as reading a just-updated balance), and centralized command-and-control workflows that are easy to reason about.

Weight the notification hat for small, lightweight use cases where data replication would be an unnecessary burden, and weight the replication hat in larger, more complex architectures so each service has greater autonomy over the data it queries.
Communication between microservices should be based on asynchronous message passing while the logic inside each microservice runs synchronously.
exception: applies to a strict definition of microservices where services are independently deployable; looser industry interpretations may not warrant so strong an assertion

statement: In the Event Collaboration pattern no single service owns the whole business workflow; each service owns a subset of state transitions, reacting to events and raising new events that trigger the next step in the chain.

Choreographed (event-collaboration) systems are pluggable: a service can change its internal event types and processing without affecting others as long as its agreed output event remains, whereas in an orchestrated system every workflow change must be made in the central controller.

Orchestration's advantage is that the whole workflow is written down in code in one place and is easy to reason about, but it tightly couples the model to the controller; choreography better suits larger implementations that span teams and change independently.
The notification and replication duality of events maps cleanly onto stateless and stateful stream processing respectively.

Stateful stream processing by event-carried state transfer requires the entire dataset to be held in Kafka (for example, all customer records stored as events) and the stream processor to keep that table in in-process, disk-resident storage with no external database.
condition: the stream processor joins against a table held as state

statement: A common pattern in smaller web systems is to mix protocols: user-facing online services interact via REST while also journaling their state changes to Kafka, and offline services such as billing and fulfillment are built purely with events.
In larger systems services cluster into bounded contexts that mix request-response and event-based protocols internally, but different bounded contexts interact with one another only through events.

Following domain-driven design, reuse should be confined within a bounded context, where the domain model is shared and everything is available to everything else, while across bounded contexts there is little sharing of code, functionality, or data and interaction is through more restricted interfaces; broad reuse can be counterproductive.
Event-based methods decouple systems in time and let them evolve independently, reversing the tight runtime coupling that a growing web of synchronous calls otherwise creates as a project scales.

Dataflow and functional programming styles suit distributed, service-based design better than the imperative request-driven style, because dataflow workers act only on the availability of their data inputs and carry no hidden state to track, similar to how streaming systems operate.

In a streaming pipeline Kafka plays the role of a Unix shell pipe while stream processors provide the chained functions, with events accumulating in a processor until a condition (such as a join between two streams) is met before the pipeline continues.

Pushing data into a loosely coupled subscriber means any operations needed on that data are performed in each subscriber rather than at the source, and messaging technologies like Kafka take most of the operational stability and performance issues off the table.
Stateful stream processing has a cold-start cost: when a new node starts it must load all of its state stores before it can begin processing messages, which in the worst case can take a long time.

Kafka Streams uses standby replicas so that every table or state store on one node has an up-to-date replica on another node, allowing an immediate failover without unduly interrupting processing if a node fails.

Kafka Streams writes periodic disk checkpoints so that a failed-and-restarted node can load its previous checkpoint and then top up only the few messages it missed while offline, rather than rebuilding from scratch.
Kafka Streams uses compacted topics to keep a state dataset as small as possible, which reduces the load time of a complete state rebuild when one is necessary.

An event-driven application uses a single input stream to drive its work; a streaming application blends one or more input streams into one or more output streams; and a stateful streaming application also recasts streams into tables and stores intermediary state in the log, internalizing all the data it needs.

Stateful stream processors keep state local and make data available wherever it is required, which increases performance and autonomy because no remote calls are needed, instead of pushing the state problem down into a database.
Holding state locally lets a service process events faster because each operation runs without a network call, and frees it to perform more data-centric operations on the data it holds.

Stateful stream processing behaves like a declaratively defined cache: a query is executed continuously over incoming event streams, its result stored locally and kept up to date, replacing the hand-crafted caching and polling that a stateless model would require.

Event Sourcing stores state changes (events) immutably in the order they occurred, which provides a comprehensive audit of exactly what the system did and lets the current state be rederived at any time by replaying the log.

CQRS separates the write path from the read path and links them with an asynchronous channel (for example, writing events to Kafka as the write model and deriving a database as the read model), decoupling the two in time so each can be optimized independently.
Command Sourcing records the commands coming into a service as events before they are processed, so the service can always be rewound and replayed to recover from a corruption.

The essence of Event Sourcing is that each state change is represented as an entirely new event appended to the log rather than overwriting the existing record, in contrast to an update-in-place CRUD persistence model.

An update-in-place database is lossy because previous state is overwritten and lost, which makes recovery from a data-corruption bug hard; a replayable log instead lets you fix the bug, rewind to before it was introduced, and replay the recorded inputs to regenerate corrected state and corrected downstream events.

Event Sourcing requires little or no additional recovery code because the primary execution path is used for both runtime execution and recovery, unlike staging tables, database triggers, or bitemporal databases, which do not provide rewind-and-replay without significant programmer effort.

When a service both updates its database and separately sends a notification, the two writes must be made atomically, because a failure between them produces at best duplicate notifications and at worst a notification that is never sent.

Keeping the database record and the emitted notification as two separate copies of state tends to let them diverge as code churns, so the overall data quality of the system suffers even when the database itself is correct.

Making the event stream the primary source of truth and deriving every read model or view from it removes the dual-write atomicity and divergence problems and ensures the state a service communicates is the same as the state it saves internally.

From the perspective of other services, the data they see externally matters more than what a service stores internally, so making the event the shared source of truth makes sense even though a traditional system treats the internal database as the source of truth.

CQRS tends to give better overall read and write performance than an equivalent CRUD system because inputs are journaled to Kafka (faster than a database write) and the expensive maintenance of update-in-place structures such as indexes can be batched and applied asynchronously on the read side.

The cost of CQRS is that the asynchronously updated read model runs slightly behind the write model in time, so a user who writes and then immediately reads may not be able to read their own writes; specific strategies exist to address this.
condition: the read model is updated asynchronously from the write model

statement: A materialized view precomputes and stores the result of a predefined query and is updated whenever the underlying data changes, trading storage for fast retrieval instead of recomputing the query each time a user needs the data.

Because Kafka is publish-subscribe, a single CQRS write model can feed many independent read models or polyglot materialized views in different storage technologies, each tuned to a use case; the views are decoupled from the underlying events so they scale independently and the writing process need not wait for a view to be computed.

The MemoryImage pattern caches a whole dataset into memory where it can be queried locally instead of using an external database; it suits datasets that fit in memory and can be loaded in reasonable time, often snapshotting the event log with a compacted topic to cut load time, and can be hand-crafted or built with Kafka Streams in-memory state stores.
condition: the dataset fits in memory and can be loaded in a reasonable amount of time

statement: An event-sourced view is a query resource (database, memory image, etc.) created in one service from data authored and owned by another service; unlike a typical cache it is sourced directly from the log and can be regenerated in its entirety at any time, including after the view definition changes.
Kafka Connect's single-message transforms suit simple adjustments or enrichments, while Kafka's Streams API suits simple to very complex manipulations and precomputing views that other services need.

A read-optimized, event-sourced view can be built quickly in any of many databases using Kafka Connect sink connectors (polyglot views), for example using Elasticsearch for rich indexing and full-text search.

Aging in software is a function of how we choose to change it rather than of time, so designing for change through modularization, tests, and continuous integration or deployment is what makes a codebase last.
At company scale, system design is more about people than about software, so simply breaking a monolith into services does little to improve sustainability because the hard problem is organizational.

As a company grows it forms teams that need autonomy to make progress without extensive interaction, and the larger the company the more autonomy they need, but total independence does not work either, so an organizational balance of people, responsibility, and communication structure must be struck.

When components are operated and evolved independently, the design problem has three intrinsically linked parts — organization, software, and data — and good systems are differentiated from bad ones by their ability to manage all three as they evolve independently over time.
Reuse is double-edged: it lets software be developed quickly and succinctly, but the more a component is reused the more dependencies it accumulates and the harder it becomes to change.

The microservices pattern comes down hard on independence — services are run by different teams, have different deployment cycles, share no code, and share no databases — but replacing that sharing with a web of RPC/REST calls is not generally a preferable solution.

Encapsulation works well only when responsibilities separate cleanly (as for an SSO or logging service in a tightly bounded context); real business services rarely separate so cleanly, so new requirements crosscut service boundaries, several services must change at once, and the cross-team coordination erodes agility.
exception: the service has a genuinely clean, stable separation of concerns, like an SSO or logging service

statement: Microservices typically do not share a single domain model, because coupling the most sensitive shared logic to many programs makes that logic fiddly to change and release.

There are two fundamental differences between a service and a shared library: a service is run and operated by someone else, and a service has data of its own, whereas a library or database requires you to supply any data it needs.

Data coupling is harder to escape than functional coupling: if a service lacks a piece of functionality it can reimplement it, but if it lacks the data it needs there is literally nothing it can do, so most business services rely heavily on one another's data.

The data dichotomy is that databases are built to expose and amplify data to make it maximally useful, while services are built to hide data so they can stay decoupled, and these two fundamental forces are in constant tension in the systems we build.

In the God Service problem, a data service grows to expose an ever-increasing set of functions until it resembles a homegrown shared database, and the more functionality, data, and users it has, the more tightly coupled and the harder and more expensive it becomes to operate and evolve.

In the REST-to-ETL problem, consumers extract a data service's data to hold and manipulate it locally — to combine it with other data, bring it closer or offline, avoid the service's outages, or get functionality the service lacks — but keeping that extracted copy up to date then requires a polling mechanism.

The more mutable copies of a dataset exist, the more the data diverges over time, degrading the data quality of the whole ecosystem, and divergent datasets are very hard to fix retrospectively (master data management is only a band-aid over the problem).
A cyclical cycle of data inadequacy emerges between the drive to centralize datasets to keep them accurate and the competing temptation or need to extract datasets and go it alone.

Event Sourcing saves state using the same medium used to communicate it and records every change immutably, which makes recovery from failure or corruption simpler and more efficient than traditional application design.
The importance of CQRS is that it scales by optimizing the read and write models independently of one another.
Event Sourcing and CQRS make events first-class citizens, which lets a system relate the data that lives inside a service directly to the data it shares with others.

Stream processing can be viewed as a database turned inside out or unbundled: responsibility for data storage (the log) is segregated from the mechanism used to query it (the stream processing API), which makes it possible to create views and embed them exactly where they are needed.

There are two main drivers for pushing data to code: a performance optimization by making data local, and decoupling the data in an organization while keeping it close to a single shared source of truth.

At an organizational level the unbundled-database pattern forms a database of databases, where a single repository of event data feeds many views and each view can flex with the needs of the team that owns it.

A replayable log combined with a set of derived views is a far more malleable entity than a single shared database, because each view can be tuned to a different team's needs while all views derive from the same source of truth, the log.

Using a shared log as the source of truth keeps applications loosely coupled by making data available centrally with the simplest possible contract, while query functionality is kept private to each service so teams can move quickly by retaining control of the datasets they use.

Lean data means that, rather than collecting and curating large datasets, an application selects only the small set of data it needs at a point in time, pushed from a central event store into caches or stores it controls, supported by operational processes that make rederiving those views practical.

When the messaging layer is the durable source of truth, any data extracted from the log need not be stored reliably because it can always be re-fetched, so a downstream database or event-sourced view can be regenerated completely from the log.

Treating a database as a long-lived resource that is tweaked, tuned, and copied between environments over its lifetime inevitably lets errors and inaccuracies creep in, whereas stream processing avoids this by rederiving views from the log instead of copying files around.

Immutability through infrastructure as code makes deployments deterministic, builds identical, and rebuilds easy; streaming applies the same immutable, deterministically rederivable approach to data through lean event-sourced views.

When pulling data from Kafka into a service, take only the fields you need: this minimizes the view's size, allows it to be reshaped to be read-optimized, and reduces coupling because a schema change is less likely to affect fields the service does not store.
Keeping a derived dataset small lets you store more rows in the available memory or disk, and performance typically improves as a result.
The drawback of lean data is that needing more data requires going back to the log, and the cleanest way to obtain it is to drop the view and rebuild it from scratch.

Kafka Streams event-sourced views — whether tables that directly materialize a topic or state stores populated by a declarative transformation — are automatically rebuilt if the service's disk is lost or removed or if the Streams Reset tool is invoked.

Because worst-case regeneration time is the limiting factor when rebuilding an event-sourced view, choose a write-optimized database or cache such as an in-memory store (Redis, MemSQL, Hazelcast), a memory-optimized or journaling-disabled database (Couchbase, MongoDB), or a log-structured write/disk-optimized database (Cassandra, RocksDB).
condition: the view must be rebuilt from the log and rebuild time matters

statement: Because rebuilding an event-sourced view can take minutes or even hours, when releasing new software regenerate views in advance or in parallel and switch from the old view to the new one only once the new view is fully caught up.
condition: view rebuild has a significant lead time

statement: Rebuilding terabyte-sized datasets in a single instance of a highly indexed, disk-resident database can be prohibitively slow, whereas memory-based solutions with fast write times or horizontal scaling keep ingestion fast.
exception: very large, highly indexed disk-resident single-instance datasets, where rebuild time may be prohibitive

statement: Operators lose trust in scripts that are not regularly used, especially data-mutating ones such as database rollback scripts, so when moving between environments it is often best to recreate views directly from the log rather than copy database files across environments.

When a message schema changes in a non-backward-compatible way, holding the dataset in full in Kafka lets you simply drop and regenerate the view instead of crafting a database schema-migration script.
condition: the full dataset is retained in Kafka

statement: Data divergence behaves like a game of telephone: as data moves application to application through many translation layers (wire model, internal domain model, database model, outbound schemas) and across semantic conflicts (such as whether a contractor is an employee), errors accumulate and become laborious and expensive to fix.

Streaming platforms reduce data divergence by connecting all applications to a single shared source of truth and, because data is retained immutably in the log, making it easier to track down when an error was introduced and to apply fixes with the original data on hand.

Consistency models are optimizations that relax strict in-order execution against a single copy of data in exchange for better performance or availability; streaming systems regain strong consistency by partitioning the relevant data into stream threads and wrapping the operation in a transaction so it runs in order against a single copy.

Groups of services generally lack the strong consistency guarantees of a single database: as data moves from service to service it becomes visible to users at different times, unless all services coordinate around a single database and a single global consistency model.
exception: all services coordinate around a single database with one global consistency model

statement: Instead of sharing a global consistency model through a database, use the single writer principle to create local points of consistency connected via the event stream, where each service is the sole writer of the state changes in its own topic.
Single writers can be scaled out linearly through partitioning when implemented with Kafka's Streams API.

The Command Topic variant uses two topics per entity: a Command topic that any process may write but that carries only the initiating event, and an Entity topic that only the owning single-writer service may write; splitting them lets administrators enforce the single writer principle strictly through topic permissions.

A less stringent single-writer-per-transition variant has each service own individual state transitions rather than all transitions in a topic, for example the payment service adding a payment section to the existing order message and owning only that one transition.

Kafka transactions provide two guarantees: messages sent to different topics within a transaction are either all written or none at all, and messages sent to a single topic within a transaction are never duplicated even on failure.
Kafka transactions let Kafka Streams join writes to state stores and writes to output topics together atomically.

Identity is important and often overlooked in business systems: messages must be uniquely identified to detect duplicates, and identity is what enables optimistic concurrency control for updates made at the same time.

An entity's identity should correlate with the real world (for example an order has an OrderId and a payment a PaymentId), and a logically mutable entity should additionally carry a version identifier.
condition: the entity is logically mutable (it passes through several states or has updatable fields)

statement: Optimistic concurrency control rejects a write whose underlying data has become stale by comparing version numbers on the server before permitting the write, and it can be implemented equivalently in synchronous or asynchronous systems.

The single writer principle and related consistency patterns are useful patterns for common cases rather than general solutions, and there will always be exceptions, particularly where the implementation is constrained by legacy systems.
exception: constrained environments such as those dominated by legacy systems

statement: Global consistency can be problematic and eventual consistency is useful; the single writer principle adapts eventual consistency to avoid update collisions while keeping its lack of timeliness.

In a services context Kafka transactions do three things: they remove duplicates that would otherwise corrupt streaming results such as counts, they send groups of messages atomically to different topics, and they tie a write to a Kafka Streams state store together with an outbound message in one atomic unit.
Retrying a failed call in a distributed system can cause duplicate processing, which leads to real problems such as debiting a customer's account twice or adding duplicate items to a feed.

By the end-to-end principle, as long as deduplication happens at the end of each use case (for example a database deduplicating by primary key) it does not matter how many duplicate calls are made in between, because such a process is naturally idempotent.

For natural deduplication to work, every network call must carry an appropriate key defining its identity and be deduplicated against a store holding an extensive history of those keys; otherwise duplicates must be considered explicitly in business logic, increasing cognitive overhead.
condition: deduplication is being relied on rather than provided by exactly-once infrastructure

statement: Without exactly-once support, event-driven systems end up deduplicating on every message received before processing and assigning every outgoing message a carefully chosen ID for downstream deduplication, which is a hassle and a breeding ground for errors.

Duplication, like message ordering and redelivery, is arguably an infrastructure concern that should not leak into the application layer; Kafka transactions provide exactly-once guarantees that free services from deduplicating incoming data and choosing dedup keys for outgoing data.

Kafka's exactly-once guarantee covers only the Kafka parts of a system and the interactions between services performed through Kafka; parts of the system based on other technologies are not covered by the guarantee.
exception: system components built on technologies other than Kafka

statement: To validate each message exactly once in a consume-process-produce loop, the producer must send the output message and commit the consumer offset to the consumer_offsets topic as a single atomic unit.
Exactly-once in Kafka requires both idempotence in the broker, so duplicates cannot be created in the log, and an atomic commit layered on top that ties all the messages sent together.

A broker presents two opportunities for duplication: a send to the broker that fails before its acknowledgment returns (a retry may create a duplicate message), and a reader that fails before committing offsets (the same message may be read again on restart).

Broker idempotence gives each producer an identifier and each message a sequence number, and the broker uses the unique combination to discard a message already present in the log, which is far more efficient than storing every key ever seen in a database.

Kafka transactions use marker messages flowing through the streams (an adaptation of the Chandy-Lamport Snapshot Marker Model): begin markers are sent down each topic, then the messages, and finally a commit or abort marker concludes the transaction.

To ensure consumers read only committed data, on seeing a Begin marker a consumer buffers messages internally and holds them until the Commit marker arrives, only then presenting them to the consuming program.

Transaction atomicity is coordinated by a transaction coordinator, of which there are many spread across the cluster so there is no single point of failure, but each transaction uses exactly one coordinator.
When using the Kafka Streams API, exactly-once processing requires no extra code; the feature is simply enabled.

Adding a new field to a schema is a backward- and forward-compatible change: programs on the old schema still read new messages but do not see the new field, while programs on the new schema read the whole message; this additive evolution is how most shared messaging models are managed over time.

Fields cannot be moved or removed from a schema in a compatible way, although a move can be synthesized by cloning the field, leaving the data duplicated in two places until a breaking change can be released.

The Confluent Schema Registry maps Kafka topics to the schema they use and enforces compatibility rules before messages are added, checking every message for Avro compatibility so that incompatible messages fail on publication.

Schema-on-read lets many incompatible schemas coexist in the same topic at once by pushing format translation into the application layer; it is pragmatic because recent data is often more valuable, so programs can move forward without migrating old data, and it is simple when parsing code for previous schemas already exists.

Unless you perform a single holistic big-bang release, you will always have to handle the schema-evolution problem, either by physically migrating datasets forward or by maintaining different application-layer routines.
exception: a single holistic big-bang release of all producers and consumers

statement: The Dual Schema Upgrade Window handles a non-backward-compatible schema change by creating two topics (for example orders-v1 and orders-v2) carrying the old and new schemas, giving services a window during which they can upgrade before the old topic is archived or deleted.
condition: the schema change is non-backward-compatible

statement: Dual-publishing both schemas atomically with the transactions API, or down-converting the v2 topic to v1 with a Kafka Streams job, does not solve back-population of historic messages, so neither is appropriate for topics used for long-term storage.
exception: topics used for long-term storage, which require back-population

statement: Up-converting from the v1 topic to the v2 topic with a Kafka Streams job started from offset 0 (or migrating the dataset internally and republishing it) handles back-population, making it better suited to long-retention topics such as those used for Event Sourcing.
condition: historic messages must be ported forward (long-retention or Event Sourcing topics)

statement: The single writer principle makes schema upgrades simpler, because if several different services wrote the same entity it would be much harder to schedule a non-backward-compatible upgrade without a conjoined release.

Schemas are code and should be version-controlled, so the best way to collaborate on a schema change is through GitHub pull requests: implementers propose and code against the change while others review, comment, and approve, which reliably reaches and audits consensus without unduly impeding the implementer.

Coordinating schema change by emailing affected teams lacks structure and accountability, while routing all changes through a central team stifles progress by forcing implementers to wait for the central team and arrange sign-off.

A valid schema does not guarantee downstream applications will work, because a semantic error such as an unexpected character, invalid country code, negative quantity, or corrupt bytes can stall a process and hold up processing until the issue is fixed, which is unacceptable in some environments.

Kafka has no traditional dead letter queue, but a consumer that cannot read a message (for a semantic reason or an invalid payload such as a failed CRC check) can place it on a separate error topic so processing continues, and the error topic can be reprocessed later.

The simplest way to remove messages from Kafka is to let them expire (the default retention is two weeks and is tunable to an arbitrarily large or small period), and an Admin API also lets you explicitly delete messages older than a specified time or offset.

When using Kafka for Event Sourcing or as a source of truth you typically do not hard-delete records; instead a record is removed by writing a null value or delete marker for its key, which keeps the fully versioned history intact, and most Connect sinks are built with delete markers in mind.

For regulatory physical-deletion requirements such as GDPR's right to be forgotten, a delete marker is not enough because the data must be physically removed; compacted topics are the common tool because they allow messages to be explicitly deleted or replaced by key, while some use crypto shredding.
condition: data must be physically removed to meet a regulatory requirement

statement: Deleting from a compacted topic works like Cassandra or HBase: you write a new message with the target key and a null value (a tombstone), and the record is removed permanently when the compaction process next runs.

When the topic's key is not the key you want to delete by (for example a topic keyed by ProductId when you must delete by customer), use a composite key such as [ProductId][CustomerId] with a custom partitioner that partitions only on the ProductId, so you can still delete by the composite key.
condition: the partitioning/ordering key differs from the key you must delete by

statement: To propagate a delete from a source database through Kafka to downstream Connect sinks, a change-data-capture (CDC) enabled source connector handles it automatically, whereas without CDC you need a custom mechanism for managing deletes.
exception: a CDC-enabled connector is in use, in which case the delete propagates automatically

statement: When many services share a Kafka cluster, segregate private internal topics from shared business topics, enforcing it strictly through the authorization interface by granting read/write on internal topics only to their owning services (via runtime validation or secured with TLS or SASL) rather than relying on convention.

Kafka Streams is the core JVM API for stream processing, offering a declarative DSL to join, filter, group, or aggregate streams blended with functional per-message methods such as map, flatMap, transform, and peek, so you can mix SQL-like operations with arbitrary custom code.

KSQL is an interactive SQL-like wrapper over the Kafka Streams API for use outside the JVM; it can run standalone (for example via the Sidecar pattern) and be called remotely, with custom processing added through user-defined functions or by pushing output to a topic consumed by a native client.
Kafka Streams and KSQL let you model business operations in an asynchronous, nonblocking, and coordination-free manner.

To let a client read its own writes despite CQRS asynchronicity, implement a blocking HTTP GET that blocks until the awaited event arrives in the view or a configured timeout passes (essentially long polling), which can be implemented with nonblocking IO.

When Kafka Streams state stores are exposed over an HTTP endpoint and the service runs with multiple instances, requests must be routed to the correct partition and instance for a given key, and Kafka Streams includes a metadata service that does this routing.

An operation that mutates atomic state across topics (such as validating stock, reserving items, and emitting a validation message) works reliably only if Kafka's transactions feature is enabled and the data is partitioned by the relevant business key (for example ProductId) before the operation is performed.
condition: the operation manages atomic state across topics and is scaled across threads or machines

statement: If a multi-step state mutation fails without being wrapped in a transaction, you have no way to know what state the system is left in.

A traditional, non-stateful streaming system scaled across parallel processes runs the critical section inside a transaction in a shared database, so all instances bottleneck on the same database instance.

Stateful stream processing systems like Kafka Streams avoid remote transactions and cross-process coordination by partitioning the problem over a set of threads or processes using a chosen business key, which is the key to scaling these systems horizontally.

Partitioning in Kafka Streams reroutes messages so that all the state required for one computation is sent to a single thread; the approach is inherently parallel and enables high message-at-a-time rates, but it works only if a logical key cleanly segregates all operations, including both the state they need and the state they operate on.
condition: a logical key exists that cleanly segregates all the operations and their state

statement: Partitioning by a business key makes all operations for that key execute sequentially on the same thread so different keys need no coordination, and the resulting operation is atomic (via Kafka transactions), horizontally scalable, and free of cross-network coordination, similar to the Map phase of MapReduce.

A rekey operation repartitions a stream by pushing records into a new intermediary Kafka topic keyed by the chosen business key (and back out again), producing co-partitioned data that can be processed together; the same technique partitions reads in order to perform a join.

A Kafka Streams state store is a local, disk-resident hash table backed by a Kafka topic that you program much like a hash map or key/value store, with the benefit that its data is persisted to Kafka and restored if the process restarts, and writes to it participate in Kafka's transactions.

To join two streams on a key that is not the primary key (a foreign-key relationship), rekey and co-partition the streams by that join key so corresponding records land on the same thread, after which the join can be performed without any additional network access.

Chained operations that need different data distributions are connected with rekey operations, for example distributing data by ProductId for one stage and then rekeying back to OrderId before adding it to a destructive Orders view keyed by OrderId so that no data is lost.

The keys used to partition event streams must be invariant if ordering is to be guaranteed, so a partitioning key such as ProductId or OrderId must remain fixed across all messages relating to that entity, which is typically enforced at the domain level (for example, requiring a brand-new order when a user changes the product they are buying).
condition: ordering of the partitioned stream must be guaranteed

statement: To wait for N events that all arrive on a single topic, group by the key, count occurrences of each key using an aggregator executed within a window, and filter the output for the required count.
condition: the awaited events share a single topic

statement: Every distributed system has a baseline cost: a partitioned streaming solution gives good scalability and resiliency but is always more complex to build and run than an equivalent single-process application, so you should always weigh better nonfunctional properties against simplicity when designing a system.

A streaming platform supports stateless services, read-only stateful services (event-sourced views), and read-write stateful services (either entirely inside Kafka under its transactional guarantees or by calling out to other services or databases), letting you trade the operational ease of stateless approaches for the data-processing power of stateful ones.

Even though standby replicas, checkpoints, and compacted topics mitigate the risks of pushing data to code, there is always a worst-case scenario in which service-resident datasets must be rebuilt, and this must be considered as part of any system design.
Adopting the streaming model brings a mindset shift to a more asynchronous, functional, and data-centric style compared with the more procedural nature of traditional service interfaces.

Partition distribution across consumers is managed by Kafka itself rather than Kafka Streams, through Kafka's Consumer Group Protocol, which lets any group of consumers control how partitions are distributed across the group.

Enterprise integration connects independent applications that can each run by themselves and coordinate in a loosely coupled way, which is distinct from a distributed n-tier application whose individual tiers cannot run on their own.
Messaging transmits data or commands across a network using a send-and-forget model in which the caller dispatches the information and proceeds to other work while the messaging system delivers it.
An asynchronous call can be retried until it succeeds, making the communication more reliable than an equivalent synchronous call.
Asynchronous messaging enables throttling of requests and load balancing across consumers.
Adopting asynchronous calls and callbacks makes a design more complex than a synchronous approach, so the reliability gains come at a design-complexity cost.
Describing integration with a vendor-independent pattern vocabulary lets architects and integrators make confident design decisions and communicate across heterogeneous messaging products.
After delivering an asynchronous request the caller can optionally be notified of the result through a callback rather than blocking for the reply.

Every integration solution must contend with four fundamental challenges: networks are unreliable, networks are slow, any two applications differ in language/platform/data format, and change is inevitable.

Sending data across a network is multiple orders of magnitude slower than a local method call, so designing a widely distributed solution as if it were a single in-process application risks severe performance problems.

An integration solution should minimize dependencies between systems by using loose coupling, because a change in one tightly coupled system can cascade into an avalanche of changes across all connected systems.

There are four main integration approaches — File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation, and Messaging — each with distinct advantages and disadvantages, and a solution may combine styles so each integration point uses the style that suits it best.
File Transfer integration requires the participating applications to agree on the filename and location, the file format, the timing of writing and reading, and who deletes the file.
condition: when integrating via File Transfer

statement: Shared Database integration has multiple applications share one schema in a single physical database, so no data has to be transferred between applications.
condition: when integrating via Shared Database

statement: Remote Procedure Invocation exposes an application's functionality for remote access and communicates in real time and synchronously.
condition: when integrating via Remote Procedure Invocation

statement: Messaging integration has one application publish a message to a shared channel that others read later, requiring agreement on the channel and message format, with asynchronous communication.
condition: when integrating via Messaging

statement: A message has two parts: a header carrying meta-information used by the messaging system, and a body carrying the application payload that the messaging system ignores.
A messaging system (message-oriented middleware) overcomes inherently unreliable computers and networks by repeatedly retrying transmission until the message is delivered.

Wrapping data as an atomic message and delegating delivery to the messaging system lets delivery be retried until it succeeds, so the receiver can be assured of reliably receiving exactly one copy of the data.
Messaging moves messages using store-and-forward: the messaging system stores the message on each computer along the path and forwards it computer to computer until it reaches the receiver.
Messaging is more immediate than File Transfer, better encapsulated than a Shared Database, and more reliable than Remote Procedure Invocation.
If remote communication is not actually needed, messaging is not needed and a simpler in-process mechanism such as shared memory or concurrent collections is sufficient.
condition: only when remote, cross-process communication is required
exception: when remote communication is not needed

statement: Asynchronous (variable-timing) communication lets the sender batch requests at its own pace and the receiver consume them at its own pace, so both applications run at maximum throughput instead of waiting on each other.
Asynchronous communication enables throttling: the receiver controls the rate at which it consumes requests to avoid overload, while callers are not blocked because the communication is asynchronous.

Messaging provides reliable delivery that RPC cannot, because store-and-forward plus automatic resending overcomes network and receiver failures without the sender and receiver handling those details.
Messaging is well suited to disconnected operation: data can be queued as it is created while offline and synchronized when the application reconnects to the network.
condition: for applications that run disconnected and sync when a connection is available

statement: Using callbacks instead of blocking threads keeps the number of blocked threads to a small, known set of reply listeners, which frees most threads for real work and makes thread state easy to re-establish after a crash.

Asynchronous messaging imposes a more complex event-driven programming model in which logic is split across event handlers, making systems harder to develop and debug than a single synchronous method chain.
Message channels guarantee delivery but not timing, so messages sent in sequence can arrive out of order, and dependent messages require special handling to re-establish their sequence.
exception: when message ordering matters, extra sequencing logic is required

statement: Not every interaction can use send-and-forget; when a user needs an immediate result, the messaging solution must bridge synchronous and asynchronous styles, typically via Request-Reply.
condition: when an immediate, interactive response is required

statement: For bulk data replication, ETL (extract-transform-load) tools are more efficient than messaging because messaging adds per-message overhead; messaging is best suited to keeping systems in sync after the initial replication.
condition: for large one-time bulk data movement, prefer ETL over messaging

statement: Different messaging systems usually do not interconnect because many rely on proprietary protocols and even shared specifications like JMS do not control the physical implementation, which can create vendor lock-in and a further integration challenge.

An n-tier distributed application is distribution, not integration, because its tiers are tightly coupled, communicate synchronously, and serve human users expecting rapid response, whereas integrated applications are independent, loosely coupled, asynchronous, and tolerant of broad time constraints.

Adopting asynchronous communication means giving up a single thread of execution: results arrive via callbacks and sub-processes can complete in any order, so the caller must correlate each result to the call that produced it.

Messaging middleware is delivered in four product categories: operating-system/database services (e.g., MSMQ, Oracle AQ), application servers implementing JMS, proprietary EAI suites that bundle messaging with business-process automation and workflow, and Web services toolkits implementing reliable-messaging standards.

The same logical messaging concept maps to different vendor terminology — for example a Message Channel is a JMS Destination, an MSMQ MessageQueue, a WebSphere MQ Queue, and a TIBCO Topic — so a vendor-neutral pattern vocabulary is needed to compare solutions.

At the time of writing, Publish-Subscribe Channel had a direct equivalent in JMS (Topic) but no direct equivalent in MSMQ or WebSphere MQ, so publish-subscribe capability cannot be assumed across all messaging products.
The messaging pattern language has six root patterns derived from the central Messaging pattern: Message Channel, Message, Pipes and Filters, Message Router, Message Translator, and Message Endpoint.
A useful pattern must be prescriptive: it should tell the reader what to do to solve the problem, document why the problem is hard, and explain why rejected alternative solutions do not work well.

Independently developed applications often disagree on message format, on the form and meaning of identifiers, and on character encoding, so intermediate transformer components are required to convert messages between producer and consumer formats.
Many applications were not designed to participate in messaging, so they must be explicitly connected to the messaging system through a messaging layer that makes the application a message endpoint.
Standard UML class and interaction diagrams lack semantics to describe messaging flows; the UML Profile for EAI extends collaboration diagrams for this but does not capture every integration pattern.
Illustrative integration code samples that omit error checking, security, robustness, and scalability should not be treated as a starting point for building a production integration solution.

A typical enterprise runs hundreds to thousands of heterogeneous applications, and building one big application to run an entire business is effectively impossible because even large ERP suites cover only a fraction of required business functions.

Spreading business functions across best-of-breed applications gives flexibility but causes functional spillover and overlap between packages, so defining a clean functional separation between systems is hard.
End users execute business functions without regard to system boundaries, so a single business transaction such as placing an order can span five to seven different internal systems.
Application integration must provide efficient, reliable, and secure data exchange between multiple enterprise applications.
The true challenges of enterprise integration span both business and technical issues, so the technical infrastructure alone addresses only a small portion of integration complexity.

Because IT groups are often organized around functional areas (an instance of Conway's law), successful integration requires organizational and political change as application groups give up exclusive control when each application becomes part of an integrated flow.

Once the most critical business functions are incorporated into an integration solution, that solution becomes vital to the business, and a failing or misbehaving integration solution can cost millions in lost orders, misrouted payments, and lost customers.

Integration developers usually have limited control over the participating applications because they are legacy or packaged systems that cannot be changed, forcing developers to compensate for application deficiencies and differences at the integration layer.
condition: when participating applications are legacy or packaged systems that cannot be modified

statement: Few integration standards have firmly established themselves, and historically even standards-compliant products failed to interoperate — the lack of interoperability that hampered CORBA, now echoed by fragmentation around Web services extensions.

A common data representation such as XML does not imply common semantics; the same concept like 'account' carries different meaning and constraints in each system, and resolving these semantic differences is a particularly difficult and time-consuming task involving business and technical decisions.

Operating and maintaining an EAI solution can be more daunting than building it, because the mix of technologies and distributed nature make deployment, monitoring, and troubleshooting complex and demand skill sets that are often scarce or fragmented across IT operations.
Integration patterns are reusable nuggets of advice describing solutions to frequently recurring problems, not copy-paste code samples or shrink-wrap components.

Integration projects commonly fall into six types — Information Portals, Data Replication, Shared Business Functions, Service-Oriented Architectures, Distributed Business Processes, and Business-to-Business Integration — and a single project often combines several of them.

Data replication can be implemented in several ways: database-vendor built-in replication, exporting data to files and re-importing, or using message-oriented middleware to carry data records inside messages.

The choice between a shared business function (calling a service) and data replication is driven by how much control you have over the systems and the data's rate of change: a service call is more intrusive, while replication suits data that is read frequently but changes infrequently.
condition: deciding between service call and replication based on control and rate of change

statement: A service is a well-defined function that is universally available and responds to consumer requests, and a service-oriented architecture rests on two key elements: service discovery via a directory, and negotiation of an interface contract.

A distributed business process adds a business-process-management component that coordinates the execution of a business function across multiple existing systems, supplying the coordination the individual applications lack.

Business-to-business integration raises additional issues of transport protocols, security, and standardized data formats because communication crosses the Internet between independent business partners.
condition: when integration spans organizational boundaries over a public network

statement: The core principle of loose coupling is to reduce the assumptions two parties make about each other; more shared assumptions make communication more efficient but make the solution less tolerant of interruptions and change.

A local method call is an example of tight coupling because it assumes the same process, the same language or bytecode, exact parameter count and types, immediate synchronous execution, and no concern for eavesdropping.

RPC- and RMI-style approaches package remote data exchange in local method-call semantics to exploit developer familiarity and to defer the local-versus-remote placement decision until deployment time.

Portraying remote communication as a variant of a local method call is dangerous because remote calls invalidate local-call assumptions (shared language, low latency, reachability, security, stable signatures), typically producing brittle, hard-to-maintain, poorly scalable solutions.

A minimalist TCP/IP socket integration is fast and cheap but brittle because the two parties make four coupling assumptions: platform technology (internal number/object representation), location (hard-coded addresses), time (all components available simultaneously), and data format (matching parameter list and types).

Transmitting raw in-memory byte representations between systems corrupts data when the systems differ in integer width or byte endianness, so integration should use a self-describing, platform-independent data format such as XML.

Sending data to an addressable channel — a logical address both sender and receiver agree on without knowing each other's identity — removes the location dependency that hard-coded machine addresses create.

A connection-oriented protocol such as TCP/IP creates a temporal dependency that requires both endpoints and the network to be available at the same time; queuing sent requests inside the channel removes this temporal dependency.
To let a channel queue and buffer requests, the data must be wrapped into self-contained messages so the channel knows how much data to buffer and deliver at one time.

Performing data-format transformation inside the channel removes the shared-format dependency between systems: when one system's format changes, only the transformer changes while the other participating systems remain unaffected.

The main drawback of loose coupling is additional complexity and a harder design/build/debug experience, which is why message-oriented middleware is used to provide common formats, queuing channels, and transformers so loosely coupled exchange becomes almost as easy as a naive direct call.

A basic integration solution requires two elements: a communications channel that moves information between applications, and a message — a snippet of data with an agreed-upon meaning to both applications — placed inside that channel.
Because an application's internal data format often cannot be changed, the middleware must provide a translation step that converts one application's data format into another's.

Requiring each sending application to know and target every recipient system does not scale, because the sender must know all others and every newly added system forces a change to the sender; a routing component such as a message broker should instead deliver messages to the correct destinations.

An integration solution needs a systems-management function that monitors the data flow, verifies that all applications and components are available, and reports error conditions to a central location.

Most packaged, legacy, and many custom applications are not prepared to participate in an integration solution, so a message endpoint — custom code or a vendor-provided Channel Adapter — is needed to connect each application explicitly.

A Channel Adapter attaches to an application and publishes a message to a channel when an event occurs inside the application (for example via database triggers), can also work in reverse by consuming messages to trigger application actions, and may operate without the application being aware of it.
Use a Messaging Gateway to isolate application code from messaging-specific code.

Use Message Translators to convert each source application's format into a common message that conforms to a Canonical Data Model — a message format independent of any specific application — so all applications communicate in one shared format.

With a Canonical Data Model there are two message classes — canonical (public) and application-specific (private) — and an application-specific message should be consumed only by its related application and that application's Message Translator.

Reinforce the public/private message split with a naming convention: prefix application-specific channels with the application name (e.g., WEB_NEW_ORDER) and name canonical channels by the message's intent without a prefix (e.g., NEW_ORDER).
Connect each order source to its Message Translator via a Point-to-Point Channel when each message must be consumed exactly once.
condition: when each message must be consumed by exactly one receiver

statement: Prefer a consistent Message Translator over hand-coding transformation logic inside the gateway, because hand-coded transformation is tedious and error-prone and a separate translator shields the downstream flow from minor source-format changes.
A Datatype Channel carries messages of only one type, which makes it easy for consumers to know exactly what type of message to expect on that channel.
A Document Message passes a document to any interested recipient who is free to decide how to process it, rather than instructing the receiver to take a specific action.
Integrating existing parallel systems can be cheaper than rewriting them into a single system, so operating and integrating redundant applications is sometimes the more economical choice.
condition: when rewrite cost exceeds the cost of operating parallel systems

statement: Designing an Aggregator requires three key decisions: correlation (which messages belong together), the completeness condition (how to know all messages have arrived), and the aggregation algorithm (how to combine the messages into one result).

Correlate related messages by a unique per-transaction identifier such as an order ID rather than by a shared attribute like customer ID, because the same customer may place multiple orders in quick succession.
A Content Enricher is a component that adds missing data items to an incoming message.
Asynchronous messaging lets communication happen at the pace of the components, so a slow step that holds a message does not block independent steps that can proceed concurrently.
A Publish-Subscribe Channel lets you add additional subscribers without disturbing the existing flow of messages.

To observe messages travelling over a Point-to-Point Channel, where each message can be consumed by only one subscriber, insert a Wire Tap that consumes a message from one channel and republishes it to two channels.
condition: when monitoring a Point-to-Point Channel whose messages have a single consumer

statement: Storing messages in a central Message Store lets later components retrieve the data they need without every intermediate step carrying that data along — the Claim Check pattern, which checks data for later retrieval.
A Process Manager is a central component that stores data between messages and tracks progress to determine the next step, replacing fixed channel-to-channel wiring of components.
Coordinating systems through a Process Manager turns the individual systems into shared services that any process can access, which increases reuse and allows rapid change and maintenance.

For a synchronous status query where the user expects an immediate response, accessing the database directly as a Shared Database is the simplest and most efficient approach and always shows current data, at the cost of tightly coupling the querying application to the database.
condition: when an immediate, always-current synchronous read is required and the coupling cost is acceptable

statement: To participate in a service-oriented architecture each service must expose an interface contract, and each request-reply service must support a Return Address so the consumer specifies the reply channel, enabling the service to be reused across different contexts.

Wrap a legacy system that lacks service features such as Return Address with a Smart Proxy that intercepts both request and reply messages to add the missing capability and to track quality of service such as response times.
condition: when a legacy service lacks features needed to participate in an SOA

statement: There are two basic ways to deliver address data to downstream systems: include the address in the New Order message, or replicate address changes separately; including it reuses an existing channel but carries address data on every order even though addresses change far less frequently.

When two operations must occur in a specific order, such as updating an address before sending the bill, insert a Process Manager that receives one message and publishes the two ordered messages to the target system.
condition: when the order of two dependent operations matters

statement: Prefer external Message Translators over embedding transformation logic in the Process Manager, so the Process Manager's logic is insulated from the possibly complicated proprietary data formats required by applications.

Propagating address changes through a dedicated Publish-Subscribe Channel reduces message traffic when addresses change less often than orders are placed and reduces coupling because any interested system can subscribe without affecting others, at the cost of building a new consume interface in each system.
condition: when the replicated data changes less frequently than the transactions that use it

statement: Use Message Filters so that each system receives only the messages matching its criteria — for example, preventing a billing-only address change from being sent to the shipping system.

Prefer coarse-grained, self-contained business actions over fine-grained interfaces in integration, because fine-grained interfaces cause excessive remote calls, message-synchronization overhead, and tight coupling — yet interfaces that are too coarse limit flexibility, so the right granularity is a balanced trade-off.

Use File Transfer rather than real-time messaging when data changes infrequently, such as catalogs updated quarterly, also because files transport efficiently over public networks via FTP whereas most asynchronous messaging infrastructures do not work well over the public Internet.
condition: when data changes infrequently or must traverse the public Internet

statement: Process bulk data with translators that transform a whole batch at once rather than one item at a time, which is much more efficient when handling large amounts of same-format data.
condition: when transforming large volumes of same-format data

statement: A Publish-Subscribe Channel has two notable drawbacks: any subscriber can listen to published messages without the publisher's knowledge, and over wide-area networks it must send a separate copy of each message to every recipient, causing unnecessary traffic for uninterested recipients.

To send individual messages only to interested and authorized recipients with tight control over who receives them, use a Dynamic Recipient List — a Recipient List whose routing is driven by a Dynamic Router that updates from subscription control messages.

The routing solution is independent of transport technology: recipient channels can be implemented as email addresses via mailing lists or as Web service URIs via SOAP, showing the patterns describe design independent of a specific transport.

To verify billing for a metered external service, insert a Smart Proxy that counts requests and measures request-to-reply elapsed time by replacing the consumer's Return Address with a fixed reply channel and restoring the original to forward the reply.
A Control Bus collects metrics such as response times from many different components into a central management console.

To detect a service that returns validly formatted but incorrect data, periodically inject a Test Message with a known expected result and use a Test Data Verifier to check the reply's accuracy, and additionally take a statistical sample such as alerting when too many consecutive rejections occur.

The four integration styles are File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation, and Messaging, presented in increasing order of sophistication where each addresses shortcomings of its predecessor.

Do not pick one integration style to use always; choose the best style for each integration opportunity, and two applications may integrate using multiple styles so each integration point uses what suits it best.

The great advantage of File Transfer is that integrators need no knowledge of an application's internals: the file's contents and format become the application's interface, so each application can change internally as long as it keeps producing the same file format.

File Transfer requires developers to agree on file naming conventions and directories, keep filenames unique, agree which application deletes old files and when, and use a locking or timing convention so a file is not read while still being written; if applications do not share a disk, one must transfer the file.
condition: when integrating via File Transfer

statement: File Transfer's main weakness is that infrequent updates let systems drift out of synchronization, so the file-production frequency must be chosen according to consumers' data-freshness needs, and longer intervals make inconsistency more likely and more painful.

Messaging can be understood as File Transfer that produces a file for every change; once files become this fine-grained, managing them exceeds what file systems can do, so it is better treated as messaging.

A Shared Database keeps a family of integrated applications consistent because they all rely on the same data, and transaction-management systems handle simultaneous updates about as gracefully as possible while small inter-update times make errors easy to find and fix.

Shared Database integration is eased by ubiquitous SQL relational databases, avoids multiple file formats, and forces semantic-dissonance problems to be confronted before go-live rather than left to fester into incompatible data.

The biggest difficulty with a Shared Database is designing a unified schema that meets multiple applications' needs — technically hard, often politically contentious, and frequently impossible because external packages will not work with a schema other than their own.

Multiple applications frequently reading and modifying the same Shared Database can cause performance bottlenecks and deadlocks from locking, and distributing the database to co-locate with applications adds data-placement and locking-conflict performance problems.

Sharing data alone is often insufficient because a data change may need to trigger processes in other applications, and doing this through shared data would require applications to know too much about each other's internals.

Remote Procedure Invocation applies the principle of encapsulation to integration: an application requests data or modification from the owning application, so each application maintains the integrity of its own data and can change its internals without affecting others.

Remote Procedure Invocation has many variants — CORBA, COM, .NET Remoting, Java RMI, and Web Services using SOAP and XML — and Web services are valuable because they work easily over HTTP, which passes through firewalls.

The familiarity of Remote Procedure Invocation's procedure-call semantics is more disadvantage than advantage, because remote and local calls differ greatly in performance and reliability, and misunderstanding this leads to slow and unreliable systems.

Even though encapsulation reduces coupling, Remote Procedure Invocation still leaves applications fairly tightly coupled, and the required sequencing of remote calls makes it difficult to change the integrated systems independently.
Designers often build integration the way they would build a single application, unaware that the rules change once issues cross application boundaries.

Messaging transfers packets of data frequently, immediately, reliably, and asynchronously using customizable formats, combining File Transfer's decoupling and RPC's behavior invocation while adding a retry mechanism and asynchrony so the sender does not wait on the receiver.

Thinking about communication asynchronously forces developers to recognize that working with a remote application is slower, which encourages designing components with high cohesion (much work done locally) and low coupling (selective remote work).

Messaging lets messages be transformed in transit without the sender or receiver knowing, enabling broadcast to many receivers, choosing one of many potential receivers, and other topologies that separate integration from application development.
The high frequency of messages reduces but does not entirely remove the inconsistency and lag problems of File Transfer, because systems are still not updated perfectly simultaneously.
exception: some update lag remains even with frequent messaging

statement: Messaging's downsides include a learning curve for asynchronous design, harder testing and debugging, and the message-transformation independence often leaving integrators to write a lot of messy glue code.

Once messaging is chosen, four root mechanisms answer the core questions: a Message carried on a Message Channel transfers data, a Message Router directs data when the sender does not know the receiver, a Message Translator converts formats when sender and receiver disagree, and Message Endpoints connect an application to the messaging system.

Messaging rests on six basic concepts: Channels, Messages, multi-step delivery via Pipes and Filters, Routing via a Message Router, Transformation via a Message Translator, and Endpoints via Message Endpoints.
A newly installed messaging system contains no channels, so developers must determine how their applications need to communicate and create the necessary channels.

Connect applications with a Message Channel where one application writes information and another reads it, and use a different channel per information type so a receiver selecting a channel is assured of getting only the kind of information it wants.

Channels are logical addresses whose physical implementation — direct endpoint connections, a central hub, or several logical channels multiplexed onto one physical channel — is hidden from the applications.
The number and purpose of channels tend to be fixed at deployment time, because every application that needs a channel must know about it, which makes runtime channel creation rarely useful.

Calling client code such as JMS createQueue or .NET new MessageQueue does not allocate a new queue resource; it only provides access to a resource that already exists, created separately through the messaging system's administration tools.

Channels are cheap but not free: each consumes memory and persistent channels consume disk, and every messaging implementation has practical limits, so if you may need thousands of channels you must choose and test a highly scalable messaging implementation.
condition: when an application may require very large numbers of channels

statement: Mixing different data types on the same channel causes confusion, so use separate Datatype Channels each carrying a single message type.
Applications that use messaging benefit from a dedicated Invalid Message Channel to which messages that cannot be processed are diverted.
A well-designed set of channels forms a Message Bus that acts like a shared messaging API for a whole group of applications.
There are two kinds of message channels: Point-to-Point Channels and Publish-Subscribe Channels.
Many messaging systems support hierarchical channel naming similar to a file system of folders and subfolders, which helps organize large numbers of channels.

Two separate processes exchanging data must marshal it into a byte stream, copy it, and unmarshal it in the receiver, so the receiver obtains its own local copy rather than a shared reference to the sender's data.
Any data to be transmitted via messaging must be packaged into one or more Messages — data records the messaging system can transmit through a channel.

Choose the message style by intent: use a Command Message to invoke a procedure in another application, a Document Message to pass data, an Event Message to notify of a change, and Request-Reply when a reply is expected.

If the data exceeds what one message can hold, split it into a Message Sequence; if the data is only useful for a limited time, set a Message Expiration; and since all senders and receivers must agree on format, specify it via a Canonical Data Model.
To the messaging system all messages are alike — a body described by a header — so the distinction between command, document, and event message types is purely an application-level concern.

Connecting components with asynchronous Message Channels lets each stage run in its own thread or process and begin the next message immediately, enabling concurrent pipeline processing that significantly increases throughput over strictly sequential processing.

A processing pipeline's throughput is limited by its slowest stage, so deploy multiple parallel instances of the slowest filter using a Point-to-Point Channel with Competing Consumers, where each message is consumed by exactly one of the N processors.
Running parallel instances of a filter can cause messages to be processed out of order, so if the message sequence is critical you must run only one instance of that component or use a Resequencer.
condition: when message ordering must be preserved

statement: Parallelizing filters works best when each filter is stateless and returns to its prior state after processing a message; a stateful component such as a de-duplication filter that retains message history cannot easily be run in multiple parallel instances.
