exception: a stateful filter cannot be safely parallelized

statement: Integration implementations of Pipes and Filters use active filters that independently pull, process, and push to queuing pipes, unlike the classic assumption that every data element undergoes the same fixed sequence of steps.

A simple non-transactional filter loses the message if an error occurs before the message is sent to the output channel, which is undesirable in production, so use a Transactional Client to prevent message loss.
condition: in production where message loss is unacceptable

statement: Solving routing by creating a separate Datatype Channel per message type forces message originators to know the processing-selection criteria, can cause an explosion in the number of channels, and cannot express routing decisions that do not depend on message origin.

Letting the receiving component decide whether to process a message it has already consumed is problematic, because a consumed message cannot simply be returned to the channel and embedding selection logic ties the component to a message type, reducing reuse and composability.

In most integration solutions the components are large packaged or legacy applications that cannot be modified, making it uneconomical or impossible to adjust the producing or consuming applications to the needs of the messaging system.

Insert a Message Router that consumes a message from one channel and republishes it to a different channel based on a set of conditions, without modifying the message content — it concerns itself only with the message's destination.

The key benefit of a Message Router is that the destination decision criteria are maintained in a single location, so adding message types or components or changing routing rules requires changing only the router, and routing all messages through one router preserves their order.

A Message Router can re-couple a system because it must know every possible destination; when the destination list changes frequently the router becomes a maintenance bottleneck, so prefer reactive filtering — a Publish-Subscribe Channel with Message Filters letting recipients self-select — over predictive routing.
condition: when the set of possible destinations changes frequently

statement: A Message Router adds a processing step and message decode/re-encode overhead that can become a performance bottleneck; running routers in parallel or adding hardware can preserve throughput, but the latency for a single message to traverse the system will almost certainly increase.

Heavy use of routers and loose coupling makes the overall message flow hard to understand, complicating testing, debugging, and maintenance, which can be mitigated with Message History at runtime or static analysis of each component's published and subscribed channels, often aided by a central EAI repository.

Message Router variants include the fixed router (single input and output, used to decouple subsystems or relay between solutions, often combined with a Message Translator or Channel Adapter), the Content-Based Router (decides on message content, type, or field values), and the Context-Based Router (decides on environment conditions for load balancing, testing, or failover).

A Message Channel already provides basic round-robin load balancing through competing consumers without any router, whereas a Message Router can add smarter, intelligence-driven routing beyond simple round-robin.

Message Routers are stateless when they decide using only the current message, or stateful when they consider the content of previous messages, such as a router that eliminates duplicates by retaining a list of messages already seen.

Connecting a Message Router to a Control Bus lets the routing criteria change at runtime without code changes or interrupting the message flow — for example switching the system from test to production mode — and a Dynamic Router configures itself from control messages issued by potential recipients.

A Message Broker — central to virtually all commercial EAI tools — accepts, validates, transforms, and routes messages so applications need not be aware of one another, enabling non-intrusive integration of packaged and legacy applications by placing all routing logic in the middleware; it is the integration equivalent of the Mediator pattern.
The Message Translator is the messaging equivalent of the Adapter pattern: it converts a message from one component's format or interface into another so it can be used in a different context.

Message translation occurs at four layers loosely borrowed from the OSI model: Transport (communication protocols), Data Representation or syntax (data formats, character sets, encryption/compression), Data Types (field names, types, value domains, constraints), and Data Structures or application layer (entities, associations, cardinality).
The Transport layer provides complete and reliable data transfer across network segments, and translation between different transport protocols is provided by the Channel Adapter pattern.

The Data Representation layer converts complex data structures to and from the character or byte streams the transport carries, which may require decrypting, decompressing, and parsing the input, then rendering, compressing, and encrypting the output.

The Data Types layer handles application-domain type decisions such as date representation, time zones, and postal-code semantics — often captured in Data Dictionaries — and these issues go well beyond whether a field is a string or an integer, including reconciling mismatched value domains like differing region-code schemes.

The Data Structures (application) layer defines the logical entities an application deals with, such as Customer, Address, and Account, and their relationships and cardinality, which is the domain of entity-relationship and class diagrams.

Decoupling is an essential tool for managing change: Message Channels decouple applications from each other's location and a Message Router decouples them from agreeing on a destination, but they remain coupled through data formats until a Message Translator removes that dependency.

Because many scenarios require transformation at more than one layer, a layered transformation model lets each layer be treated independently of the lower layers so designers can work at different levels of abstraction.

Chain one Message Translator per transformation layer using Pipes and Filters so each translator is reusable across scenarios and individual layers are interchangeable — for example swapping the data-representation step from fixed-format output to comma-separated output without changing the structural transformation.

Message Translator specializations include the Content Enricher (adds information), the Content Filter (removes information), the Claim Check (removes information but stores it for later retrieval), the Normalizer (converts many formats into one consistent format), the Canonical Data Model (uses multiple translators for format decoupling), and the Messaging Bridge (translates the transport layer by connecting messaging systems).

XSLT is a W3C-standard, rules-based language that transforms one XML document into another format by matching elements of the source document, reflecting that structural transformation is a common enough need to warrant a standard language.
When collapsing source data into a target that has room for only one value, such as a single address or phone number, you must select which source value to use based on business rules.
condition: when the target structure cannot hold all source values

statement: Visual drag-and-drop transformation editors dramatically shorten the learning curve for building a Message Translator, but they become a liability for debugging or complex solutions, so good tools let you switch between the visual view and the underlying XSL.

The application and the messaging system are separate software — the messaging system being a specialized server like a database manager or web server — so they require explicit connecting code to work together.
Once a call is packaged as a message on a channel many receivers could perform it, so to guarantee exactly one receiver receives and performs a given message, send it on a Point-to-Point Channel.
condition: when exactly one receiver must process each message

statement: A Point-to-Point Channel ensures only one receiver consumes any given message even when the channel has multiple receivers, so the receivers need not coordinate, while still allowing multiple receivers to consume different messages concurrently.

Multiple consumers on a Point-to-Point Channel become Competing Consumers, making message consumption highly scalable because the work can be load-balanced across consumers running on multiple applications and computers.
To implement RPC over messaging, use Request-Reply with a pair of Point-to-Point Channels, where the call is a Command Message and the reply is a Document Message.
To broadcast an event to all interested receivers, send it on a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which delivers a separate copy of the event to each subscriber.
condition: when every interested receiver must get the event

statement: A Publish-Subscribe Channel splits one input into one output channel per subscriber and delivers a copy of each published message to each output, so every subscriber consumes its own copy exactly once and consumed copies disappear.

A Publish-Subscribe Channel is a useful debugging tool because you can eavesdrop on a channel without disturbing the existing message flow — for example a program that logs all channel traffic to a file, giving benefits similar to a Message Store.

The ability to eavesdrop on a Publish-Subscribe Channel is also a security risk, so subscribing to a channel should be restricted by security policies; peek functions let consumers view messages without consuming them, and many but not all commercial implementations enforce such restrictions.

Many messaging systems let subscribers use wildcard characters to subscribe to multiple hierarchical channels at once, but only subscribers may use wildcards while publishers must always publish to a specific channel, and the syntax varies by vendor.

An Event Message is usually sent on a Publish-Subscribe Channel because multiple dependents are often interested in the event, and if notifications must be acknowledged, use Request-Reply with the notification as the request and the acknowledgement as the reply.
Concurrent subscribers on a Publish-Subscribe Channel share the event by each receiving a copy rather than competing for it, in contrast to Competing Consumers on a Point-to-Point Channel.
A receiver moves a message it cannot process to an Invalid Message Channel, while the messaging system moves a message it cannot deliver to a Dead Letter Channel.
The messaging system may fail to deliver a message because of a misconfigured or deleted channel, message expiration or timeout, a Selective Consumer that everyone ignores, or a malformed header.

A dead message is one the messaging system cannot deliver — determined automatically from the message header — whereas an invalid message is properly delivered but cannot be processed by the receiver based on its body or specific header fields.

A developer is limited to whatever dead-message handling the messaging system provides but can design custom handling for invalid messages, including for seemingly dead messages the system does not handle.

Each machine typically has its own local Dead Letter Channel so a dying message moves between local queues without networking uncertainty, while recording which machine it died on and the channel it was meant for.

Use Guaranteed Delivery to persist messages to a built-in local data store so they survive a messaging-system crash: the send does not complete until the message is safely stored, and a message is not deleted from one store until it is stored in the next.

Persistence increases reliability at the expense of performance, so if it is acceptable to lose messages when the messaging system crashes, avoid Guaranteed Delivery so messages move through the system faster.
condition: when message loss on a crash is acceptable

statement: Guaranteed Delivery can consume large amounts of disk space in high-traffic scenarios such as a multi-hour outage with thousands of messages per second, so some systems provide a retry-timeout parameter to bound buffering, and event messages can often be safely discarded after a short time via Message Expiration.
condition: in high-throughput scenarios where buffered messages could exhaust disk

statement: Turn off Guaranteed Delivery during testing and debugging so channels can be purged by restarting the server, because leftover queued messages are a common debugging pitfall in asynchronous guaranteed messaging.
condition: during testing and debugging

statement: Reliability is measured in the number of 9s, with cost rising exponentially toward higher reliability, so Guaranteed Delivery is designed to be resilient against expected outages like machine or network failure but is usually not 100% bulletproof — disk failure or a disk filled during a long outage can still lose messages.

Apply Guaranteed Delivery selectively: use it for critical messages such as trade requests, confirmations, and address changes, but not for high-frequency loss-tolerant data such as price updates where the overhead is prohibitive, and consider providing separate guaranteed and non-guaranteed channels for the same data.

Persistence configuration is platform-specific: JMS sets persistence per message, MSMQ requires a transactional channel and Transactional Client senders, and JMS Publish-Subscribe Guaranteed Delivery only reaches active subscribers unless a Durable Subscriber is used.

Use a Channel Adapter to connect an application to the messaging system: it accesses the application's API or data to publish messages onto a channel and receives messages to invoke functionality inside the application, acting as a messaging client.
A Channel Adapter can connect at different layers of an application's architecture: the user interface, the business-logic API, or the database.

A User Interface (screen-scraping) Channel Adapter needs no access to application internals and suits platforms the messaging system does not support, but it is brittle and slow because user interfaces change frequently and screen rendering and re-parsing add unnecessary overhead.

If an application exposes a well-defined API, a Business Logic Channel Adapter using that API is usually the best approach because such interfaces are more stable and more efficient than the user interface.
condition: when the application exposes a well-defined, stable API

statement: A Database Channel Adapter extracts or inserts data directly and can use triggers to emit messages on change, making it efficient, non-intrusive for reads, and fairly universal, but reaching into internals is dangerous for writes and brittle because vendors often treat the schema as unpublished and subject to change.

Channel Adapters require message formats that closely mirror the adapted component's internal structure, such as database table and field names, which is a poor format for inter-application integration, so most adapters must be combined with a Message Translator to produce Canonical Data Model messages.

A Channel Adapter can run on a separate computer and connect via protocols like HTTP or ODBC to avoid installing software on the application or database server, but those protocols do not provide messaging's quality of service such as guaranteed delivery, and some adapters are unidirectional.

A Metadata (Design-Time) Adapter extracts metadata describing an application's internal data formats — via database system tables or component reflection — to configure Message Translators or detect changes in the application's data formats.

A Messaging Bridge is a special Channel Adapter that connects one messaging system to another rather than to an application, and a Channel Adapter is typically implemented as a Transactional Client so each unit of work succeeds in both the messaging system and the adapted system.

A Messaging Bridge connects two messaging systems so they act as one, letting a merged company integrate two existing messaging systems without redesigning half of its applications onto a single system.
condition: when two separately-built messaging systems must interoperate

statement: A Message Bus combines a common data model, a common command set, and a messaging infrastructure so that different systems communicate through a shared set of interfaces, analogous to a hardware communications bus.

A Message Bus comprises three parts: a common communication infrastructure (the messaging system acting as a cross-platform universal adapter, possibly with routers and publish-subscribe channels), adapters (Channel Adapters and Service Activators over a shared Canonical Data Model), and a common command structure understood by all participants.

Rewriting working but non-integrated systems onto a common technology is usually prohibitively expensive, so a Message Bus that lets them coordinate in a loosely coupled way is preferable to replacement.

Building each unified front-end application to integrate directly with all back-end systems duplicates the integration complexity across every new front-end and still does not help the back-ends integrate with each other, which favors a shared Message Bus.

A Message Bus forms a simple service-oriented architecture in which each service has a request channel of agreed format and usually a corresponding reply channel, and the request channels act as a directory of available services.
A Message Bus requires every application using it to share the same Canonical Data Model.

A single intermediary application that offers all services tends to become a bottleneck and single point of failure, whereas a Message Bus is preferable because it can be distributed across multiple computers for load distribution and fault tolerance.

Once a Message Bus is in place, adding or removing back-end applications and developing new front-end applications is simple, because the other applications keep sending messages on the bus's channels and need not change.

A message's intent determines its type: a Command Message tells the receiver what code to run, a Document Message transmits a data structure without specifying what to do with it, and an Event Message notifies the receiver of a change without dictating how to react.

In a Request-Reply exchange the request is usually a Command Message and the reply a Document Message containing a result or exception; the requestor specifies a Return Address for the reply channel and the reply carries a Correlation Identifier so it can be matched to the originating request.

There are two common Request-Reply scenarios: Messaging RPC, where the requestor wants the invoked function's return value, and Messaging Query, where the requestor runs a query remotely and receives the results in the reply.
When a data structure is too large for a single message, break it into manageable chunks and send them as a Message Sequence so the receiver can reconstruct the original structure.
condition: when data does not fit in a single message

statement: For time-sensitive messages, use Message Expiration: the messaging system discards a message it cannot deliver by its expiration, and a receiver discards a message it receives after the expiration.
condition: when message contents become useless after a deadline

statement: Use a Command Message — a regular message that encapsulates a request as in the Command pattern — to reliably invoke a procedure in another application, and send it on a Point-to-Point Channel so the command is consumed and invoked exactly once.

Invoking a procedure asynchronously via a message lets the call keep retrying until the remote procedure is successfully invoked, unlike synchronous RPC which fails outright if the network is down or the remote process is not currently listening.

Use a Document Message to reliably transfer a data structure: it passes data and lets the receiver decide what to do, avoiding the over-specificity of a Command Message, is more reliable than RPC, and can use a Point-to-Point Channel for single delivery or a Publish-Subscribe Channel to give every interested receiver a copy.

Use an Event Message for reliable asynchronous event notification so the subject can send when ready and each observer can receive if and when it is ready, avoiding RPC's requirement that the receiver accept immediately and that the announcer know every listener.

An Event Message differs from a Document Message in timing and content: an event's content is often minimal — many events are empty and their mere occurrence signals the observer to react — while the event's timing is critical.
Guaranteed Delivery is usually unhelpful for events because they are frequent and must be delivered quickly, whereas Message Expiration helps ensure an event is processed promptly or discarded.

Observer notification over messaging trades a push model against a pull model: the push model combines document and event in one message (efficient only if all observers want the details, otherwise a large frequently-ignored message), while the pull model sends a small Update event plus a State Request command and State Reply document so only interested observers fetch details at the cost of more channels and traffic.

Event messages are usually broadcast on a Publish-Subscribe Channel rather than a Point-to-Point Channel, and their subscribers can often be non-durable because a busy receiver can safely ignore events.
To make messaging two-way, send a pair of Request-Reply messages each on its own channel, because a single Message Channel transmits messages in only one direction.

In Request-Reply the request channel can be Point-to-Point or Publish-Subscribe depending on whether the request should be processed by one consumer or broadcast, but the reply channel is almost always Point-to-Point because replies should go only to the requestor.

A requestor can receive a reply two ways: a Synchronous Block where one thread sends and blocks as a Polling Consumer (simple but hard to recover after a crash and implying one outstanding request or a private reply channel), or an Asynchronous Callback where a separate thread listens and invokes a callback (supporting many outstanding requests over one reply channel and easy crash recovery, at the cost of callback-context complexity).

There are three Request-Reply types: Messaging RPC (a command request and a document reply carrying the return value or exception), Messaging Query (a command query and a result reply, perhaps a Message Sequence), and Notify/Acknowledge (an event notification and a document acknowledgement).
Like a method return, a reply is one of three kinds: Void (notifying completion so the caller can proceed), a Result value, or an Exception indicating the method aborted and why.

A JMS TemporaryQueue is private to its connection and convenient as a reply channel via the reply-to property, but its messages are lost when the connection closes and it cannot provide Guaranteed Delivery.

The request message should carry a Return Address indicating where to send the reply, so the replier asks the request rather than hard-coding reply channels, which encapsulates channel knowledge within the requestor and keeps the replier flexible.
A Return Address is placed in the message header because it is not part of the transmitted data, analogous to the reply-to field of an email.
A reply generally needs both a Return Address, which tells the replier which channel to use, and a Correlation Identifier, which tells the requestor which request the reply belongs to.

A requestor may direct replies to a separate callback processor monitoring a different channel, so the reply channel is not necessarily the requestor itself, which is a further reason to specify the destination explicitly with a Return Address.
A Correlation Identifier in a reply is set to the original request's message ID so the requestor can match each reply to the request that produced it.

There are practical limits on how much data a single message can hold — absolute implementation limits, performance penalties for large messages, or producer/consumer constraints such as COBOL and mainframe systems handling only 32 KB chunks — so very large data must be split.
When a large data set must be broken into message-size chunks, send it as a Message Sequence and mark each message with sequence-identification fields.
condition: when data exceeds the single-message size limit

statement: A Message Sequence uses three identification fields: a sequence identifier distinguishing the cluster, a position identifier ordering each message, and a size or end indicator giving the message count or marking the last message.

Position plus size-or-end fields let the receiver reassemble the parts even if they arrive out of order, and an end-indicator design should be used when the sender does not know the total count in advance, such as when streaming.

If a receiver expects a Message Sequence, every message sent to it should be sent as a sequence — even a sequence of one — otherwise the missing sequence fields may cause the receiver to treat the message as invalid.
If a receiver gets some but never all of the messages in a sequence, it should reroute the messages it did receive to the Invalid Message Channel.
condition: when a sequence is received incomplete

statement: Use a Transactional Client for sequences: send all messages in one transaction so none are delivered until all are sent, and receive them in one transaction so none are consumed until all arrive, rolling back if incomplete; many implementations then preserve send order, simplifying reassembly.

When a Message Sequence is the reply in a Request-Reply, the sequence identifier and the Correlation Identifier are usually the same, separating only if the requestor expects multiple multi-part responses to one request.

A Message Sequence is incompatible with Competing Consumers and the Message Dispatcher, because consumers each receiving different parts cannot reassemble the data, so a sequence must be transmitted over a channel with a single consumer.
An alternative to a Message Sequence is the Claim Check: if both applications share a database or file system, store the large document and transmit only a receipt in a single message.
condition: when both applications share a common datastore

statement: Sequence fields are easier to filter on when stored in the message header rather than the body, but since JMS allows application-defined header properties and .NET does not, application-defined sequence fields may have to be placed in the message body.

Asynchronous messaging decouples timing so a requestor can successfully send a request even when the replier is not yet running, because the messaging system holds the message until the replier is available.

In Request-Reply the request and reply are distinct, separate messages with different message IDs, and the reply carries the request's message ID as its Correlation Identifier so the requestor can match them.
A Durable Subscriber is an observer that must not miss notifications even if it is temporarily disconnected when the notification is sent.
Encapsulate messaging code behind a Messaging Gateway so that the application objects acting as subject and observer are not themselves messaging-specific.

A Datatype Channel guideline governs publish-subscribe channel design: whether two unrelated subjects can share one channel to update the same group of observers depends on keeping each channel to a single message type.
Designing a complex enterprise with many subjects notifying many observers requires deliberately planning an adequate set of channels rather than reusing channels arbitrarily.

Pair endpoint consumer styles to roles: a Requestor that awaits a single expected reply can use a Polling Consumer, while a Replier should use an Event-Driven Consumer because it cannot predict when a request will arrive.
A replier typically runs continuously because it cannot predict when a request will arrive, whereas a requestor that needs only one reply can send the request, receive the reply, and exit.

When configuring a message-reading endpoint, set it to read all of the message's properties and apply the correct formatter (for example an XML formatter for string contents) so the message and its metadata are interpreted correctly.
A Publish-Subscribe Channel implements the Observer pattern and makes it much easier to use among distributed applications.

Implementing Observer over publish-subscribe takes three steps: an administrator creates the channel (a JMS Topic), the application acting as Subject creates a publisher to send messages, and each Observer creates a subscriber to receive them, analogous to attaching an observer.
Once subject and observers are connected through a Publish-Subscribe Channel, the subject announces a change by sending a single message and the channel ensures every observer receives a copy.

A Subject can contain several independently changing pieces of state called aspects, and a single Observer may be interested in several aspects across multiple Subjects of different classes, which makes update semantics complex.

Two different message types should not share a channel: the Datatype Channel rule requires one message type per channel, and the audiences interested in each type usually differ, so separate channels avoid delivering unwanted notifications.
Creating a separate channel for every aspect of an entity that can change leads to a channel explosion.

Large numbers of channels tax the messaging system: low-traffic channels waste resources and complicate load distribution, many channels require many senders, receivers, and threads checking mostly-empty channels, and dependents become confused about which channels to subscribe to.

Send similar notifications that go to the same observers on one channel — for example unifying address-changed and credit-rating-changed under a common CustomerChange root element with optional nested elements — while keeping unrelated audiences such as product versus customer notifications on separate channels.

When messages share a channel but some observers want only a subset, use Selective Consumers; if selective consumers become too complicated and the messaging system supports many channels cheaply, separate channels may be the better choice.

The goal of channel design is to ensure observers receive only the notifications they need, without a channel explosion and without burdening a typical observer with many threads and consumers monitoring many channels.
For distributed notification the push model is simpler and often more efficient than the pull model, although the pull model can also be implemented over messaging.
Even if applications need messaging for nothing else, it can be worth adopting messaging solely to use Publish-Subscribe Channels for change notification.

Message Routing patterns fall into three groups: Simple Routers (variants of the Message Router routing from one inbound channel to one or more outbound channels), Composed Routers (combining simple routers for complex flows), and Architectural Patterns (router-based architectural styles).

A Content-Based Router inspects message content and routes each message to the proper destination, letting producers send to a single channel and avoiding coupling the producer to specific destination channels.

A Message Filter is a special Content-Based Router that passes a message to another channel only if it matches criteria and otherwise discards it; it lives in the messaging system, whereas a Selective Consumer is built into a Message Endpoint.

Routing can be done predictively with a Content-Based Router, which has total control but depends on knowing all possible destination channels, or reactively with an array of Message Filters on a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which spreads routing logic across filters and avoids a single component dependent on all destinations.
A Dynamic Router lets routing logic be modified at runtime by sending control messages to a designated control port, and its dynamic behavior can be combined with most forms of Message Router.
A Recipient List is a Content-Based Router that routes a single message to more than one destination channel while maintaining control over the set of recipients.

A Splitter splits a message containing a list of items into individual messages for separate routing and processing, and an Aggregator recombines related messages; the Aggregator is a stateful router that stores messages until its completeness conditions are met and may consume many messages before publishing one.

A Resequencer reorders out-of-sequence messages where components such as ledger-based systems depend on order; it is stateful but ultimately publishes the same number of messages it consumed, unlike the Aggregator.
EAI tools let routing logic be built with drag-and-drop so only the actual decision logic must be coded, and they provide transactionality, thread management, and systems management for free.
Solutions built with visual UI tools are hard to document because many important settings are hidden in property fields not visible on screen.

The most basic way for a component to receive only relevant messages is to subscribe only to the channels that carry relevant messages, which leverages publish-subscribe routing and lets new subscribers join without changing the system.

Channel subscription is a binary all-or-nothing condition, so achieving finer granularity requires more channels, and combining multiple parameters causes channel explosion — for example two item types times three price-change thresholds already needs six channels.

Making a Content-Based Router or Recipient List send each recipient only its relevant messages burdens the message originator with maintaining every subscriber's preferences, which becomes a maintenance nightmare if recipients or preferences change quickly.

Broadcasting all messages and filtering inside each component assumes you control the component (often false for packaged or legacy applications) and couples the component to a specific message type, reducing its reuse.

Use a Message Filter to eliminate undesired messages from a channel based on criteria: it has a single output channel and routes matching messages there while discarding the rest, equivalent to a Content-Based Router routing to either the output or a null channel.

A Message Filter is stateless when it decides per message, which allows running parallel instances to speed processing, but it can be stateful — for example eliminating duplicates by storing the identifiers of messages already seen.

Hierarchical channel naming with wildcard subscriptions lets subscribers refine channel semantics by appending qualifying parameters, but it is less flexible than a Message Filter, which can express conditions like a price change greater than 11.5% that channel names cannot.

A Selective Consumer (message selector) filters within the receiving application by evaluating header or property expressions before the application sees the message, and unlike a Message Filter — which removes messages from the input channel and republishes only matches — a Selective Consumer leaves non-matching messages on the channel unconsumed.

Registering a filter expression with the messaging infrastructure lets it propagate the filter closer to the message source, avoiding the wasteful network traffic of routing a message just to discard it while keeping routing control with the subscriber, behaving like a dynamic Recipient List.

A Content-Based Router delivers each message to exactly one consumer with central predictive control but must know all participants, while a Publish-Subscribe Channel with Message Filters allows multiple consumers with distributed reactive control and needs no knowledge of participants, making routers suit business transactions and filter arrays suit event notifications.

Decide between a Content-Based Router and a filter array by who should control and maintain the routing and whether multiple recipients must process the same message, and always use a Content-Based Router for sensitive data only certain recipients may see rather than trusting other recipients to filter it out.

Network conditions drive the router-versus-filter choice: filters with efficient broadcast such as internal-network IP multicast avoid a single-router bottleneck, but over the Internet where only point-to-point connections exist a router is more efficient, and a dynamic Recipient List can pass control to recipients while still using a router for network efficiency.

Reactive filtering and Routing Slip solutions are less efficient than a Message Router because they use trial-and-error across destinations, and distributed routing risks having multiple recipients or none, which can go undetected without a central routing element.

Use a Dynamic Router that self-configures from control messages sent by destinations on a dedicated control channel, achieving efficient predictive routing without the router depending on hard-coded knowledge of all destinations.

A Dynamic Router must store its routing rules persistently to survive a restart, can configure itself from start-up announcements or from a broadcast trigger (more robust but requiring a Publish-Subscribe Channel), and may support subscribe and unsubscribe control messages for runtime changes.

A Dynamic Router must resolve rule conflicts when multiple recipients claim the same message type, using strategies such as rejecting conflicting control messages, sending to the first match, or sending to all matches — the last of which turns it into a Recipient List and violates the one-output-per-input rule.

A common use of the Dynamic Router is dynamic service discovery in service-oriented architectures, where it maintains a service directory mapping service names to channels and routes by requested service name, allowing a service to be provided by more than one provider behind a single client-facing channel.

Publish-Subscribe Channel subscriptions are relatively static and binary, so they cannot change the set of recipients on a message-by-message basis, which means dynamic per-message recipient control needs a different mechanism.

Use a Recipient List to route to dynamically specified recipients: define a channel per recipient, inspect each incoming message, compute the list of desired recipients, and forward a copy of the message to each recipient's channel.

A Recipient List has two logical parts — compute the recipient list, then traverse it sending a copy to each recipient — and like a Content-Based Router it usually does not modify the message content.

A Recipient List's list can be supplied externally by attaching it to the message (useful when destinations come from user selection) or computed internally from message content and rules; when supplied externally, the Recipient List should remove it before forwarding to reduce message size and hide the other recipients.
To preserve a Recipient List's control over message flow, ensure recipients cannot subscribe directly to its input channel and bypass the control it exercises.

A robust Recipient List must be atomic and restartable, only consuming the input message after all outbound messages are successfully sent, achievable via a single transaction across channels, a persistent record of which recipients were already sent to, or idempotent receivers that tolerate resending all messages on restart.

An idempotent function does not change system state when the same message is processed twice; messages can be inherently idempotent or made idempotent with a duplicate-eliminating Message Filter, which lets a sender safely resend when delivery is uncertain, much like TCP/IP.

A Dynamic Recipient List lets recipients configure the rule set via a control channel, combining a Dynamic Router with a Recipient List so subscribers control their own filtering while the system still sends only to interested parties.

Whether broadcast-and-filter or individual Recipient-List delivery is more efficient depends on the infrastructure: IP-multicast publish-subscribe can reach many local recipients in a single transmission, but the further apart recipients are — especially across the Internet which requires point-to-point connections — the more efficient a Recipient List becomes.

Broadcast efficiency also depends on the proportion of interested recipients: if most recipients want the message it can be more efficient to broadcast and let the few non-participants filter it out, but if only a small fraction are interested a Recipient List is almost guaranteed to be more efficient.

When sending a message to multiple recipients you may reconcile the responses in an Aggregator — waiting for all to compare and choose the best, or taking the first available to optimize throughput — and Scatter-Gather names the pattern of sending one message to many recipients and recombining their responses into one.

A dynamic Recipient List can emulate a Publish-Subscribe Channel on a system that provides only Point-to-Point Channels by tracking the point-to-point channels subscribed to a topic, and it can enforce access control to the data source as long as recipients cannot access its input channel directly.
condition: when the messaging system lacks native publish-subscribe channels

statement: Requiring the message originator to publish individually to each recipient burdens the originator with delivery and embeds routing logic in the application, which is unrealistic for packaged or legacy applications that are often unaware they participate in an integration solution.

Broadcasting a message and having each recipient check an attached recipient list is inefficient because every recipient must process every message, and it relies on an honor system, which is undesirable when a request must reach only a select subset such as a request for quote sent to chosen suppliers.

When a Splitter breaks a composite message into item messages, enrich each item with the shared context such as order date, order number, and customer ID so each message is self-contained and the consumer need not store context across messages, which is essential when the items are processed by stateless servers.
Include a correlating field such as the order number in each split item message so the items can later be re-aggregated by an Aggregator.
Use a Splitter to iterate over the repeating elements of a message containing a list and emit one individual message per element for separate downstream routing and processing.

An Aggregator correlates related messages through a Correlation Identifier such as an auction ID, holds active aggregates keyed by that identifier, and applies an aggregation strategy with a completeness condition such as waiting for a minimum number of messages before publishing a combined result.

Keep an Aggregator's aggregation strategy independent of the messaging API by converting incoming message data into strongly-typed domain objects and wrapping the domain class with an Adapter, so the domain logic carries no references to the messaging API.

A channel abstraction such as the JMS Destination lets messaging code be written independently of whether the channel is a queue or a publish-subscribe topic, which is useful for testing and debugging by listening in via topics and switching to queues in production.

A Resequencer buffers out-of-order messages keyed by their sequence index and forwards them in order only once the next consecutive message is available, while tracking a sliding buffer range of expected indices.

Use a Composed Message Processor to handle a composite message by splitting it, routing the sub-messages to the appropriate destinations, and re-aggregating the responses into a single message; to the rest of the system it appears as a single filter with one input and one output channel.

A Composed Message Processor uses an Aggregator to reconcile the dispatched responses, and because all sub-messages originate from one message it can pass the sub-message count to the Aggregator to define a more efficient completeness strategy.

Splitting an order into independent sub-orders processed per fulfillment system is sometimes the only option when you lack control over the downstream process, but it can degrade the customer experience with multiple shipments and invoices and harder returns, especially when order items depend on each other.

Dispatching one sub-item at a time and waiting for each response simplifies temporal dependencies but is inefficient, so prefer dispatching sub-messages in parallel to exploit the fact that each system can process them simultaneously.

A Composed Message Processor must handle missing or delayed responses such as an unavailable subsystem, choosing among delaying all affected work, routing to a human exception queue, or resending the request.
Composing individual patterns into a larger pattern provides an abstraction that hides the complex internal workings and lets implementation details change without affecting other components.

Use a Scatter-Gather to broadcast a message to multiple recipients and re-aggregate their replies into a single response, combining the routing logic, recipients, and post-processing into one logical component so other components stay independent of the routing.

A Scatter-Gather has two distribution variants: via a Recipient List, which controls the recipients but must know each recipient's channel, or auction-style via a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which uses a single channel but relinquishes control over who participates.

A Scatter-Gather must be prepared to receive responses from some but not all recipients because it may not know how many participate, and adding a Return Address lets all responses be processed through a single channel.

Synchronizing parallel activities holds up subsequent processing until the slowest subtask completes, so a cascading Aggregator is a useful compromise that lets subsequent tasks begin with only a subset of the results available.

A single solution can use multiple Aggregators for different purposes — for example one that selects the best bid without necessarily waiting for all responses and using a complex selection algorithm, and another that concatenates all item responses but must ensure every response arrives and handle missing items.

When components are legacy or packaged and cannot host routing logic, implement a Routing Slip with an external router that communicates with each component via messaging, which increases the number of channels and components but still gives the best trade-off of efficiency, flexibility, and maintainability.
condition: when components cannot be modified to carry routing logic

statement: A Routing Slip is most useful for a sequence of binary validation steps where each step can abort or pass the message on, for stateless transformation steps configured per message source, and for steps that only gather data while postponing the decision to the end.
If the flexibility to reconfigure step order is not actually needed, a simple hard-wired Pipes and Filters chain may suffice instead of a Routing Slip.

A Routing Slip used as a Chain of Responsibility lets each component accept or pass the message, avoids duplicate processing, and makes it easy to detect a message no component processed, while the central component must know all participants but not which messages each consumes.

Compared to a Content-Based Router that publishes a single message regardless of the number of systems, a Routing Slip publishes on average about half the number of systems, trading more network traffic and slower processing for distributed decision-making.

When routing needs branching conditions, forks, joins, or decisions based on intermediate results, use a Process Manager rather than a Routing Slip, and avoid overburdening a Routing Slip with conditional logic — switch to a Process Manager once that complexity is required.

A dynamic Routing Slip combines a central point of maintenance with hard-wired efficiency, but as complexity grows it becomes harder to analyze and debug because routing state is distributed across the messages and the process-definition configuration becomes hard to understand.

A Routing Slip can implement a composed service in an SOA: a lookup component fetches the required fine-grained steps from a service directory, adds the channel list and a return channel to the message header, and the steps execute in sequence while appearing externally as a single request-reply exchange.

Use a Process Manager to route a message through multiple processing steps when the required steps may be unknown at design time or may not be sequential, such as when steps run in parallel or depend on intermediate results.

A Process Manager returns control to a central component after each step that determines the next step(s), and to keep processing units decoupled from the central unit, the central unit should maintain its own memory of the last-executed step rather than forcing units to carry extraneous routing data.

A Process Manager produces a hub-and-spoke message flow initialized by a trigger message, with all traffic running through the central hub, which risks turning the Process Manager into a performance bottleneck.

A Process Manager's versatility is both its strength and weakness: it can execute any sequential or parallel sequence so almost any integration problem can be solved with it, but using it for every situation is overkill that distracts from the core design and adds significant performance overhead.

A Process Manager must maintain the current position in the process between messages rather than tying that knowledge to a processing unit, because the same unit may appear at multiple steps and the same reply must trigger different next steps depending on process context.

A Process Manager can also store intermediate results relevant to later steps, acting as a Claim Check, which keeps individual processing steps independent because they need not carry data produced or consumed by other units.
Connecting each application to every other with individual point-to-point channels causes a channel explosion known as integration spaghetti, which undermines the benefits of channel-based routing.

Requiring each application to communicate explicitly with every other hampers maintainability, because adding a new system that needs shared data such as a customer address forces changes to every system that produces it.

Use a central Message Broker that receives messages from multiple sources, determines the correct destination, and routes each message accordingly, implementing its internals using the routing design patterns — the hub-and-spoke architectural style.

The Message Broker is an architecture pattern comparable to Pipes and Filters rather than a single design pattern, is not monolithic, and internally is built from many of the message routing patterns.

A central Message Broker can become a serious bottleneck, but if its design is stateless you can deploy multiple broker instances to improve throughput, with a Point-to-Point Channel ensuring only one instance consumes each incoming message.
condition: when the broker is composed only of stateless components

statement: In complex solutions, use multiple specialized Message Brokers to avoid an unmaintainable über-broker, accepting the loss of a single maintenance point, and organize them as a Message Broker hierarchy where local brokers route within a subsystem and a central broker decouples whole subsystems.

A Message Broker usually must translate data formats between applications and often uses a Canonical Data Model internally to avoid the N-square problem, where the number of translators needed grows with the square of the number of participants.

Commercial EAI tools simplify building Message Brokers by providing built-in endpoint code, visual design tools for routers, decision points, and transformers, and runtime support for deployment and traffic monitoring.

Integrated applications rarely agree on a common data format — differing in their notion of an entity like Customer and in relational versus flat or XML storage — and since the applications often cannot be modified, the integration solution must accommodate and resolve these differences.

Wrap message payload in an Envelope Wrapper that complies with the messaging infrastructure's header and format requirements, and combine multiple wrappers when a message must cross different messaging infrastructures.

Message-format dependencies make channel decoupling partly illusory: if a sender must format messages in the receiver's format, switching receivers still forces a change to the sender, a dependency that Message Translators remove.

An integration solution can be viewed as two parallel systems, one handling the actual message data and one handling the metadata that describes the message data, and many message-flow patterns apply equally to managing the metadata.

A Channel Adapter can extract metadata from applications into a central metadata repository, which integration developers then use to define transformations between application formats and the Canonical Data Model, commonly expressed as XSD for XML messages.
Transformation principles apply beyond messaging, since File Transfer and Remote Procedure Invocation must also transform between systems' differing data formats.

An Envelope Wrapper is needed because messaging-infrastructure header fields such as security credentials and encryption are required by routing components but unknown to or considered invalid by endpoint applications, so raw messages must be wrapped to comply, analogous to network tunneling.
Encrypting message content prevents eavesdropping by unauthorized listeners, which is a particularly important concern with publish-subscribe mechanisms.

Use a Content Enricher to access an external data source and augment a message with information the originator cannot supply; it is a special case of Message Translator that injects new data rather than merely rearranging existing fields.

The alternatives to a Content Enricher — storing extra data in the source system, having the source fetch it before sending, routing through the data-owning system, or having the receiver fetch it — each introduce tight coupling or require modifying packaged applications, so a dedicated Content Enricher decouples the participants better.

In a loosely coupled system, do not have one system instruct the next what to do; send an Event Message and let others decide, because building the downstream requirements into the source system shifts the message's semantics from an event toward a command and tightly couples the systems.

A Content Enricher's added data comes from one of three sources: computation from the message itself with no external source, the operating environment such as a timestamp, or another system such as a database, file, LDAP directory, or manual user entry, the last being the most common.

Because a Content Enricher must wait synchronously for its data source, a synchronous protocol like HTTP or ODBC may perform better than asynchronous messaging, and since the enricher and its data source are inherently tightly coupled, channel-based loose coupling matters less for that interaction.

Use a Content Enricher to resolve references by passing small messages that carry keys or IDs and restoring full data via lookup; references help most when a message passes through many intermediaries before the final recipient, where you enrich just before delivery, but whether they improve performance depends on how many components can operate on references versus how many must enrich.

When communicating with external parties using verbose standards like ebXML or RosettaNet, keep internal messages simple and use a Content Enricher to add required fields on the way out and a Content Filter to strip unneeded fields on the way in.
Use a Content Filter to remove unimportant data items from a message, leaving only the important ones.

Two main reasons to use a Content Filter are security — removing data a requestor is not authorized to see when the provider always returns everything — and simplification, since large standardized documents with hundreds of nested fields are hard to work with and break visual transformation tools and debugging.

A Content Filter can also flatten an over-nested tree structure, such as one modeled after normalized database tables, into a simpler list of elements that other systems can understand and process more easily.
Multiple Content Filters can act as a Filtering Splitter to break one complex message into individual messages each dealing with a certain aspect of the original.

Database adapters often emit messages that mirror the database schema, including multiple linked tables and primary and foreign keys irrelevant to the receiver, so use a Content Filter to flatten the structure and extract only the relevant fields.

An alternative to a Content Filter for flattening database-adapter output is a database view that resolves the table relationships, but adding views may violate the goal of keeping enterprise integration as non-intrusive as possible.

Translating directly between each pair of integrated applications causes the number of Message Translators to grow with the square of the number of applications, becoming unmanageable, and each translator still depends on both applications' formats.

Design a Canonical Data Model independent of any specific application and require every application to produce and consume messages in this common format, so that adding a new application needs only translation to and from the canonical model regardless of how many applications already participate.

A Canonical Data Model pays off as the number of applications grows: six mutually communicating applications need thirty translators with direct translation but only twelve with a Canonical Data Model.
A Canonical Data Model makes replacing an application later much cheaper, because switching from one system to another is far easier if the indirection was built into the original solution.

There are three ways to make applications conform to a common format: change the application's internal format (usually impractical, and if it were easy a Shared Database would be better than messaging), implement a Messaging Mapper inside the application (custom applications only), or use an external Message Translator.

Choose between a Messaging Mapper and an external Message Translator based on transformation complexity and application maintainability: packaged applications rule out a Mapper because their source is unavailable, and visual tools speed simple mappings but become unwieldy for complex transformations.

A Canonical Data Model introduces double translation — source to canonical to target — versus direct translation, adding latency, so for very high throughput systems direct translation may be the only choice; prefer the more maintainable canonical model unless performance requirements forbid it, mitigated by parallelizing stateless translators.

A Canonical Data Model only needs to model the portion of data that participates in messaging, not the complete data model of every application, which significantly reduces the complexity of creating it.

A Canonical Data Model has political and communication benefits because it lets developers and business users discuss the integration in business-domain terms rather than a specific package's implementation, and defining it is often the first step to resolving semantic dissonance between applications.

Dependencies between applications exist at multiple levels, each removed by a different mechanism: Message Channels remove transport-protocol dependency, Message Routers remove location dependency, a common representation such as XML removes data-type dependency, and a Canonical Data Model removes data-format and semantic dependency.
Because the canonical format is likely to change over time, a Canonical Data Model should specify a Format Indicator.

An external service's WSDL effectively specifies a Canonical Data Model that both parties must use, with double translation provided by a Messaging Mapper or Gateway in the consumer and a Remote Facade in the provider.

A loan broker acts as an intermediary that gathers customer data once, obtains the credit score, selects the most suitable banks, collects their quotes, and returns the best offer, illustrating how routing and transformation patterns compose into a larger solution.

SOAP was designed for synchronous RPC-style calls, and because most Web services use HTTP — which is ubiquitous and passes firewalls but is inherently unreliable and synchronous, reusing one connection for request and response — HTTP-based Web services invariably use synchronous request/response messaging.

A synchronous Web service keeps the client connection open until the response arrives, which lets the client quickly learn the operation's status, but it forces the server to manage many concurrent open connections, increasing server complexity and requiring per-invocation failure trapping and recovery.

SOAP encoding style is either 'encoded' (the obsolete Section-5 type mapping) or 'literal', where type information comes from an external XML Schema such as a WSDL; literal encoding has superseded SOAP encoding since the adoption of XML Schema.

WSDL binding style is either RPC, which strictly requires the wrapper element to match the operation name with parts matching parameters in name and order and a single named response, or Document, which only requires well-formed XML; Document plus Literal is commonly used to convey RPC semantics as a Command Message.
Choosing SOAP over HTTP with synchronous communication and RPC binding makes a Web service behave essentially like a Remote Procedure Invocation.
A Web services framework such as Apache Axis can act as the message channel, handling all message processing on behalf of the application so that the application code contains only business logic.
A Service Activator connects a Message Channel to a synchronous service in an application so that when a message is received the corresponding service is invoked.

A Web service's deployment scope determines instance lifecycle: request scope creates a new instance per request (the default), session scope keeps an instance across a single client's requests, and application scope makes the service a singleton for the application's lifetime.

Generating proxies and skeletons from a WSDL document encapsulates all SOAP-related code so the developer writes only business logic in the generated method bodies, keeping messaging concerns out of the application code.

Implement a Content Enricher by encapsulating access to an external data source such as a credit agency behind a gateway class, so the calling logic depends only on a domain interface and not on the external system's API.

A WSDL document's binding and body elements reveal the chosen binding style (RPC versus Document) and encoding (SOAP encoding versus doc/literal), so inspecting the generated WSDL confirms the actual on-the-wire contract.

Encapsulating each external provider, such as an individual bank, behind its own service interface lets a broker treat heterogeneous providers uniformly when sending requests and collecting responses.
Factor common messaging-endpoint behaviour such as receiving requests and sending replies into a reusable base service class, so each concrete service only overrides the message-processing logic.
An asynchronous request-reply service receives a request message and sends back a correlated reply on a separate channel, decoupling the sender and receiver in time.
A gateway class encapsulates the protocol and message construction needed to call an external service such as a credit bureau, isolating application code from the messaging and transport details.

In an asynchronous process triggered by an incoming message, the logic is not contained in a single method but spread across event handlers driven by a sequence of external events such as a new request, a credit reply, and a bank quote.

Because asynchronous process logic is spread across event handlers, maintain state across them with an Asynchronous Completion Token — an object reference passed with the request that the gateway returns with the reply — so each handler can recover the original call's context.

An Asynchronous Completion Token should hold what later handlers need, such as the original request message (for its message ID and reply address) and the request data structure, and storing strongly-typed duplicate data is worth the few extra bytes for the convenience.

Separate business logic from messaging functions by encapsulating messaging in a base class and moving the business logic into a class with no messaging dependency, so it can be unit-tested with a tool like nUnit; note that inheritance still carries dependencies from a subclass to its base, so a fully separate class is cleaner.

To test code that uses the messaging layer without the dependency and performance cost of real queues, provide a mock implementation of the message sender and receiver interfaces that triggers the message handler directly.
A mock messaging layer must reply with a message of the correct type, such as a canned reply, because you cannot simply pass the request message back as the reply.

A production messaging system must handle errors by routing error messages to a central console so operators are notified in a unified way, typically using systems-management patterns such as the Control Bus, which simple examples often omit.

Without transactional queues, a crash mid-flow leaves partial work — some recipients get the request while others do not, or a reply never reaches the client — so such actions must be encapsulated in transactions where an incoming message is not consumed until the corresponding outbound message has been sent.

A single-threaded endpoint that does not begin receiving the next message until the previous one finishes is acceptable for examples, but a high-throughput environment should use a Message Dispatcher that manages multiple performer threads.
condition: in high-throughput environments

statement: Even a simple asynchronous messaging application is far more complex than a monolithic one — operations taken for granted like a method call require significant coding effort — but design patterns provide a shared language for the trade-offs without descending into vendor jargon.

Commercial EAI suites add substantial functionality over basic channel APIs, including visual drag-and-drop configuration of Message Translators and Process Managers plus sophisticated system and metadata management.

An auction-style Scatter-Gather uses a Publish-Subscribe Channel to broadcast a request to an unknown number of recipients — a dynamic Request-Reply with an unknown number of listeners — unlike a Recipient List that sends to a predefined set.
A broker can present a synchronous Request-Reply facade to its clients while performing asynchronous operations such as an auction Scatter-Gather behind that facade.

In an auction-style Scatter-Gather the Aggregator's completeness condition relies on a timeout rather than waiting for all responses: each received bid resets the timeout, responses arriving after timeout are ignored, and if none arrive a no-quotes response is returned.
Publishing bids on a public Publish-Subscribe Channel lets other participants listen to competitors' bids and place counter-bids, which is a confidentiality consequence to weigh.

When multiple asynchronous request-reply flows such as auctions run concurrently, use a Correlation Identifier together with a Selective Consumer so each process instance receives only the replies it cares about rather than all replies.

Ideally correlation filtering would occur at the channel level with a dynamic channel per pending flow, but process engines often require subjects to be registered up front, which precludes dynamic runtime channels and makes process-level filtering an acceptable fallback.

A process engine queues inbound messages on its registered subjects to prevent a timing bug where, in an asynchronous world, a reply arrives before the process transitions into the state that listens for it.
Assign a unique Correlation Identifier per process or auction, propagate it to each downstream request and back in every reply, and filter replies by matching the correlation identifier.

A Publish-Subscribe Channel makes monitoring easy because you can listen to all messages on the bus and log them to inspect the message flow, while private inbox reply channels remain invisible to such general monitoring.

A Messaging Gateway exposes a public API of methods and events that make no reference to messaging, so the calling application issues domain-level calls and need not worry about how messages are sent or correlated.

A gateway stores the caller's Asynchronous Completion Token in a dictionary indexed by the request's Correlation Identifier and retrieves the associated context when the reply arrives, so the calling application does not handle correlation itself.

Messages differ fundamentally from objects: most messaging infrastructures support only scalar data such as strings, numbers, and dates and not inheritance or object references, because they must interoperate with non-object-oriented applications — a key difference between RPC/RMI and asynchronous messaging.

Passing an object reference inside an asynchronous message is problematic because resolving it requires a request-reply that defeats loose coupling, and the referenced object may no longer exist by the time the message is received.

Including an object's entire dependency tree in a message ensures the receiver has all referenced data but can make messages explode in size when the domain model is fine-grained and highly interrelated.

Serializing an object into an opaque string data field is universally supported but prevents a Message Router from routing on properties, hampers testing and debugging, prevents type-based routing and format validation, and breaks cross-language serialization.

Separate the mapping code from the domain object, because mixing low-level messaging code with application logic blocks parallel work by messaging and domain teams and makes the domain object depend on the messaging infrastructure, impeding its reuse outside messaging.

Create a separate Messaging Mapper that holds the mapping logic between domain objects and the messaging infrastructure such that neither the domain objects nor the infrastructure are aware of the Messaging Mapper's existence.

A Messaging Mapper differs from a messaging abstraction layer or Gateway: with an abstraction layer the domain objects still know about the abstraction, whereas with a Messaging Mapper the domain objects have no awareness that messaging is involved at all.

Because neither side knows about the Messaging Mapper, invoke it through events — for example implementing a message-listener interface for inbound messages and using the Observer pattern for domain events — and if it must be invoked directly, depend on a Messaging Mapper interface rather than its implementation.

Reduce Messaging Mapper boilerplate with a reflection-based generic mapper that works when field names match, or with a configurable code generator that allows flexible field naming and reference handling but is harder to test and debug.

Do not let a framework auto-serialize domain objects one-to-one into messages, because message design criteria differ from domain-object criteria; instead define interface objects resembling Data Transfer Objects that match the desired message structure and have the Messaging Mapper translate between true domain objects and those interface objects.

Even with a Messaging Mapper, also use a Message Translator to convert the mapper's output into Canonical Data Model messages: let the mapper resolve object references and data-type conversions and let the translator handle structural mapping, accepting an extra component and a small performance penalty for the added decoupling.
Complex transformations are sometimes easier to implement in the application's programming language than in an integration vendor's drag-and-drop tooling.

To coordinate a message with a database, start a transaction, receive the message, update the database, then commit (or update the database, send a notifying message, then commit), so the message is not removed unless the database is updated and the database change does not stick if the message cannot be sent — behavior often implemented by a Channel Adapter.

To coordinate a message with a workflow, use Request-Reply inside transactions — acquire the work item, send the request, and commit, then receive the reply, complete or abort the work item, and commit — so the application never loses received messages nor forgets to send a required message and can roll back and retry on failure.
Coordinating a messaging system with a database or a workflow engine requires a distributed transaction because the messaging system and the other resource each have their own transaction manager.

Transactional clients do not work as expected with Event-Driven Consumers, because the consumer must commit the receive before passing the message to the application, so the application cannot roll back the consume — an event-driven consumer behaves the same whether or not its client is transactional.

Messaging systems can participate in distributed XA transactions where supported — JMS via XASession under the Java Transaction API, MSMQ via its transactional queue support — and the JMS spec recommends clients rely on the J2EE application server's distributed-transaction support rather than handling distributed transactions directly.

Transactional Clients work well with a single Polling Consumer and are useful in Request-Reply, Pipes-and-Filters filters, Message Sequence, and Channel Adapter, but do not work well with Event-Driven Consumers or Message Dispatchers and can cause problems for Competing Consumers.
Under a transactional session, a consumed message is only consumed within the consumer's transactional view until commit, remaining available to other consumers until the commit succeeds.

To make a filter transactional as a Send-Receive Message Pair, open a transaction before consuming the input message and commit after publishing the output, and on any exception abort to roll back both the consumption and publication, returning the input message to the queue for other consumers.
Competing Consumers consume messages from a single channel in parallel, each running in its own thread to load-balance message processing across consumers.
A JMS session must be single-threaded and serializes message consumption, so each competing consumer needs its own Session and MessageConsumer to consume messages in parallel.

The JMS specification does not define the semantics of concurrent QueueReceivers acting as Competing Consumers or require that the approach work at all, so applications using this technique are not guaranteed portable and may behave differently across JMS providers.
Competing consumers can share a single Connection but must each create their own Session because a JMS session supports only a single thread.

Do not use Selective Consumers to hide messages of a certain type from certain consumers, because messaging systems usually do not authorize a consumer's selection criteria, so a malicious but channel-authorized consumer can change its criteria to access unauthorized messages; use separate Datatype Channels to securely lock applications out.

A Message Dispatcher is an alternative to Selective Consumers that holds the selection criteria, routes each message to the matching performer, and reroutes unmatched messages to the Invalid Message Channel; if the messaging system lacks a Selective Consumer feature you must implement the behavior yourself with a Message Dispatcher.

To handle messages that match no consumer, implement a default consumer using a Message Dispatcher with a default case rather than a Selective Consumer, because a default selective consumer would have to match all selector values and thus compete with every other consumer.

A Selective Consumer delivers all messages and has each receiver ignore the unwanted ones, which suits cases where other receivers want those messages, whereas a Message Filter prevents unwanted messages from ever reaching the receiver's channel, which suits messages no receiver wants.

A Content-Based Router is a more static approach where each new routing option needs a new channel and consumer and in-flight messages may land on the wrong channel during a change, while a Selective Consumer is more dynamic because each new filtering option only needs a new consumer that is easy to create at runtime.
A message's selection value should be specified in its header rather than its body so a Selective Consumer can evaluate it without having to parse the message body.

A Selective Consumer makes a single channel act like multiple Datatype Channels, can be implemented as either a Polling Consumer or an Event-Driven Consumer, and can be part of a Transactional Client.
Two message types can safely share one channel by giving each a selector value, with senders setting the type selector and each Selective Consumer consuming only messages of its type.

In .NET, which lacks JMS-style message selectors, prefer ReceiveById over Peek-then-Receive because the message returned by Receive may not be the one that was Peeked, and use ReceiveByCorrelationId so a requester receives the reply specific to its request.

On a Publish-Subscribe Channel, which subscribers receive a message depends entirely on who is subscribed when it is published, so a subscriber that is not yet subscribed misses the message and should subscribe before messages of interest are published.
By default a publish-subscribe subscription lasts only as long as the connection, and a subscriber unsubscribes simply by closing its connection, with no explicit unsubscribe action required.

A third subscriber state, inactive — disconnected but still subscribed — is needed so the messaging system saves messages published during a connection lapse and delivers them on reconnect, distinguishing an inactive subscriber from an unsubscribed one.

Design a Service Activator that connects messages on a channel to the service being invoked, so a single service can support both synchronous and asynchronous invocation and multiple messaging technologies without being reimplemented for each style.

A Service Activator handles all messaging details — receiving as a Polling or Event-Driven Consumer and extracting which service and parameters to use — then invokes the service synchronously like any other client, so the service is written as if always synchronous and is unaware it is being invoked via messaging.
