Orchestration-driven service-oriented architecture was built around an enterprise-wide reuse philosophy (born of an era of scarce, expensive licensed resources), organizing services into a taxonomy of business, enterprise, application, and infrastructure services tied together by an orchestration engine.

The reuse goal of SOA failed because business components are not durable like construction materials: reuse breeds coupling, so a change to a shared canonical service (e.g., Customer) ripples across consumers, forcing coordinated deployments and holistic testing and burdening each consumer with details it does not need.

Pushing technical partitioning to the SOA extreme grinds domain concepts to dust, so a trivial change like adding an address line to a checkout flow can require changes across dozens of services and tiers.

Because SOA shares a database and routes everything through a single orchestration engine, it is a single architecture quantum despite being distributed, inheriting the disadvantages of both monolithic and distributed architectures and teaching that distributed transactions and extreme technical partitioning are impractical.

Reuse and coupling are linked by the First Law of Software Architecture: favoring reuse (via inheritance or composition) also favors coupling, so when the goal is high decoupling, prefer duplication over reuse.

Microservices is the physical embodiment of domain-driven design's bounded context: each service models a domain or workflow and includes everything it needs (its own classes and database schema), never coupling to another context's data or class definitions.

In microservices, performance is a common negative side effect of distribution because network calls and per-endpoint security add latency, and architects should avoid transactions across service boundaries, making service granularity the key to success.
A frequent microservices mistake is making services too small (because 'microservice' is a label, not a description), which forces excessive inter-service communication to do useful work.
exception: treating the 'micro' label as a commandment to make services as small as possible

statement: Find microservice boundaries using three guides: purpose (a service should be functionally cohesive, contributing one significant behavior), transactions (entities that must cooperate in a transaction suggest a boundary, and avoiding distributed transactions yields better designs), and choreography (bundle services back together if they require extensive communication).
Iteration is the only reliable way to get service design right; architects rarely discover the correct granularity, data dependencies, and communication styles on the first pass.

Microservices require data isolation: avoid shared schemas and databases used as integration points; each service owns its data, and the lost single source of truth is handled either by designating one domain as authoritative and coordinating with it or by using replication/caching.

Data isolation lets each service team choose the most appropriate database or tool for its needs and change it later without affecting other teams, since others cannot couple to its implementation details.

A microservices API layer is optional and useful for indirection, proxying, and hosting operational facilities like a naming service, but it must not be used as a mediator or orchestrator, because all interesting logic should live inside a bounded context.
exception: using the API layer for orchestration would violate the bounded-context philosophy

statement: Microservices split domain logic (which prefers duplication) from operational concerns that genuinely benefit from coupling; the sidecar pattern places common operational concerns (monitoring, logging, circuit breakers) in each service so a shared infrastructure team can upgrade them centrally.
Connecting each service's sidecar forms a service mesh that gives unified, holistic control of cross-cutting operational concerns across all microservices.
Service discovery builds elasticity into microservices by routing requests through a tool that monitors load and spins up new service instances, often hosted in the service mesh or API layer.

Microservices typically use protocol-aware heterogeneous interoperability: services know or discover which protocol to call each other with (no central hub), may run on different technology stacks (polyglot), and collaborate over the network.

The goal of microservices technology choice is to fit the correct-scale technology to a narrow problem (sometimes even enforcing heterogeneous stacks to prevent accidental coupling), not to standardize a single enterprise stack.

Choreography (no central coordinator, like a broker EDA) preserves maximum decoupling and is symbiotic with microservices, but makes error handling and coordination more complex; orchestration introduces a localized mediator that concentrates coupling into one service while leaving the others less affected.

Domain/architecture isomorphism — matching the shape of the architecture to the problem — should guide style selection; e.g., microkernel fits customizability, space-based fits many discrete operations, and a highly coupled problem fits a less decoupled style (service-based) better than microservices.

Architects should not build transactions across microservice boundaries — doing so violates the decoupling principle and creates connascence of value — and a need for cross-service transactions usually signals services that are too granular.
exception: rare cases where two services need very different characteristics yet still require transactional coordination

statement: When cross-service transactions are unavoidable, use the saga pattern (a mediator coordinating compensating transactions) sparingly; compensating/undo logic is far more complex than the forward operation, and if transactions dominate the architecture, the design went wrong.

Microservices depends on the DevOps automation revolution and rates highly on scalability, elasticity, and evolutionary change, but performance is often a weakness due to network calls and per-endpoint security, mitigated by caching/replication and by preferring choreography over orchestration.

Choosing an architecture style is fundamentally contextual ('it depends') — the culmination of trade-off analysis over architecture characteristics, domain considerations, and strategic goals — and architects must understand the rules well enough to break them intelligently.

Preferred architecture styles shift over time, driven by past pain points, ecosystem changes, new capabilities/paradigms, accelerating change, domain shifts, technology changes, and external factors, so architects must track current trends to know when to follow them and when to make exceptions.

Before choosing a style, an architect should be comfortable with the domain, the architecture characteristics that impact structure, the data architecture (in collaboration with DBAs), organizational factors, and the maturity of process/teams/operations — since styles that rely on Agile engineering practices struggle where that maturity is absent.

To decide monolith versus distributed, use quanta: a single set of architecture characteristics implies a monolith is suitable, while different parts needing different characteristics imply a distributed architecture.

Architects should default to synchronous communication and use asynchronous only when necessary, because synchronous is simpler to design, implement, and debug, while asynchronous adds headaches like data synchronization, deadlocks, race conditions, and harder debugging despite its performance and scale benefits.

The output of the style-selection design process is an architecture topology, plus architecture decision records for the hardest decisions, plus fitness functions to protect important principles and operational characteristics.

A modular monolith builds domain-centric components over a single database deployed as one quantum; separating tables by domain alongside the components eases a future migration to a distributed architecture.

The Backends-for-Frontends (BFF) pattern makes the API layer a set of thin adaptors that translate generic backend output into the format each frontend device expects, enabling richer device-specific UIs.

A good GGG-style design that resolves to multiple quanta is not the 'correct' or only or even best design — it simply has the least-worst set of trade-offs — and quantum analysis at component-design time helps identify service, data, and communication boundaries.

Making an architecture decision means gathering enough relevant information, justifying it (technically and for the business), documenting it, and effectively communicating it to the right stakeholders; a good decision guides teams toward the right technical choices.

The Covering Your Assets anti-pattern is avoiding or deferring a decision out of fear of being wrong; overcome it by deciding at the last responsible moment (enough information without blocking teams or risking analysis paralysis) and by continually collaborating with development teams to confirm the decision is implementable.

The Groundhog Day anti-pattern is a decision being re-debated because no one knows why it was made; overcome it by recording both a technical and a business justification, since the presence of business value is also a litmus test for whether the decision is worth making at all.

The four most common business justifications for an architecture decision are cost, time to market, user satisfaction, and strategic positioning, and the chosen justification must match what the business stakeholders actually care about.

The Email-Driven Architecture anti-pattern is decisions being lost or forgotten; overcome it by never putting the decision in an email body (which creates multiple systems of record), linking instead to a single record, and notifying only the people the decision directly impacts.

A technology choice is an architecture decision when it directly supports an architecture characteristic; per Nygard, architecturally significant decisions are those affecting structure, nonfunctional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques.

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) are short one-to-two-page documents with the sections Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences (often plus Compliance and Notes), kept consistent and concise.
An ADR's status (Proposed, Accepted, Superseded) keeps a historical record: a superseded ADR is cross-linked to the one that replaced it, preserving why each decision was made and changed.

Adding a Request-for-Comments status with a deadline to a draft ADR avoids the Analysis Paralysis anti-pattern, and the Status section forces an explicit conversation about which decisions an architect may approve alone versus escalate, using criteria like cost, cross-team impact, and security.

An architecture decision should be escalated rather than self-approved when its cost exceeds an agreed threshold (effort estimated as hours times the FTE rate), when it impacts other teams, or when it has any security implication, and these limits should be documented for all architects.
State an ADR's decision in an affirmative, commanding voice ('we will use…') rather than a passive opinion, so it is unambiguous that a decision has actually been made.

The Decision section should emphasize why over how, because knowing the rationale prevents harmful refactoring — e.g., replacing gRPC (chosen to reduce latency) with messaging can reintroduce latency and upstream timeouts.

The Consequences section should record an architecture decision's impacts (good and bad) and its trade-off analysis, forcing the architect to weigh whether the downsides outweigh the benefits and preserving the trade-off reasoning for future challengers.
A Compliance section should state how a decision will be governed — manually or via an automated fitness function — so important decisions are measurably enforced.

Each ADR should be its own file or wiki page; storing ADRs in the application Git repo suits app-scoped decisions but not larger organizations, where wiki or shared storage organized by application/common/integration/enterprise scope is better for access and for non-application-scoped decisions.

ADRs are an effective way to document software architecture, because the Context describes the situation and alternatives, the Decision captures the all-important why, and the Consequences capture the trade-offs.

Using ADRs for standards lets an architect justify why a standard must exist; if a standard cannot be justified in the Decision and Consequences sections, it probably should not be made, and developers who understand why a standard exists are more likely to follow it.
Every architecture decision, no matter how obvious, should be documented and justified.
Continually analyzing architecture risk lets architects find deficiencies and take corrective action to mitigate them.

The architecture risk matrix qualifies risk as the product of impact and likelihood (each rated low=1, medium=2, high=3), giving 1-2 low, 3-4 medium, and 6-9 high, and should be applied by considering impact first and likelihood second.

A risk assessment accumulates matrix-qualified risk by assessment criteria and by domain/service area, should be filtered (e.g., show only high-risk) for signal-to-noise, and should indicate the direction of risk using unambiguous notation derived from continuous fitness-function measurements.

Risk direction notation must be unambiguous: bare up/down arrows are interpreted oppositely by roughly half of people, so use a clear convention (e.g., plus/minus signs or an arrow pointing to the target risk number) rather than relying on a legend.
exception: ambiguous up/down or left/right arrows without a clear, persistent key cause misinterpretation

statement: No single architect can determine a system's overall risk (they miss areas and lack full knowledge), so risk storming is a collaborative exercise that should include senior developers and tech leads.

Risk storming has three activities — identification (done individually and non-collaboratively so participants do not bias each other), consensus, and mitigation (both collaborative) — conducted against an up-to-date architecture diagram, and should be restricted to a single risk dimension when possible.

In risk storming consensus, focus discussion on items where participants disagree or where only one person flagged risk, because a lone high rating often reflects firsthand knowledge (e.g., a component known to fail under load) the others lack.
For unproven or unknown technologies, always assign the highest risk rating (9), because the impact/likelihood matrix cannot be applied to something whose behavior is unknown.
condition: the technology in question is unproven or unknown to the team

statement: Bringing developers and tech leads into risk storming is valuable both because they add implementation perspective and because a developer not knowing a technology is itself a useful signal of risk.

Risk mitigation is the most important risk-storming activity; because mitigation usually incurs cost, stakeholders must decide whether the cost outweighs the risk, and architects should offer cheaper partial-mitigation alternatives when the full fix is rejected.

The risk matrix can also assess Agile story-completion risk, scoring the impact if a story is not finished in the iteration against the likelihood it will not finish, so teams can track and prioritize high-risk stories.

Availability risk from external systems you do not control can be mitigated by checking their published SLA or SLO — an SLA being a legally binding contractual guarantee and an SLO not — and recording those figures on the architecture diagram.
condition: depending on external systems outside your control

statement: Risk storming is a continuous process throughout a system's life, typically run on a chosen dimension after a major feature is added or at the end of each iteration, to catch risks before they reach production.

Communication is critical to an architect's success: no matter how brilliant the technical idea, it never manifests unless the architect can convince managers to fund it and developers to build it, making diagramming and presenting essential soft skills.
Apply representational consistency: always show how a detailed view relates to the overall architecture before drilling into it, to avoid confusing viewers about scope.

Use low-fidelity, ephemeral artifacts early in design to avoid the Irrational Artifact Attachment anti-pattern, in which attachment to a diagram grows in proportion to the time invested in it, discouraging needed revision.

Architects should master their diagramming tool's layers (hide/show detail and build incremental presentations), stencils/templates (consistent reusable components), and magnets (line-snapping for alignment).

Among diagramming standards, UML survives mainly as class and sequence diagrams, C4 (Context, Container, Component, Class) suits monolithic architectures better than distributed ones, and ArchiMate is a deliberately minimal enterprise modeling language.

A widely shared diagram convention is that solid lines indicate synchronous communication and dotted lines indicate asynchronous communication; otherwise architects must define and consistently apply their own shapes and line semantics.
Include a key whenever diagram shapes could be ambiguous, because a diagram that leads to misinterpretation is worse than no diagram at all.

The fundamental difference between a presentation and a document is time: in a presentation the speaker controls the pace an idea unfolds, so manipulating time with transitions and animations is a key architect skill.

Use subtle transitions and animations to hide slide boundaries and stitch slides into one story, and a distinctly different transition to signal moving to a new topic, rather than splashy effects or padding content to fill a slide.

Avoid the Bullet-Riddled Corpse: a presenter has two channels (verbal and visual), and putting full text on slides while reading it aloud overloads one channel and starves the other, so build information up incrementally instead.

Distinguish infodecks from presentations: an infodeck is standalone, contains all the information, and needs no time elements, whereas presentation slides are deliberately only half the message — the speaker is the other half — so do not cram all content into the slides.
The invisibility pattern — inserting a blank slide — refocuses the audience's attention on the speaker by turning off the visual channel.

An architect must guide the development team through implementation rather than designing in a silo and handing the architecture off, since making teams productive is what differentiates effective architects.

A core architect responsibility is to create and communicate the constraints — the box — within which developers implement the architecture; boundaries that are too tight frustrate teams (causing attrition), and boundaries too loose force the team to act as architect, causing confusion and lost productivity.

The control-freak architect makes overly fine-grained, low-level decisions that steal the art of programming from developers; this is an easy trap when moving from developer to architect because of the temptation to keep doing class design and choosing design patterns.

It is the architect's role to identify components, their core operations, and their interactions, but not to design a component's internal implementation (class diagrams and design patterns) — that is the developer's role.
exception: a project's complexity or low team skill may sometimes require the architect to exert control-freak-level detail

statement: The armchair architect has not coded recently, stays disconnected from teams, and produces uselessly high-level diagrams and loose boundaries; key indicators are too little time with the team, weak domain/technology understanding, and not considering implementation implications.
An effective architect provides the right constraints and tools, removes the team's roadblocks, collaborates closely, and earns the team's respect.

How much control an architect should exert (Elastic Leadership) depends on five factors: team familiarity, team size, overall experience, project complexity, and project duration — more control for newer, larger, more junior, more complex, and longer projects.

Project duration counterintuitively requires more control for longer projects and less for shorter ones, because a short project carries built-in urgency a control-freak would impede, while a long project lets teams relax and needs the architect to keep momentum.
exception: this duration relationship is the reverse of the naive intuition

statement: The control factors should be re-analyzed continually across the project lifecycle (and may be weighted), because the appropriate level of control changes as the team and system evolve.

Three warning signs indicate a development team has grown too large: process loss (Brooks's law — actual productivity falls below group potential, signaled by frequent merge conflicts), pluralistic ignorance, and diffusion of responsibility.
To counter process loss, structure work into parallel streams on separate services or areas, and question adding a team member when no parallel work stream exists for them.

Pluralistic ignorance is when team members publicly accept but privately reject a norm because they fear missing something obvious; an effective architect watches body language and facilitates, drawing out and supporting the dissenter.

Checklists make teams more effective for processes that lack procedural ordering or dependencies and that are error-prone or have frequently skipped steps, but they should not be used for dependent procedural sequences or simple, frequent, error-free tasks.
condition: the process is non-sequential and error-prone or has frequently missed steps

statement: Keep checklists as small as possible and remove anything that can be automated, because over-using checklists triggers the law of diminishing returns and developers stop following oversized ones.
Do not omit obvious steps from a checklist, because it is the obvious tasks that are most often skipped or missed.

The Hawthorne effect — people change behavior when they believe they are observed — can be used to enforce checklist compliance by spot-checking while letting the team believe every checklist is verified.

Three high-value checklists are the developer code-completion checklist (a definition of done), the unit/functional testing checklist (edge cases, growing with each QA-found defect), and the software release checklist (the most volatile, extended with the root cause of every failed deployment).

Architects guide teams by communicating design principles that define the box developers work in, and before adopting a new library they should make developers answer whether it overlaps existing functionality and what its technical and business justification is.
Requiring a business justification (not just a technical one) for technology desires is a powerful technique, as it forces awareness of business value and can defuse disruptive technology advocacy.

Decision authority over third-party libraries should be graduated by category: developers may decide special-purpose libraries alone, may recommend general-purpose libraries subject to architect approval, and must leave framework libraries to the architect.

Making development teams effective is part of the architect's role, not something to delegate entirely to a development or project manager, and it is what differentiates an effective architect from a merely technical one.

Negotiation is one of the most important architect skills, because almost every architecture decision is challenged by developers, other architects, or stakeholders, and the architect must resolve disagreements into solutions all parties accept.

In stakeholder negotiations, decode buzzword grammar ('zero downtime', 'needed it yesterday', 'lightning fast') to identify the stakeholder's real underlying concern (availability, time to market, performance).

Gather as much information as possible before a negotiation and translate vague vernacular into concrete terms — e.g., convert 'five nines' into actual minutes/seconds of yearly downtime — to ground the conversation.

Raise cost and time only as a last resort in a negotiation, because opening with 'that costs too much' or 'we don't have time' starts it on the wrong foot before more meaningful justifications are tried.
Use divide-and-conquer to qualify a demanding requirement to only the specific part of the system that truly needs it, reducing the scope and cost of both the requirement and the negotiation.

When negotiating with another architect, remember that demonstration defeats discussion: run a comparison in a production-like environment rather than arguing, because every environment differs and a generic answer cannot settle it.
Avoid letting a negotiation become argumentative or personal; calm leadership with clear, concise reasoning prevails, and when things get heated the best move is to pause and reengage later.
Architects should not dictate to developers from on high (the Ivory Tower anti-pattern) but earn respect; when asking developers to adopt a decision, provide a justification rather than a command.

State the justification first and avoid commanding language like 'you must', because people stop listening once they hear something they disagree with, and leading with the reason ensures it is heard while depersonalizing the request.

When a developer disagrees with a decision, let them try to arrive at the solution themselves: either they discover the constraint firsthand and buy in, or they find a genuinely better option — both outcomes are wins.
Roughly half of being an effective software architect is people, facilitation, and leadership skills.

Distinguish essential complexity ('we have a hard problem') from accidental complexity ('we made a problem hard'); architects who add accidental complexity to prove their worth or for job security become ineffective leaders.

Avoid accidental complexity by practicing the 4 C's of architecture — communication, collaboration, clarity, and conciseness — which together make an architect an effective communicator and trusted go-to leader.

An effective architect must be both pragmatic and visionary: visionary strategic planning kept practical by accounting for budget, time, team skill level, trade-offs, and technical limitations, which earns respect from both stakeholders and developers.

A pragmatic approach to a hard problem like elasticity is to first find and isolate the actual bottleneck (e.g., the database) and consider simpler mitigations like caching before adopting an elaborate theoretical solution.
Effective architects lead by example rather than by title, earning respect, because rank means little when it comes to leading people and most problems are ultimately people problems.
Dismissing a developer's suggestion (e.g., 'that's a dumb idea') shuts down the whole team's willingness to collaborate.

Phrase guidance as questions ('have you considered…', 'what about…') instead of commands ('you must', 'what you need to do is'), because questions put control back on the developer and create a collaborative conversation.
Basic people skills build respect: use and correctly pronounce people's names, offer a firm handshake with eye contact, and avoid hugs in professional settings due to discomfort and harassment risk.
Turning a request into a favor often succeeds where a command fails, because people resist being told what to do but generally want to help.

To become the team's go-to leader, take initiative regardless of title — step in to help with technical struggles, offer personal support while reading cues to avoid being pushy, and host brown-bag lunches to share knowledge and practice mentoring.

To make more time for the development team, control meetings: for meetings you are invited to, ask why you are needed and request the agenda, attend only the relevant portions, and attend in a team member's place to protect their focus.

For meetings you call, keep them to a minimum (an email often suffices), set and stick to an agenda, and respect developer flow by scheduling meetings at the start, just after lunch, or end of day rather than mid-day when developers are deep in flow.

Architects should sit with the development team, since an isolated office or cubicle signals unavailability; if that is impossible, walk around, be seen, and block time to converse, answer questions, and coach.

Architects must keep learning continuously because technology changes at a dizzying pace, and the 20-minute rule — spending at least 20 minutes a day learning, ideally first thing in the morning before checking email — maintains the technical breadth architects need.

Architects should avoid technology bubbles and echo chambers (especially vendor-created ones), because honest appraisals are rare inside them and a collapsing bubble is not noticed from within until too late.

A technology radar is a living document for assessing the risks and rewards of existing and emerging technologies, organized into four quadrants (tools, languages/frameworks, techniques, platforms) and four rings: hold (don't start anything new with it), assess (worth exploring), trial (pilot on a low-risk project), and adopt.

A personal radar can extend the hold ring to include bad habits an architect is trying to break, use the assess ring as a staging area for promising-but-unexamined technologies, and use the trial ring for active spike experiments that enable real trade-off analysis.

Architects should not be laissez-faire about their technology portfolio; treat it like a financial portfolio and diversify — track some widely in-demand skills while also taking gambits like open source or emerging areas, reinforcing breadth over depth.

In building a technology radar, the exercise of thinking and conversation matters more than the visualization output, because it forces busy architects to carve out time to deliberately consider their technology investments.

An architect's next opportunities and outside-experience advice are more likely to come from weak links (casual acquaintances) than strong links, so architects should use social media to follow respected technologists and surface new technologies to assess.

Architecture skill is built through deliberate practice (e.g., architecture katas), and there is no answer key because there are no right or wrong answers in architecture — only trade-offs — and the why behind a design matters more than the how.
The layered (n-tier) architecture organizes components into horizontal layers, each performing one specific role such as presentation, business, persistence, or database.
Most layered architectures use four standard layers (presentation, business, persistence, database), but smaller applications may use three and larger, more complex ones five or more.
condition: layer count varies with application size and complexity

statement: The business and persistence layers can be merged into a single business layer when persistence logic (e.g., SQL) is embedded directly in the business components.
condition: when persistence logic is embedded in business-layer components

statement: Each layer should form an abstraction (separation of concerns) so that it handles only its own logic and need not know how lower layers fulfill a request.
In a closed layer, a request must pass through every layer directly beneath it in sequence before reaching lower layers (presentation -> business -> persistence -> database).

Use closed layers to enforce layers of isolation so that a change confined to one layer does not affect components in other layers, provided the inter-layer contracts (e.g., the model) stay unchanged.
condition: inter-layer contracts/model remain stable

statement: Mark a layer open when requests should be permitted to bypass it and go directly to the layer below.

Place a shared-services layer below the business layer and mark it open, so the presentation layer is architecturally barred from the shared services while the business layer can still bypass it to reach persistence.
Document which layers are open or closed and why; failing to communicate this generally produces tightly coupled, brittle architectures that are hard to test, maintain, and deploy.
Watch for the architecture sinkhole anti-pattern, where requests flow through multiple layers as simple pass-through processing with little or no logic performed in each layer.

Apply the 80-20 rule to the sinkhole anti-pattern: about 20% pass-through requests is typical and acceptable, but if the majority of requests are simple pass-through, consider making some layers open.
condition: majority of requests are simple pass-through

statement: Opening layers to mitigate the sinkhole anti-pattern reduces layer isolation and makes change harder to control, so it is a deliberate trade-off.
The layered pattern tends toward monolithic applications, which poses potential issues for deployment, robustness/reliability, performance, and scalability.
The layered architecture is a solid general-purpose pattern and a good default starting point, particularly when the best-suited pattern is not yet known.
condition: when the best-fit pattern is still uncertain

statement: The layered architecture rates LOW on overall agility because of its typically monolithic nature and tight coupling of components.

The layered architecture rates LOW on ease of deployment because one small component change can require redeploying a large portion or all of the application, making it a poor fit for continuous delivery.
The layered architecture rates HIGH on testability because layers can be mocked or stubbed to isolate testing within a single layer.
The layered architecture rates LOW on performance because each business request must traverse multiple layers.
The layered architecture rates LOW on scalability because its broad granularity and monolithic tendency make scaling expensive.
The layered architecture rates HIGH on ease of development because it is well known, not overly complex, and maps naturally onto teams organized by layer skill set (Conway's law).

Event-driven architecture is a distributed, asynchronous pattern of highly decoupled, single-purpose event-processing components that asynchronously receive and process events, used to build highly scalable and adaptable applications.

Event-driven architecture has two main topologies: the mediator topology for orchestrating multiple steps of an event through a central mediator, and the broker topology for chaining events together without a central mediator; choose based on whether central orchestration is needed.
Use the mediator topology of event-driven architecture for events that have multiple steps and require orchestration to determine step order and which steps run serially versus in parallel.
condition: the event requires multi-step orchestration

statement: The mediator topology has four component types: event queues, an event mediator, event channels, and event processors; the flow runs client -> event queue -> event mediator -> event channels -> event processors.
The mediator topology distinguishes two event types: the initial event received by the mediator, and the processing events the mediator generates and dispatches to event processors.
The event mediator orchestrates the steps of the initial event but does not itself perform the business logic; it only knows the steps required to process the event.

Event channels can be message queues or message topics, but message topics are most widely used with the mediator topology so a processing event can be handled by multiple event processors each performing a different task.

Each event processor should be self-contained and perform a single business task without relying on other event processors to complete its task, even though processor granularity can range from fine-grained to coarse-grained.

Match the event-mediator implementation to the orchestration complexity: open-source integration hubs (Spring Integration, Apache Camel, Mule ESB) for simpler flows, BPEL with an engine (e.g., Apache ODE) for more sophisticated orchestration, and a business process manager (e.g., jBPM) for very large applications needing complex orchestration including human interaction.

Mismatching the mediator implementation to the need is a recipe for failure: using an open-source integration hub for very complex business-process orchestration, or a BPM for simple routing, both fail.

It is common to have anywhere from a dozen to several hundred event queues in an event-driven architecture, and the pattern does not specify their implementation (message queue, web service endpoint, or a combination).

Use the broker topology when the event-processing flow is relatively simple and you do not need central event orchestration; the message flow is distributed across event processors in a chain through a lightweight message broker (e.g., ActiveMQ, HornetQ).
condition: event flow is simple and central orchestration is unnecessary

statement: The broker topology has two component types: a broker (centralized or federated, holding all event channels) and event processors; channels can be message queues, topics, or both.

In the broker topology each event processor processes an event and publishes a new event describing the action it performed, and the event chain continues until no more events are published for the initiating event.
In the broker topology, once an event processor hands off (publishes) its event it is no longer involved in processing that event, analogous to a relay-race handoff.
An event published in the broker topology may not be consumed by any processor, which is common when evolving an application or providing for future functionality and extensions.

Event-driven architecture is relatively complex to implement, primarily because of its asynchronous distributed nature, requiring you to address remote process availability, lack of responsiveness, and broker/mediator reconnection logic on failure.

Event-driven architecture lacks atomic transactions across a single business process because the decoupled distributed processors make a transactional unit of work very hard to maintain; if a single undivided transaction must be split across event processors, this is probably not the right pattern.
condition: a single unit of work would have to span multiple event processors

statement: When using event-driven architecture, plan event-processor granularity around which events can and cannot run independently, settle on a standard data format (e.g., XML, JSON, Java Object), and establish a contract versioning policy from the start, because contract creation, maintenance, and governance are the hardest aspects of the pattern.
Event-driven architecture rates HIGH on overall agility because single-purpose, fully decoupled event processors let changes be isolated to one or a few processors and made quickly.

Event-driven architecture rates HIGH on ease of deployment, and the broker topology tends to be easier to deploy than the mediator topology because the mediator is somewhat tightly coupled to the processors, so a processor change may also require a mediator change.
Event-driven architecture rates LOW on testability because generating events requires a specialized testing client or tool and the asynchronous nature complicates testing.
Event-driven architecture rates HIGH on performance because its decoupled parallel asynchronous operations generally outweigh the cost of queuing and dequeuing messages.
Event-driven architecture rates HIGH on scalability because each event processor can be scaled separately, allowing fine-grained scalability.

Event-driven architecture rates LOW on ease of development because of its asynchronous nature, contract creation, and the advanced error handling needed for unresponsive processors and failed brokers.

The microkernel (plug-in) architecture is a natural fit for product-based applications that are packaged and released in versions, and for internal business applications released like products, adding features as plug-ins to a core for extensibility and feature isolation.

The microkernel architecture consists of two component types: a core system containing the minimal functionality to make the system operational (for business apps, the general business logic without custom special-case code), and stand-alone plug-in modules that extend it with specialized processing and custom code.
Keep plug-in modules independent of one another and keep inter-plug-in communication to a minimum to avoid dependency issues, even though a plug-in may be designed to require another plug-in.
Let the core system discover plug-ins through a plug-in registry that records each plug-in's name, data contract, and remote access protocol details.

Plug-ins can connect to the core via OSGi, messaging, web services, or point-to-point binding; the choice depends on application type and needs, and the pattern requires only that plug-in modules remain independent of one another.

For third-party plug-ins with contracts you do not control, create an adapter between the plug-in contract and your standard contract so the core system needs no specialized code per plug-in, and define a contract versioning strategy from the start.
condition: plug-ins are supplied by third parties with contracts you do not control

statement: The microkernel pattern can be embedded within another architecture pattern (e.g., a layered architecture) to handle a specific volatile area of an application.
The microkernel pattern supports evolutionary design and incremental development: build a solid core first, then add features over time without significant changes to the core system.

For product-based applications, make the microkernel architecture your first choice as the starting architecture, especially when releasing additional features over time and controlling which users get which features; refactor later if it stops meeting requirements.
condition: the application is product-based

statement: The microkernel architecture rates HIGH on agility, ease of deployment (plug-ins can be hot-deployed at runtime), and testability (plug-ins tested in isolation and easily mocked), because changes are isolated to loosely coupled plug-ins and the core tends to stabilize quickly.

The microkernel architecture can perform well because you can streamline the application to only the features you need (as JBoss does by trimming unused features), but it rates LOW on scalability because implementations are typically smaller product-based single units, and LOW on ease of development because of the contract governance, versioning, registry, granularity, and connectivity complexity it requires.

The microservices architecture is a distributed architecture of separately deployed units (service components) accessed through a remote access protocol (e.g., JMS, AMQP, REST, SOAP, RMI); deploying each component separately yields easier deployment, increased scalability, and a high degree of decoupling.

In microservices, design around service components (which can range in granularity from a single module to a large portion of the application) rather than around services, and recognize that choosing the right service-component granularity is one of the biggest challenges of the pattern.

The microservices architecture evolved from real problems with prior patterns: from monolithic layered applications (driven by continuous delivery) and from overly complex, expensive SOA, and it simplifies the notion of a service, eliminates orchestration needs, and simplifies connectivity.
The microservices architecture has three common topologies: API REST-based, application REST-based, and centralized messaging.

Use the API REST-based topology for websites that expose small, self-contained services: very fine-grained service components (one or two modules) accessed through a REST interface implemented by a separately deployed web-based API layer.
condition: exposing small, self-contained single-purpose services

statement: Use the application REST-based topology when client requests come through traditional web or fat-client business screens: a separately deployed UI web application remotely accesses coarser-grained service components via REST; it suits small-to-medium business applications of relatively low complexity.
condition: UI is delivered through business application screens of low-to-medium complexity

statement: In the centralized messaging topology, use a lightweight centralized message broker (e.g., ActiveMQ, HornetQ) only as transport: it must not perform orchestration, transformation, or complex routing, and it should not be confused with SOA or treated as 'SOA-Lite'.

The centralized messaging topology suits larger business applications needing sophisticated transport control, offering advanced queuing, asynchronous messaging, monitoring, error handling, and better load balancing; address the broker's single-point-of-failure and bottleneck risk through broker clustering and federation.
condition: larger applications needing sophisticated transport control

statement: Choosing the correct service-component granularity is a main challenge of microservices: too coarse-grained loses the deployment, scalability, testability, and loose-coupling benefits, while too fine-grained creates orchestration needs that turn lean microservices into heavyweight SOA.

Treat the need to orchestrate service components from the UI or API layer, or the need for inter-service communication to process a single request, as a signal that the service components are too fine-grained or not partitioned correctly by business functionality.
Satisfy a service component's data needs from another component through a shared database rather than by invoking the other service component, to avoid undesired coupling between components.

For shared functionality, it is acceptable to copy the shared logic across service components (violating DRY) to keep them independent and separately deployable, trading redundancy for independence; small utility classes commonly fall into this category.

If you cannot avoid service-component orchestration regardless of granularity, microservices is probably not the right pattern, because its distributed nature makes a single transactional unit of work across components very hard and would require a complex transaction-compensation (rollback) framework.
condition: orchestration across service components is unavoidable

statement: Microservices generally yields more robust applications, better scalability, and easier continuous delivery than monoliths and SOA because major components are split into smaller, separately deployed units.

Microservices enables real-time production deployments (deploying only the changed service components), reducing big-bang monthly or weekend deployments; for a single instance, detect the hot-deployment in the UI and redirect users to a wait/error page, or swap multiple instances in and out for continuous availability.

Because microservices is a distributed architecture, it inherits event-driven architecture's hard problems: contract creation, maintenance, and governance, remote system availability, and remote access authentication and authorization.

The microservices architecture rates HIGH on overall agility, ease of deployment, testability, scalability, and ease of development, because separately deployed, loosely coupled service components isolate change and scaling to individual components.
The microservices architecture rates LOW on performance because its distributed nature does not naturally lend itself to high-performance applications.

In the standard web request flow (browser -> web server -> app server -> database), increasing user load moves bottlenecks down the stack; scaling web servers is easy and cheap but shifts the bottleneck to the application server and then the database, which is hardest and most expensive to scale and is usually the final limiting factor for concurrent transactions.

Use the space-based architecture to solve extreme scalability and concurrency problems and to handle variable, unpredictable concurrent user volumes; solving scalability architecturally is often better than scaling out a database or retrofitting caching into a non-scalable architecture.
condition: application has extreme or variable/unpredictable concurrent load

statement: The space-based architecture achieves high scalability by removing the central-database constraint and keeping application data in replicated in-memory data grids across all active processing units, while dynamically starting and stopping processing units as load changes.

The space-based architecture has two primary components: a processing unit (containing application modules, an in-memory data grid, an optional asynchronous persistent store for failover, and a replication engine) and virtualized middleware.
Split a space-based application into multiple processing units by functional area for larger applications, while smaller web applications can deploy into a single processing unit.
condition: application is large enough to warrant functional partitioning

statement: In space-based architecture, the messaging grid manages input requests and session information and forwards each request to an available processing unit, using anything from a round-robin to a next-available algorithm.

The data grid is the most crucial space-based component: it works with each processing unit's replication engine so that every processing unit holds exactly the same in-memory data, replicating updates in parallel asynchronously and very fast (sometimes within microseconds).

The processing grid is an optional space-based component that mediates and orchestrates requests requiring coordination between different processing-unit types (e.g., an order unit and a customer unit).

The deployment manager is critical to variable scalability in space-based architecture: it continually monitors response times and user load and dynamically starts processing units as load increases and shuts them down as load decreases.

The space-based architecture is complex and expensive to implement and is a good fit for smaller web applications with variable load (e.g., social media, bidding/auction sites) but is not well suited to traditional large-scale relational-database applications with large amounts of operational data.

Although space-based architecture does not require a centralized datastore, one is commonly included to perform the initial in-memory data-grid load and to asynchronously persist updates; partition the data to isolate volatile, widely used transactional data from non-active data to reduce each processing unit's in-memory footprint.
The space-based ('cloud') architecture's processing units and virtualized middleware do not have to run on cloud or PaaS hosting and can run on local servers.

Because space-based product implementations (e.g., GemFire, JavaSpaces, GigaSpaces, IBM ObjectGrid, nCache, Oracle Coherence) vary greatly in cost and capability (especially data-replication times), establish your specific goals and needs before selecting a product.

The space-based architecture rates HIGH on overall agility, ease of deployment, performance, and scalability, because processing units start and stop quickly, in-memory data access and caching deliver performance, and the lack of central-database dependency removes the scaling bottleneck.

The space-based architecture rates LOW on testability (achieving very high user loads in a test environment is expensive and time-consuming) and LOW on ease of development (sophisticated in-memory grid and caching products are unfamiliar and demand care that source code not impede performance and scalability).

Use the pattern-analysis summary to match an architectural priority to candidate patterns; for example, when scalability is the primary concern, the event-driven, microservices, and space-based patterns are good choices, whereas the layered pattern carries deployment, performance, and scalability risk.

Choosing an architecture pattern requires analyzing more than the characteristic ratings, including infrastructure support, developer skill set, project budget, deadlines, and application size, and the choice is critical because an architecture is very hard and expensive to change once in place.

Enterprise applications center on displaying, manipulating, and storing large amounts of often complex data and on supporting or automating business processes; they differ from embedded systems, control systems, telecoms, and desktop productivity software.
Architecture patterns drawn from enterprise applications do not necessarily transfer to other domains such as embedded, control, telecom, or desktop software.
condition: when the target system is not an enterprise application

statement: Patterns and their code examples are starting points to be adapted to the specific application, not canned solutions to be copied verbatim.
Architecture has two recurring elements: the highest-level breakdown of a system into its parts, and the decisions that are perceived as hard to change.
What is architecturally significant is subjective and can change over a system's lifetime; once something proves easy to change it ceases to be architectural.
Most nontrivial enterprise applications use a layered architecture of some form, and layering is the most widely useful structuring approach for them.
exception: in some situations other approaches such as pipes and filters are more valuable

statement: Practice iterative development: deliver software as soon as you have something useful to the user, even if it is not complete.
The primary benefit of objects is making complex business logic tractable; a well-developed Domain Model is the payoff for a complex business problem.

Enterprise application data is persistent and long-lived: it must survive many program runs, often outlasting the hardware, operating systems, and compilers that created it, and must be migrated through structural changes and replacement applications.

Enterprise applications typically hold large data volumes (a moderate system exceeds 1 GB over tens of millions of records), so data management is a major part of the system and modern systems use relational databases.
Many users access enterprise data concurrently, creating concurrency-control problems that transaction-manager tools only partly handle and that often cannot be hidden from application developers.

Enterprise applications rarely stand alone; they must integrate with heterogeneous systems built at different times with different technologies, and face semantic/conceptual dissonance where the same data field means different things in different divisions.
Business logic is arbitrary and full of one-off special cases; because the only certainty is that it will change over time, organize it so it can absorb change.

Not all enterprise applications are large; small systems carry disproportionate cumulative value, and one of the best things you can do is turn a large project into a small one by simplifying its architecture and process.
No single architecture is right for all enterprise applications; choose an architecture by understanding the particular problems of your system, and distrust anyone who says 'always do this.'
Beware adding flexibility speculatively: complexity added for flexibility's sake, if the guess is wrong, can make the system harder to evolve and delay deployment and its benefits.
condition: when flexibility is added before it is needed and the prediction turns out wrong

statement: Delaying an enterprise application's business benefits costs money, so unnecessary up-front complexity that slows delivery has a real cost.
Pick as small a set of tools as you can, but recognize different tools suit different purposes; using a tool suited to a different kind of application can hinder more than help.
For most performance issues, get the system running, instrument it, and optimize through a disciplined process based on measurement rather than speculation.
Some architectural decisions affect performance in ways that are difficult to fix with later optimization, so a subset of performance-relevant decisions must be considered early.
Treat any performance advice as unproven until measured on your own configuration; designs are often wrongly accepted or rejected on performance assumptions that measurement later refutes.
Whenever you perform a performance optimization, measure both before and after; otherwise you may merely make the code harder to read with no gain.

A significant configuration change (virtual machine, hardware, or database upgrade) can invalidate prior performance facts and even turn a past optimization into a regression, so re-measure and re-verify optimizations after such changes.
Minimize remote calls: latency is usually the dominant cost in remote systems and the application developer can do little to improve it.

Response time, responsiveness, and latency are distinct: response time is the time to process a request, responsiveness is how quickly the system acknowledges a request, and latency is the minimum time to get any response even for no work.

Throughput is work done per unit time (transactions per second for enterprise apps, against a chosen common transaction set); efficiency is performance divided by resources; capacity is maximum effective throughput or load.

Scalability measures how adding resources affects performance and is distinct from capacity and efficiency: vertical scalability (scaling up) adds power to a single server, horizontal scalability (scaling out) adds more servers.

For enterprise systems it often makes sense to build for hardware (horizontal) scalability rather than raw capacity or efficiency, because adding servers is frequently cheaper than adding programmers or optimizing software for weaker hardware.
condition: provided the system is genuinely scalable

statement: Patterns are discovered (not invented) common, effective solutions to recurring problems; their chief value for experienced designers is creating a shared design vocabulary, which is why pattern naming matters.
For every pattern, ask 'When would I NOT use this?'; few patterns are always the right choice, and that question surfaces the alternatives.
A code example illustrates a pattern but is not the pattern: examples are deliberately simplified (omitting error handling and production scaffolding) and must be reworked for your environment.

Layering yields key benefits: you can understand one layer without the others, substitute alternative implementations of a layer, minimize inter-layer dependencies, standardize at layer boundaries, and reuse a built layer across many higher-level services.
Layering has costs: it can cause cascading changes (a new field must be threaded through every layer) and extra layers can hurt performance through per-layer representation transforms.
exception: encapsulating an underlying function often yields efficiency gains that more than compensate

statement: The hardest part of a layered architecture is deciding what layers to have and what each layer's responsibility should be.
A layer is a logical division that need not run on a separate machine, whereas a tier implies physical separation; the two terms are not synonyms.

Enterprise applications decompose into three principal layers: presentation (handles user interaction), domain/business logic (the real point of the system), and data source (communication with databases, messaging, transaction managers, and other packages).

Presentation is an external interface for a service your system offers to others, while data source is your interface to services others provide you; this asymmetry is worth preserving because the kind of client changes how you design the service.

Always separate presentation, domain, and data source in some form, choosing the separation mechanism (subroutines, then classes, then packages) appropriate to the application's complexity, but do at least subroutine-level separation.
Enforce the dependency rule: domain and data source code must never call into presentation; this lets you substitute presentations and change the UI without deep ramifications.

To detect leaked domain logic, imagine adding a radically different layer (a command line to a web app, or an XML file instead of a relational database); any functionality you would have to duplicate marks domain logic that has leaked into presentation or data source.
Keep presentation decisions out of the domain: put the domain decision (e.g., whether a product's sales are improving) in the domain layer and let presentation only choose how to display the result.

Running all layers on the server is usually the simplest choice and best for ease of upgrade and maintenance, because deployment is confined and there is no desktop synchronization or compatibility burden.
The argument for running logic on the client rests on responsiveness or disconnected operation, since server-side logic requires a network roundtrip and an available connection.
The data source layer almost always runs only on servers; presentation placement follows the UI choice (rich client runs presentation on the client, a web interface runs it on the server).
exception: except when server functionality is duplicated onto a powerful client for disconnected operation

statement: Prefer a Web presentation if you can and a rich client only if you must, since web front ends are increasingly usable and avoid client deployment problems.

If domain logic must run on the client, prefer running all of it in one place; splitting domain logic across client and server is worst-of-both-worlds because you no longer know where any piece of logic lives.
exception: unless only a small, self-contained piece of domain logic must run on the client, isolated in a module runnable on either side

statement: Keep all code in a single process (on one node or replicated across a cluster) and do not separate layers into discrete processes unless you absolutely must, because distribution degrades performance and adds complexity such as Remote Facade and Data Transfer Object.

Treat distribution, explicit multithreading, the object/relational paradigm chasm, multiplatform development, and extreme performance (e.g., over 100 transactions per second) as complexity boosters that each carry high development and maintenance cost; adopt them only when genuinely required.

Transaction Script organizes domain logic as one procedure per user action; it is a simple procedural model most developers understand, works with Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway, and has obvious transaction boundaries.
Transaction Script degrades as domain-logic complexity grows: it tends to duplicate code that is hard to spot and remove, producing a tangled web of routines without clear structure.
condition: as the complexity of the domain logic increases

statement: Domain Model organizes logic around domain objects (the nouns of the domain), letting you absorb increasingly complex logic in a well-structured, extensible way (e.g., add a new strategy object rather than another conditional branch).

Domain Model carries costs: a real learning/paradigm-shift curve (often months) and a more complex relational mapping (typically Data Mapper); a sophisticated data source layer behaves like a fixed cost that pays off once built.

Table Module is a middle ground: one instance per table operating on a Record Set, giving more structure than Transaction Script while lacking Domain Model's fine-grained OO techniques (inheritance, strategies); its biggest advantage is fitting GUI/platform environments built around SQL Record Sets such as COM and .NET.

The choice among Transaction Script, Table Module, and Domain Model depends mainly on domain-logic complexity: with simple logic the Domain Model's cost is not repaid, but as complexity rises the simpler approaches hit a wall where adding features becomes exponentially harder.
There is no way to measure domain-logic complexity numerically, so the decision relies on experienced people making a judgment call from an initial analysis of the requirements.
A team already familiar with Domain Model lowers its initial cost, so the stronger the team, the more inclined you should be to use a Domain Model.
condition: when the team is experienced with rich object models

statement: Table Module is attractive only when the environment provides strong common Record Set tooling (e.g., .NET); with such tooling prefer it over Transaction Script, and without it do not bother with Table Module.
condition: depending on Record Set support in the development environment

statement: The domain-logic structuring choice is tricky to change later, so invest upfront thought; if you started with Transaction Script and chose wrong, refactor toward Domain Model, but moving from Domain Model back to Transaction Script is rarely worthwhile unless you can also simplify the data source layer.
The three domain-logic patterns are not mutually exclusive; it is common to use Transaction Script for some logic and Table Module or Domain Model for the rest.

A Service Layer sits over a Domain Model or Table Module as the application's API through which presentation interacts with the domain; it is usually warranted only with a Domain Model or Table Module, not with Transaction Script alone.
The Service Layer is a good place to put transaction control and security, described per method (e.g., via a properties file or code attributes).

Prefer the thinnest Service Layer you can, or none at all: assume you do not need one and add it only if the application demands it, while recognizing that some good designers succeed with a rich Service Layer.
If you decide to use a Domain Model, make it dominant rather than mixing a controller-entity style, because use-case controllers (Transaction Scripts) tend to encourage duplicated code.
exception: unless improving an existing Transaction Script + Row Data Gateway design, where moving duplicated behavior into the gateways yields a simple Active Record Domain Model

statement: Separate SQL access from domain logic into dedicated classes organized one per table (a Gateway), so all SQL is easy to find, the rest of the application knows nothing about SQL, and database specialists have a clear place to work.

Row Data Gateway has one instance per returned row; Table Data Gateway has one instance per table and returns a Record Set, making it the obvious gateway for Table Module and a way to encapsulate stored-procedure access.

For a simple Domain Model that closely matches the tables, use Active Record (each domain object loads and saves itself); for a rich Domain Model use Data Mapper, and do not use a plain Gateway as the primary persistence mechanism for a Domain Model.

Active Record breaks down as the Domain Model grows richer: the one-to-one class-to-table match fails, relational databases cannot represent inheritance (blocking strategy and other OO patterns), and you increasingly need to test domain logic without touching the database.
condition: as the domain logic becomes more complex

statement: Data Mapper is the most complex mapping architecture but completely isolates the Domain Model from the database, letting the two vary independently.

Pick a single primary persistence mechanism and do not mix them, because mixing gets messy; you may still use a data Gateway to wrap tables or services treated as external interfaces even under Data Mapper.
Mapping a Domain Model to a relational database is estimated anecdotally at roughly a third of programming effort, a cost that continues during maintenance.
Most projects choose relational over object-oriented databases primarily because of risk: relational databases are proven, vendor-backed, and offer SQL as a relatively standard tool interface.

If you have a Domain Model, seriously consider buying an O/R mapping tool, since mature commercial tools exceed hand-built mappers; weigh the licence cost against the cost of building and maintaining the layer yourself, but expect that using and tuning the tool still takes significant work.

Use Unit of Work to track every object read and modified and to orchestrate all database writes on a single commit, concentrating complex commit sequencing (including key dependencies) in one place; it is essential when database interactions become awkward.
Use an Identity Map to record every row read so the same row is never loaded into two in-memory objects; its primary purpose is maintaining correct identity, with caching as only a secondary benefit.

Use Lazy Load (a placeholder standing in for an object reference) so the real object is fetched only when the link is followed, preventing a single read from pulling an enormous object graph out of the database.
With row-based database interaction classes, prefer separate finder objects over static find methods so database operations remain substitutable (e.g., replaceable by a Service Stub for testing).

Finder methods query database state, not in-memory object state, so objects added in memory are not returned by a query; therefore it is usually wise to run queries at the beginning of a unit of work.

When reading data, pull back multiple rows at once and never issue repeated queries on the same table; prefer one over-fetching query to many small ones, and use joins to load multiple tables at once, but bear in mind databases optimize only about three or four joins per query before performance suffers.
exception: beware locking too many rows when using pessimistic concurrency control

statement: General performance rules only guide thinking; always profile your application against your specific database and data and set aside time for tuning, because caching schemes and surprising exceptions vary by environment.

Objects and relations represent links differently: objects use direct references and can hold multivalued collections, while relational normalization forces single-valued foreign keys, which reverses the relationship direction (the child row holds the key to the parent).

Bridge the object/relational link mismatch with Identity Field (store each object's relational key), Identity Map (key-to-object lookup on read), and Foreign Key Mapping (wire inter-object references from foreign keys), falling back to a database fetch or Lazy Load when a key is not in the Identity Map.
Map a many-to-many relationship with an Association Table Mapping (a dedicated link table), because relational databases cannot represent a collection on both ends directly.

Avoid relying on collection ordering when persisting to a relational database; prefer unordered sets, or apply an explicit sort per query, because arbitrary order is hard to maintain across persistence.

If the database can defer referential-integrity checks to the end of the transaction, use that capability; otherwise order updates deliberately (topological sort or a hardcoded table write order) to satisfy per-write checks and reduce deadlock-induced rollbacks.
condition: depending on whether the database supports deferred referential-integrity checking

statement: Do not give small Value Objects (such as date ranges or money) their own table; embed their fields into the owning row as an Embedded Value and skip the Identity Map, since value objects have value semantics.

Use a Serialized LOB to store a clustered group of objects as a single column (e.g., XML) to avoid many small database calls for hierarchic structures like org charts or bills of materials, but only when you do not need to query the parts, and do not overuse it or the database degenerates into a transactional file system.
condition: best when the stored group is relatively isolated and not separately queried

statement: There are three ways to map a class inheritance hierarchy to tables: Single Table Inheritance (one table for the whole hierarchy), Concrete Table Inheritance (one table per concrete class), and Class Table Inheritance (one table per class), trading data-structure duplication against access speed.

Inheritance-mapping trade-offs: Class Table Inheritance is cleanest but needs multiple joins to load one object; Concrete Table Inheritance avoids joins but is brittle to superclass changes and complicates key management; Single Table Inheritance wastes space on empty columns and can be an access bottleneck but keeps everything in one place for easy modification and no joins.

Inheritance-mapping patterns can be mixed within one hierarchy at the cost of added complexity; with no clear winner, a reasonable default is Single Table Inheritance for its simplicity and refactoring resilience, reaching for the others as wasted-column issues demand, and consulting DBAs.

With a Domain Model, beware a model shaped like the database: build the Domain Model without regard to the database to simplify domain logic and treat the schema purely as a way to persist object data; Data Mapper gives the most flexibility, or Active Record when an isomorphic schema genuinely makes sense.

Build the database incrementally within each short iteration (no more than six weeks, preferably fewer) rather than building a database-free Domain Model for months before persisting it, which risks crippling performance problems too costly to refactor.

When the same data is drawn from multiple similar-but-different sources, a two-step mapping (in-memory schema to a logical data store schema to the physical schema) reduces duplication, but it only pays off when the sources share many commonalities.
condition: when physical data stores are similar but annoyingly different

statement: Repetitive mapping code signals a design problem; factor out common behavior, or adopt Metadata Mapping (a metadata file describing column-to-field mappings) driving code generation or reflection, which is why commercial O/R tools are metadata-based.

Metadata Mapping is the foundation for a Query Object (queries expressed over in-memory objects without knowing SQL or the schema) and a Repository (which hides the database so callers cannot tell whether objects came from memory or disk); Repository fits rich Domain Model systems.

Treat database connections as expensive resources that must be closed as soon as you are done; use connection pooling when creation is costly, but most platforms pool for you, so verify that pooling actually helps before implementing it yourself.

Tie a connection to its transaction: open on transaction begin and close on commit or rollback, letting the transaction own the connection so you deal only with the transaction; a Unit of Work naturally manages both.

Do not rely on garbage collection to close database connections, because the close is deferred until the memory is reclaimed; prefer explicit or transaction-tied closing and treat garbage collection only as a backup.
Make a connection available where needed via a thread-scoped Registry rather than threading it through many method parameters, since the same connection must not be shared across threads.

Avoid 'select *' combined with positional column indices, because adding or reordering a column breaks the code; column-name indices are clearer and safe with 'select *', and if performance matters, measure.
Keep simple create/read/update/delete test cases for each database mapping structure to catch when the SQL drifts out of sync with the code.
Prefer static, precompilable SQL over dynamic SQL recompiled each time, avoid assembling SQL by string concatenation, and batch multiple SQL statements into a single database call in production code.

The script style of web program (CGI, servlet) is best at interpreting requests while the server-page style (PHP, ASP, JSP) is best at formatting responses, so the natural split is a script for request interpretation and a server page for response formatting, which is the Model View Controller pattern.

Apply Model View Controller to keep the domain models completely separate from the web presentation, which makes the presentation easy to modify or add to and the domain logic easy to test; this matters most when a server page is the view.

In web MVC the input controller pulls information off the request, forwards business logic to a model object, then selects a view and passes it the response data (often via a shared HTTP session object).

Use an Application Controller when the machine controls screen flow and navigation order; you do not need one when the user is free to reach any screen in any order (test: machine in control means you need it, user in control means you do not).
An Application Controller can be made presentation-independent and reused across presentations that share the same flow, though it is often best to give different presentations a different flow.

Template View (server pages with embedded dynamic markers) is powerful but tends toward messy, hard-to-maintain code, so keep programming logic out of the page structure, typically by delegating to a helper object.
Transform View (e.g., XSLT) is effective when the domain data is in XML or easily converted to it.
condition: when working with XML-formatted domain data

statement: Two Step View concentrates the HTML decision in one place, making global HTML changes easy and supporting multiple front-end appearances or output devices from a shared logical screen, but it only works when screens share a common logical structure.
condition: when different screens use the same basic logical layout

statement: Page Controller uses one input controller per page or action, while Front Controller routes all requests through a single object that interprets the URL and delegates, centralizing HTTP handling and avoiding web-server reconfiguration when the site's action structure changes.
Separate an input controller's two responsibilities, handling the HTTP request and deciding what to do with it, often into distinct objects.
Concurrency is hard to reason about and hard to test; even a large automated test suite gives weak security against concurrency defects.

Transaction managers let enterprise developers take a relatively naive view of concurrency: as long as all data manipulation happens within a transaction, the most dangerous concurrency problems are avoided.
condition: provided all data manipulation occurs inside a transaction

statement: Offline concurrency (concurrency control for data manipulated across multiple database transactions) cannot be handled by a single system transaction and must be managed explicitly.
The two essential concurrency problems are lost updates and inconsistent reads, both of which are correctness/safety failures caused by concurrent access to the same data.

Concurrency control trades correctness (safety) against liveness (how much concurrent activity is possible); you often sacrifice some correctness for liveness depending on the likelihood and seriousness of the failures.
If you can tolerate the concurrency problems, you can avoid concurrency control entirely; this is rare but occasionally valid.
condition: when the consequences of the concurrency problems are tolerable
