statement: Two key defenses for enterprise concurrency are isolation (partition data so only one active agent can access a piece) and immutability (data that cannot change needs no concurrency control).

Design concurrency by creating isolated zones in which programmers need not think about concurrency and pushing as much code as possible into them; forcing everyone to worry about concurrency everywhere reliably causes trouble.
Identify immutable (or almost-always-immutable) data and share it widely, and route read-only applications to copied data sources so their concurrency controls can be relaxed.
Optimistic locking is conflict detection (agents edit copies and a conflict is caught at commit), whereas pessimistic locking is conflict prevention (the first to check out blocks others).

Choose between optimistic and pessimistic locking by the frequency and severity of conflicts: when conflicts are rare or low-consequence prefer optimistic locks (better concurrency, easier to implement), but when conflict consequences are painful for users use pessimistic locks.

Pessimistic locking reduces concurrency because others must wait, while optimistic locking allows better progress but shifts the cost to conflict resolution; business data usually cannot be auto-merged, so resolving an optimistic conflict often means discarding the work and redoing it.
Pessimistic locks prevent inconsistent reads using read/write (shared/exclusive) locks: many readers may hold a shared lock, but a write lock excludes all other locks.

Optimistic locks detect conflicts via a version marker (timestamp or counter): compare your marker with the shared data on update for lost updates, and compare the marker of every datum read to detect inconsistent reads.

Controlling concurrency on every datum read causes needless conflicts and waits, so distinguish data you merely read from data you actually used to make decisions, recognizing that classifying them correctly requires careful analysis (e.g., a zip code matters when tax depends on location).
Deadlock is a particular risk of pessimistic locking: two or more parties each hold a lock the other needs so none can progress, and in complex multi-party chains deadlocks are hard to foresee.

Deadlocks can be handled after the fact by detection (choose a victim who loses work and locks) or by lock timeouts (easier to implement but victimizes some holders even when no real deadlock exists), or prevented by acquiring all locks up front, forcing a global lock-acquisition order, or auto-victimizing a later requester.

For enterprise applications prefer very simple, conservative deadlock schemes (even combining all-locks-up-front with a timeout), accepting some unnecessary victims, because missing a deadlock scenario is far worse and supposedly deadlock-proof schemes are easy to get wrong.

A transaction is a bounded sequence of work with well-defined start and end that completes on an all-or-nothing basis and leaves all participating resources in a consistent state at both start and end.

Software transactions are characterized by ACID: Atomicity (all steps commit or all roll back), Consistency (resources valid at start and end), Isolation (results invisible to other open transactions until commit), and Durability (committed results survive any crash).
A transactional resource is anything that uses transactions to control concurrency (databases, message queues, printers, ATMs), not just databases.
Keep transactions as short as possible for throughput, and as a general rule never let a transaction span multiple requests (a long transaction).

Starting a transaction at the beginning of a request and ending it at request end is a simple model; opening the transaction late (only at the first write) minimizes transaction time and can improve liveness but leaves you exposed to inconsistent reads, so it is usually not worth it unless contention is heavy or business transactions span requests.
condition: unless there is very heavy contention or business transactions already span multiple requests

statement: Be aware of what a transaction locks: row locks let transactions share a table, but locking too many rows makes the database escalate to a table lock that excludes everyone, so avoid a single shared 'object' or Layer Supertype table that is a lock-escalation magnet.
Reducing transaction isolation buys liveness at the cost of correctness; the SQL standard defines four isolation levels, each weaker level admitting a specific inconsistent-read error.
Isolation levels and the errors they allow are: Read Uncommitted (dirty, unrepeatable, phantom), Read Committed (unrepeatable, phantom), Repeatable Read (phantom only), and Serializable (none).

Serializable isolation guarantees correctness but severely harms liveness, so you often must lower it for throughput; since you need not use the same isolation level for every transaction, decide the error-versus-performance trade-off per transaction.

A system transaction (RDBMS or transaction monitor) is reliable but meaningless to the user, whereas a business transaction is the user's logical unit of work that may span multiple requests and should still exhibit ACID properties.

Implementing a business transaction as a single long system transaction is acceptable only with modest concurrency needs; if you can get away with it, do it because it avoids many problems, but it will not scale (the database becomes a bottleneck) and refactoring from long to short transactions is complex and poorly understood.
condition: only when the database has modest concurrency needs

statement: When you cannot use long transactions, break the business transaction into a series of short system transactions and supply the application-level glue to preserve ACID across them; this is offline concurrency.

Atomicity and durability are the easiest business-transaction properties to support by running the final commit phase inside one system transaction, with a Unit of Work tracking the change set accurately for a Domain Model.

Isolation is the hard business-transaction property to enforce, and isolation failures cause consistency failures such as one session overwriting another's work or inconsistent reads accumulating across system transactions.
Assume all business transactions execute within a single client session, because designing multiple sessions for one business transaction is a reliable way to get badly confused.
As much as possible, let the transaction system handle concurrency; only take on concurrency control that spans system transactions when you genuinely have to.

For offline concurrency, make Optimistic Offline Lock your first choice (easier to program, best liveness); switch to Pessimistic Offline Lock when late failure discovery at commit is too costly (e.g., users could lose an hour of work), accepting that it is harder to program and reduces liveness.

Reduce offline-locking complexity with a Coarse-Grained Lock (lock a group of related objects together) and an Implicit Lock (free developers from managing locks directly), which avoids hard-to-find bugs from forgetting to lock.

Concurrency control is not a purely technical decision to defer until after requirements: the optimistic-versus-pessimistic choice shapes the whole user experience and requires domain input from the system's users.

Avoid explicit multithreaded programming with locks and synchronization as much as possible, because it easily introduces defects that are almost impossible to reproduce, and application developers should almost never have to handle explicit concurrency mechanisms.

Application-server request-handling options trade isolation against resource cost: process-per-session gives full isolation but is expensive, pooled process-per-request gives almost the same isolation with far fewer processes (provided resources are released at request end), and thread-per-request is most efficient but provides no isolation between threads.

Prefer process-per-request over thread-per-request: it is equally scalable and more robust (a runaway thread can crash an entire process), and avoiding threading headaches is worth the extra hardware, especially with a less experienced team.

If you must use thread-per-request, create an isolated zone by having each thread create fresh objects per request and never publishing them where other threads can see them (e.g., static variables); object creation is cheap in modern environments, and fresh per-session objects avoid concurrency bugs and can improve scalability.

In threaded servers avoid static, class-based, or global variables and singletons (their access must be synchronized); use a thread-scoped Registry for any global memory and pool only genuinely expensive-to-create objects such as database connections, with synchronized access.
A 'stateless server' usually means an object that retains no state between requests (its field values are undefined when a method is invoked), not a literally fieldless object.

The chief value of a stateless server is resource efficiency: because no state is kept between calls, any object can service any request, so objects can be pooled and far fewer objects serve more (especially idle) users; statelessness also fits HTTP's stateless protocol and high-traffic web sites.

Many client interactions are inherently stateful (e.g., a shopping cart spanning a session), so you cannot avoid the state; the real decision is what to do with it, since you can implement a stateful session on a stateless server but may not want to.

Session state is data relevant only to one session within a business transaction and must be committed to become shared record data; it is distinct from cached data, which can be lost without losing correctness.
Session state carries transaction-like (ACID) properties and is often invalid while being edited, only needing to satisfy validation rules when the business transaction commits.

The biggest difficulty with session state is isolation: concurrent edits and inconsistent reads (such as a risk value depending on a zip code changed by another user mid-edit) must be handled explicitly.

There are three basic ways to store session state: Client Session State (URL, cookie, hidden field, or rich-client objects), Server Session State (in memory or serialized to file or a shared store), and Database Session State (broken into tables and fields like record data).

Use Client Session State only when the session state is small, because all of it must travel over the wire on every request, and encrypt it because an unencrypted client-held state can be edited by a malicious user.
condition: when the amount of session state is small

statement: Session data must be isolated from other sessions, and with Database Session State you must work hard to keep the session data isolated from the record data living in the same database.

When clustering, choose between session migration (sessions move server-to-server for better load balancing, good for long sessions) and server affinity (one server handles a session); affinity keyed on client IP can backfire when many clients share a proxy IP and overload one server.

Choose a session-state approach by data size and user idleness: Database Session State suits public retail systems (little data per session, many idle users) while Server Session State suits data-heavy sessions (e.g., leasing) to avoid moving masses of data to and from the database each request.

Account for failure and cancellation: Client Session State makes abandoned sessions trivial to forget; Database Session State best survives client, server, and network failures; Server Session State survives only if backed to nonvolatile store; and non-client approaches need explicit cleanup and timeout for cancelled sessions.

Server Session State is usually cheapest on development effort (especially when not persisted between requests); a reasonable default is Server Session State with a remotely stored memento to survive crashes, Client Session State for session IDs and tiny data, and Database Session State only when you need failover and clustering and cannot store remote mementos.

Distributing objects has far more pitfalls than commonly realized; vendor middleware can make local and remote calls look identical (transparency), but it cannot make remote-call performance transparent.
A procedure call within a process is very fast, a call between processes is orders of magnitude slower, and a call to another machine is another order or two slower again.

An object's remote interface must differ from its local interface: local interfaces should be fine-grained (many small methods for OO flexibility) while remote interfaces must be coarse-grained (fewer, bulkier calls) to minimize round trips, accepting a more awkward programming model.

First Law of Distributed Object Design: do not distribute your objects; basing distribution on individual classes produces too many remote calls and a system that is awkward to build, deploy, and modify even with coarse-grained interfaces everywhere.

To use multiple processors, prefer clustering: put all classes in a single process and run multiple copies of that process across nodes, so each process uses fast local calls and fine-grained interfaces.

Minimize distribution boundaries and be parsimonious with object distribution; the genuinely unavoidable boundaries are the client/server desktop divide, the application-server/database divide (where SQL is designed as a remote interface), the web-server/application-server divide, package/vendor boundaries, and rare genuine application-server splits.

At a distribution boundary, keep fine-grained objects internal and place a coarse-grained Remote Facade at the boundary whose only job is to expose a remote interface to the fine-grained objects, making the remote-call cost explicit rather than transparent.

Pair Remote Facade with Data Transfer Object to move data across the wire in one coarse-grained block, and ensure a Data Transfer Object references only other Data Transfer Objects and fundamental objects (such as strings) since it appears on both sides of the wire.

XML-over-HTTP interfaces (e.g., SOAP) usefully send lots of structured data in one roundtrip and ease cross-platform communication and firewall traversal, but add marshalling overhead; when both sides share a platform, use that platform's native remote-call mechanism and reserve XML web services for when a more direct approach is not possible.
An asynchronous, message-based approach is often preferable to synchronous RPC for distributed systems and is arguably the best use of web services.
Architectural decisions are not cast in stone: architectural refactoring is hard and its full costs are poorly understood, but it is not impossible.
Adopt continuous integration, test-driven development, and refactoring so you can change architectural decisions later, because you will need to change them.

The central enterprise design decision is the domain-logic approach (Transaction Script, Table Module, or Domain Model), driven mainly by domain-logic complexity and secondarily by the difficulty of the database connection.
Transaction Script fits simple applications well (e.g., a basic catalog and shopping cart) but its difficulties multiply exponentially as the domain logic grows complex.
A rich Domain Model best handles genuinely complex domain logic but requires real skill (done poorly it is a disaster) and brings a messy relational-database connection.
Table Module is an attractive middle ground that handles domain logic better than Transaction Script and fits relational databases and Record Set tooling well, making it especially strong on .NET.
Tools affect architecture: ideally you choose tools to fit your architecture, but in practice you often must match your architecture to your available tools.

Separate database logic from a Transaction Script even in the simplest applications, choosing Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway, with strong Record Set tooling tilting you toward Table Data Gateway.

With a Transaction Script you can usually wrap the whole script in a single system transaction because it corresponds closely to one, except when one request reads data for editing and a later request saves it, where Optimistic Offline Lock is almost always the best choice.
exception: when editing spans two requests (read in one, save in another), use Optimistic Offline Lock

statement: For a simple Domain Model close to the database use Active Record; as it grows complex use Data Mapper (most independent of other layers but most complex), get a mapping tool unless you have a strong team or simplifications, and use Unit of Work as the focal point for concurrency control.

Presentation is relatively independent of the lower layers: prefer an HTML browser interface if you can get away with it and a rich client if you cannot, with Model View Controller as the underpinning.

Choose input controller and view by tooling and site nature: Page Controller suits document-oriented sites with mixed static and dynamic pages, Front Controller suits complex navigation; pick Template View versus Transform View by whether the team uses server pages or XSLT, and Two Step View for one site with multiple looks.

Patterns outlive technologies, so cross-platform experience (Forte, CORBA, Smalltalk) translates effectively to Java and .NET; the same architectural decisions apply across platforms even as the technologies change quickly.
You do not need EJB to build a good J2EE application; a great deal can be done with plain old Java objects (POJOs) and JDBC.
For a complex Domain Model, keep it entirely independent of the EJB container by using POJOs, so you can write, run, and test the domain logic without dealing with the container's vagaries.

Never give entity beans a remote interface: they act as Domain Models or Row Data Gateways needing fine-grained interfaces, whereas a remote interface must always be coarse-grained, so keep entity beans local only.

On .NET, Table Module is the default domain-logic choice because the platform's tooling orbits the data set acting as a Record Set, leaving little reason to use Transaction Script except in the very simplest cases.

Web services are for application integration, not application construction: do not split a single application into web services that talk to each other unless you really need to; instead build the application and expose parts as Remote Facades, and do not let web-service hype make you forget the First Law of Distributed Object Design.

Stored procedures are often the fastest option because they run in the database process, but they lock you into a vendor and lack good structuring mechanisms, so avoid putting business logic in them for modularity and portability unless there is a strong performance gain, and then treat it as a targeted optimization step rather than an architectural principle.
exception: unless a clear, strong performance gain justifies moving a specific method into a stored procedure

statement: Treat mediating layers (such as Application Controller between presentation and domain, or Data Mapper between domain and data source) as optional extras: start from the three base layers and add a mediating layer only when one base layer becomes too complex.
Splitting a Service Layer from the domain layer separates workflow/use-case logic from pure domain logic; it is occasionally useful rather than mandatory, and respected designers disagree on it.
A Domain Model is less worthwhile for smaller systems, and you can reasonably skip a separate domain layer in a small system.

Transaction Script organizes all the domain logic for one system transaction primarily as a single procedure that calls the database directly or through a thin wrapper, with common subtasks factored into shared subprocedures.
A benefit of Transaction Script is independence: when writing one script you need not worry about what other transactions are doing.

Separate Transaction Scripts as much as possible (at least into distinct subroutines, better into classes separate from presentation and data source) and never call presentation logic from a Transaction Script, to make the code easier to modify and test.

Organize Transaction Scripts into classes either as several related scripts per class grouped by subject area (best for most cases) or as one script per class using the Command pattern (which allows manipulating scripts as runtime objects but is rarely needed).
Instantiating a fresh object per Transaction Script can help with threading because it makes it easier to isolate data.
Transaction Script's strength is simplicity: it adds very little overhead in performance or in understanding and is natural for applications with only a small amount of logic.

As business logic grows, Transaction Script becomes hard to keep well-designed, with code duplication between transactions as the particular danger, since each script handles one transaction and common code tends to be copied.
condition: as the business logic becomes more complicated

statement: Because refactoring a Transaction Script design into a Domain Model is harder than it should be, choosing a Domain Model early is often best when you expect the domain logic to become complex.
Do not rule out Transaction Script however object-oriented you become: many problems are simple, and a simple solution gets you running much faster.
When a calculation is simple enough, replace an in-memory script loop with a single SQL statement using an aggregate function.

In a Domain Model, place behavior on the object that needs to know it (e.g., whether a revenue recognition is recognizable by a date), which avoids duplication and reduces coupling even though it spreads behavior across many small collaborating objects.
Use the Strategy pattern in a Domain Model to provide well-contained plug points: add a new algorithm by creating a new subclass and overriding its method, making algorithmic behavior easy to extend.

A Domain Model replaces conditional logic by moving complexity out of algorithms and into the relationships between objects: the decision path is fixed when objects are wired together, so similar conditionals factor into the object structure and are reused across the system.
A core purpose of a Domain Model is to hide the database, both from the upper layers and from the people working within the Domain Model itself.
Table Module organizes domain logic as one class per table (or view or query) with a single instance handling all rows, in contrast to a Domain Model which has one object per row.
A Table Module has no notion of object identity, so every operation must pass in an identity reference, usually the database primary key.
Table Module's strength is packaging data with behavior while playing to the strengths of a relational database, operating on a table-oriented backing structure (a Record Set produced by a SQL call).

A Table Module can be implemented as an instance initialized with a record set rather than as static methods, which enables specialization through inheritance (e.g., a rush-contract module extending a contract module).
A benefit of the Table Module style is testability: you can test it by creating a Record Set in memory without going to the database.
A Table Module's structure follows the virtual tables the application perceives (including views and queries), not strictly the physical database tables.

Use Table Module when accessing tabular data via a Record Set and when access to that structure is fairly straightforward; because it lacks the full power of objects (no direct instance-to-instance relationships and weak polymorphism), prefer a Domain Model for complex domain logic.

Table Module beats a Domain Model with Active Record when other parts of the application are built around a common table-oriented data structure (such as COM/.NET Record Sets); when Domain Model objects and tables are similar, a Domain Model with Active Record may be better.

Identify Service Layer operations from the use-case model and the user-interface design, since the UI is typically the first and most significant client and is built to support the use cases actors want to perform.
There is almost always a one-to-one correspondence between CRUD use cases and Service Layer operations.

A Service Layer operation's responsibility is to coordinate and atomically transact the application's full response to a use case (e.g., validation plus notifying other people and integrated applications), which can be far from trivial.

Grouping operations into Service Layer abstractions follows only vague heuristics: one abstraction for a small application, one per subsystem (vertical slice) for larger ones, or abstractions reflecting domain partitions or thematic behaviors.

Implementing a Service Layer class as a POJO versus a stateless session bean trades ease of testing (POJOs run and test without an EJB container) against ease of transaction control (session beans get container-managed distributed transactions but must be deployed to test).

Service Layer (which factors responsibility to avoid duplication and promote reusability and transcends any particular technology) is distinct from Session Facade (which is motivated by avoiding the performance penalty of too many remote invocations on entity beans).

Use a Service Layer when an application's business logic has more than one kind of client and its use-case responses span multiple transactional resources, and design it in from the start once you foresee a second client or a second transactional resource.

You probably do not need a Service Layer when the business logic has only one client and use-case responses do not span multiple transactional resources; in that case Page Controllers can manage transactions and delegate to the Data Source layer.
condition: when there is a single client and no multi-resource transactional responses

statement: Keep application-specific logic out of domain object classes (which become less reusable across applications if they carry it) and out of the data source layer, encapsulating it instead in a dedicated higher Service Layer so domain objects stay reusable and that layer's implementation can later change (e.g., to a workflow engine).

Service Layer combines operation scripting with domain object classes, scripting the application logic while delegating domain logic to domain objects, and can be designed for local invocation, remote invocation, or both.

Combat duplicated logic in Service Layer operation scripts by factoring responsibilities into reusable objects (such as Gateways) accessed via delegation, with a Layer Supertype providing convenient access to them.
Embedding database access code in in-memory objects increases complexity when those objects also carry business logic and makes testing slower because tests then hit the database.

A Row Data Gateway is an object that exactly mimics a single record (one field per column) and hides all data-source access behind its interface; it must contain only database-access logic and no domain logic (the presence of domain logic makes it an Active Record instead).
Row Data Gateway works particularly well with Transaction Script, factoring out database access code so it can be reused across scripts.
With a Row Data Gateway, prefer separate finder objects over static find methods so finders remain polymorphic and substitutable across different data sources.

Do not use a Row Data Gateway with a Domain Model: use Active Record for simple mappings (no extra layer) and Data Mapper for complex ones (better decoupling); shielding domain objects with a Row Data Gateway creates three data representations (business logic, gateway, database), which is one too many, so keep Row Data Gateways mirroring the database structure.
Row Data Gateways are tedious to write but are excellent candidates for code generation from a Metadata Mapping, so their database access code can be built automatically during the build.
Combining Row Data Gateway with Data Mapper can be effective when the Row Data Gateways are auto-generated from metadata while the Data Mappers are written by hand.
condition: when Row Data Gateways are generated from metadata and Data Mappers are hand-written

statement: When Transaction Script plus Row Data Gateway shows business logic repeated across scripts, moving that logic into the Row Data Gateway gradually turns it into an Active Record and reduces duplication.

Mappers need access to domain-object fields without exposing setters and getters meant only for persistence (and never by making fields public); options are packaging mappers close to the domain objects (which muddies dependencies), using reflection (slower but negligible against SQL time), or status-guarded public methods named so they are not mistaken for regular accessors.

When loading objects, either use a rich constructor that supplies all mandatory data (preferred, since it yields a well-formed object from the start and can enforce immutability) or create an empty object and then populate it.

A rich constructor risks infinite recursion on cyclic references, so to break cycles create a blank object with a no-arg constructor and insert it into the Identity Map immediately, so an in-progress cycle returns the partially built object instead of recursing.

Store field-to-column mapping either as explicit code (one mapper class per domain object, the simplest and often best approach) or as Metadata Mapping (data in a class or file), the latter absorbing mapping variation through code generation or reflection without extra source code.

Use Data Mapper when you want the database schema and the object model to evolve independently, most commonly with a Domain Model; its primary benefit is that you can ignore the database while designing, building, and testing the domain model.

The price of Data Mapper is an extra layer compared with Active Record, so use business-logic complexity as the test: simple logic needs neither a Domain Model nor a Data Mapper, while complex logic leads to a Domain Model and therefore to Data Mapper.

Do not use Data Mapper without a Domain Model, but you may use a Domain Model without Data Mapper (via Active Record) when the model is simple and the database is under the developers' control, refactoring database behavior into a separate layer as complexity grows.
Do not build a full-featured database-mapping layer yourself; it is complex, and for most cases you should buy a database-mapping layer rather than build one.

Writing to the database on every object-model change produces many small, slow database calls and forces a transaction to stay open for the whole interaction, which is impractical when a business transaction spans multiple requests.

A Unit of Work tracks all objects created, updated, and deleted (and optionally read, to detect inconsistent reads) during a business transaction, then on commit opens a transaction, performs concurrency checking, and writes the changes, so application programmers never explicitly call database-update methods or worry about referential-integrity ordering.

Register objects with a Unit of Work either by caller registration (flexible but error-prone, since forgetting means changes are not written) or by object registration (loading registers an object clean and setters register it dirty); object registration removes the burden from the caller but still requires registration calls in the right places.
Registration with a Unit of Work is well suited to code generation, aspect-oriented programming, or bytecode post-processing, which keep the database code separated from the regular domain code.

A unit-of-work-controller variant has the Unit of Work handle all reads, copy each object at read time, and compare at commit, which avoids registration calls and enables selective update of only changed fields at the cost of commit overhead (a hybrid copies only registered/changed objects).

For transient objects (such as domain-object tests that run faster without database writes), provide a transient constructor that does not register, or better a Special Case Unit of Work whose commit does nothing.

Avoid manual update ordering for referential integrity by configuring the database to check integrity only at commit (most databases allow this, with no good reason not to); otherwise make the Unit of Work the place that sorts update order, using explicit code for small systems and metadata with a topological sort for large ones.
Reduce deadlocks by always editing tables in the same fixed sequence, and use the Unit of Work as the ideal place to hold that fixed table-write order.
Let objects find their current Unit of Work through a thread-scoped Registry (or by passing it in), and never allow more than one thread to access a single Unit of Work.

A Unit of Work is a natural point for batch updates, sending multiple SQL commands in a single remote call, which matters when many updates, inserts, and deletes occur in rapid succession; check that batching does not interfere with statement precompilation.
A Unit of Work works with any transactional resource, not just databases, so it can also coordinate message queues and transaction monitors.

Unit of Work's strength is keeping all change-tracking in one place and serving as a firm platform for offline concurrency (Optimistic and Pessimistic Offline Lock); its alternatives are weaker, since explicit save-on-change causes too many calls, tracking changes in variables becomes unmanageable in a Domain Model, and per-object dirty flags only help when dirty objects are easy to find.
Lazy Load can be implemented four main ways: lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder, and ghost.

Lazy initialization checks each field access for null and loads the value on demand, which requires the field to be self-encapsulated (all access through a getter) and fails when null is a legal value, in which case use a different not-loaded marker or a Special Case.

Lazy initialization forces a dependency between the object and the database, so it suits Active Record, Table Data Gateway, and Row Data Gateway; with Data Mapper use a virtual proxy to add the needed layer of indirection.

A virtual proxy looks exactly like the real object and loads it on first method call, but because it is not the real object it can cause identity problems (multiple proxies for one object hold different identities), so override the equality method and use it instead of identity comparison.
Virtual proxies avoid identity problems when used only for collection classes, since collections are Value Objects whose identity does not matter and there are only a few collection types to wrap.

A value holder wraps an object and loads it on first access, but the owning class must know the value holder is present and you lose strong-typing explicitness; avoid identity problems by never passing the value holder beyond its owning class.

A ghost is the real object in a partial state (initially just its ID) that loads its full state on first field access; put a ghost into the Identity Map immediately to maintain identity and avoid cyclic-reference problems when reading data.
A virtual proxy or ghost need not be entirely empty: preloading quick, commonly-used data (a 'light object') can make sense.
Inheritance complicates Lazy Load, because with ghosts (and with virtual proxies in statically typed languages) you may not know which subtype to create without loading the object properly.

Beware ripple loading: a collection filled with Lazy Loads and then iterated one at a time causes one database call per object and can cripple performance; avoid it by making the collection itself a single Lazy Load that loads all its contents at once, except for very large collections where you need a Value List Handler.

Lazy Load is a good candidate for aspect-oriented programming or bytecode post-processing, which lets you vary the lazy-load strategy separately and frees domain developers from lazy-loading concerns.

Because different use cases need different degrees of laziness, use separate database-interaction objects (e.g., an eager and a lazy mapper) or a strategy object to choose the loading pattern; in practice only two degrees are needed (a full load and enough for list identification), and more adds complexity than it is worth.

Do not use Lazy Load on a field stored in the same row as the rest of the object (there is no extra cost to fetch it); only consider Lazy Load when accessing the field requires an extra database call and the data is not used when the main object is used.
Lazy Load adds complexity, so prefer not to use it unless you actively expect to need it.
Identity Field stores the relational primary key inside the in-memory object to maintain the correspondence between an object and its database row, which is required in order to write data back.

Distrust meaningful keys (such as a Social Security number) and usually choose meaningless keys, because keys must be unique and immutable but human error makes meaningful keys neither; meaningful keys are acceptable only for small or very stable cases.
exception: meaningful keys may be tolerable for small systems or very stable cases

statement: Prefer simple (single-field) keys for the uniformity of using one code path for all key manipulation; use compound keys when one table makes sense only in another's context (e.g., order number plus line-item sequence), but remember compound keys carry meaning so guard uniqueness and immutability.

Choose a key type with fast equality (the most common key operation) and easy next-key generation, for which a long integer is often best, and avoid dates or times in keys because they are meaningful and cause portability and precision-sync problems.

Database-unique keys are often easier than table-unique keys and allow a single Identity Map, and with Class Table or Concrete Table Inheritance use keys unique across the inheritance hierarchy rather than per table.
Represent a compound key as a dedicated key class whose essential behavior is equality, and centralize key handling in a Layer Supertype with default behavior extended for exceptional cases.
There are three ways to obtain a new key: let the database auto-generate it, use a GUID, or generate your own.

Database auto-increment fields usually do not reveal the generated key before commit, so you generally cannot use them on tables where you must insert connected objects (e.g., an order and its line items that need the order's key as a foreign key).

A database counter or sequence (as in Oracle) is ideal for key generation because it runs in a separate transaction and can return multiple keys at once, but it is nonstandard and not available in all databases.
A GUID is globally unique and a safe key, but its large string form is hard to type and read and may hurt index performance.

The roll-your-own SQL max-plus-one table scan read-locks the entire table and only works when inserts are rare, and it requires full transaction isolation to avoid two transactions getting the same ID.

A better roll-your-own key scheme is a separate key table (name plus next-available value): fetch many keys at once to cut database calls and contention, and access the key table in its own short transaction so the lock is not held for the whole business transaction (the only cost being that a rolled-back insert wastes a cheap key).
Separate the new-key-generation code into its own class so it is easy to replace with a Service Stub for testing.

Use Identity Field when mapping in-memory objects to database rows (typically with a Domain Model or Row Data Gateway); it is not needed for Transaction Script, Table Module, or Table Data Gateway, and small value objects with no own table are better handled by Embedded Value while a complex unqueried object graph is better stored as a Serialized LOB.

Split mapper behavior into find (locating the right database row) and load (populating the domain object from that row), putting the default behavior for simple integral keys in a mapper Layer Supertype and overriding hook methods for more complex keys.
Extract the parts of a compound key through named helper methods rather than literal numeric indices, because literal positional indices into a key are a code smell that obscures intent.

Use a template method in the mapper supertype with hook methods for the variable parts (such as binding key parameters and creating the key), so the shared default path serves simple integral keys and only the exceptional cases override the hooks.
Creating an empty object and inserting it directly into the Identity Map removes the special handling otherwise needed when an associated object is not yet registered during loads.

Although issuing one query per table is conceptually clean, it is often inefficient because each SQL call is a slow remote call, so it is frequently worth gathering data from multiple tables in a single joined query (a multitable find).

When loading a referenced object from a multitable join, check the Identity Map first (whether it is already loaded) before constructing it, so an already-loaded object is reused rather than duplicated.

There is a genuine tension over where to place the code that maps a SQL result into a referenced object: putting it on the referenced object's own mapper keeps it with the class that usually loads it, but keeping it with the query reflects that the load logic is tightly coupled to the SQL.
Loading N objects when each requires a separate query for its associated data causes the N+1 query problem (e.g., loading a hundred employees and their skills takes 101 queries).

Multitable query optimization (one joined query that loads many objects with their associations) is more awkward, so apply it only where needed and put your energy into speeding up the slow, important queries rather than optimizing many less-important ones.
Use a method object (a complicated method turned into its own object) to hold intermediate state in fields instead of passing it through parameters; create it, run it once, and discard it.

Keep a result-set loader generic and independent of specific domain classes by passing in a small callback interface (e.g., an Adder) that the caller implements for the particular association, a role closures or function pointers would fill more naturally.

Distinguish a load method (which does whatever is needed and may advance the cursor) from a loadRow method (which guarantees to load data from a row without moving the result-set cursor) when processing a multi-row join result.

A Serialized LOB can be a BLOB (binary) or a CLOB (textual): BLOB is simplest where the platform auto-serializes and is most space-efficient, but it requires a binary type, is impenetrable to casual viewing, and most seriously suffers versioning problems when the class changes and old long-lived serializations can no longer be read.

A CLOB is human-readable (aiding casual browsing) but uses more space, may need a custom parser, and is slower than binary; XML removes the parser and standardization problems but worsens the space cost through verbosity, and a zipped XML BLOB trades readability back for space.

Beware identity and duplication with a Serialized LOB: do not embed a shared, updatable LOB (such as customer details) in another table (such as order), which copies the data per row; instead place the LOB in its own table so many rows can link to it.
exception: embedding the LOB is desirable when you deliberately want a point-in-time snapshot rather than shared, updatable data

statement: Ensure that the data inside a Serialized LOB is reachable only from the single object that owns it, to avoid duplicating data that overlaps with another LOB.

Serialized LOB works best when you can carve out a piece of the object model that will not be queried via SQL from outside the application, and works poorly when objects outside the LOB need to reference objects buried inside it (which requires an awkward referencing scheme).
The main disadvantage of a Serialized LOB is that you cannot query its internal structure with SQL.
Structures suitable for a Serialized LOB are often also suitable for a separate denormalized reporting database, into which the LOB can be transformed into table structures.

With Class Table Inheritance, give each class in the hierarchy its own mapper whose load, save, insert, and delete handle only that class's table (chaining to the superclass mapper via base calls), and have a top-level mapper dispatch to the correct concrete mapper by type code on find and by runtime type on update, insert, and delete.

Caching query results in an in-memory data set lets you make several accesses to the table-based data without a high performance cost; when going directly to the database instead, reduce the load (for example, by joining across all the hierarchy's tables).
Insertion under inheritance mapping has two stages: first create the new database rows, then use the per-class save methods to populate those blank rows with data.

Metadata Mapping manifests in running code two ways: code generation (a program turns the metadata into mapper source built before compilation) or reflective programming (reading field and method names from metadata and invoking them dynamically).
Treat generated mapping code as never hand-edited: integrate generation fully into the build and do not keep the generated classes in source control.

Although reflection is generally worth avoiding (slower and harder to debug), it is appropriate for database mapping because you are reading field and method names from a file, and its overhead is usually small relative to the SQL call, but you should measure in your environment.

Reflection is the more dynamic approach (you can change the metadata file, even at runtime, without recompiling) whereas code generation requires recompiling and redeploying, though mapping changes are rare because they imply database or code changes.
Generated mapping code is more explicit and easier to debug, so a reasonable default is to prefer code generation over reflection, especially for less sophisticated developers.

Hold mapping metadata in a separate file (XML is popular, giving hierarchic structure without a custom parser), directly in source code (avoids parsing but is harder to edit), or in the database itself (keeping the mapping with the data so schema changes are co-located).
Metadata access and parsing performance is mostly negligible, since code generation parses only at build time and reflection parses once at startup and then caches the in-memory representation.
Evolve metadata complexity as your needs grow rather than building a fully general mapping scheme up front, because it is not hard to add new capabilities to metadata-driven software.

Handle special cases that would over-complicate a simple metadata scheme by overriding the generic code with handwritten subclasses of the generated or reflective routines, isolating a single overridable method per special case.
Reduce hand-coding effort by writing a good Layer Supertype that handles the common behavior, leaving only a few hook routines per mapping, which Metadata Mapping can then reduce further.

Metadata Mapping can interfere with code refactoring because automated tools cannot find field names hidden in a mapping file (renaming a private field can silently break the application, with no warning under reflection), but it can make database refactoring easier since the metadata states the schema interface.

A Query Object expresses a query in the language of domain objects and fields rather than table structure, holding the target class and a collection of criteria corresponding to where-clause predicates, and then translating itself into SQL.
Build complex query criteria as polymorphic subclasses (e.g., a case-insensitive pattern-match criterion) so that each criterion knows how to generate its own SQL fragment.

A Repository mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers through a collection-like interface: clients build query specifications (criteria) declaratively and submit them for satisfaction, and the encapsulated mapping code performs the operations behind the scenes.
A Repository concentrates query-construction code in one place and minimizes duplicate query logic, which becomes important when there are many domain classes or heavy querying.
A Repository supports a clean separation and one-way dependency between the domain and data-mapping layers and presents the persistence layer as an in-memory collection of domain objects.

A Repository replaces specialized finder methods with specification-based object selection, so client code never thinks in SQL and works purely in terms of objects, treating queries as the satisfaction of a specification rather than as execution.
Remember that a Repository's apparent in-memory collection may map to a huge table, so operations like all() on a catalog's ProductRepository over hundreds of thousands of rows are unwise.
A Repository's object source need not be a relational database: because the data-mapping component can be swapped via strategy objects, Repository suits systems with multiple schemas or sources.

Repository shines with multiple data sources and for testing: backing it with an in-memory data store lets unit-test suites run entirely in memory (much faster) and simplifies fixtures, since you just construct domain objects and add them to a collection rather than saving and deleting them in setup and teardown.

Under the covers a Repository combines Metadata Mapping with a Query Object to generate SQL automatically from the criteria, and some domain objects (such as immutable ones) can be kept in memory and never queried for again once loaded.

A Page Controller handles a request by creating the necessary model objects, placing the information the view needs into the HTTP request, and then forwarding to the view; because forwarding is common, it naturally sits on a Page Controller superclass.
The main point of coupling between a Template View and its Page Controller is the request parameter names used to pass the objects the view needs.

You may use model objects directly as view helpers (instead of a separate helper class) when the helper would only be a dumb forwarder, but ensure the model class contains no servlet-dependent code, which belongs in a separate helper class.
Scriptlet code in server pages is bad design, so when a server page acts as the request handler delegate the controller function to a helper class to keep the logic out of the page.

When the handler server page is also the default view, control reverts to it unless the controller forwards elsewhere, which is convenient when the page acts as the view most of the time and matches the natural association between a web page and its server page.
Replace a clumsy helper-initialization scriptlet in a server page with a custom tag that creates, registers, and initializes the helper object, keeping logic out of the page.

A Front Controller routes all requests through a single handler that instantiates the appropriate command (e.g., named by a URL command parameter), initializes it, and runs its process method, with commands sharing data and behavior through a command superclass that defines common init/forward and an abstract process.
Use a Special Case (such as an UnknownCommand) for an unrecognized request to avoid a lot of extra error-checking code.
Generating HTML by concatenating strings in code is painful, so compose a dynamic page like a static page but embed markers that resolve into calls gathering the dynamic information (Template View).
Embed Template View markers as HTML-like tags (which work well with WYSIWYG and XML tools), as special text markers (easier syntax but editors may mangle them), or as your own custom-defined tags.

Avoid embedding programming logic (scriptlets) in server pages, because a page is a poor program module that loses structural and modular features, prevents nonprogrammers and designers from editing it, and makes it too easy to mingle layers and duplicate domain logic across pages.
Avoid scriptlets by giving each page a regular helper object that holds all the real programming logic, so the page only calls into it and remains a pure Template View editable by nonprogrammers.

Treat general-purpose conditional tags (such as a generic IF) as a bad smell because they turn templates into a programming language; instead move the condition into the helper (returning an empty string when false) or use a focused tag driven by a single Boolean helper property.
Any condition evaluated in a page must rest on a single Boolean property of the helper, since putting a more complex expression in the page is putting logic into the page.

A Template View should ideally play only the view in Model View Controller; where it must take on controller or model responsibilities, ensure that program logic lives in the helper rather than the page.
Template processing is done by compiling the page after creation, compiling it on first request, or interpreting it on each request, the last being a poor choice when interpretation is slow.
Guard exception handling in a Template View, because an exception reaching the web container can yield odd half-rendered output instead of a redirect, so catch exceptions in the helper class.
Transform View renders the model's data into HTML by treating it as a transformation: the program walks the domain data and, recognizing each element type, writes out the HTML for it.

Template View and Transform View differ in organization: a Template View is organized around the output, while a Transform View is organized around separate transforms per input element dispatched by a simple loop, so a Transform View's rules can be arranged in any order without affecting the output.

To run an XSLT Transform View, feed it XML, ideally the natural return type of the domain logic, otherwise produce the XML via a Data Transfer Object that serializes itself (or a Transaction Script returning XML directly), and pass a DOM rather than a string unless a string form is needed to cross a communication line.

Choose between Transform View and Template View mostly by the team's preferred environment and tool availability, noting that HTML editors are more mature than XSLT tools and XSLT's functional style and XML syntax are awkward to master.
A strength of XSLT is portability to almost any web platform, since the same XSLT can transform XML produced from J2EE or .NET, helping put a common HTML view over data from different sources.

Transform View avoids two of Template View's biggest problems: it is easier to keep the transform focused only on rendering (avoiding excess logic in the view), and it is easy to run and capture its output for testing without a web server.

Because Transform View transforms directly to HTML, a site-wide appearance change can force changes across multiple transforms; reduce this with common transforms (e.g., XSLT includes, which are easier to call than in Template View), or use a Two Step View when you need easy global changes or multiple appearances for the same data.

An object-based (non-XSLT) Two Step View constrains site-layout uniformity less, letting a page author slip in individual HTML more easily, but that same openness permits inappropriate use, so the team must weigh flexibility against the way constraints prevent mistakes.

An Application Controller centralizes screen-navigation and application-flow logic (such as wizard-style ordered screens or conditional screens), removing the duplication that arises when multiple input controllers each need to know what to do; input controllers then ask it for the command and view to use given the context.

An Application Controller has two responsibilities, deciding which domain logic to run and which view to display, typically holding two collections of references (domain commands and views) stored as Commands, function references, or strings invoked by reflection.

Prefer an Application Controller with no links to the UI machinery, because that lets you test it independently of the UI and reuse it across multiple presentations, which is why many treat it as an intermediate layer between presentation and domain.
An application can use multiple Application Controllers split by broad areas of the user interface, while a simple application needs only one.

The same Application Controller can serve multiple presentations (web, rich client, PDA), but do not be too eager, because different UIs often need different screen flow for usability; reusing one may cut development effort at the cost of a more awkward UI.

A user interface is well modeled as a state machine (events trigger different responses depending on state), and an Application Controller is well suited to representing that control flow as metadata, set up either in code or in a separate configuration file.

Keep request-specific domain logic out of the Application Controller; because the domain/application boundary is murky, a few such cases may live there, but if the logic recurs in many places, drive it from the Domain Model instead.

Use an Application Controller when there are definite rules about the order pages are visited and state-dependent view choices, and skip it when any screen can be visited in any order; a good signal to introduce one is having to make similar changes in many places whenever the application flow changes.

In Enterprise Java a session bean (stateful or stateless remote object) is a good distributed facade, and plain Java objects run fine inside an EJB container, so domain objects need not be entity beans.

Offer remote method variants that move data either as a Data Transfer Object or as an XML string so the client can choose by its nature and connection, accepting that this multiplies the number of methods on the facade.
A distributed facade should be a long list of very short methods with very little logic, each merely delegating to another object, because the facade is only a packaging mechanism.
Keep as much testing as possible in a single process by instantiating and testing the session bean (Remote Facade) implementation directly, outside the EJB container, for a faster testing turnaround.

A web service is fundamentally a remote interface (plus a slow string-parsing step), so the basic Remote Facade advice holds: build the functionality fine-grained and layer a Remote Facade over it to expose web services.
Use assembler objects to move data between the domain objects and the Data Transfer Objects so the facade stays thin.
A Data Transfer Object is a plain data holder that flattens the domain structure for transfer over the wire.
For a very simple domain you are better off using a Table Data Gateway to build the Data Transfer Objects directly rather than introducing a full Domain Model.

A Data Transfer Object collapses and flattens a domain object graph for transfer (for example, folding the artist into the album DTO and representing performers as an array of strings), written from the domain model by an assembler that the Remote Facade calls.
When updating the domain from a Data Transfer Object, decide per case whether to update the existing domain object or replace it with a new one, based on whether other objects reference it.

Native binary serialization requires the Data Transfer Object classes on both sides of the wire to stay in sync (a server-side change without a matching client change causes transfer errors), whereas a map-based serialization makes the transfer more tolerant, since added server fields are simply ignored by older clients.
Avoid tedious hand-written Data Transfer Object serialization by using a reflective routine on a Layer Supertype, which handles most cases (with extra code needed for primitives).
In Java, free binary serialization via a marker interface is the first choice for a Data Transfer Object, but text-based serialization such as XML is often necessary.
Always check the Identity Map on load so different versions of the same object are not loaded within one business transaction, which would cause undefined behavior and corrupt version checks.

Set version and modification fields in the mapper rather than through a constructor, so that version-storage responsibility is not pushed down to each concrete mapper and domain object, which would weaken the Implicit Lock.

Implement Optimistic Offline Lock by bundling a version check into the UPDATE and DELETE statements and verifying that exactly one row was affected; a row count of zero means the lock could not be obtained, so throw a concurrency exception.
Acquire Optimistic Offline Locks within the same system transaction that commits the changes, in order to maintain record-data consistency.
On detecting a concurrency violation during commit, roll back the system transaction (a step that must not be forgotten).
Detect inconsistent reads, when the isolation level is unknown, by registering read objects and incrementing their version during commit.

Pessimistic Offline Lock prevents conflicts by forcing a business transaction to acquire a lock before using data, so once begun it is likely to complete, in contrast to optimistic locking where a victim does all the work only to fail at commit, which becomes unpopular for lengthy transactions.

Pessimistic Offline Lock offers three lock types: an exclusive write lock (acquire to edit, ignoring reads, fine when stale views are acceptable), an exclusive read lock (acquire even to load, which severely restricts concurrency), and a read/write lock (mutually exclusive read and write but allowing concurrent read locks, maximizing concurrency at the cost of complexity).

Choose a lock type to maximize concurrency, meet business needs, and minimize complexity, treating locking as a domain decision (include Pessimistic Offline Lock in the domain model), because a wrong locking strategy cannot be rescued by a correct technical implementation.

Use a single lock manager as the only code that touches locks, backed by exactly one lock table (a singleton in-memory hash table, or a database table when the application server is clustered), and keep lock objects private to the manager.
Generally acquire the lock before loading the data so you are guaranteed the latest version, and lock the ID or primary key rather than the object, which lets you lock before loading.
Release locks when the business transaction completes, and do not release early without a specific reason such as a serious liveness problem.

When a lock cannot be acquired, abort immediately by throwing an exception rather than waiting, which avoids deadlock and timeout complexity; acquire contentious locks as early as possible, ideally all before the user begins work.

Serialize access to the lock table, and with a database-backed lock table interact within a system transaction and use serializable isolation for read/write locks to avoid inconsistent reads, optionally isolating lock acquisition in its own serializable transaction to ease the performance cost.
Reduce contention on the inherently serial lock table by using coarser lock granularity, such as a Coarse-Grained Lock.

Manage lock timeouts for lost sessions (e.g., crashed web clients) by preferring the application server's session-timeout mechanism to release locks when the HTTP session invalidates, or by timestamping each lock and treating old ones as invalid.

Use Pessimistic Offline Lock only when the chance or cost of conflict is high, treating it as complementary to Optimistic Offline Lock and never locking every entity, which would create tremendous contention.

If you must use Pessimistic Offline Lock, also consider a long transaction (sometimes no more damaging and easier to program, so load-test first), and do not use offline locking at all when business transactions fit within a single system transaction, where built-in mechanisms like SELECT FOR UPDATE or entity-EJB locking suffice; all offline-locking techniques depend on having a real transaction monitor.
exception: when each business transaction fits in one system transaction, use built-in system-transaction locking instead

statement: Implement a database lock manager as your own application lock table (not the database's internal locking), where acquiring a lock inserts a row and releasing deletes it, using a system-wide-unique long primary key as the lockable ID and the HTTP session ID as the owner.

Have acquireLock first verify the owner does not already hold the lock (session code commonly re-acquires), but recognize that these repetitive lock-table reads add contention, so consider carefully caching owned locks at the session level.

The layers beneath the web tier need their own session concept (an application session distinct from the HTTP session) that stores an ID, user, and Identity Map and is bound to the executing thread (e.g., via thread-local storage) so it can be found.
When starting a new business transaction, release any locks held by a prior application session, and register a listener to release an application session's locks when its HTTP session expires.

Execute all locking and standard domain business for a single request within one system transaction (e.g., by decorating the command with a transactional command), and mandatorily roll back the system transaction on a concurrency or any other exception to keep conflicting changes out of the permanent record data.

Implement a Coarse-Grained Lock by sharing one version object across a group of related objects, ensuring all of them reference the exact same version instance by caching versions in a session-scoped Identity Map.

Separate a shared version's database insert from its creation so insertion can be deferred until at least one owner is inserted, and have the version track whether it is new so it is inserted only once.

Have a shared version increment its database row once per change set (checking it is not already locked first) and, after the update, verify the affected row count is non-zero, where zero signals a concurrency violation.

Increment the shared version only in the system transaction that commits the business transaction, because an optimistic lock is acquired only at commit, and use a separate checkCurrent method to verify data is still current in an earlier transaction without updating.

Deleting a shared version is tricky: for an aggregate, delete the version right after deleting the aggregate root; otherwise consider reference counting, which complicates the version, possibly enough to make it a full domain object.
Have the Data Mapper insert the shared version before inserting the corresponding domain objects and increment it before updating or deleting an object.

In its simplest form Server Session State holds session objects in memory on the application server keyed by session ID, which assumes enough memory, no clustering, and that a server failure can simply abandon the session.

To avoid holding memory resources, serialize Server Session State to a memento for persistent storage in as simple a form as possible: binary serialization is easy and compact but is not human-readable and risks versioning breakage, while textual/XML needs more code.

Store serialized Server Session State either on the application server (file or local database, simple but poor for clustering and failover) or somewhere generally accessible such as a shared server or a database session table (a Serialized LOB), which supports clustering and failover at the cost of slower, cacheable activation.
When storing Server Session State in a database, provide a mechanism to expire old sessions (e.g., a cleanup daemon, or rotating partitioned table segments) to avoid contention on the session table.

Do not assume stateless session beans are always better than stateful ones for performance: load-test first, because the difference appears only under heavy load, and if the advantage is insignificant and stateful beans are easier, use them.
Database Session State pulls the data needed for a request from the database at the start and saves it back at the end, requiring only a session ID (the keys) to be held on the client.

Because session data is local to a session and must not affect the rest of the system until committed, separate pending session data from record data, either via a session-ID/pending field (invasive, since every application must filter it out) or via separate pending tables cloned from the real tables (less invasive but adds table-selection logic), with pending tables also letting you defer integrity and validation rules.
Provide a mechanism to clean up cancelled or abandoned session data, using the session ID to find it plus a timeout daemon driven by a table tracking each session's last interaction.

Rolling back updates to existing record data within a session is hard, so one simple option is to disallow session cancellation and let updates to record data become permanent at the end of each request, which often fits users' expectations.

If pending tables are only read by the objects handling a session, there is little point in tabularizing the data, so use a Serialized LOB instead (which crosses into Server Session State); better still, where feasible design so all data is record data to avoid pending-data hassles entirely.

Database Session State enables stateless server objects (allowing pooling and easy clustering) at the cost of reading and writing data each request (caching reduces the read cost), and its clustering and failover are usually more straightforward than Server Session State's.

A Mapper is an insulating layer between subsystems that controls their communication without either being aware of it; since neither subsystem can invoke it directly, a third subsystem drives it or it observes events in one of them.

To decouple parts of a system choose between Mapper and Gateway: Gateway is far more common because it is simpler to write and use, so use a Mapper only when neither subsystem may depend on the interaction, typically a complicated and independent interaction such as a database (Data Mapper).

Use a Layer Supertype (a superclass for all objects in a layer, such as a Domain Object superclass) to hold common features like Identity Field handling without duplication, and use more than one Layer Supertype when a layer has more than one kind of object.

Use a Separated Interface to break a dependency that contradicts the general dependency structure by defining the interface in one package and implementing it in another, exploiting that an implementation depends on its interface but not vice versa, so other packages depend only on the interface.

Place a Separated Interface in the client's package when there is a single client or all clients share a package (making the client responsible for defining it), or in a third package when there are multiple clients or when the interface is not the client developers' responsibility.
An abstract class can serve as a good interface because it can carry common but optional implementation behavior.

Bind a Separated Interface's implementation through a separate factory (itself behind a Separated Interface) with a Plugin to defer the choice to configuration time, or more simply let a startup package that knows both interface and implementation wire things up.

Do not write a separate interface for every class, which is excessive for application development; use one only to break a dependency or to allow multiple independent implementations, since separating them later is a simple refactoring you can delay.
A Registry is a well-known, apparently global object used to find common objects and services when you lack an appropriate object to navigate from.
Design a Registry's interface separately from its implementation, preferring a static-method interface that is easy to find anywhere and can encapsulate delegation.

Represent monetary values with a dedicated Money class holding an amount and a currency, because money is not a first-class type and naive handling causes currency-mixing errors and lost pennies from rounding.
Store a money amount as an integral or fixed-decimal type and absolutely avoid floating point, which reintroduces the rounding errors Money exists to prevent.
Use distinct types for whole-unit money and fractional-unit money, since they behave differently under arithmetic, and make it clear which kind you are working with.
Because Money is a Value Object, override its equality and hash-code operations to be based on currency and amount.
Make money arithmetic currency-aware: treat adding monies of different currencies as an error, or use a money bag that holds multiple currencies in one object.

Allocating a sum across multiple places cannot use a general rounding scheme without losing or gaining pennies, so prefer an allocator function that distributes by ratios and scatters the remainder pennies, distinguishing proportional charge (use multiplication) from allocation (use an allocator).

Do not convert currency by simply multiplying by an exchange rate, because specific rounding rules (as for the fixed euro currencies) break that, so encapsulate the conversion algorithm in a convertor object.
Encapsulate currency-aware printing and parsing inside Money to ease user-interface and report display and input, leveraging the platform's globalization number formatters.

Store Money via Embedded Value (a currency per money), but when an account is single-currency you can store the currency on the account and pull it during mapping to avoid the overkill of repeating it on every entry.

Use a Money type for essentially all numeric calculation in object-oriented environments to encapsulate rounding and ease multi-currency work, since the common performance objection rarely matters and the encapsulation makes tuning easier.
Always question accessors on a Value Object, because there is almost always a way that does not break encapsulation (database mapping via Embedded Value being a rare unavoidable exception).

Enterprise systems often depend on problematic third-party services (credit scoring, tax, pricing) whose unpredictability slows development and, worse, can stop tests from running, which breaks the development process.
Replace a problematic external service during testing with a Service Stub that runs locally, fast, and in memory, to improve the development experience.

Define access to the service through a Gateway implemented as a Separated Interface (not a class) so you can have one implementation that calls the real service and at least one Service Stub loaded via a Plugin, and keep the Service Stub as simple as possible because complexity defeats its purpose.

When a dynamic Service Stub needs test-setup methods not on the Gateway interface, add those methods to the Gateway and make the real-service implementation throw assertion failures if they are called.
Use a Service Stub whenever dependence on a particular service hinders development and testing (Extreme Programming practitioners call this a Mock Object).

Data-aware UI tools make relational display and simple updates easy but provide no good place for business logic, which then gets jammed into stored procedures or mingled with UI code; a Record Set (an in-memory tabular structure that looks like a query result yet can be manipulated by other code) provides both.

A Record Set is usually provided by the platform (e.g., ADO.NET data set, JDBC row set), and disconnecting it from the data source lets you pass it across a network and serialize it as a Data Transfer Object.
A disconnected Record Set can act as a Unit of Work: modify it and return it to the data source to commit, with Optimistic Offline Lock checking for conflicts before writing.

Prefer an explicit, typed interface over an implicit one for Record Sets, because implicit interfaces (generic field-name access, or passing data in dictionaries) hide which fields exist and lose type information in statically typed languages; use strongly typed data sets (as in ADO.NET) or code generation for explicit Record Sets.

Use Record Set together with Table Module when your environment relies on the Record Set as its common data structure: fetch a Record Set, pass it to a Table Module to calculate derived information, to the UI for display and editing, back to the Table Module for validation, then commit the updates.
Guard against overly complex solutions during design, because excessive system complexity directly limits the ability to scale.
Overengineering takes two forms — exceeding the useful requirements of a product, and making a product overly complex — and the complexity form is the larger threat to scalability.

Test a design for excess complexity by having the engineer present it to engineering peers of varying experience; if any group cannot understand and re-explain it unassisted, treat the design as too complex.

A system can be overly complex in three ways: making the system work harder than necessary, making the user work harder than necessary, or making engineers work harder than necessary to understand it.
Do not build features that only a small fraction of users want.
condition: a feature is wanted by only a small fraction of the user base

statement: Simple, easy-to-understand systems are cheaper to maintain, faster to troubleshoot and restore, and let less-senior engineers contribute, which increases organizational scalability.
Apply the Design-Implement-Deploy (D-I-D) process: design for 20x capacity, implement (code) for 3x capacity, and deploy for roughly 1.5x capacity.
Designing and discussing how to scale is far cheaper than implementing it, so scale design (targeting 20x to infinite) should happen early and frequently at low engineering and asset cost.
In the implement phase, narrow the scale target to roughly 3x-20x current size and code the change about a month before the capacity is needed.
Deploy capacity just-in-time (days before demand) to avoid idle assets diluting shareholder value; keep roughly 1.5x peak for moderate growth and up to ~5x peak for hyper-growth.
condition: moderate-growth versus hyper-growth company

statement: Use the cloud for burst capacity rather than holding idle owned hardware for sudden demand.
Scale is elastic — capacity needs contract as well as expand — so solutions should be designed to flex in both directions.
Simplify a solution in three places: its scope, its design, and its implementation.
Simplify scope with the Pareto (80/20) principle: deliver the roughly 20% of features that produce ~80% of the value and cut the rest.
Cutting unnecessary features reduces dependencies between functions, which makes the system scale more effectively and cost-effectively.

Simplify implementation by reusing proven work: prefer widely-adopted open-source or third-party solutions, then an internally proven solution, then a legally-copyable external approach, and build your own only as a last resort.
The simplest implementation is usually one that has already been built and proven scalable.
Reduce the number of DNS lookups required to download a page, balanced against the browser's limit on simultaneous connections.
condition: web pages where performance matters

statement: Every distinct domain that serves page objects requires a DNS lookup (from cache or a name server), which can cost up to hundreds of milliseconds.
Reduce the number of objects on a page, since object count drives page download time, balanced against maximizing simultaneous connections.
