Passive sniffing aggregation manufactures logs from observed network traffic without reconfiguring publishers, but it requires a single egress monitoring point (rare in large or global topologies), cannot read SSL traffic, and silently drops logs under resource saturation — a bad idea when logs are vital.

Logging done right delivers all logs reliably in real-time, optionally to redundant servers, and turns the stream into operational business-level monitors (bounds on 500/404 rates, requests per second versus trend) that trigger immediately rather than from 24-hour roll-ups.
Support many log subscribers cheaply with reliable IP multicast (such as Spread), so adding subscribers does not require scaling up network infrastructure or bring the system to its knees.

Separate logging roles — web servers publish, log servers journal and retain, log monitors analyze and alert, casual monitors do ad-hoc inspection — so each role can have its own uptime, service level, and ownership.

A group-communication publish/subscribe substrate (such as Spread) makes log aggregation simpler and more elegant than batch, unicast, or sniffing approaches, needing only three components: a publication mechanism, a journaling subscriber, and the messaging substrate.
Keep the log-journaling component brain-dead simple (subscribe to groups, write messages to files), because simplicity makes it reliable and fast.

Do not let inertia or fear of code modification entrench the wrong technology — integrating a new approach is often an hour's work (such as a log4j-to-Spread bridge), and refusing it forfeits large advantages.
Routing logs through a publish/subscribe substrate instruments the whole architecture for performance assessment, debugging, monitoring, and auditing with little effort.

Build your own real-time web-cluster monitoring tools from the log stream, because web clusters lack the per-node real-time tooling (iostat, vmstat) that single systems have, and once the data is at your fingertips such tools are quick to write.
Log per-request service time, and per-statement database execution time, into the log stream so you can report average, minimum, and maximum latencies like iostat.

Keep your engineering-analytical thinking while taking a macroscopic business view: monitor technical business metrics (registrations, orders, click-through), because you uniquely see both technical and business metrics and the business reports already draw on your logs and databases.
Correlating business and technical metrics for a healthy system lets you recognize an unhealthy situation as it forms, using minute-level real-time trends.
Visualization is priceless for large datasets — graphs sharing a common time axis make cause-and-effect correlation across systems easy where raw numbers do not.
Set up metric collection before problems occur (as part of launching a service), not during troubleshooting, or you will have no historical baseline to compare against.

Choose the metric-collection interval from how long it takes to fully understand a graph (collect roughly twice that often); finer resolution is expensive and adds little, while multi-resolution retention (fine recent, coarse for years) covers history.
Metrics split into SNMP-queryable (easy — tools like Cacti auto-collect and auto-build the round-robin databases) and non-SNMP custom business metrics that need one-off collection scripts.
Maintain one-off custom collection scripts for non-SNMP business metrics — they are simple, similar to one another, and reusable across the organization.
Smuggle a custom field into an existing but unused log field (such as remote_user) so you add data without changing the log format or breaking existing parsers.

Define your metrics precisely and graph the right breakdown: a definition mismatch hid a problem (a 'hits up 2%' figure counted all log lines, not just 200 responses), and graphing by HTTP response code instantly exposed a 404 spike.
Centralized, remote logging gives a single audit portal and, critically, access to a misbehaving machine's logs even when the machine itself is unreachable.

Most development is feature design — adding to an already-designed application — which is the most common ground for mistakes; the core application should be designed once and well, since it is the basis for all later work.
Feature-design mistakes are smaller and easier to recover from than core redesign, but recognize bad design and refactor it, because death by pin pricks is a bad way to die.

Define the size and scope of the problem before building a solution — building first and sizing later wastes effort (a MySQL 'who's online' attempt reached only ~800 operations/second against a 9,000/second requirement).
Do not default to the tool that is already there (such as the site's RDBMS) merely because it is there; match the tool to the problem.

An RDBMS is the wrong tool when ACID is not needed — for a 30-minute 'who's online' view, durability, isolation, and multi-row consistency are irrelevant, so paying ACID's cost (full table scans, query-cache invalidation, sorts) is pure waste.

SELECT COUNT(*) and ORDER BY ... LIMIT can be far more expensive than they look: databases rarely keep accurate cardinality (so COUNT does real work), and a LIMITed top-N still fully sorts the resultset despite an index.

Never make a non-essential side task (such as view-tracking) synchronous with serving the request — if the side write slows, the whole site stalls; the right behavior is to serve slightly stale data while the back end catches up.

Process derived or auxiliary data passively from the already-flowing (free) log stream instead of synchronously in the request path, achieving near-real-time accuracy where the only failure mode under a surge is a small lag behind reality.
'Too slow' usually means 'inappropriate' — the tool is not necessarily slow, it is the wrong tool for the job.

For a hot in-memory lookup service, choose a platform that does not touch storage and whose data structures answer your exact questions cheaply (for example a purpose-built C service) rather than a general-purpose database.
Reuse infrastructure already privy to the needed data — a passive log subscriber that already receives all logs and supports loadable modules is a natural platform for a new log-driven service.

Do not be intimidated by bending tools to your will (poking a user ID into Apache's connection record, writing a PHP C extension to hook request shutdown); a working end-to-end prototype can take about an hour.
Use a compact binary protocol (length-prefixed fields in network byte order) for a fast internal service.
Eliminate expired data at maintenance time rather than at query time — pre-cull old entries (popping the oldest off a time-ordered index is O(1)) so queries never have to filter by age.

Choose data structures that answer your exact questions cheaply — for example a hash of URL counts plus a multi-indexed skiplist indexed exactly as the equivalent SQL (unique user ID, ordered hit-date, ordered URL-and-hit-date) — so an in-memory service mirrors the required access patterns.
Use C, or any language with cheap data management and granular control of data structures, for a performance-centric service that must sustain thousands of queries per second.
A non-blocking socket service must track partial-read progress per connection and resume when more data arrives (returning on EAGAIN).

Test against a dataset that fairly represents production, not arbitrary data; a passive, off-critical-path tracker can be tested on a fresh instance fed real production logs with almost no test-harness investment.
Warm the system up before measuring — a 30-minute activity window means realistic data exists only after 30 minutes of operation.

When performance is surprising, profile rather than guess: a 43 queries/second result was traced to Math::BigInt dominating, and passing the 64-bit ID as two 32-bit halves raised throughput to about 2,859 queries/second.

Test in the real deployment shape — run the client in parallel from many servers (eight nodes reached about 12,000 queries/second aggregate) — and aim for confidence rather than overengineering the test or chasing human-timing precision.

A service scales when it collects its information outside the critical service path (passive, log-stream-fed), so it can run on every web server without adding load to any other component — that, not raw per-box throughput, is the real testament to scalability.

Know your tools: understand the principles behind a tool's features to pick the right ones, weigh the cost of features you do not need (do not squash a mosquito with a cannon), and learn its quirks and caveats.

Use the group-communication paradigm for multi-party messaging where the participant set is small, identities matter, and members both send and receive; point-to-point among all participants is expensive and chaotic, while reliable IP-multicast fits a single sender broadcasting to many anonymous receivers.
A group-communication system provides group membership (the current member set plus join/leave notifications) and broadcast primitives characterized by reliability and ordering.
Message ordering guarantees are FIFO (per-sender order), causal (FIFO plus cross-sender happened-before), and total (all receivers see the same order).

Match the delivery guarantee to the need — the strongest guarantee (a SAFE/EVS delivery, given only once all daemons hold the message) is significantly slower than agreed or FIFO delivery, so do not use it casually.
Keep configuration identical across all nodes, because slightly different configs can leave daemons that appear healthy yet cannot communicate.

Use a publish-to-a-group messaging bus to decouple clients from servers: a client sends one message to the group and the bus reliably fans it out, so the client need not know or connect to each server individually (as in a distributed cache purge).

Match the consistency cost to the data's forgiveness — for cache-coherence purges, RELIABLE delivery suffices because a node that missed a purge (through a crash or partition) can simply clear its whole cache on restart and repopulate on demand, avoiding the expense of SAFE delivery and extra logic.

Diagnose messaging-substrate failures with raised debug verbosity, then revert; common failures are binding the wrong node name, a firewall blocking both the configured port and the port immediately above it, and multicast silently falling back to unicast (which then fails at three or more nodes).

Test application robustness against network faults by injecting artificial partitions (for example via spmonitor) and watch daemon health metrics (membership changes, retransmission counts) for signs of an unstable network.
Many hard problems in modern software architecture have no single best solution and instead present a collection of messy trade-offs that must be weighed case by case.
Data tends to outlive the systems and architectures that process it, so it warrants diligent design attention.
Modern architecture decisions increasingly hinge on data concerns: who can and should read data, who can and should write it, and how to separate analytical from operational data.
Trade-off decisions about data are made better by incorporating both an architecture-to-data and a data-to-architecture perspective.
Architects should treat trade-off analysis as a repeatable process, paying attention to the method used to reach the trade-offs rather than only the final answer.
Architects should not try to find the best design; they should strive for the least-worst combination of trade-offs.
The notion of a best design is misleading because best implies maximizing all competing architecture factors simultaneously, which cannot be achieved.
An architect's real job is to objectively determine and assess the set of trade-offs on both sides of a consequential decision and resolve it as well as possible.

No single technology or management technique by itself promises an order-of-magnitude improvement in productivity, reliability, or simplicity within a decade, so architects should not seek silver-bullet solutions.
Most architecture problems are novel to an organization's exact environment and circumstances, so prior blog posts or Stack Overflow answers rarely transfer directly.
Software architecture is the set of structural decisions that are hard to change later, so it should change much less than design because it provides the foundation.
This book deliberately focuses on how architects make decisions and weigh trade-offs rather than on technology or implementation details.
The software development ecosystem evolves unpredictably, with each new capability enabling further ones until the ecosystem replaces itself one piece at a time.
When evaluating an architecture style, especially a historical one, architects must consider the constraints in place at the time that made that style dominant.

Microservices became viable largely because infrastructure became operationally free, as tools like Puppet and Chef and later containers and Kubernetes let teams programmatically provision environments.
All software architecture ultimately serves data by ensuring the right data is available and usable across the enterprise.
Many data architects' instincts to build tightly coupled systems conflict with the needs of modern distributed architectures.
In microservices following the bounded-context idea, data and transactionality become architectural concerns because data moves inside the service boundary.
Operational data is the transactional OLTP data the business runs on (sales, inventory, transactions); interrupting it stops the organization from functioning.

Analytical data is used by data scientists and analysts for prediction, trending, and business intelligence; it is often non-transactional and not critical to day-to-day operation but drives long-term strategy.
Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) are an effective way to document an architecture decision, typically as a short one-to-two-page text file.
An ADR should capture Context (the problem and alternative solutions), Decision (the decision and its justification), and Consequences (results and trade-offs considered).
Documenting an architecture decision is a separate concern from governing the proper use of that decision.
Architecture governance is any organized oversight of aspects of software development, needed to ensure design principles become reality when the architect is not the implementer.
Manual governance such as code reviews and review boards is error-prone and lets important details slip through.
Automation and feedback are central tenets of effective software development, as shown by continuous integration in XP and later by DevOps.
An architecture fitness function is any mechanism that performs an objective integrity assessment of one or more architecture characteristics.
Architecture characteristics must be defined as objective, measurable values to be governed by fitness functions, so a goal like high performance must be expressed as a measurable threshold.

Architects should beware composite architecture characteristics such as agility that are not directly measurable, and decompose them into measurable contributors like deployability, testability, and cycle time.
The inability to measure an architecture characteristic often signals that its definition is too vague.
Fitness functions have two scopes: atomic, which handles a single architecture characteristic in isolation, and holistic, which validates a combination.
Holistic fitness functions validate a combination of interlocking architecture characteristics to ensure their combined effect does not harm the architecture.

Architecture characteristics can conflict or show synergy, so improving one may degrade another, for example improving security often affects performance and scalability can be at odds with elasticity.
Fitness functions validate architecture characteristics, not domain criteria, whereas unit, functional, and acceptance tests validate domain criteria.
To decide between a fitness function and a unit test, ask whether any domain knowledge is required to execute the test: if yes use a unit/functional/acceptance test, if no use a fitness function.
exception: The separation is not purely binary; some fitness functions touch the domain and vice versa.

statement: Arbitrarily importing classes or components across a codebase destroys modularity because a component cannot be reused without dragging its coupled components along, trending toward a Big Ball of Mud.
Code reviews catch structural governance problems too late in the development cycle to reliably prevent architectural decay.
Architects should automate prevention of component cycles with a fitness function wired into the continuous build, for example using a dependency tool that fails the build when cycles exist.
Fitness functions can govern macro structure such as layered-architecture access rules, for example using ArchUnit or NetArchTest to forbid disallowed cross-layer dependencies.
An objective fitness-function outcome need not be static; dynamic fitness functions return context-based values, such as allowing performance per user to decline gradually as concurrent users rise.
Most fitness functions should be automated and run continually, but some must be manual, such as a legal review of sensitive changes; a validation that does not run validates nothing.

Giving each team's deployment pipeline a shared governance slot lets a security team universally automate checks and respond to a zero-day exploit by failing builds that contain a dangerous framework version.
Manual security and governance processes are error-prone and let affected systems escape detection, as in the Equifax breach where a known Struts vulnerability went unpatched on many systems.
Architects should not overuse fitness functions; they should serve as an executable checklist of important-but-not-urgent principles rather than an ivory-tower set that frustrates developers.
Codifying quality, structure, and safeguard rules as continually-running fitness functions prevents the we-will-fix-it-later slippage that is a frequent cause of technical debt.
Architects should keep architecture and design separate and understand why a choice has better trade-offs before how to implement it, reflecting the rule that why is more important than how.
Two artifacts, including services, are coupled if a change in one might require a change in the other to maintain proper functionality.
A service is a cohesive collection of functionality deployed as an independent executable.
A component is an architectural building block providing a business or infrastructure function, usually manifested as a package, namespace, or directory grouping of source files.
Communication is synchronous when the caller must wait for the response before proceeding, and asynchronous when the caller does not wait and may be notified later through a separate channel.
A workflow is orchestrated when a dedicated service coordinates it, and choreographed when no orchestrator exists and the participating services share coordination responsibility.
A workflow is atomic if all of its parts maintain a consistent state at all times, in contrast to the spectrum of eventual consistency.
A contract is the interface anywhere two software parts join, including method calls, remote integration calls, and dependencies.

Abstract architecture concepts should be grounded against a concrete running example, and that example should start from an existing system because many real-world problems exist within existing systems rather than greenfield development.
A large monolith with reliability problems makes change slow and risky, where edits take too long and break other things and crashes take down all functionality at once.

When all components share a single database schema, breaking the application into a distributed architecture requires the architecture team to collaborate with the database team to decompose the data.
To understand trade-offs in distributed architectures, architects should pull the moving pieces apart and analyze them in isolation before putting them back together.

Coupling in architecture can be split into static coupling, which is how parts are wired together through dependencies and connection points, and dynamic coupling, which is how parts call one another at runtime.
Static coupling can often be measured at compile time because it represents the static dependencies within the architecture.
Dynamic coupling concerns the kind of runtime communication, the information passed, and the strictness of contracts between parts.

Generic advice to decouple as much as possible is harmful when taken to the extreme, because fully decoupled parts cannot communicate; coupling is not inherently bad and must be applied appropriately.
No single tool or approach such as sagas, an enterprise service bus, Kafka, or orchestration is a silver bullet for distributed architecture, and comparing them is often an apples-to-oranges mistake.
Architects struggle with granularity and communication decisions because no universal best practices apply to real-world complex systems, so trade-offs must be determined case by case.

Microservices complexity rose because modeling bounded contexts made transactionality a first-class architectural concern, since moving the database inside the service boundary turns data concerns into architecture concerns.
Trade-off analysis is a core skill modern architects must build because software architecture is the kind of problem you cannot simply Google an answer for.
Existing frameworks such as ATAM lack focus on the real problems architects face on a daily basis.

Architects should perform trade-off analysis in three steps: find what parts are entangled, analyze how they are coupled, and assess trade-offs by determining the impact of change on interdependent systems.
Under the simplest definition, two parts of a software system are coupled if a change in one might cause a change in the other.

An architecture quantum is an independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion, high static coupling, and synchronous dynamic coupling, a common example being a well-formed microservice within a workflow.
Static coupling represents how static dependencies such as operating system, frameworks, and libraries resolve within the architecture via contracts.
Dynamic coupling represents how quanta communicate at runtime synchronously or asynchronously, so fitness functions for these characteristics must be continuous and typically use monitors.
A monolithic architecture deployed as a single unit is by definition a single architecture quantum.
condition: The architecture is deployed as a single unit.

statement: The architecture-quantum boundary provides a common language that aligns architects, developers, and operations on a shared scope of coupling, behavior, and deployability.

Architecture quantum and its static coupling is one of the forces architects must weigh when choosing service granularity, alongside trade-offs like release cadence, affected services, and engineering practices.

Data-intensive applications are assembled from standard building blocks, each suited to one need: databases (store and later retrieve data), caches (remember results of expensive operations to speed reads), search indexes (keyword search and filtering), stream processing (asynchronous message handling), and batch processing (periodic crunching of accumulated data).

When no single tool can meet all of an application's storage and processing needs, decompose the work into tasks each handled by the tool best suited to it and integrate those tools with application code.
condition: a single tool cannot meet all the application's data needs

statement: When several tools are combined behind a service API, the application code becomes responsible for upholding the composite system's guarantees, such as keeping caches and search indexes in sync with the primary database and invalidating or updating them correctly on writes.
condition: multiple data tools are composed behind one service interface

statement: Reliability, scalability, and maintainability are the three concerns that matter in most data systems and should be treated as the primary goals driving design.
A fault is one component of the system deviating from its specification, whereas a failure is the system as a whole ceasing to provide the required service to users; the two are distinct.
Because the probability of a fault cannot be reduced to zero, design fault-tolerance mechanisms that prevent faults from escalating into failures rather than attempting to eliminate faults entirely.
condition: fault probability cannot be reduced to zero

statement: Deliberately inducing faults in a running system (for example by randomly killing processes, as the Netflix Chaos Monkey does) continually exercises the fault-tolerance machinery and increases confidence that real faults will be handled correctly.
condition: the system is designed to be fault-tolerant

statement: Many critical bugs in deployed systems trace back to poor error handling.

Prefer tolerating faults over preventing them, except where no cure exists; security breaches are such a case, because a compromise or leak of sensitive data cannot be undone, so prevention is the only option.
exception: no cure exists for the fault, e.g. a security compromise or data leak that cannot be reversed

statement: At datacenter scale hardware faults are routine: with hard-disk mean time to failure of roughly 10 to 50 years, a cluster of 10,000 disks should expect on average about one disk failure per day.

The traditional first response to hardware faults is component-level redundancy (RAID disk arrays, dual power supplies, hot-swappable CPUs, backup batteries and generators), which lowers the rate of single-machine failure but cannot by itself prevent all hardware-caused failures.

As an application spreads across more machines, the aggregate rate of hardware faults rises proportionally, and on cloud platforms virtual-machine instances commonly become unavailable without warning because the platforms prioritize elasticity over single-machine reliability.

Favor software fault-tolerance that survives the loss of entire machines, alongside or instead of hardware redundancy, because it enables rolling upgrades that patch one node at a time with no whole-system downtime, whereas a single-server system requires planned downtime to reboot.
condition: the system runs across multiple machines

statement: Hardware faults are largely random and independent across machines (with only weak correlations from common causes such as rack temperature), so a large number of hardware components failing simultaneously is unlikely.
Systematic software faults are correlated across nodes and harder to anticipate than hardware faults, so they tend to cause many more system failures than uncorrelated hardware faults.

Software bugs that cause systematic faults often lie dormant for a long time and are triggered only by unusual circumstances that violate an assumption the software made about its environment which was usually but not permanently true.

There is no single fix for systematic software faults; reduce them with many small measures: carefully examining assumptions and interactions, thorough testing, process isolation, allowing processes to crash and restart, measuring and monitoring behavior in production, and having the system continuously check its own guarantees and alert on any discrepancy.
In one study of large internet services, configuration errors by operators were the leading cause of outages, while hardware faults played a role in only 10-25% of outages.

Minimize opportunities for human error by designing abstractions, APIs, and admin interfaces that make the right thing easy and the wrong thing discouraged, but avoid making them so restrictive that people work around them and negate the benefit.
exception: interfaces that are too restrictive, which people then circumvent

statement: Decouple the places where people make the most mistakes from the places where those mistakes cause failures, for example by providing fully featured non-production sandbox environments where people can experiment safely with real data without affecting real users.

Test thoroughly at all levels, from unit tests through whole-system integration tests to manual tests; automated testing is especially valuable for covering corner cases that rarely arise in normal operation.

Enable quick and easy recovery from human error: make configuration changes fast to roll back, roll out new code gradually so unexpected bugs affect only a small subset of users, and provide tools to recompute data when an earlier computation turns out to be wrong.

Set up detailed, clear monitoring (telemetry) of performance metrics and error rates; it provides early warning signals, lets you check whether assumptions or constraints are being violated, and is invaluable for diagnosing problems when they occur.

Reliability matters even for noncritical and mundane applications because failures cause lost productivity, legal risk, lost revenue, and reputational damage; reliability may be deliberately sacrificed to cut development or operational cost, but only as a conscious, explicit decision.
exception: prototypes for unproven markets or very thin-margin services, where reduced reliability may be a conscious tradeoff

statement: Scalability is not a one-dimensional label, so calling a system simply scalable or not scalable is meaningless; instead frame it as concrete questions about how the system will cope if it grows in a particular way and how resources can be added to handle the added load.

Describe a system's current load with a small set of load parameters chosen to fit its architecture (for example requests per second, the read-to-write ratio, simultaneously active users, or cache hit rate), recognizing that the average case or a few extreme cases may dominate.

Twitter's scaling challenge for timelines came from fan-out (the distribution of followers per user), not from raw tweet write volume, which illustrates that the true load parameter may not be the obvious request rate.
When reads vastly outnumber writes, prefer doing more work at write time and less at read time, for example precomputing per-user results into a cache, so that the frequent read path is cheap.
condition: the read rate is much higher than the write rate

statement: Precomputing at write time shifts cost onto writes and can explode for high-fan-out entities (a single post by an account with tens of millions of followers becomes tens of millions of writes), so a hybrid that fans out for most entities but merges at read time for extreme outliers delivers more consistent performance.
condition: some entities have extremely high fan-out

statement: For batch processing systems the key performance metric is throughput (records per second or total job time), whereas for online systems it is response time (the time between a client sending a request and receiving the response).

Latency and response time are not the same: response time is what the client sees and includes service time plus network and queueing delays, while latency is the duration a request spends waiting to be handled.

Treat response time as a distribution of values to be measured rather than a single number, because it varies from request to request even for identical requests due to causes such as context switches, packet loss and TCP retransmission, garbage-collection pauses, and page faults.

Use percentiles such as the median (p50), p95, p99, and p999 rather than the arithmetic mean to characterize response times, because the mean does not reveal how many users actually experienced a given delay.

High-percentile tail latencies directly shape user experience and often hit the most valuable customers (those with the most data); Amazon specifies internal response-time targets at the 99.9th percentile and has observed that a 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by about 1%.
Optimizing very high percentiles (such as the 99.99th) often yields diminishing returns because they are dominated by random events outside your control, so the cost may not be worth the benefit.

Percentiles are used in service level objectives (SLOs) and service level agreements (SLAs) that define expected performance and availability and let customers demand remedies such as refunds when the agreed thresholds are not met.

Queueing delays (head-of-line blocking) account for much of the response time at high percentiles, because a server processes only a few requests in parallel and a few slow requests hold up those behind them; therefore measure response times on the client side.

When load-testing, the load-generating client must keep sending requests independently of response times; if it waits for each request to finish before sending the next, it artificially shortens the queues and skews the measured response times to look better than reality.

Tail latency amplification: when a single end-user request requires multiple backend calls, even made in parallel, the request waits for the slowest call, so even a small fraction of slow backend calls makes a much larger fraction of end-user requests slow.

Compute response-time percentiles efficiently over a rolling window using approximation algorithms such as forward decay, t-digest, or HdrHistogram, and never average percentiles to combine machines or reduce resolution; the correct way to aggregate response-time data is to add the histograms.

An architecture suited to one level of load is unlikely to cope with ten times that load, so on a fast-growing service expect to rethink the architecture on roughly every order-of-magnitude increase in load.

Scaling up (vertical, a more powerful machine) and scaling out (horizontal, distributing load across many machines in a shared-nothing architecture) are complementary, and good architectures usually combine them pragmatically rather than committing to one extreme.

Elastic systems that automatically add resources on detecting a load increase are useful when load is highly unpredictable, but manually scaled systems are simpler and have fewer operational surprises.
condition: load is highly unpredictable

statement: Distributing stateless services across machines is straightforward, but making a stateful data system distributed adds substantial complexity, so keep a database on a single node (scale up) until scaling cost or high-availability requirements force you to distribute it.
exception: scaling cost or high-availability requirements that force distribution

statement: There is no generic one-size-fits-all scalable architecture; a large-scale architecture is highly specific to its application and is built around assumptions about which operations will be common and which rare.

If the load-parameter assumptions behind a scalable architecture turn out to be wrong, the scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive, so in an early-stage or unproven product it is usually more important to iterate quickly on features than to scale for hypothetical future load.
condition: the product is early-stage or its load is unproven

statement: The majority of the cost of software lies in ongoing maintenance (fixing bugs, keeping it operational, investigating failures, adapting it, repaying technical debt, adding features), not in initial development.

Design software for three maintainability principles: operability (make it easy for operations to keep the system running), simplicity (make it easy for new engineers to understand by removing complexity, distinct from UI simplicity), and evolvability (make it easy to change the system for unanticipated future requirements).

Good operations can often work around limitations of bad software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations, so invest in operability: provide runtime visibility through monitoring, support automation and standard tooling, avoid dependence on individual machines, supply good documentation and a predictable operational model, give good overridable defaults, and allow both self-healing and manual control.

Complexity slows down everyone who works on a system and raises maintenance cost; its symptoms include an explosion of the state space, tight coupling of modules, tangled dependencies, inconsistent naming, performance hacks, and special-casing to work around problems elsewhere (a big ball of mud).

Complex software increases the risk of introducing bugs when making changes, because hidden assumptions and unexpected interactions are more easily overlooked; reducing complexity therefore improves maintainability, so simplicity should be a key design goal.

Complexity is accidental when it is not inherent in the problem the software solves (as seen by users) but arises only from the implementation; simplifying a system can remove accidental complexity without reducing its functionality.

Abstraction is one of the best tools for removing accidental complexity: a good abstraction hides implementation detail behind a clean facade, is reusable across many applications, and raises overall quality because improvements to the shared component benefit every user, though finding good abstractions (especially in distributed systems) is hard.

A system's requirements are very unlikely to stay fixed: new facts, unanticipated use cases, shifting business priorities, new feature requests, platform changes, regulatory changes, and growth all drive change, so design for change rather than assuming stable requirements.

Evolvability, the ease of modifying a data system to meet changing requirements, is closely linked to its simplicity and its abstractions: simple, easy-to-understand systems are usually easier to modify than complex ones.
The choice of data model profoundly affects both how software is written and how its builders think about the problem, so it is important to choose a data model appropriate to the application.

Applications are built by layering data models (application objects and APIs, then a general-purpose model such as JSON, relational tables, or a graph, then bytes in memory or on disk), where each layer hides the complexity of the layers below behind a clean model so different teams can work together effectively.

Every data model embodies assumptions about how it will be used: some kinds of usage are easy and some unsupported, some operations are fast and some perform badly, and some transformations feel natural while others are awkward.

In the relational model (Codd, 1970) data is organized into relations (tables in SQL), each an unordered collection of tuples (rows), and its goal was to hide the internal data representation behind a cleaner interface than earlier models exposed.

Relational databases generalized well far beyond their original business-data-processing scope to a broad variety of use cases, while successive rivals (the network, hierarchical, object, and XML database models) each generated hype but never lasted.

The main driving forces behind NoSQL adoption are the need for greater scalability than relational databases easily provide (very large datasets or very high write throughput), a preference for free and open source software, specialized query operations poorly supported by the relational model, and frustration with the restrictiveness of relational schemas.

Because different applications have different requirements, the best technology for one use case often differs from another, so relational and nonrelational datastores are expected to coexist, an approach called polyglot persistence.

Storing object-oriented application data in relational tables requires an awkward translation layer known as the object-relational impedance mismatch; object-relational mapping frameworks reduce the boilerplate but cannot completely hide the difference between the two models.

For self-contained, document-like data with one-to-many tree structure (such as a resume), a JSON or document representation has better locality than a normalized multi-table schema, because the whole record is fetched in one query instead of multiple queries or a multi-way join.
condition: the data is mostly self-contained with a one-to-many tree structure

statement: When a value meaningful to humans is referenced from many records, store an ID rather than duplicating the text: the ID never needs to change, the human-meaningful information lives in exactly one place, and duplicating it instead incurs write overhead and risks inconsistency; removing such duplication is the key idea behind normalization.

Normalization requires many-to-one relationships, which fit the document model poorly: relational databases make the needed joins easy, but document databases often support joins weakly or not at all, forcing you to emulate joins in application code and shifting that work from the database to the application.
condition: the schema is normalized and needs many-to-one relationships

statement: Even if an application initially fits a join-free document model, data tends to become more interconnected as features are added and many-to-many relationships emerge, so anticipate future joins when choosing a model.

The document model echoes the older hierarchical model (IBM IMS): both handle one-to-many relationships well but make many-to-many relationships difficult and lack joins, forcing developers to denormalize data or resolve references manually.

The network (CODASYL) model generalized the hierarchical model by letting a record have multiple parents, which allowed many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, but links were pointer-like and the only way to reach a record was to follow an access path from a root record.

Manual access-path selection in the hierarchical and network models made querying and updating code complicated and inflexible, because if you lacked a path to the data you wanted you had to change the access paths and rewrite the hand-written query code, making changes to an application's data model difficult.

The relational model lays all data out in the open as tables of rows with no access paths to follow, so you can read or insert any row matching an arbitrary condition without first arranging foreign-key navigation.

In a relational database the query optimizer automatically decides which indexes and join methods to use and in what order, so developers rarely manage access paths; declaring a new index makes existing queries use it without rewriting them, which makes adding new features easier.

A key insight of the relational model is that you build the general-purpose query optimizer once and every application using the database benefits; hand-coding access paths is easier for a single query but the general-purpose optimizer wins in the long run.

For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships relational and document databases are not fundamentally different: in both, the related item is referenced by a unique identifier (a foreign key in the relational model, a document reference in the document model) that is resolved at read time using a join or follow-up queries.

The main arguments for the document model are schema flexibility, better performance through locality, and closeness to the application's own data structures, while the relational model counters with better support for joins and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.

Use a document model when the data has a document-like structure (a tree of one-to-many relationships where the whole tree is typically loaded at once); shredding such a structure into multiple relational tables tends to produce cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code.
condition: the data is a document-like tree of one-to-many relationships loaded together

statement: A limitation of the document model is that you cannot reference a nested item directly but must address it by position (like an access path), though this is usually not a problem as long as documents are not too deeply nested.
exception: documents that are deeply nested

statement: Choose the data model by the shape of the relationships in the data: tree-structured or relationship-free data fits the document model, simple many-to-many fits the relational model, and highly interconnected data with common many-to-many relationships is most naturally modeled as a graph; there is no general best answer.

Calling document databases schemaless is misleading because the reading code assumes an implicit structure; the real distinction is schema-on-read (the structure is implicit and interpreted only when data is read) versus schema-on-write (the relational approach where the schema is explicit and the database enforces it on every write).

Schema-on-read is analogous to dynamic (runtime) type checking and schema-on-write to static (compile-time) type checking, and like that debate the enforcement of schemas in databases is contentious with no universally right answer.

To change a data format, a schema-on-read database lets you write new documents with the new fields and handle old ones in application code, while a schema-on-write database needs a migration; most relational systems run ALTER TABLE in milliseconds (MySQL is a notable exception that copies the whole table), but an UPDATE that rewrites every row is slow on any database, so a lazy default-and-backfill-at-read approach may be preferable.

Schema-on-read is advantageous when the data is heterogeneous (many object types not practical to give separate tables, or a structure controlled by external systems that may change), whereas when all records are expected to share the same structure an explicit schema is a useful mechanism for documenting and enforcing it.
condition: the collection holds heterogeneous records
exception: records are all expected to share the same structure

statement: The locality benefit of storing a document as one continuous string only applies when you need large parts of the document at once; the database typically loads the entire document even to read a small portion, and updates usually rewrite the whole document, so keep documents fairly small and avoid writes that increase their size.
condition: the application frequently needs large parts of a document at once

statement: Grouping related data together for locality is not unique to the document model; relational systems achieve the same effect, for example Google Spanner interleaving child rows within a parent table, Oracle multi-table index cluster tables, and the column-family concept in the Bigtable model used by Cassandra and HBase.

A declarative query language such as SQL, where you specify the pattern of the results you want rather than how to compute them, is preferable to an imperative query API because it is more concise, hides engine implementation so the database can introduce performance improvements without changing queries, and lends itself to automatic optimization and parallel execution; imperative code over-specifies order and is hard to parallelize.

The advantage of declarative over imperative specification also appears on the web: declarative CSS or XPath selectors automatically apply and stop applying as the matched state changes and let browser vendors improve performance without breaking pages, whereas imperative DOM manipulation in JavaScript is longer, more error-prone, and must be rewritten to use new APIs.

MapReduce is a low-level model between declarative and imperative in which query logic is written as map and reduce code snippets called by the framework; these functions must be pure (using only their input, performing no additional database queries, and having no side effects) so the database can run them anywhere, in any order, and rerun them on failure.

MapReduce queries require two carefully coordinated functions, which is often harder than writing one query and gives the optimizer fewer opportunities, so MongoDB added a declarative aggregation pipeline; this illustrates that a NoSQL system can end up accidentally reinventing SQL.

A graph data model consists of vertices (nodes/entities) and edges (relationships/arcs) and becomes the natural choice when many-to-many relationships are common and the connections in the data grow complex, whereas the relational model handles only simple many-to-many cases comfortably.
condition: many-to-many relationships are common and connections are complex

statement: Graphs are not limited to homogeneous data; an equally powerful use is to store completely different types of objects in a single datastore, as Facebook does with one graph whose vertices are people, locations, events, checkins, and comments and whose edges encode the relationships among them.

In the property graph model each vertex has a unique id, sets of incoming and outgoing edges, and a collection of key-value properties, and each edge has a unique id, a tail and head vertex, a label describing the relationship, and properties; this can be stored as two relational tables (vertices and edges) with indexes on both the tail and head vertex columns to traverse the graph in both directions.

The property graph model is flexible because any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex with no schema restricting associations, you can efficiently find a vertex's incoming and outgoing edges and traverse forward and backward, and using different edge labels lets you keep several kinds of relationships in one clean graph.

Graphs are good for evolvability: as features are added to an application, the graph can be extended easily to accommodate new data structures, for example by introducing new vertex and edge types without restructuring existing data.

Cypher and SPARQL are declarative graph query languages in which you specify the pattern to match (including variable-length traversals such as following an edge zero or more times) and the query optimizer automatically chooses the most efficient execution strategy, so you need not specify execution details.

Graph data stored relationally can be queried in SQL only with difficulty, because a relational query usually fixes its joins in advance while a graph traversal needs a variable number of joins; SQL:1999 recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE) can express variable-length traversal but far more clumsily than Cypher or SPARQL, illustrating that different data models suit different use cases.

The triple-store model is essentially equivalent to the property graph model: each fact is a (subject, predicate, object) triple where the subject is a vertex and the object is either a primitive value (so predicate and object act as a property key and value) or another vertex (so the predicate is an edge label, the subject the tail vertex, and the object the head vertex).

The triple-store data model is independent of the semantic web, which was overhyped in the early 2000s and has largely not been realized; triples can still be a good internal data model for applications even if you never publish RDF data.

Graph databases are not a re-emergence of the CODASYL network model: a graph database imposes no schema restricting which vertices can connect, lets you reach any vertex directly by id or index rather than only by traversing a fixed access path, leaves vertices and edges unordered, and supports high-level declarative query languages, whereas CODASYL required schema-restricted nesting, mandatory access-path traversal, maintained ordering, and imperative queries.

Datalog (a subset of Prolog) defines rules that derive new predicates from stored data or from other rules; because rules can be combined and reused across queries and built up a piece at a time, Datalog is less convenient for simple one-off queries but copes better when the data and queries are complex.

The two main NoSQL directions target opposite relationship profiles: document databases suit use cases where data comes in self-contained documents with rare relationships between documents, while graph databases suit use cases where anything is potentially related to everything; the relational model sits between, and each of the three is best in its own domain.

One data model can be emulated in terms of another (for example graph data represented in a relational database), but the result is often awkward, which is why specialized systems exist for different purposes rather than a single one-size-fits-all solution.

Document and graph databases typically do not enforce a schema, which makes it easier to adapt applications to changing requirements, but the application still assumes some structure, so the real question is only whether the schema is explicit and enforced on write or implicit and handled on read.

Some data needs fall outside all general-purpose database models and require specialized or custom systems, for example genome sequence-similarity search, petabyte-scale particle-physics analysis, and full-text search.

B-trees are the most widely used indexing structure and the standard implementation in almost all relational databases and many nonrelational ones; like SSTables they keep key-value pairs sorted by key, enabling efficient key lookups and range queries.

B-trees break the database into fixed-size pages (traditionally about 4 KB) read and written one at a time to match the disk's block layout, with pages referencing each other by on-disk address to form a balanced tree of depth O(log n) that typically fits in three or four levels, in contrast to log-structured indexes that use variable-size segments written sequentially.

A B-tree lookup starts at the root page and follows child references chosen by key-range boundaries down to a leaf page that holds the value inline or a reference to it; the number of child references per page (the branching factor) is typically several hundred, so few page reads are needed.

A B-tree write overwrites a page in place (so existing references remain valid), unlike append-only log-structured indexes, and operations that touch several pages (such as splitting an overfull page, which rewrites two child pages and their parent) risk leaving a corrupted index if the database crashes part way through.

To make a B-tree resilient to crashes, implementations commonly use a write-ahead log (also called a redo log): an append-only file to which every modification is written before being applied to the tree pages, so the tree can be restored to a consistent state after a crash.

In-place page updates in a B-tree require careful concurrency control (typically latches, which are lightweight locks) so concurrent threads do not see an inconsistent tree, whereas log-structured approaches avoid this because they merge in the background and atomically swap old segments for new ones.

Common B-tree optimizations include copy-on-write (writing a modified page to a new location with new parent versions instead of using a write-ahead log, which also aids concurrency control), abbreviating keys in interior pages to raise the branching factor and reduce depth, laying out leaf pages sequentially on disk for range scans, and adding sibling pointers between leaf pages for in-order scanning.

As a rule of thumb LSM-trees are typically faster for writes and B-trees faster for reads (LSM reads must check several SSTables at different compaction stages), but storage-engine benchmarks are workload-sensitive and often inconclusive, so you must test with your own workload to make a valid comparison.

Write amplification, where one logical write to the database causes multiple writes to disk over time (a B-tree writes to the WAL and the page and again on splits; an LSM-tree rewrites data during repeated compaction), has a direct performance cost in write-heavy applications because it consumes finite disk bandwidth, and it wears out SSDs, which can be overwritten only a limited number of times.

LSM-trees can sustain higher write throughput than B-trees, partly through sometimes-lower write amplification and partly by writing compact SSTable files sequentially rather than overwriting several tree pages (especially important on magnetic disks where sequential writes are much faster than random writes), and they compress better with lower fragmentation and storage overhead.

A downside of LSM-trees is that background compaction competes with ongoing reads and writes for limited disk bandwidth, so high-percentile response times can spike (B-trees are more predictable), and at high write throughput compaction may fail to keep up, causing unmerged segments to accumulate until the disk fills and reads slow down; since SSTable engines usually do not throttle incoming writes, explicit monitoring is needed to detect this.
condition: write throughput is high or compaction is not configured carefully

statement: An advantage of B-trees is that each key exists in exactly one place in the index (a log-structured engine may hold multiple copies in different segments), which makes B-trees attractive for strong transactional semantics because range locks for transaction isolation can be attached directly to the tree; there is no quick rule for which engine is better, so test empirically.

Beyond the primary-key index that uniquely identifies a row, document, or vertex, secondary indexes (created with CREATE INDEX) are often crucial for performing joins efficiently; their keys are not unique, which is handled either by storing a list of matching row identifiers per key or by appending a row identifier to the key, and both B-trees and log-structured indexes can serve as secondary indexes.

An index value can be the actual row or a reference to the row stored in a heap file (unordered storage); the heap file avoids duplicating data when several secondary indexes exist because each index just points at the one heap location, and in-place updates work when the new value fits, otherwise the record is moved and either all indexes are updated or a forwarding pointer is left behind.

A clustered index stores the indexed row directly within the index (for example InnoDB's primary key) and a covering index stores some of the table's columns so a query can be answered from the index alone; both speed up reads but, like any data duplication, require additional storage, add overhead on writes, and demand extra effort to preserve transactional consistency.

A concatenated index combines several fields into one key by appending columns in a specified order, so it can serve queries on a leading prefix of those fields (for example last name, or last name plus first name) but is useless for querying a non-leading field alone (for example first name only).

Querying several columns simultaneously (such as a geospatial range over latitude and longitude) cannot be answered efficiently by a standard one-dimensional B-tree or LSM-tree index; multi-dimensional indexes such as R-trees, or mapping coordinates through a space-filling curve into a regular B-tree, are needed, and the same technique applies to non-geographic ranges like color or (date, temperature).

Exact-match indexes cannot search for similar or misspelled keys; fuzzy and full-text search require different techniques such as synonym expansion, ignoring grammatical variants, proximity search, and matching within a bounded edit distance (for example Lucene's use of a Levenshtein automaton).

Disks are tolerated despite their awkward layout requirements because they are durable (contents survive power loss) and cheaper per gigabyte than RAM; as RAM gets cheaper and many datasets are not large, keeping data entirely in memory has become feasible, leading to in-memory databases.

In-memory databases that need durability achieve it with battery-backed RAM, by writing a change log to disk, by writing periodic snapshots, or by replicating in-memory state to other machines; the system is still in-memory because the disk serves only as an append-only durability log while reads are served entirely from memory.

The performance advantage of in-memory databases is not avoiding disk reads (a disk-based engine may never read from disk if memory is large enough, because the operating system caches disk blocks); rather, they are faster because they avoid the overhead of encoding in-memory data structures into a form that can be written to disk.

In-memory databases can also offer data models that are hard to implement on disk (such as Redis's priority queues and sets), and the anti-caching approach can extend them beyond available memory by evicting least-recently-used records to disk at record granularity, though the indexes must still fit entirely in memory.

A transaction is a group of reads and writes that form a logical unit and need not have ACID properties; transaction processing means allowing clients to make low-latency interactive reads and writes, as opposed to batch processing jobs that run only periodically.

Online transaction processing (OLTP) looks up a small number of records by key through an index and inserts or updates them from interactive user input, whereas online analytic processing (OLAP) scans a huge number of records reading only a few columns each and computes aggregates such as count, sum, or average to support business decisions rather than returning raw records.

OLTP and analytic (OLAP) systems differ across read pattern (a few records fetched by key versus aggregation over many), write pattern (low-latency user writes versus bulk ETL or event streams), users (customers via an application versus internal analysts), what the data represents (latest state versus a history of events), and dataset size (gigabytes-to-terabytes versus terabytes-to-petabytes).
SQL works for both OLTP and OLAP queries, but from the late 1980s companies began running analytics on a separate database called a data warehouse rather than on their transaction-processing systems.

OLTP databases are closely guarded for high availability and low latency, so administrators are reluctant to let analysts run ad hoc analytic queries directly on them, because those queries scan large parts of the dataset and harm the performance of concurrent transactions.

A data warehouse is a separate, read-only copy of the data from a company's OLTP systems that analysts can query freely without affecting OLTP operations; data is loaded by Extract-Transform-Load (extract via periodic dump or continuous stream, transform into an analysis-friendly schema, clean it, then load).

A key advantage of a separate data warehouse is that it can be optimized for analytic access patterns, because the indexing algorithms that work well for OLTP are not good at answering analytic queries; behind a common SQL interface, OLTP and warehouse systems increasingly use different storage and query engines.

Analytics uses far less data-model diversity than transaction processing; most data warehouses follow a star schema (dimensional modeling) with a central fact table whose rows are individual events and foreign keys to dimension tables that capture the who, what, where, when, how, and why of each event.
Capture facts as individual events to allow maximum flexibility of later analysis, accepting that the fact table can become extremely large (tens of petabytes at big enterprises).
A snowflake schema further normalizes dimension tables into subdimensions, but star schemas are often preferred because they are simpler for analysts to work with.

Most OLTP databases lay out storage row-oriented (all values of a row stored together), which is inefficient for analytic queries that touch only a few of a fact table's 100-plus columns, because the engine still loads, parses, and filters whole wide rows from disk.

Column-oriented storage stores all the values of each column together (often in separate files) so that a query reads and parses only the columns it uses, which saves substantial work for analytic queries; it relies on every column file holding the rows in the same order so a full row can be reassembled by taking the nth entry from each file, and it applies to nonrelational data too (for example the Parquet format).

Column data is often repetitive and compresses well; bitmap encoding turns a column with n distinct values into n bitmaps (one bit per row), and sparse bitmaps are further run-length encoded for very compact storage, which also makes common warehouse filters fast (WHERE col IN (...) becomes a bitwise OR of bitmaps, and conjunctions across columns become a bitwise AND).

The column families of Cassandra and HBase (inherited from Bigtable) are misleadingly named, because within a column family they store all of a row's columns together with a row key and do not use column compression, so that model is still mostly row-oriented rather than column-oriented.

Column-oriented storage also uses CPU cycles efficiently through vectorized processing: a chunk of compressed column data fits in the CPU's L1 cache and is iterated in a tight loop with operators working directly on the compressed chunk, so analytical databases optimize not only disk bandwidth but also main-memory-to-CPU bandwidth, branch prediction, and SIMD instructions.

A column store can impose a sort order to act as an index, but the data must be sorted an entire row at a time (never per column, or rows could not be reassembled); the administrator chooses the sort columns from knowledge of common queries, for example putting date_key first when queries target recent date ranges, with a second sort key ordering rows that tie on the first.

Sorting a column store also aids compression: when the first sort column has few distinct values it forms long runs of repeated values that run-length encode to a few kilobytes even for billions of rows, with the compression effect strongest on the first sort key and progressively weaker on later sort keys.

Because data must be replicated across machines for fault tolerance anyway, a column store (as in C-Store and Vertica) can store the same data sorted in several different ways so each query uses the sort order that best fits its pattern, unlike a row store whose secondary indexes only hold pointers to rows.

Column storage, compression, and sorting speed reads but make writes harder, because update-in-place is not possible with compressed columns and inserting into a sorted table would rewrite all column files; the solution is the LSM-tree approach of buffering writes in memory and merging them into the column files in bulk, with the query optimizer combining on-disk columns and recent in-memory writes transparently.
A materialized view caches the results of a query as an actual copy written to disk, in contrast to a virtual view that is merely a query shortcut expanded on the fly at read time.

A materialized view must be updated whenever the underlying data changes because it is a denormalized copy, which makes writes more expensive, so materialized views are rarely used in OLTP databases but can make sense in read-heavy data warehouses.
condition: the workload is read-heavy, as in a data warehouse
exception: write-heavy OLTP workloads, where the update cost outweighs the benefit

statement: A data cube (OLAP cube) is a grid of aggregates grouped by several dimensions; because the aggregates are precomputed, certain queries become very fast, but a cube cannot answer queries on attributes that are not among its dimensions, so warehouses keep as much raw data as possible and use cubes only as a performance boost for specific queries.

Storage engines split into OLTP-optimized engines (user-facing, huge request volume, each query touching a few records by key through an index, where disk seek time is the bottleneck) and analytics-optimized engines (low query volume but each scanning millions of records, where disk bandwidth is the bottleneck and column-oriented storage is an increasingly popular solution).

OLTP storage engines come from two schools: the log-structured school, which only appends to files and deletes obsolete ones but never updates in place (Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase, Lucene), and the update-in-place school, which treats the disk as overwritable fixed-size pages (B-trees, used in all major relational databases); the log-structured idea of turning random writes into sequential writes enables higher write throughput.
Understanding storage-engine internals lets an application developer choose the storage tool best suited to the application and reason about the likely effect of adjusting tuning parameters.

Forward compatibility means old code can read data written by new code, and backward compatibility means new code can read data written by old code; both are needed for evolvability so that different parts of a system can be upgraded independently rather than all at once.

In tag-based formats like Protocol Buffers and Thrift, every field added after the initial schema deployment must be optional or have a default value, because a new required field would break backward compatibility when new code reads data written by old code; forward compatibility holds because old code skips fields with tag numbers it does not recognize.

In tag-based formats you may only remove a field that is optional, never a required field, and you can never reuse a tag number, because data written somewhere may still include the old tag and must continue to be ignored by new code.

Changing the datatype of a field may be possible but risks losing precision or truncation; for example widening a 32-bit integer to 64-bit lets new code read old data, but old code reading a new 64-bit value into a 32-bit variable will truncate it if it does not fit.

Avro encodes data as concatenated values with no field or datatype identifiers, so it can only be decoded with a compatible schema; the writer's schema and reader's schema need not be identical because the Avro library resolves differences by matching fields by name, ignoring fields present only in the writer's schema and filling fields present only in the reader's schema from declared defaults.

To keep an Avro schema compatible you may only add or remove a field that has a default value: adding a field without a default breaks backward compatibility (new readers cannot read old data) and removing a field without a default breaks forward compatibility (old readers cannot read new data).

Avro does not make values nullable by default; to allow null you must use a union type (such as union{null, long}) and null is only a valid default when it is a branch of the union, which is more verbose but prevents bugs by making explicit what can and cannot be null.

In Avro, changing a field name is backward but not forward compatible (the reader's schema can list aliases to match an old writer's field names), and adding a branch to a union type is likewise backward but not forward compatible.

Because Avro data cannot be decoded without the writer's schema, the schema must be conveyed by context: include it once at the start of a large file (object container files), store a version number in each record plus a registry of schema versions (for databases), or negotiate the schema on connection setup (for RPC); a schema-version registry also serves as documentation and lets you check compatibility before deploying.

Avro is friendlier than Thrift or Protocol Buffers to dynamically generated schemas because it has no tag numbers: you can generate an Avro schema from a relational schema and regenerate it whenever the database schema changes, with fields matched by name, whereas tag-based formats need an administrator to assign and carefully never-reuse field tags on every schema change.

Code generation from a schema (Thrift, Protocol Buffers) is valuable in statically typed languages for efficient in-memory structures, compile-time type checking, and IDE autocompletion, but adds little in dynamically typed languages; Avro can be used with or without code generation, and its object container files are self-describing because they embed the writer's schema.

Schema-based binary encodings are a viable alternative to textual JSON, XML, and CSV: they are more compact because field names can be omitted, the schema is always-current documentation because it is required for decoding, a schema registry allows checking forward and backward compatibility before deployment, and code generation enables compile-time type checking; overall schema evolution gives schema-on-read-like flexibility plus better data guarantees and tooling.

Whenever you send data to a process with which you do not share memory (over the network or to a file) you must encode it as a sequence of bytes, and compatibility is fundamentally a relationship between the process that encodes the data and the process that decodes it.

Data flowing through a database needs both backward and forward compatibility, because during a rolling upgrade newer and older versions of the code access the database concurrently, so a value written by newer code may later be read by older code still running.

When older code reads, updates, and rewrites a record that contains a field it does not know about, it should preserve that unknown field intact; encoding formats support this, but you must take care at the application level because decoding a value into model objects and re-encoding them can silently drop unknown fields.

Data outlives code: a deployed application version can be replaced in minutes, but database contents remain in their original encoding for years unless explicitly rewritten, and migrating a large dataset is expensive, so most relational databases instead allow adding a nullable column without rewriting existing rows and fill in nulls when old rows are read; schema evolution then makes the whole database appear as one schema even though storage holds many historical versions.

An archival snapshot (for backup or loading into a data warehouse) is written once and is thereafter immutable, so it should be encoded consistently in the latest schema, and immutable formats such as Avro object container files, or an analytics-friendly column-oriented format like Parquet, are a good fit.

Unlike a database that allows arbitrary queries, a service exposes an application-specific API that permits only the inputs and outputs predetermined by its business logic, which provides encapsulation by letting the service impose fine-grained restrictions on what clients can and cannot do.

A central goal of a service-oriented or microservices architecture is to make the application easier to change by making each service independently deployable and evolvable, owned by one team that can release frequently without coordinating with others; this means old and new versions of servers and clients run simultaneously, so the data encoding must remain compatible across versions of the service API.

REST is a design philosophy built on HTTP principles (simple data formats, URLs to identify resources, and HTTP features for caching, authentication, and content-type negotiation) and has gained popularity for cross-organization integration and microservices, whereas SOAP is an XML-based protocol that avoids most HTTP features, carries a sprawling set of WS-* standards, depends heavily on tooling and code generation, suffers interoperability problems between vendors, and has fallen out of favor in smaller companies.

The RPC model tries to make a remote network call look like a local function call (location transparency), but this is fundamentally flawed because a network request is unpredictable and can be lost, can time out leaving you unsure whether it succeeded, can be silently duplicated by retries unless the protocol is idempotent, has much higher and more variable latency, requires all parameters to be encoded to bytes, and may cross language boundaries with mismatched types.
Do not try to make a remote service look like a local object, because it is a fundamentally different thing; part of REST's appeal is that it does not hide the fact that it is a network protocol.

Newer RPC frameworks (such as Finagle, Rest.li, and gRPC) are explicit that a remote request differs from a local call: they use futures or promises to encapsulate asynchronous actions that may fail and to combine parallel requests, gRPC supports streams of multiple requests and responses, and some provide service discovery so a client can locate a service's address.

A custom binary RPC protocol can outperform generic JSON-over-REST, but REST has significant advantages for experimentation and debugging (callable from a browser or curl with no code generation), universal language and platform support, and a vast tooling ecosystem, so REST predominates for public APIs while RPC frameworks focus on requests between services owned by the same organization within a datacenter.

For RPC evolvability you can assume all servers are updated before all clients, so you only need backward compatibility on requests and forward compatibility on responses, and the scheme inherits its compatibility properties from the underlying encoding format.
condition: servers are upgraded before clients

statement: Service compatibility is harder when RPC crosses organizational boundaries because the provider cannot force clients to upgrade, so compatibility must be maintained for a long time, perhaps indefinitely, often by running multiple versions of the API side by side; there is no agreed standard for API versioning (a version number in the URL or HTTP Accept header, or a per-client stored version, are common).

Asynchronous message passing sits between RPC and databases: it delivers a message to another process with low latency like RPC, but routes it through an intermediary message broker that stores the message temporarily like a database.

A message broker offers advantages over direct RPC: it buffers messages when the recipient is unavailable or overloaded (improving reliability), can redeliver messages to a crashed process (preventing loss), frees the sender from knowing the recipient's address (useful when cloud VMs come and go), can deliver one message to several recipients, and logically decouples sender from recipient.

Message brokers do not enforce a data model (a message is just bytes plus metadata, so any encoding can be used), and if the encoding is both backward and forward compatible you have the greatest flexibility to change publishers and consumers independently and deploy them in any order; a consumer that republishes messages must take care to preserve unknown fields.

The actor model encapsulates concurrency in actors, each typically representing one entity with private local state that communicates only by asynchronous messages, avoiding threads, locks, and deadlock; message delivery is not guaranteed, and distributed actor frameworks reuse the same message-passing across nodes, which makes location transparency work better than in RPC because the model already assumes messages may be lost.

Rolling upgrades, which deploy a new version of a service to a few nodes at a time, enable releases without downtime (encouraging frequent small releases over rare big ones) and reduce risk by allowing a faulty release to be detected and rolled back before it affects many users, but they require all data flowing through the system to be both backward and forward compatible because nodes run different versions of the code simultaneously.
