Among encoding formats, language-specific encodings are restricted to one language and often lack forward and backward compatibility, textual formats like JSON, XML, and CSV are widespread but vague about datatypes and have compatibility that depends on usage, and binary schema-driven formats like Thrift, Protocol Buffers, and Avro give compact encoding with clearly defined compatibility and useful schemas at the cost of not being human-readable.

The reasons to distribute a database across multiple machines are scalability (spreading data, read, or write load beyond what one machine can handle), fault tolerance and high availability (redundancy so the system survives the loss of a machine, the network, or a datacenter), and latency (placing servers near geographically distributed users).

A shared-memory architecture (scaling up) joins many CPUs, RAM, and disks under one operating system to act as a single machine, but its cost grows faster than linearly, a machine twice the size cannot necessarily handle twice the load because of bottlenecks, its fault tolerance is limited, and it is confined to a single geographic location.

A shared-disk architecture uses several machines with independent CPUs and RAM but a shared array of disks connected by a fast network; it is used for some data-warehousing workloads, but contention and the overhead of locking limit its scalability.

A shared-nothing architecture (scaling out) gives each node its own CPU, RAM, and disk and coordinates between nodes only in software over a conventional network; it needs no special hardware so you can use the best price-performance machines, can spread data across geographic regions to reduce latency and survive a datacenter loss, and is now feasible even for small companies on cloud virtual machines.

A shared-nothing distributed architecture demands the most caution from the application developer because the database cannot hide the constraints and trade-offs of distribution; it usually adds application complexity and can limit the expressiveness of the data models you can use, and in some cases a simple single-threaded program outperforms a cluster of over 100 CPU cores, so distribution should not be adopted reflexively.

Data is distributed across nodes in two complementary ways: replication keeps a copy of the same data on several nodes for redundancy and performance, and partitioning (sharding) splits a large database into subsets assigned to different nodes; they are separate mechanisms but often used together.

Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple networked machines for three reasons: to keep data geographically close to users and reduce latency, to keep the system working when some parts fail and increase availability, and to scale out the machines serving read queries and increase read throughput.

Replicating unchanging data is trivial; all the difficulty of replication lies in handling changes, and almost all distributed databases use one of three approaches to replicate changes between nodes: single-leader, multi-leader, or leaderless replication.

In leader-based replication one replica is the leader that accepts all writes to its local storage and streams the change log to its followers, which apply the writes in the same order; clients may read from the leader or any follower but may write only to the leader.

With synchronous replication the leader waits for a follower to confirm a write before reporting success, which guarantees the follower has an up-to-date copy, but means the leader must block all writes if that synchronous follower stops responding.

Making all followers synchronous is impractical because any single node outage would halt the whole system, so in practice a semi-synchronous configuration keeps one follower synchronous and the rest asynchronous (promoting another to synchronous if it fails), guaranteeing an up-to-date copy on at least two nodes.

Fully asynchronous leader-based replication lets the leader keep processing writes even when all followers lag, but if the leader fails unrecoverably any writes not yet replicated are lost, so a confirmed write is not guaranteed durable; this trade-off is nonetheless widely used, especially with many or geographically distributed followers.

A new follower can usually be set up without downtime by taking a consistent snapshot of the leader (ideally without a full lock), copying it to the follower, having the follower request all changes since the snapshot's exact replication-log position (such as a PostgreSQL log sequence number or MySQL binlog coordinates), and applying that backlog until it has caught up.

A follower recovers from a crash or network interruption by catch-up recovery: because it keeps a local log of changes received from the leader, on restart it knows the last transaction it processed and requests all changes since then, applies them, and resumes the live stream.

Leader failure is handled by failover: detect the failure (usually via a timeout because there is no foolproof way to tell what went wrong), choose a new leader (by election or an appointed controller, preferring the replica with the most up-to-date data, which is a consensus problem), reconfigure clients to the new leader, and ensure the old leader steps down to a follower if it returns.

Failover is fraught with hazards: with asynchronous replication the new leader may be missing the old leader's last writes and discarding them violates durability (and is especially dangerous when external systems are coordinated, as when reused autoincrement keys caused cross-store inconsistency at GitHub), split brain where two nodes both believe they are leader can lose or corrupt data, and the failure-detection timeout is hard to tune because too long delays recovery while too short triggers unnecessary failovers that worsen an already struggling system.
Because automatic failover is fraught with problems, some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually even when the software supports automatic failover.

Node failures, unreliable networks, and the trade-offs among replica consistency, durability, availability, and latency are fundamental problems of distributed systems, not incidental implementation details.

Statement-based replication (logging each write statement) can break down on nondeterministic functions like NOW() or RAND(), on order-dependent or autoincrementing statements, and on statements with side effects such as triggers, so other methods are now generally preferred unless transactions are required to be deterministic.

Write-ahead-log shipping replicates by sending the storage engine's low-level log of changed disk bytes to followers, which tightly couples replication to the storage format so leader and followers usually cannot run different software versions; this blocks zero-downtime upgrades that would otherwise upgrade followers first and then fail over.

Logical (row-based) log replication uses a row-level log of inserts, deletes, and updates that is decoupled from the storage engine internals, so it can stay backward compatible across database versions and storage engines (enabling zero-downtime upgrades) and is easier for external systems to parse, which is the basis of change data capture.

Trigger-based replication moves replication into the application layer using custom code run on writes, which provides flexibility (replicating only a subset of data, replicating across different kinds of databases, or applying conflict-resolution logic) at the cost of greater overhead and more bugs than the database's built-in replication.
condition: you need to replicate a subset, replicate across database types, or apply custom conflict resolution

statement: A read-scaling architecture distributes read-only queries across many followers to offload the leader, which suits read-heavy web workloads, but it realistically requires asynchronous replication, because synchronously replicating to all followers would make any single node failure or network outage halt all writes, and more nodes make such an outage more likely.
condition: the workload is mostly reads with a small fraction of writes

statement: Reading from an asynchronous follower can return stale data when the follower has fallen behind, so the same query against the leader and a follower may differ; this inconsistency is temporary and resolves once writes stop and the follower catches up, a property known as eventual consistency.

The word eventually in eventual consistency is deliberately vague: replication lag is usually a fraction of a second, but near capacity or during network problems it can grow to seconds or minutes, at which point the resulting inconsistency becomes a real problem for applications rather than a theoretical one.

Read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency guarantees that a user always sees their own submitted updates after reloading, while making no promise about other users' updates; it is needed because reading from an asynchronous follower immediately after a write can return stale data that looks to the user like their input was lost.

Read-after-write consistency can be implemented by reading anything the user may have modified from the leader (for example always reading a user's own profile from the leader), or by reading from the leader for a short window after the user's last update or while a follower's lag exceeds a threshold, or by having the client remember the timestamp of its last write and ensuring the serving replica reflects updates at least up to that timestamp.

Providing read-after-write consistency across a user's multiple devices is harder, because the last-write timestamp must be centralized rather than held on one device, and requests from different devices may be routed to different datacenters, so approaches that read from the leader may require routing all of a user's devices to the same datacenter.
condition: the same user accesses the service from multiple devices

statement: Monotonic reads guarantee that a user making several reads in sequence will not see time move backward (will not read older data after having read newer data); it is stronger than eventual consistency but weaker than strong consistency, and one way to achieve it is to route each user's reads to the same replica, chosen for example by a hash of the user ID.

Consistent prefix reads guarantee that if writes happen in a certain order, anyone reading them sees them in the same order, which prevents causality violations such as seeing an answer before its question; this is a particular problem in partitioned databases that lack a global write ordering, and it can be addressed by writing causally related writes to the same partition or by explicitly tracking causal dependencies.

When using an eventually consistent system, consider how the application behaves if replication lag grows to minutes or hours, and if that produces a bad user experience, design for a stronger guarantee such as read-after-write rather than pretending that asynchronous replication is synchronous, which causes problems later.

Handling replication-lag guarantees in application code is complex and easy to get wrong, which is why transactions exist: they let the database provide stronger guarantees so the application can be simpler, and the claim that distributed systems must abandon transactions for eventual consistency is overly simplistic.

Multi-leader replication lets more than one node accept writes, with each leader also acting as a follower to the other leaders and forwarding its changes to them; this overcomes single-leader replication's downside that all writes must go through one node that you might be unable to reach.

Multi-leader replication rarely makes sense within a single datacenter because its benefits seldom outweigh the added complexity, but it is reasonable for multi-datacenter operation, for clients that must keep working offline, and for real-time collaborative editing.
condition: the deployment spans datacenters, needs offline operation, or supports collaborative editing
exception: within a single datacenter, where it is usually not worth the complexity

statement: In a multi-datacenter deployment, a multi-leader configuration with one leader per datacenter outperforms single-leader on write latency (writes are processed locally and replicated asynchronously, hiding inter-datacenter delay), tolerates datacenter outages (each datacenter keeps operating and catches up later), and tolerates unreliable inter-datacenter links better because replication is asynchronous.

The big downside of multi-leader replication is that the same data can be concurrently modified on different leaders, producing write conflicts that must be resolved; because it is often a retrofitted feature with subtle pitfalls around autoincrementing keys, triggers, and integrity constraints, multi-leader replication is frequently considered dangerous and avoided when possible.

An application that must keep working while offline is essentially multi-leader replication taken to the extreme, where each device is a local leader accepting writes and an asynchronous sync process reconciles the devices, with replication lag possibly lasting hours or days depending on connectivity.

Real-time collaborative editing is a replication problem: locking the document before editing is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader, while making the unit of change very small and avoiding locks enables simultaneous editing but brings all the challenges of multi-leader replication, including conflict resolution.

In a single-leader database a conflicting second writer is blocked or aborted and retried, but in multi-leader replication both writes succeed and the conflict is detected only asynchronously later, when it may be too late to ask the user to resolve it; making conflict detection synchronous would forfeit multi-leader's main advantage of independent writes, so you might as well use single-leader.

The simplest and frequently recommended strategy for multi-leader conflicts is conflict avoidance: ensure all writes for a given record go through the same leader (for example routing each user to a home datacenter), so conflicts cannot occur; but this breaks down when the designated leader must change, such as after a datacenter failure or when a user relocates.
exception: the designated leader for a record must change, for example on datacenter failure or user relocation

statement: Every replication scheme must ensure all replicas eventually converge to the same final value, so because multi-leader replication has no defined ordering of writes, applying writes simply in the order each replica receives them would leave replicas in divergent, inconsistent states, which is unacceptable.

Convergent conflict resolution can be achieved by last-write-wins (picking the write with the highest unique ID or timestamp, which is popular but dangerously prone to data loss), by letting a higher-numbered replica win (also lossy), by merging the values, or by recording the conflict in an explicit structure that preserves all versions for later resolution such as prompting the user.

Custom conflict-resolution logic can run on write (a fast background handler that cannot prompt the user, as in Bucardo) or on read (all conflicting versions are stored and returned to the application on the next read for it or the user to resolve, as in CouchDB), and resolution usually applies at the level of an individual row or document rather than an entire transaction.

Custom conflict-resolution code is error-prone (Amazon's shopping cart once preserved added items but not removed ones, so removed items reappeared); research into automatic resolution includes conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) for sets, maps, and counters, mergeable persistent data structures using Git-like three-way merges, and operational transformation behind collaborative editors like Google Docs.

Conflicts can be subtler than two writes to the same field: for example a meeting-room booking system can produce overlapping bookings even when the application checks availability first, because two bookings made on two different leaders do not see each other.

A replication topology is the set of paths along which writes propagate between nodes; with more than two leaders the options include a circular topology (each node forwards to one other), a star or tree (a root forwards to the rest), and all-to-all (every leader sends to every other).

In circular and star topologies a write passes through several nodes, so to prevent infinite replication loops each write is tagged with the identifiers of all nodes it has passed through and a node ignores any change already tagged with its own identifier.

Circular and star topologies have a single point of failure because one failed node interrupts replication between the others until it is fixed (usually requiring manual reconfiguration), whereas a densely connected all-to-all topology is more fault tolerant because messages can travel along alternate paths.

All-to-all multi-leader topologies can deliver writes out of order when some links are faster than others, causing causality violations such as an update arriving before the insert it depends on; timestamps cannot fix this because clocks are not sufficiently synchronized, so version vectors are needed, and because conflict detection is poorly implemented in many multi-leader systems you should read the documentation and test the guarantees thoroughly.

Leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication, used by Riak, Cassandra, and Voldemort, abandons the leader and lets any replica accept writes directly from clients; there is no failover, so a client sends each write to all replicas in parallel and considers it successful once a configured number acknowledge, and sends reads to several nodes in parallel, using version numbers to pick the newest value.

A leaderless replica that missed writes while down catches up through read repair (a parallel read detects a stale replica and writes the newer value back, which works only for frequently read values) and an anti-entropy background process (which copies missing data between replicas in no particular order); without anti-entropy, rarely read values can be missing from replicas and so have reduced durability.

In a quorum, with n replicas a write must be acknowledged by w nodes and a read must query r nodes, and if w + r > n the read and write node sets overlap so at least one read node holds the latest value; a common choice is an odd n with w = r = (n+1)/2.

The quorum parameters w and r are tunable trade-offs: setting them below n keeps reads or writes available when nodes are down (n=3,w=2,r=2 tolerates one failure), while a read-heavy workload might set w=n and r=1 for fast reads at the cost that a single failed node blocks all writes; if fewer than w or r nodes are available the operation returns an error.

Even with w + r > n, quorums do not absolutely guarantee a fresh read: stale values can still be returned with sloppy quorums (no guaranteed read-write overlap), with concurrent writes (which must be merged, since last-write-wins loses data to clock skew), when a write overlaps a read, when a partially failed write is not rolled back, or when a node restored from an old replica drops the new value below w, so treat w and r as knobs on the probability of staleness rather than as absolute guarantees.

Leaderless quorum replication usually does not provide the read-your-writes, monotonic-reads, or consistent-prefix-reads guarantees, so those anomalies can occur in applications; obtaining stronger guarantees generally requires transactions or consensus.

Monitor replica staleness even when the application tolerates stale reads, alerting when replication falls significantly behind; leader-based systems can expose replication lag by comparing each follower's log position to the leader's, but leaderless systems lack a fixed write order which makes monitoring harder, and read-repair-only systems can return arbitrarily old values for rarely read keys, so quantifying eventual consistency matters for operability.

A sloppy quorum accepts the required w or r responses from reachable nodes that are not among a value's designated n home nodes during a network interruption, then forwards those writes to the home nodes once it heals (hinted handoff); this increases write availability but means that even with w + r > n a read may not see the latest value, so it is really only a durability assurance rather than a true quorum.

Leaderless replication supports multi-datacenter operation because it is designed to tolerate concurrent writes, network interruptions, and latency spikes: the replica count n can span datacenters while a client typically waits only for a quorum of nodes in its local datacenter, with higher-latency writes to other datacenters happening asynchronously.

Because leaderless databases let several clients write the same key concurrently, conflicts occur even with strict quorums (and also during read repair or hinted handoff), and since events arrive in different orders at different nodes due to variable delays, naively overwriting on each received write would leave the replicas permanently inconsistent.

Most database implementations handle concurrent-write conflicts poorly, so to avoid losing data the application developer must understand the internals of the database's conflict handling rather than assuming the database resolves conflicts correctly on its own.

Last-write-wins forces an arbitrary order on concurrent writes by keeping the one with the highest timestamp and discarding the rest, which achieves convergence but sacrifices durability because concurrent writes all reported successful are silently dropped except one and clock skew can even drop non-concurrent writes; it is acceptable for caching but a poor choice when data loss is unacceptable, and is safe only if each key is written once and treated as immutable (for example using a UUID key).
exception: caching or other contexts where lost writes are acceptable

statement: Operation A happens before operation B if B knows about, depends on, or builds upon A, and two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other; the later of two ordered operations should overwrite the earlier, while two concurrent operations constitute a conflict that must be resolved.

Concurrency does not require operations to overlap in physical time: two operations are concurrent whenever each is unaware of the other, regardless of when they occurred, because distributed-system clocks cannot reliably establish simultaneity and network delays can leave time-separated operations unaware of each other.

A server can detect concurrency using per-key version numbers: it increments the version on each write, returns all not-yet-overwritten values plus the latest version on a read, and requires a client to read before writing and to include the prior version and a merge of the values it read; on receiving a write the server overwrites all values at or below that version but keeps higher-versioned values as concurrent, and a write with no version number is concurrent with everything and overwrites nothing.

The version-number algorithm drops no data but requires clients to merge concurrently written values (which Riak calls siblings); merging is the same problem as multi-leader conflict resolution, and since last-write-wins loses data you may need more intelligent merge logic in application code.

Merging siblings by taking their union works for add-only data like a shopping cart, but if items can be removed, a plain union resurrects removed items, so the system must leave a deletion marker (a tombstone) with an appropriate version number rather than truly deleting the item, so removals survive the merge.
condition: the data allows removals, not only additions

statement: Because merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone, conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) such as those in Riak can merge concurrent values automatically in sensible ways, including correctly preserving deletions.

With multiple leaderless replicas a single version number per key is insufficient; instead each replica keeps a version number per key and tracks the versions it has seen from every other replica, and this collection across replicas (a version vector, sent to clients on reads and returned on writes) lets the database distinguish overwrites from concurrent writes and makes it safe to read from one replica and write to another, creating siblings but losing no data when they are merged correctly.

Single-leader replication is popular because it is easy to understand and needs no conflict resolution, whereas multi-leader and leaderless replication are more robust to faulty nodes, network interruptions, and latency spikes but are harder to reason about and provide only weak consistency guarantees.

When a single machine cannot hold a very large dataset or sustain a high query throughput, the data must be broken into partitions (sharding), where normally each record belongs to exactly one partition and each partition is effectively a small database of its own; the main motivation is scalability, distributing data across many disks and query load across many processors in a shared-nothing cluster.

Partitioning is usually combined with replication so that copies of each partition live on multiple nodes; a node may hold several partitions, acting as leader for some and follower for others, and the choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme.

The goal of partitioning is to spread data and query load evenly across nodes; uneven distribution is called skew, and a partition with disproportionately high load is a hot spot that undermines partitioning by concentrating load on one node while others sit idle.
Assigning records to nodes at random avoids hot spots but makes it impossible to know which node holds a given item without querying all nodes in parallel, so a smarter partitioning scheme is needed.

Key-range partitioning assigns each partition a contiguous range of keys with boundaries that adapt to the data distribution (set manually or automatically) and keeps keys sorted within a partition, which makes range scans and concatenated-index lookups easy; its downside is that some access patterns create hot spots (for example a timestamp key sends all of today's writes to one partition), which can be mitigated by prefixing the key with another field at the cost of needing a separate range query per prefix.

Hash partitioning applies a hash function (which need not be cryptographically strong, though language built-in hashes that vary across processes are unsuitable) to spread even skewed keys uniformly, assigning each partition a range of hash values; it distributes load fairly (and is called consistent hashing when boundaries are pseudorandom) but loses the ability to do efficient range queries.

Consistent hashing (Karger's CDN load-distribution scheme with random partition boundaries to avoid central coordination) actually works poorly for databases and is rarely used; the term is confusing and unrelated to replica or ACID consistency, so it is clearer to call the technique hash partitioning.

Cassandra compromises between key-range and hash partitioning with a compound primary key whose first column is hashed to choose the partition while the remaining columns form a concatenated sorted index, so you cannot range-query the first column but, with the first column fixed, you can efficiently range-scan the others, which elegantly models one-to-many data such as (user_id, timestamp) to fetch a user's updates in a time range on a single partition.

Hashing a key reduces but cannot eliminate hot spots, because if all reads and writes target the same key (such as a celebrity's user ID) the identical hash routes everything to one partition; most systems cannot auto-compensate, so the application must reduce the skew, for example by appending a random suffix to a known-hot key to split it across many keys at the cost of reads having to combine all those keys and bookkeeping which keys are split.
condition: a small number of keys carry disproportionately high load

statement: Secondary indexes do not map neatly to partitions, and there are two main approaches to partitioning them: document-based (local) indexes and term-based (global) indexes.

A document-partitioned (local) secondary index has each partition index only its own documents, so writes touch just one partition, but a query on the index must scatter/gather across all partitions because matching documents are not co-located, which is widely used yet prone to tail-latency amplification; vendors recommend structuring partitions so an index query can be served from one partition, though that is not always possible.

A term-partitioned (global) secondary index covers all partitions and is itself partitioned by term (by the term value for range scans or by a hash of the term for even load), which makes reads efficient because a query hits only the partition holding the term, but makes writes slower and more complex because one document's terms may span many index partitions; keeping it synchronous would require a distributed transaction, so global index updates are often asynchronous.

Rebalancing moves data and requests between nodes when query throughput grows, the dataset grows, or a machine fails, and regardless of scheme it should leave load fairly shared, keep the database serving reads and writes throughout, and move no more data than necessary to stay fast and limit I/O.
Do not assign keys to nodes with hash mod N, because when the node count N changes most keys must move between nodes, making rebalancing excessively expensive.

A fixed-partition rebalancing scheme creates many more partitions than nodes and assigns several to each node, so adding or removing a node only moves whole partitions (the partition count and key-to-partition mapping stay fixed, only partition-to-node assignment changes, and the old assignment serves requests during transfer) and powerful nodes can be given more partitions; the fixed count caps the maximum number of nodes and must be chosen high enough for growth but not so high that per-partition overhead dominates.

Dynamic partitioning, used by key-range databases like HBase and RethinkDB, splits a partition when it exceeds a configured size and merges it when it shrinks, so the number of partitions adapts to the data volume; a caveat is that an empty database starts with a single partition so one node handles all early writes, which is mitigated by pre-splitting when the key distribution is known.

Partitioning proportionally to nodes, as in Cassandra and Ketama, keeps a fixed number of partitions per node so each partition's size stays stable as both data and nodes grow, with a new node randomly splitting some existing partitions and taking half of each; this requires hash-based partitioning and corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing.

Fully automatic rebalancing reduces operational work but is unpredictable and dangerous when combined with automatic failure detection, because a temporarily slow overloaded node can be declared dead and trigger a rebalance that adds load and causes cascading failure, so keeping a human in the loop is slower but helps prevent operational surprises.

Routing a client request to the partition holding a key is an instance of service discovery, addressed in three ways: clients contact any node which forwards as needed, a partition-aware routing tier forwards requests, or partition-aware clients connect directly; the core challenge in all three is propagating changes in the partition-to-node assignment so every participant agrees.

Many distributed data systems use a coordination service such as ZooKeeper as the authoritative map of partitions to nodes that routers and clients subscribe to (as in HBase, SolrCloud, Kafka, and Espresso via Helix), while Cassandra and Riak instead use a gossip protocol among nodes, which adds node complexity but avoids an external dependency; client IP addresses change slowly enough that DNS usually suffices.

Massively parallel processing (MPP) relational databases used for analytics support far richer queries than single-key NoSQL stores: the MPP query optimizer breaks a complex query of joins, filters, grouping, and aggregation into execution stages and partitions that run in parallel across cluster nodes, which especially benefits queries that scan large parts of the dataset.

A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit that executes all-or-nothing (it either commits or aborts and rolls back, after which it is safe to retry), which simplifies application error handling by removing the need to reason about partial failure; transactions are not a law of nature but were deliberately created to simplify the programming model.

Not every application needs transactions, and weakening or abandoning transactional guarantees can buy higher performance or availability while some safety properties are achievable without transactions, so decide whether you need them by understanding exactly what guarantees they provide and what they cost.

Both the claim that transactions are the antithesis of scalability and the claim that transactions are essential for any serious application are hyperbole; like every technical design choice, transactions have both advantages and limitations that must be weighed.

The transaction safety guarantees are summarized as ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability), but one database's implementation differs from another's (the meaning of isolation in particular is ambiguous), so an ACID-compliant claim does not tell you what guarantees to expect and the term has become largely a marketing label, while BASE is even vaguer and effectively just means not ACID.

ACID atomicity is not about concurrency but about fault handling: if a fault occurs partway through a transaction's writes, the aborted transaction discards or undoes all writes it has made so far, giving an all-or-nothing guarantee so the application can safely retry without risking duplicate or partial data; a more accurate name would be abortability.

ACID consistency is an application-specific notion that certain invariants about the data stay true, and it is the application's responsibility to define transactions that preserve those invariants; the database cannot guarantee it in general (it can only enforce specific constraints like foreign keys or uniqueness), so consistency is really a property of the application rather than of the database.

ACID isolation means concurrently executing transactions do not interfere with each other, formalized as serializability where each transaction behaves as if it were the only one running and the committed result is as if they ran serially; but serializable isolation is rarely used because of its performance penalty (for example Oracle's serializable level actually implements the weaker snapshot isolation).

ACID durability is the promise that once a transaction commits its data will survive a hardware fault or crash, implemented on a single node by writing to nonvolatile storage plus a write-ahead log and in a replicated database by copying to some number of nodes, with the database waiting for those writes or replications to complete before reporting the commit as successful.

Perfect durability does not exist and no single technique provides absolute guarantees: disk-only data is inaccessible if the machine dies, correlated faults can knock out all replicas, asynchronous replication can lose recent writes, SSDs can violate fsync on power loss, firmware and filesystem bugs can corrupt files, silent corruption can spread to replicas and backups, and many SSDs develop bad blocks within a few years, so combine writing to disk, replication, and backups and treat any guarantee skeptically.

Multi-object transactions are needed when several pieces of data must stay in sync, such as a denormalized unread-message counter alongside the messages themselves: isolation prevents another transaction from reading a half-updated state (a dirty read) and atomicity prevents the pieces from being left out of sync if an error occurs partway through.

Multi-object transactions need a way to group which operations belong together: relational databases typically use the client's TCP connection (everything between BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT), which is imperfect because a dropped connection after a commit request leaves the client unsure whether it committed, whereas many nonrelational databases lack grouping entirely, so even a multi-key operation may succeed for some keys and fail for others, leaving partial state.

Storage engines almost universally provide atomicity and isolation at the level of a single object on one node (atomicity through a crash-recovery log and isolation through a per-object lock), so an interrupted or partial single-object write is never visible to readers.

Single-object atomic operations such as increment and compare-and-set avoid read-modify-write race conditions and can prevent lost updates, but they are not transactions in the usual sense of grouping multiple operations on multiple objects, so marketing them as lightweight transactions or ACID is misleading.

Multi-object transactions coordinate writes across several objects: they keep relational foreign-key references (and graph edges) valid, keep denormalized data in sync when one logical change spans several documents, and keep secondary indexes consistent so a record cannot appear in one index but not another; an application can run without transactions, but error handling becomes much harder and the lack of isolation causes concurrency problems.

A key feature of a transaction is that it can be aborted and safely retried after an error, and ACID databases follow the philosophy of abandoning a transaction entirely rather than leaving it half-finished, whereas leaderless-replication datastores work on a best-effort basis that does not undo what it has already done, leaving error recovery to the application.

Retrying an aborted transaction is simple and effective but imperfect: a commit whose acknowledgment is lost in the network causes the work to be done twice unless there is application-level deduplication, retrying on overload makes it worse (so limit retries and use exponential backoff), only transient errors are worth retrying (not permanent ones like constraint violations), side effects outside the database such as sending email may repeat (use two-phase commit to commit across systems), and a client that dies while retrying loses its write.

Concurrency bugs are hard to find by testing because they depend on unlucky timing that is rare and hard to reproduce, and hard to reason about in a large application, which is why databases hide concurrency from developers by providing transaction isolation.

Serializable isolation makes transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, but it carries a performance cost that many databases avoid by using weaker isolation levels that protect against some concurrency issues but not all, which are harder to understand and can lead to subtle bugs.

Concurrency bugs from weak isolation are real, having caused financial loss, audits, and data corruption, and the advice to just use an ACID database misses the point because many relational databases considered ACID use weak isolation by default, so you should understand the concurrency problems that exist and how to prevent them rather than blindly trusting the tools.
Read committed, the most basic isolation level, makes two guarantees: no dirty reads (you only see data that has been committed) and no dirty writes (you only overwrite data that has been committed).

Preventing dirty reads stops other transactions from seeing a partially updated multi-object state or data that is later rolled back, and preventing dirty writes stops conflicting writes from different transactions being mixed up (such as a car sale awarded to one buyer but invoiced to another), but read committed does not prevent the lost-update race because the second write occurs after the first transaction has already committed.

Read committed is usually implemented by preventing dirty writes with row-level locks held until commit or abort, but it does not prevent dirty reads with read locks (a long write would block many readers and harm response time and operability) and instead remembers both the old committed value and the new uncommitted value, serving readers the old value until the write commits.

Read committed still permits read skew (a nonrepeatable read), where a query running during a transfer sees one account before the change and another after it and so observes an inconsistent total; this is considered acceptable under read committed because each value read was committed at the time it was read.

Read skew is intolerable for operations that read large parts of the database over time, such as backups (where parts copied before and after a change make the inconsistency permanent on restore) and long-running analytic queries or integrity checks (which return nonsensical results when they observe the database at different points in time).

Snapshot isolation has each transaction read from a consistent snapshot of all data committed at the moment the transaction started, unaffected by later changes, which is a boon for long-running read-only queries such as backups and analytics because the data they operate on does not change underneath them.

Snapshot isolation is implemented with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC): write locks prevent dirty writes but reads take no locks, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers, and the database keeps several committed versions of each object so in-progress transactions can see the state at different points in time (read committed using a fresh snapshot per query, snapshot isolation one snapshot per transaction).

In MVCC, each transaction gets an increasing transaction ID and rows are tagged with the IDs that created and deleted them; an object is visible to a reader only if its creating transaction had committed before the reader started and it is either not deleted or was deleted by a transaction that had not committed before the reader started, so writes by in-progress, aborted, or later transactions are ignored, giving a consistent snapshot at small overhead by never updating in place.

Isolation-level names are unreliable: snapshot isolation is called serializable in Oracle and repeatable read in PostgreSQL and MySQL, and because the SQL standard's definition of isolation levels is ambiguous and flawed, databases claiming repeatable read provide widely differing guarantees, so the name alone does not tell you what protection you get.

The lost-update problem occurs when two transactions concurrently run a read-modify-write cycle and the later write clobbers the earlier one (as in concurrent counter increments, edits to a list inside a JSON document, or two users saving an entire wiki page), and neither read committed nor snapshot isolation prevents it.

Atomic write operations such as an in-database increment, MongoDB's local document updates, or Redis data-structure operations remove the need for a read-modify-write cycle and are usually the best solution against lost updates when the change can be expressed that way (implemented via an exclusive lock taken on read, called cursor stability, or single-threaded execution), but object-relational mapping frameworks make it easy to accidentally write unsafe read-modify-write code instead.
condition: the update can be expressed as a built-in atomic operation

statement: When a database's built-in atomic operations are insufficient (for example a move that must also obey application rules), explicit locking with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE prevents lost updates by locking the rows to be updated so concurrent readers wait, but it requires careful reasoning because it is easy to forget a lock somewhere and reintroduce a race condition.
condition: built-in atomic operations cannot express the needed update logic

statement: Automatic lost-update detection lets read-modify-write cycles run in parallel and aborts and retries a transaction when a lost update is detected; it integrates efficiently with snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL repeatable read, Oracle serializable, and SQL Server snapshot isolation detect it, though MySQL/InnoDB repeatable read does not), and it is less error-prone than locks or atomic operations because it needs no special application code.

Compare-and-set prevents lost updates in databases without transactions by allowing an update only if the value has not changed since it was read, retrying otherwise, but it is unsafe if the database lets the comparison read from an old snapshot, so you must verify your database's compare-and-set is safe before relying on it.
exception: the database allows the compare condition to read from a stale snapshot

statement: Locks and compare-and-set assume a single up-to-date copy of the data and therefore do not apply to multi-leader or leaderless replication, where the common approach is to let concurrent writes create conflicting siblings that are merged afterward; commutative atomic operations like incrementing a counter or adding to a set merge cleanly across replicas (as in Riak datatypes), whereas last-write-wins is prone to lost updates yet is the default in many replicated databases.

Write skew is a race condition where two transactions read the same objects and then update different objects in a way that together violates an invariant spanning those rows (such as both on-call doctors taking themselves off call after each sees that two are on call); it generalizes the lost-update problem and is only automatically prevented by true serializable isolation.

Options for preventing write skew are limited: single-object atomic operations do not help because multiple objects are involved, automatic lost-update detection does not catch it, and multi-object constraints are rarely supported (sometimes approximated with triggers or materialized views), so if you cannot use serializable isolation the next-best option is to explicitly lock the rows the transaction depends on with SELECT FOR UPDATE.

Write skew arises in many check-then-act scenarios where the write changes the precondition that was checked, including meeting-room double-booking, conflicting moves in a multiplayer game, two users claiming the same username, and double-spending an account balance; some of these (like a unique username) can be fixed with a unique constraint.

A phantom is when a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another transaction; snapshot isolation avoids phantoms in read-only queries but they cause tricky write skew in read-write transactions, and SELECT FOR UPDATE cannot help when the check is for the absence of rows because there are no existing rows to lock.

Materializing conflicts works around phantoms by precreating lock rows (such as one row per room and time slot) so a transaction can lock concrete rows and turn the phantom into an ordinary lock conflict, but it is hard and error-prone and leaks concurrency control into the data model, so it should be a last resort and serializable isolation is preferable.

Serializable isolation is the strongest level, guaranteeing the outcome is as if transactions ran one at a time and thus preventing all race conditions, and it is the researchers' long-standing answer to the mess of weak isolation; the three techniques databases use to implement it are literal serial execution, two-phase locking, and serializable snapshot isolation.

Weak isolation levels persist because they are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented across databases, it is difficult to tell whether application code is safe at a given level (especially in a large codebase), and there are no good tools to detect race conditions since testing for them is nondeterministic.

Actual serial execution runs one transaction at a time on a single thread, which is serializable by definition; it became feasible around 2007 because RAM grew cheap enough to keep the active dataset in memory and because OLTP transactions are typically short and small (long read-only analytic queries run separately on a snapshot), but its throughput is limited to a single CPU core.

Single-threaded serial execution requires submitting each transaction ahead of time as a stored procedure rather than running interactive multi-statement transactions, because interactive transactions waste most of their time on network round-trips waiting for the application's next query; transactions must also stay short and avoid waiting for user input, for example by committing within a single HTTP request.

Stored procedures earned a bad reputation for vendor-specific archaic languages and being hard to debug, version, test, and monitor, and because a badly written one can harm a shared database more than equivalent application code, but modern implementations use general-purpose languages (VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic Java or Clojure, Redis Lua), and VoltDB even replicates by re-executing the same deterministic stored procedure on each replica.

Serial execution scales beyond a single core only by partitioning the data so that each transaction touches a single partition (each partition then runs its own transaction thread for near-linear scaling), because cross-partition transactions need lock-step coordination and are vastly slower (VoltDB reports about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second); whether single-partition transactions are feasible depends on the data structure, with key-value data partitioning easily and multiple secondary indexes requiring cross-partition coordination.

Serial execution achieves serializable isolation only within constraints: every transaction must be small and fast because one slow transaction stalls all processing, the active dataset must fit in memory, and write throughput must fit on a single CPU core or be partitioned without requiring cross-partition coordination.

Two-phase locking (2PL) is distinct from two-phase commit (2PC) and provides serializability: several transactions may read an object concurrently, but a writer needs exclusive access, so a reader blocks writers and a writer blocks readers (the opposite of snapshot isolation's readers-never-block-writers), which lets 2PL prevent all the race conditions including lost updates and write skew.

2PL is implemented with a per-object lock in shared (read) or exclusive (write) mode: many transactions can hold a shared lock together, an exclusive lock must be held alone, a transaction that reads then writes upgrades its shared lock to exclusive, and every lock is held until the transaction commits or aborts (the two phases being acquiring locks during execution and releasing them at the end).

Because 2PL uses so many locks, deadlocks (transaction A waiting on B while B waits on A) occur easily and far more often than under read committed; the database detects them and aborts one transaction, which the application must retry, and frequent deadlocks waste significant work through repeated retries.

The big downside of 2PL is performance: throughput and latencies are much worse than under weak isolation due to lock overhead and especially reduced concurrency, and because traditional databases do not bound transaction duration, waits can be unbounded, latencies unstable, and high percentiles very slow under contention, so a single slow or lock-heavy transaction can grind the system to a halt.

To prevent phantoms, serializable 2PL conceptually needs a predicate lock, which locks all objects matching a search condition, including objects that do not yet exist but might be added, so concurrent inserts, updates, or deletes matching the condition must wait.

Because predicate locks perform poorly when there are many active locks, most 2PL databases instead use index-range (next-key) locking, a safe over-approximation that locks a larger set of objects attached to an index entry (and falls back to a table-level shared lock when no suitable index exists), trading some precision for much lower overhead while still preventing phantoms and write skew.

Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) provides full serializability with only a small performance penalty over snapshot isolation (used in PostgreSQL's serializable level and FoundationDB); it is an optimistic technique in which transactions proceed without blocking and the database checks at commit time whether isolation was violated, aborting and retrying the transaction if so.

Pessimistic concurrency control (two-phase locking, serial execution) blocks whenever something might go wrong, whereas optimistic control (SSI) lets transactions proceed and aborts on conflict; optimistic control performs badly under high contention because many aborts and retries worsen an already-loaded system, but outperforms pessimistic control when there is spare capacity and low contention, and commutative atomic operations help by reducing contention.

SSI provides serializability by detecting when a transaction acted on a premise that is no longer true, using two checks: detecting reads of a stale MVCC version (an ignored uncommitted write that later commits) and detecting writes that affect another transaction's prior reads; it performs the check at commit rather than immediately, to avoid unnecessary aborts of read-only transactions and of cases where the other transaction ultimately aborts.

SSI tracks which transactions read which data via index entries (or at table level) and uses that as a non-blocking tripwire: when a transaction writes, it notifies recent readers that their read may be stale rather than blocking them, and the conflict is resolved at commit where the first transaction to commit succeeds and a conflicting later one aborts.

SSI's performance hinges on read/write tracking granularity (detailed tracking aborts fewer transactions but costs more bookkeeping) and on the abort rate, so read-write transactions should be kept fairly short; its key advantages are that it never blocks (giving predictable, low-variance latency and lock-free read-only queries, ideal for read-heavy workloads) and, unlike serial execution, it is not limited to a single CPU core.

Transactions are an abstraction that lets an application pretend certain concurrency problems and hardware or software faults do not exist, reducing a large class of errors to a retryable abort; simple single-record access can manage without them, but for complex access patterns transactions hugely reduce the error cases the developer must reason about, and they are valuable regardless of the data model.

The major isolation anomalies map to isolation levels as follows: dirty reads and dirty writes are prevented by read committed and above, read skew (nonrepeatable reads) by snapshot isolation (usually via MVCC), lost updates by some snapshot-isolation implementations automatically or otherwise by an explicit lock, write skew only by serializable isolation, and phantom reads by snapshot isolation for read-only queries but, in the write-skew case, only by index-range locks or serializable isolation.

A timeout is the only sure way to detect a node fault, but there is no simple right value: a long timeout means a long wait before a node is declared dead, while a short timeout detects faults faster but more often falsely declares a merely slow node dead.

Prematurely declaring a live node dead is harmful: an action it was performing may be done twice when another node takes over, and transferring its responsibilities adds load to other nodes and the network, which under high load can cascade into total failure as nodes declare each other dead.

With a bounded network delay and bounded request-handling time you could use a timeout of twice the delay plus the handling time, but real asynchronous networks have unbounded delays and servers cannot guarantee a maximum handling time, so a single transient spike in round-trip times can throw a system with a low timeout off balance.

The variability of network packet delays is most often caused by queueing: at congested switches (whose full queues drop packets that must be resent), in the operating system when all CPU cores are busy, during virtual-machine pauses, and at the sender due to TCP flow control; queueing delays are worst when a system is near its maximum capacity because long queues then build up quickly.

In shared multi-tenant clouds and datacenters a noisy neighbor consuming many shared resources can make network delays highly variable, so timeouts must be chosen experimentally by measuring the round-trip-time distribution over time and across machines and then trading off failure-detection delay against the risk of premature timeouts.

Rather than configured constant timeouts, a system can continually measure response times and their jitter and adjust timeouts automatically to the observed distribution, as a Phi Accrual failure detector does (used in Akka and Cassandra).

UDP trades reliability for lower delay variability by not performing flow control or retransmitting lost packets, which makes it a good choice when delayed data is worthless, such as voice or video calls where there is no time to retransmit and the retry effectively happens at the human layer.
condition: delayed data is worthless to the application

statement: Telephone circuits are synchronous with bounded delay because a fixed amount of bandwidth is reserved end to end so there is no queueing, whereas datacenter and internet networks use packet switching (Ethernet and IP) that suffers queueing and unbounded delays; packet switching is chosen because it is optimized for bursty traffic and lets TCP adapt to available bandwidth, while circuits would waste capacity on bursty transfers.

Variable network delays are a consequence of dynamic resource partitioning: statically partitioned resources (dedicated bandwidth or hardware) give latency guarantees at the cost of lower utilization and higher expense, while dynamically shared resources give better utilization and lower cost but variable delays, so variable delay is a cost-benefit trade-off rather than a law of nature, and because quality of service is not enabled in clouds or on the internet you must assume congestion and unbounded delays and set timeouts experimentally.

Rapid feedback that a remote node is down (a TCP acknowledgment, an ICMP Destination Unreachable, or a switch management interface) is useful but unreliable, because even a delivered packet may not have been handled if the application crashed first, so to be sure a request succeeded you need a positive response from the application itself.

Time is hard in a distributed system because communication is not instantaneous, so a message is always received later than it was sent by an unknown amount due to variable network delay, which makes it difficult to determine the order in which events happened across multiple machines.

Every machine has its own imperfect quartz hardware clock that runs slightly fast or slow, giving each its own notion of time, which is synchronized to a degree using the Network Time Protocol (NTP) that in turn draws from a more accurate source such as GPS.

Computers have two distinct clocks: a time-of-day clock that gives calendar wall-clock time (NTP-synchronized but able to jump backward on reset and to ignore leap seconds, making it unsuitable for measuring elapsed time) and a monotonic clock that always moves forward and whose absolute value is meaningless, so durations such as timeouts and response times should be measured with the monotonic clock.

Clock synchronization is unreliable in many ways: quartz clocks drift with temperature (Google assumes 200 ppm, roughly 17 seconds of drift per day if synced daily), clocks can be forcibly reset and jump, a node firewalled off from NTP can go unnoticed, NTP accuracy is limited by network delay (about 35 ms minimum over the internet), some NTP servers are simply wrong, leap seconds have crashed systems, and virtual-machine and untrusted-device clocks can jump or be deliberately wrong.

Very high clock accuracy is achievable (for example MiFID II requires high-frequency trading clocks within 100 microseconds of UTC) using GPS receivers and the Precision Time Protocol with careful deployment and monitoring, but it requires significant effort and expertise and degrades quickly if NTP is misconfigured or blocked.

Robust software must be prepared for incorrect clocks just as for faulty networks, because a defective clock or misconfigured NTP usually goes unnoticed (most things keep seeming to work while the clock drifts) and tends to cause silent, subtle data loss rather than a dramatic crash.

If you use software that requires synchronized clocks, you must carefully monitor the clock offsets between all machines and declare any node whose clock drifts too far from the others as dead and remove it, so that broken clocks are noticed before they cause too much damage.
condition: the software depends on synchronized clocks

statement: Do not use time-of-day clock timestamps to order events across nodes, because even with clock skew under a few milliseconds a causally later write can carry an earlier timestamp, so last-write-wins conflict resolution will keep the earlier-timestamped value and silently drop the later write.

Last-write-wins by clock timestamp has several pitfalls: writes can silently disappear because a node with a lagging clock cannot overwrite a fast-clock node's value until the skew elapses, it cannot distinguish writes made in quick succession from truly concurrent ones (so causality tracking like version vectors is needed), and two nodes can generate the same timestamp requiring a tiebreaker that can itself violate causality.

NTP cannot be made accurate enough to guarantee correct ordering of events across nodes, because its accuracy is itself bounded by the network round-trip time, and correct ordering would require the clock source to be significantly more accurate than the network delay being measured.

Logical clocks, based on incrementing counters rather than a quartz oscillator, are a safer way to order events than physical clocks because they capture only the relative ordering of events (whether one happened before another) rather than measuring elapsed time.

A clock reading should be treated not as a point in time but as a range within a confidence interval determined by drift, NTP error, and network round-trip time, so when uncertainty is around 100 ms the microsecond digits are meaningless; most systems do not expose this uncertainty, an exception being Google's TrueTime, which returns an earliest and latest possible timestamp.

A global monotonically increasing transaction ID across partitions is hard to generate because it requires coordination that reflects causality and becomes a bottleneck under many small transactions; Spanner instead uses TrueTime confidence intervals for cross-datacenter snapshot isolation, deliberately waiting the width of the confidence interval before committing a read-write transaction so that timestamps reflect causality, which is why it keeps clock uncertainty small with a GPS or atomic clock per datacenter.

A node in a distributed system must assume that its execution can be paused for a significant time at any point, even mid-function, due to stop-the-world garbage-collection pauses (sometimes minutes), virtual-machine suspension or live migration, laptop sleep, operating-system context switches and steal time, synchronous disk I/O including surprise class loading and page-fault swapping, or a SIGSTOP signal, and during the pause the rest of the system keeps moving and may declare the node dead.

Single-machine thread-safety tools like mutexes, semaphores, and atomic counters do not translate to distributed systems, because a distributed system has no shared memory and communicates only by messages over an unreliable network.

Code that relies on synchronized clocks or assumes that very little time passes between checking a condition and acting on it is unsafe, because an unexpected pause can let a lease or lock expire between the check and the action without the thread noticing, after which it proceeds to do something unsafe such as writing under an expired lease.

Hard real-time systems guarantee a response by a deadline in all circumstances, which requires a real-time operating system, documented worst-case execution times, restricted dynamic memory allocation, and extensive testing, making them very expensive and restricting the usable languages and tools; real-time is not the same as high performance and is uneconomical for most server-side systems, which must therefore tolerate process pauses and clock instability.

Garbage-collection pauses can be mitigated without real-time scheduling by treating a GC pause as a brief planned outage: warn the application, stop routing new requests to the node, drain outstanding requests, then collect; or use the collector only for short-lived objects and periodically restart processes (shifting traffic away first, like a rolling upgrade) before long-lived objects accumulate.

In a distributed system a node cannot know anything for certain and can only make guesses from the messages it receives or fails to receive, and the state of a non-responding remote node is fundamentally unknowable because a problem in the network cannot reliably be distinguished from a problem at the node.

Make a distributed system reliable by stating the assumptions it makes as an explicit system model and designing the system to meet them, because algorithms can be proven correct within a system model, so reliable behavior is achievable even when the underlying model provides very few guarantees, though doing so is not straightforward.

Truth in a distributed system is defined by the majority: a node cannot trust its own judgment and the system must not depend on any single node, so many algorithms use a quorum (voting among nodes) for decisions including declaring a node dead, and a node declared dead by a quorum must step down even if it still feels alive.

A majority quorum of more than half the nodes lets the system keep working despite failures (three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two) while remaining safe, because there can be only one majority at a time and therefore no two conflicting majority decisions.

Enforcing that there is only one of something (one partition leader, one lock holder, one owner of a username) needs care, because a node believing it is the chosen one does not mean a quorum still agrees: it may have been demoted during a network interruption or GC pause while another was elected, and if it keeps acting on its stale belief it can corrupt the system, as in the HBase bug where a client wrote under an expired lease and corrupted a file.

Fencing protects a locked resource by having the lock server return a monotonically increasing fencing token with each grant, requiring every write to include its token, and having the resource reject any write whose token is older than one it has already processed, which stops a node that falsely believes it still holds the lock from corrupting the resource; ZooKeeper's zxid or cversion can serve as the token.

Fencing requires the resource itself to actively check and reject stale tokens, because relying on clients to check their own lock status is insufficient, and it is generally wise for a service to protect itself rather than assume its clients (often run by people with different priorities) will always behave correctly.

A Byzantine fault is a node sending arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses (lying), and reaching agreement despite such nodes is the Byzantine Generals Problem; this book otherwise assumes nodes are unreliable but honest, meaning they may be slow, unresponsive, or have outdated state but tell the truth when they do respond.

Byzantine fault tolerance is relevant in specific settings such as aerospace systems (where radiation can corrupt memory) and multi-organization systems where participants may cheat (for example blockchains coordinating mutually untrusting parties), but it is usually unnecessary in a single-organization datacenter and its protocols are complicated and impractical for most server-side data systems.
condition: nodes may be malicious or subject to arbitrary corruption, as across organizations or in aerospace
exception: a single-organization datacenter where all nodes are trusted

statement: A Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm cannot save you from a software bug deployed identically to all nodes (since it needs over two-thirds correct, you would need independent implementations) nor from security compromises (an attacker who breaks one node can likely break all running the same software), so traditional mechanisms like authentication, access control, encryption, and firewalls remain the main protection, and web applications instead make the server the authority and rely on input validation, sanitization, and output escaping against malicious clients.

Even when assuming honest nodes, it is worth adding cheap pragmatic guards against weak forms of lying from hardware faults, bugs, and misconfiguration, such as application-level checksums (because TCP and UDP checksums occasionally miss corruption), sanity-checking and size-limiting user inputs to prevent denial of service, and configuring NTP with multiple servers so a misconfigured one is detected as an outlier.

A system model formalizes the faults an algorithm may assume; the three common timing models are synchronous (bounded delay, pauses, and clock error, which is unrealistic for most systems), partially synchronous (synchronous most of the time but occasionally exceeding the bounds, which is realistic), and asynchronous (no timing assumptions and not even a clock, which is very restrictive).

The common node-failure models are crash-stop (a node fails only by crashing and never returns), crash-recovery (a node may crash and later recover, with stable disk storage surviving but in-memory state lost), and Byzantine (a node may do anything, including deceiving others); the partially synchronous model combined with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful for modeling real systems.

An algorithm's correctness is defined by the properties it must satisfy, and an algorithm is correct within a system model if those properties always hold in every situation that the model assumes can occur.

Distinguish safety properties (nothing bad happens; a violation occurs at an identifiable moment and cannot be undone) from liveness properties (something good eventually happens; may not hold now but can be satisfied later, often containing the word eventually), and require safety to hold in all situations of the system model while allowing liveness to be conditioned on caveats such as a majority of nodes surviving and the network eventually recovering.

A system model is a simplified abstraction, so a real implementation must still handle cases the model assumes cannot happen (for example stable storage being corrupted or wiped, which breaks crash-recovery and quorum assumptions), even if that handling only alerts a human operator to clean up.

Proving an algorithm correct in a system model does not guarantee its real implementation always behaves correctly, but it is a valuable first step that can uncover problems which would otherwise stay hidden until unusual circumstances defeat the assumptions, so theoretical analysis and empirical testing are equally important.

Partial failures are the defining characteristic of distributed systems: whenever software does anything involving other nodes, that interaction may occasionally fail, go slow, or never respond, so you must build tolerance of partial failures into the software so the system as a whole keeps functioning when some parts are broken.

Detecting faults is hard because most systems lack accurate failure detection and rely on timeouts, which cannot distinguish network failures from node failures and falsely suspect nodes under variable delay, and a degraded or limping node (such as a network interface that drops to a tiny fraction of its throughput) can be even harder to handle than one that has cleanly failed.

Because distribution brings partial failures, unreliable clocks, and process pauses, prefer keeping things on a single machine when you can (a single computer can do a lot and avoids these problems), and adopt a distributed system only when scalability, fault tolerance, or low latency genuinely require it.
exception: scalability, fault tolerance, or low latency goals that a single node cannot meet

statement: Supercomputers assume reliable components and must be stopped and restarted entirely when one fails, whereas distributed systems can run continuously at the service level by handling faults and maintenance at the node level, though a bad configuration change rolled out to all nodes will still bring a distributed system down.

Linearizability is a recency guarantee that makes a system appear as if there is a single copy of the data on which every operation takes effect atomically at one point in time, so that once any read returns a new value, all subsequent reads by any client must return that value or a newer one; returning a stale value after someone has already observed the new value violates linearizability.

Linearizability and serializability are different guarantees: serializability is an isolation property of multi-object transactions ensuring they behave as some serial order (possibly different from the real order), while linearizability is a recency guarantee on a single object that does not group operations and therefore does not by itself prevent write skew; providing both together is called strict serializability.

Serializability implemented by two-phase locking or actual serial execution is typically linearizable, but serializable snapshot isolation is not linearizable, because it deliberately reads from a consistent snapshot that excludes writes more recent than the snapshot.

Linearizability is required for locking and leader election (all nodes must agree which node holds the lock, which is why coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd use consensus to provide linearizable locks) and for hard uniqueness constraints such as a username, email, or filename, which behave like an atomic compare-and-set lock, as do guarantees that a balance never goes negative or a seat is not double-booked, all of which need a single up-to-date value that all nodes agree on.

Not every constraint needs linearizability: foreign-key and attribute constraints can be enforced without it, and some constraints can be treated loosely and compensated for afterward (such as moving customers off an overbooked flight), but a hard uniqueness constraint of the kind found in relational databases does require linearizability.

Cross-channel timing dependencies create race conditions when two communication channels connect the same components (for example a file store plus a message queue): if the storage is not linearizable, the queue can outrun the storage's internal replication so a consumer sees a stale or missing object and the results become permanently inconsistent, and linearizable storage is the simplest way to avoid this.

A single copy of the data is linearizable but not fault-tolerant, so fault tolerance requires replication, and the replication methods differ in linearizability: single-leader replication is potentially linearizable (reading from the leader or synchronously updated followers, but not if it uses snapshot isolation, a delusional leader serves reads, or asynchronous failover loses writes), consensus algorithms are linearizable because they prevent split brain and stale replicas, multi-leader replication is not linearizable, and leaderless replication probably is not.

Strict quorum reads and writes (w + r > n) in a Dynamo-style system are not automatically linearizable, because variable network delays allow a read that begins after another read completes to return an older value, and last-write-wins conflict resolution or sloppy quorums make linearizability impossible.

Dynamo-style quorums can be made linearizable at a performance cost by having readers perform read repair synchronously before returning and writers read the latest quorum state before writing, but only for read and write operations, since a linearizable compare-and-set requires a consensus algorithm, so it is safest to assume a leaderless Dynamo-style system does not provide linearizability.

Linearizability has a fundamental cost under network partitions: if an application requires linearizability, replicas disconnected from the others cannot process requests (they must wait or return errors, becoming unavailable), whereas if it does not require linearizability each replica can keep processing independently and stay available, so non-linearizable applications tolerate network problems better.

The linearizability-versus-availability trade-off applies to any linearizable database on an unreliable network, regardless of how it is implemented and not only in multi-datacenter deployments, which is the essence of the CAP theorem.

CAP is widely misunderstood: the pick-two-of-three framing is misleading because network partitions are a fault you cannot choose to avoid, so it is better phrased as choosing consistency or availability when partitioned, and because CAP's formal scope is narrow (only linearizability and only network partitions, with an idiosyncratic definition of availability) it has little practical value for designing systems and is best avoided.

Partitioning a single-leader database so each partition has its own leader does not affect linearizability, because linearizability is a single-object guarantee; cross-partition transactions are a separate and harder matter.

Surprisingly few systems are actually linearizable (even RAM on a multi-core CPU is not, because per-core caches and store buffers require explicit memory barriers), and the usual reason for dropping linearizability is performance rather than fault tolerance, since linearizability is slow all the time, not only during a network fault.

Linearizability is provably slow: the response time of linearizable reads and writes is at least proportional to the uncertainty of network delays, so on a highly variable network it is inevitably high and no faster algorithm exists, whereas weaker consistency models can be much faster, which matters for latency-sensitive systems.

Causality imposes an ordering on events (cause before effect, a message sent before it is received, a question before its answer), and a system that obeys this ordering is causally consistent; snapshot isolation provides causal consistency because a consistent snapshot is consistent with causality, while read skew is reading a state that violates causality.
