Causality defines a partial order in which concurrent operations are incomparable, whereas linearizability defines a total order in which any two operations can be compared along a single timeline with no concurrency, so a linearizable datastore has no concurrent operations.

Linearizability is stronger than causal consistency and implies it, so a linearizable system automatically preserves causality even across multiple communication channels without passing extra metadata, which makes linearizable systems simple to understand but comes at a cost in performance and availability.

Causal consistency is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down under network delays and stays available during network failures (the CAP trade-off does not apply to it), and because many systems that appear to need linearizability really only need causal consistency, preserving causality can often be implemented far more efficiently than full linearizability.

To maintain causal consistency a replica must process an operation only after all operations that causally precede it have been processed, waiting if any is missing, which requires tracking causal dependencies across the whole database (a generalization of version vectors) and knowing which version of the data each read observed.

Because tracking every causal dependency is impractical when clients read a lot before writing, a better approach is to order events with compact sequence numbers or logical-clock timestamps, which provide a total order that can be made consistent with causality (if A causally precedes B then A gets a lower number, while concurrent operations are ordered arbitrarily).

In single-leader replication the replication log already defines a total order of writes consistent with causality, because the leader can increment a counter per operation, so a follower that applies writes in log order is always causally consistent even when lagging behind.

Without a single leader, common sequence-number generators (per-node odd/even numbers, physical-clock timestamps, or preallocated blocks of numbers) scale better than funneling everything through one leader but are not consistent with causality, because nodes process operations at different rates, physical clocks suffer skew, and block ranges can be assigned out of causal order.

Lamport timestamps generate a total order consistent with causality using a (counter, node ID) pair where every node and client tracks the maximum counter value it has seen and raises its own counter to any higher value it receives, so every causal dependency increases the timestamp; they are more compact than version vectors but, unlike version vectors, cannot distinguish whether two operations are concurrent or causally dependent.

A total order of operations alone is not sufficient for problems like a uniqueness constraint, because the total order only emerges after all operations have been collected, so a node deciding immediately whether a username creation succeeds would have to check every other node and would halt if one were unreachable; you also need to know when the total order is finalized.

Total order broadcast (atomic broadcast) is the problem of getting all nodes to agree on one total order of messages, defined by two safety properties that must hold even under faults: reliable delivery (a message delivered to one node is delivered to all) and totally ordered delivery (every node receives the messages in the same order), with the algorithm retrying until the network recovers while still preserving order.

Partitioned databases with a single leader per partition usually maintain ordering only within each partition, so they cannot offer cross-partition consistency guarantees such as consistent snapshots or foreign-key references without additional coordination to establish a total order across partitions.

Total order broadcast is exactly what database replication needs: if every message is a write and every replica processes the same writes in the same order, the replicas stay consistent aside from lag (a principle called state machine replication), and the same approach implements serializable transactions when each message is a deterministic transaction applied in the same order on every node.

Total order broadcast fixes the message order at delivery time so a node cannot retroactively insert a message earlier once later ones are delivered, which makes it stronger than timestamp ordering; it is effectively a way to build a log where delivering a message is appending, and it can implement a fencing-token lock service whose monotonically increasing log sequence number serves as the token (ZooKeeper's zxid).

Total order broadcast is asynchronous (messages are delivered reliably in a fixed order but with no guarantee of when), whereas linearizability is a recency guarantee, yet you can build a linearizable compare-and-set on top of total order broadcast by appending a tentative claim, waiting for your own message to come back, and treating the first claim for that key as the winner.

Building writes on top of a log gives linearizable writes but not linearizable reads (a read from an asynchronously updated store can be stale, which is sequential rather than linearizable consistency), so to make reads linearizable you can sequence the read through the log, fetch the latest log position in a linearizable way and wait for it (as ZooKeeper's sync does), or read from a synchronously updated replica.

A linearizable compare-and-set (or increment-and-get) register, total order broadcast, and consensus are all equivalent problems, so a solution to one can be transformed into a solution for the others, and any linearizable sequence-number generator inevitably ends up being a consensus algorithm.

Consensus is getting several nodes to agree on something, and although it sounds simple many broken systems have been built assuming it is easy; its key uses include leader election (agreeing on the single leader to avoid a split-brain situation where two leaders diverge) and atomic commit (getting all nodes to agree whether a multi-node transaction commits or aborts).

The FLP result proves that no algorithm can always reach consensus when a node may crash, but only in the asynchronous model that forbids clocks and timeouts; allowing the algorithm to use timeouts (or even just randomness) to suspect crashed nodes makes consensus solvable, so distributed systems can achieve consensus in practice.

On a single node, atomic commit depends on the order in which data is durably written to disk (first the data, then the commit record), with the moment the commit record is durably written being the irrevocable deciding point, so a single disk controller makes the commit atomic; across multiple nodes you cannot simply send commit to all and commit independently, because it could succeed on some and fail on others and violate atomicity.

A transaction commit must be irrevocable: once committed, the data becomes visible and other transactions may rely on it (the basis of read committed isolation), so you cannot retroactively abort a committed transaction, and undoing its effects requires a separate compensating transaction.

Two-phase commit achieves atomic commit across nodes using a coordinator: in phase one it sends a prepare request and each participant ensures it can definitely commit (writing its data to disk and checking conflicts) before voting yes and surrendering its right to abort; in phase two the coordinator decides to commit only if all voted yes, durably writes that decision to its log (the commit point), and then sends the commit or abort, retrying until it succeeds.

Two-phase commit (atomic commit in a distributed database) and two-phase locking (serializable isolation) are entirely different things that merely share a similar name and should be kept as separate concepts.

The atomicity of two-phase commit rests on two points of no return: when a participant votes yes it irrevocably promises it can commit later, and once the coordinator writes its decision it cannot be reversed, which is the distributed analogue of single-node commit lumping both events into writing one commit record.

Two-phase commit is a blocking protocol: after a participant votes yes it cannot abort unilaterally and must wait for the coordinator, so if the coordinator crashes the participant is left in doubt and can do nothing but wait (it can neither safely abort nor commit, even on timeout), and the transaction completes only when the coordinator recovers and reads its log, treating any transaction without a commit record as aborted.

Three-phase commit, proposed as a nonblocking alternative, assumes bounded network delay and bounded response times and therefore cannot guarantee atomicity in real systems with unbounded delay and process pauses; nonblocking atomic commit needs a perfect failure detector, which a timeout is not on an unbounded network, so two-phase commit continues to be used despite its coordinator-failure problem.

Distributed transactions implemented with two-phase commit have a mixed reputation because, while they provide a hard-to-achieve safety guarantee, they cause operational problems and a heavy performance penalty (distributed transactions in MySQL are reported to be over ten times slower than single-node ones, owing to extra fsync disk forcing and network round-trips), which is why many cloud services avoid them.

Two distinct kinds of distributed transaction are often conflated: database-internal transactions, where all participating nodes run the same database software and can use technology-specific optimizations so they often work well, and heterogeneous transactions across different technologies or vendors (including non-database systems like message brokers), which must ensure atomic commit across entirely different systems and are much more challenging.

Heterogeneous distributed transactions enable exactly-once message processing by atomically committing a message-queue acknowledgment together with the database writes for processing it, so that if either fails both abort and the broker safely redelivers; this works only if every affected system uses the same atomic commit protocol, because a side effect on a system that does not support two-phase commit (such as sending an email) could be performed more than once on retry.
condition: all systems involved support the same atomic commit protocol

statement: X/Open XA is a widely implemented standard (a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator, not a network protocol) for two-phase commit across heterogeneous relational databases and message brokers, where the coordinator is often a library inside the application process that keeps a commit/abort log on local disk; if that process crashes, prepared participants are stuck in doubt until the server is restarted and the coordinator reads its log.

An in-doubt two-phase-commit transaction is dangerous because it must hold its locks (exclusive locks on modified rows, and shared locks on read rows under two-phase locking) for the entire in-doubt period, so a crashed coordinator can hold those locks for minutes or, if its log is lost, indefinitely, blocking other transactions and making parts of the application unavailable.

Orphaned in-doubt transactions occur in practice when the coordinator's log is lost or corrupted, and because a correct two-phase-commit implementation must preserve in-doubt locks even across restarts, they can only be resolved by an administrator manually deciding commit or abort; XA's heuristic decisions, which let a participant unilaterally decide, are a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity and are meant only for catastrophes.

A transaction coordinator is itself a kind of database storing transaction outcomes and must be treated with the same care: a non-replicated coordinator is a single point of failure (and many implementations are not highly available by default), and embedding it in the application server makes the coordinator's log crucial durable state, which breaks the otherwise stateless application-server model.

XA is a lowest-common-denominator protocol that cannot detect deadlocks across different systems and does not work with serializable snapshot isolation, and because two-phase commit requires every participant to respond for a transaction to commit, any broken part fails the whole transaction, so distributed transactions tend to amplify failures, working against the goal of fault tolerance.

A consensus algorithm is formalized by four properties: uniform agreement (no two nodes decide differently), integrity (no node decides twice), validity (any decided value was proposed by some node), and termination (every non-crashing node eventually decides); agreement and integrity are the core, validity rules out trivial always-decide-null solutions, and termination is the fault-tolerance requirement that the system must make progress.

Without fault tolerance consensus is trivial (hardcode one dictator node), but that node failing halts all decisions, which is exactly the two-phase-commit coordinator problem; since the consensus model assumes a crashed node never returns, any algorithm that must wait for a node to recover (such as 2PC) cannot satisfy the termination property.

Any consensus algorithm requires a majority of nodes to be working to assure termination (the majority forms a quorum), but the safety properties of agreement, integrity, and validity are maintained even if a majority fails or the network is severely disrupted, so a large outage can stop the system from making progress but cannot corrupt it into making invalid decisions; most consensus algorithms assume no Byzantine faults.

Total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus, with each decision corresponding to one message delivery (agreement gives the same messages in the same order, integrity prevents duplicates, validity prevents corruption or fabrication, and termination prevents loss), and algorithms like Viewstamped Replication, Raft, and Zab implement total order broadcast directly because it is more efficient than deciding one value at a time, as does Multi-Paxos.

Single-leader replication is essentially total order broadcast, but a manually chosen leader is a dictator-style consensus that fails the termination property because recovering from leader failure needs human intervention, while automatic leader election approaches fault-tolerant consensus yet is circular, since electing a leader without split brain itself requires consensus.

Consensus protocols break the leader-election circularity with epoch numbering: each election gets a monotonically increasing epoch (the ballot, view, or term number) guaranteeing a unique leader per epoch, a higher-epoch leader wins conflicts, and before deciding anything a leader must gather votes from a quorum of nodes, each of which votes only if it is unaware of any leader with a higher epoch.

Fault-tolerant consensus uses two rounds of voting, to elect a leader and to vote on each proposal, whose quorums must overlap so that any successful proposal includes a voter from the latest election, letting the leader confirm no higher epoch exists before deciding; this differs from two-phase commit in that the leader is elected rather than fixed, only a majority must agree rather than every participant, and there is a recovery process that keeps the safety properties intact.

Consensus comes at real costs: its proposal voting is a form of synchronous replication (so it cannot avoid the latency that asynchronous replication trades for performance), it needs a strict majority so a network split lets only the majority side progress, most algorithms assume a fixed node set, and reliance on timeouts means that in highly variable or geographically distributed networks transient delays trigger false leader failures and frequent elections that can wreck performance.

Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd hold small, in-memory, disk-durable data replicated by fault-tolerant total order broadcast and provide a useful bundle for distributed coordination: linearizable atomic operations (a compare-and-set implements a distributed lock, usually a lease with an expiry), total ordering that yields monotonic fencing tokens, failure detection via session heartbeats with ephemeral nodes that auto-release locks on timeout, and change notifications so clients watch instead of poll; only the linearizable atomic operations strictly require consensus.
Do not implement a consensus system yourself, because it is hard to get right; rely instead on a proven coordination service that already implements total order broadcast and consensus.

The ZooKeeper/Chubby model fits tasks like electing a leader or primary with automatic failover (for single-leader databases, job schedulers, and other stateful systems) and assigning partitions to nodes during rebalancing, achieved with atomic operations, ephemeral nodes, and notifications so the application recovers from faults without human intervention, which is hard but far better than implementing the consensus algorithms yourself.

ZooKeeper runs a fixed small number of nodes (usually three or five) that perform majority votes among themselves while serving many clients, thereby outsourcing the work of consensus, operation ordering, and failure detection to an external service, because majority votes over thousands of nodes would be terribly inefficient.

ZooKeeper is intended for small, slow-changing coordination data such as which node is the leader for a partition (changing on a timescale of minutes or hours), not for application runtime state that changes thousands or millions of times per second, for which other tools should be used.

Service discovery (registering service network endpoints so others can find them, useful in clouds where VM addresses change) does not actually require consensus, since the traditional approach is DNS with heavy caching whose reads are non-linearizable and tolerate staleness in exchange for availability; leader election does require consensus, so a consensus system can additionally expose the leader, optionally through read-only caching replicas that serve non-linearizable reads.

A membership service couples failure detection with consensus so that nodes agree on which nodes are currently alive; a live node may still be wrongly declared dead, but having agreement on the membership is valuable because operations like choosing the lowest-numbered member as leader only work if all nodes share the same view of who the members are.

Linearizability is appealing because it makes a database behave like a single variable in a single-threaded program, but it is slow especially under large network delays, whereas causal consistency is a weaker model that permits concurrency (a branching and merging version history) yet avoids linearizability's coordination overhead and is far less sensitive to network problems.

A wide range of problems are equivalent and reducible to consensus, including linearizable compare-and-set registers, atomic transaction commit, total order broadcast, locks and leases, a membership or coordination service given a failure detector, and uniqueness constraints; all of them are straightforward on a single node or with a single decision-maker but require consensus to be made fault-tolerant.

A single-leader database vests all decision-making in the leader, which is why it can provide linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, and a totally ordered replication log, but it cannot make progress if the leader fails or becomes unreachable, leaving three options: wait for the leader to recover (blocking, which fails the termination property, as XA coordinators do), fail over manually by human decision (slow), or automatically elect a new leader using a proven consensus algorithm.

Having a single leader does not avoid consensus but only kicks the can down the road, because consensus is still required to maintain the leadership and to handle leadership changes, just less frequently than on every write.

If you need something reducible to consensus and want it fault-tolerant, use a proven coordination service like ZooKeeper rather than developing your own algorithms, but recognize that not every system requires consensus, since leaderless and multi-leader replication deliberately avoid global consensus and instead cope with branching and merging version histories in place of linearizability.

The theoretical results of distributed-systems research, even when their assumptions are unrealistic, are valuable for practical work because they clarify what can and cannot be done and reveal the counterintuitive ways in which distributed systems are flawed.

Real applications integrate several datastores, indexes, caches, and analytics systems because no single database satisfies all access patterns, so integrating disparate data systems into one coherent architecture is one of the most important tasks in a nontrivial application, a point often overlooked by vendors who claim one product serves all needs.

A system of record (source of truth) holds the authoritative, typically normalized data where each fact is represented once and which wins any discrepancy, whereas a derived data system holds data transformed from another source that can be recreated if lost, such as caches, denormalized values, indexes, and materialized views.

Derived data is redundant because it duplicates existing information, but it is often essential for good read performance and is commonly denormalized, and several different derived datasets can be built from one source to view the data from different perspectives.

Whether a store is a system of record or a derived data system depends on how it is used in the application rather than on the tool itself, and being explicit about which data is derived from which other data brings clarity to an otherwise confusing architecture by making the dataflow, inputs, and outputs visible.

Data systems fall into three types with different performance priorities: online services that wait for requests and are measured by response time and availability, batch processing systems that turn a large fixed input into output and are measured by throughput (usually run periodically with no user waiting), and stream processing systems that consume inputs and produce outputs like batch jobs but act on events shortly after they happen for lower latency.

The Unix philosophy is a set of design principles that transfer to large-scale data systems: make each program do one thing well, expect each program's output to become another's input (so avoid cluttered or rigidly columnar or binary formats), build software to be tried early and rebuilt when clumsy, and prefer building tools to lighten a task.

A program that does one thing well, like the Unix sort utility (which spills to disk for larger-than-memory data and parallelizes across cores, beating most language standard libraries), is barely useful in isolation but becomes powerful when composed with other tools through a shell.

Choosing between in-memory aggregation and sorting depends on the working set (the memory the job needs for random access, which equals the number of distinct keys): an in-memory hash table works when that set fits in memory, but when it is larger, sorting wins because it uses the disk efficiently through mergesort's sequential access and spill-to-disk, leaving disk read rate as the bottleneck.

Composability requires a uniform interface, which in Unix is the file (an ordered sequence of bytes) so that files, pipes, sockets, and devices can all be plugged together, and many tools further agree to treat input as ASCII text split into newline-separated records, a shared convention that lets independently written programs interoperate.

Unix separates logic from wiring by having tools read standard input and write standard output, so the shell user composes programs (a form of loose coupling and inversion of control) without the program knowing where its input comes from or output goes; the limits are that multiple inputs or outputs are tricky, you cannot pipe output directly to a network connection, and any I/O a program wires up itself reduces that flexibility.

Unix tools support experimentation through transparency: input files are treated as immutable so commands can be rerun safely with different options, the pipeline can be ended early and piped into a pager to inspect intermediate output for debugging, and a stage's output can be written to a file so later stages can be restarted without rerunning the whole pipeline; their biggest limitation is running only on a single machine.

MapReduce resembles Unix tools but distributed across thousands of machines: a job takes one or more inputs and produces one or more outputs, normally does not modify its input or have side effects beyond the output, and writes its output files once sequentially, reading and writing a distributed filesystem instead of standard input and output.

HDFS follows the shared-nothing principle with a daemon on each machine exposing that machine's disks and a central NameNode tracking which blocks live where, conceptually forming one big filesystem over all machines' disks, in contrast to shared-disk NAS or SAN architectures that use a centralized appliance with custom hardware, so HDFS needs no special hardware.

HDFS tolerates machine and disk failures by replicating file blocks across machines, either as full copies or with an erasure-coding scheme like Reed-Solomon that lowers storage overhead, all over a conventional datacenter network without special hardware, and it has scaled to tens of thousands of machines and hundreds of petabytes at far lower cost than a dedicated storage appliance.

HDFS can schedule a computing task on the machine that stores a copy of the needed file, a locality advantage when network bandwidth is the bottleneck, whereas object stores keep storage and computation separate; this locality advantage is lost when erasure coding is used because the data from several machines must be combined to reconstruct the file.

A MapReduce job runs four steps: split the input into records, call a stateless mapper that extracts zero or more key-value pairs from each record, sort all pairs by key (done implicitly by the framework), and call a reducer that iterates over the values for each key; you write only the mapper (which prepares data for sorting) and the reducer (which processes the sorted data).

MapReduce parallelizes a computation across many machines without you writing parallelism code, because the mapper and reducer each operate on one record at a time and need not know where input comes from or output goes, and the parallelization is based on partitioning, with each input file or block processed by a separate map task.

The MapReduce scheduler puts the computation near the data by trying to run each mapper on a machine that already stores a replica of its input file (if that machine has spare resources), which avoids copying the input over the network and increases locality.

The MapReduce shuffle partitions each mapper's output by reducer using a hash of the key, writes each partition as a sorted file to the mapper's local disk, and has each reducer fetch and merge its partition from every mapper while preserving sort order, so records with the same key from different mappers end up adjacent in the reducer's input.

Because a single MapReduce job is limited, jobs are commonly chained into workflows where one job's output directory is the next job's input directory; unlike Unix pipes these pass data through files rather than streaming, and a job can start only after the jobs producing its inputs have completed successfully (failed jobs discard their partial output), so workflow schedulers are used to manage the dependencies.

MapReduce has no indexes and reads the entire content of its input files (a full table scan), which is outrageously expensive for fetching a few records but reasonable for analytic aggregates over many records, especially when parallelized, so a join in batch processing means resolving all occurrences of an association across the whole dataset rather than looking up one record.

Do not query a remote database once per record in a batch job, because throughput would be limited by the database round-trip time, caching would depend on data distribution, parallel queries could overwhelm the database, and the job would become nondeterministic as the remote data changes; instead copy the data into the same distributed filesystem (for example via ETL) and join it locally.

A reduce-side sort-merge join has mappers extract the join key from both inputs so that the framework's partitioning and sorting place all records with the same key adjacent at one reducer (a secondary sort can make one input arrive first), letting the reducer perform the join while holding only one record in memory and making no network requests.

MapReduce separates the physical network communication of getting data to the right machine (the output key acts like a destination address, since all pairs with the same key go to the same reducer) from the application logic of processing the data, and it shields application code from partial failures by transparently retrying failed tasks.

The pattern of bringing all records with the same key to the same place serves joins, grouping (GROUP BY, by using the grouping key as the map output key so aggregation happens in the reducer), and sessionization (collating a user's activity events scattered across servers by using a session or user identifier as the grouping key).

Bringing all records for one key to the same place breaks down for hot keys (linchpin objects such as a celebrity with millions of followers), because one reducer must process far more records than the others, creating skew, and since a MapReduce job finishes only when all reducers finish, downstream jobs wait for the slowest reducer.
condition: a small number of keys carry a disproportionate share of the data

statement: Hot-key skew in joins can be mitigated by a skewed or sharded join that sends a hot key's records to several randomly chosen reducers while replicating the other input to those reducers (parallelizing the hot-key work at the cost of replication), and hot-key grouping can be done in two stages, a first stage aggregating subsets at random reducers and a second combining the partial results.

A map-side join uses no reducers and no sorting (each mapper reads one input block and writes one output file) and is faster when input properties allow it; the broadcast hash join applies when a large dataset is joined with a small one, having each mapper load the small input entirely into an in-memory hash table (or a read-only on-disk index served from the OS page cache) and look up each record of the large input.
condition: one join input is small enough to fit in each mapper's memory

statement: A partitioned hash join (bucketed map join) applies when both inputs are partitioned the same way (same key, same hash function, same number of partitions) so each mapper joins just one partition from each side and loads less into memory, and a map-side merge join applies when the inputs are additionally sorted by key so a mapper can merge them incrementally regardless of memory size.
condition: the join inputs are identically partitioned (and, for a merge join, also sorted by the join key)

statement: The choice of a map-side or reduce-side join affects the output structure (a reduce-side join's output is partitioned and sorted by the join key, while a map-side join's output matches the partitioning and sorting of its large input), so optimizing join strategies requires knowing the physical layout of datasets (the number of partitions and the keys they are partitioned and sorted by), which in the Hadoop ecosystem is tracked in HCatalog and the Hive metastore.

A batch process builds a full-text search index efficiently by having mappers partition the documents, each reducer build the index for its partition, and the immutable index files be written to the distributed filesystem; when the document set changes you can either rerun the whole workflow and replace the index files wholesale (easy to reason about but costly for small changes) or update incrementally with new segment files.

To get a batch job's output into a queryable database, do not write to the production database one record at a time from a mapper or reducer, because per-record network requests are orders of magnitude slower than batch throughput, the parallel tasks can overwhelm the database, and external writes break MapReduce's clean all-or-nothing guarantee by making partially completed output externally visible.

A better way to publish a batch job's output is to build a brand-new immutable database as files in the job's output directory and bulk-load it into read-only servers (as Voldemort, ElephantDB, and HBase bulk loading do); these read-only stores are simple (needing no write-ahead log) and the server can atomically switch to the new files while keeping the old immutable files available for easy rollback.

Treating batch inputs as immutable, fully replacing previous output, and avoiding side effects gives human fault tolerance: if buggy code produces wrong output you can simply roll back the code and rerun (or switch back to the old output directory), which read-write transactional databases cannot do because rolling back code does not undo bad data already written; this also makes feature development faster, makes automatic task retry safe, and lets the same inputs feed monitoring jobs.

Hadoop is like a distributed version of Unix, with HDFS as the filesystem and MapReduce as a process that always runs a sort between the map and reduce phases, and its biggest difference from a massively parallel processing database is that MPP focuses on parallel execution of analytic SQL queries whereas MapReduce plus a distributed filesystem is more like a general-purpose operating system that can run arbitrary programs.

Because distributed-filesystem files are just byte sequences in any model or encoding, Hadoop lets you dump raw data into storage and decide how to process it later (schema-on-read, the data-lake or sushi principle), whereas an MPP database requires careful up-front modeling; making data available quickly in raw form is often more valuable than deciding the ideal model up front and shifts the burden of interpreting the data to the consumer.

MPP databases are monolithic and tightly integrated, giving excellent SQL performance accessible to analyst tools, but not all processing fits SQL (machine learning, search relevance ranking, image analysis need arbitrary code), and MapReduce on an open platform lets many different processing models run on one shared cluster accessing the same files, so data need not be imported into separate specialized systems, which eases experimentation.

Batch processing is less sensitive to faults than online systems because it can be rerun, and this shows in design: MPP databases abort the whole query when a node crashes (acceptable for short queries) and keep data in memory, whereas MapReduce retries at the granularity of an individual task and eagerly writes to disk, which is more appropriate for large, long-running jobs likely to hit at least one task failure where rerunning everything would be wasteful.

MapReduce was designed to tolerate frequent task termination because at Google low-priority batch jobs share mixed-use datacenters and can be preempted by higher-priority work (a one-hour task has about a 5% chance of termination, so a job of 100 ten-minute tasks has over a 50% chance one is killed), so task-level recovery exists to enable better cluster utilization rather than because the hardware is unreliable, which means the design makes less sense where preemption is rare.

Implementing a complex job with the raw MapReduce APIs is hard (you must write join algorithms from scratch), so higher-level models like Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch are abstractions on top that make common batch tasks much easier; MapReduce is very robust (it can process arbitrarily large data on an unreliable multi-tenant cluster, albeit slowly) but its execution model has performance problems that abstraction cannot fix, and other tools are sometimes orders of magnitude faster.

MapReduce fully materializes intermediate state by writing each job's output to the distributed filesystem, which has downsides compared to Unix pipes: a job cannot start until all of the preceding jobs' tasks (including slow stragglers) finish, mappers are often redundant because they just re-read a reducer's output, and replicating temporary intermediate data across nodes is overkill.

Dataflow engines such as Spark, Tez, and Flink treat an entire workflow as one job of connected operators that generalize map and reduce, choosing per connection whether to repartition and sort, partition without sorting, or broadcast; this lets them sort only where needed, avoid redundant map tasks, use the full dependency graph for locality optimizations, keep intermediate state in memory or on local disk instead of replicating it to the distributed filesystem, start operators as soon as their input is ready, and reuse JVM processes to cut startup overhead.

Dataflow engines run the same computations as MapReduce workflows but usually significantly faster thanks to these optimizations, and because operators generalize map and reduce, the same workflow code written in Pig, Hive, or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with only a configuration change and no code modification.

Because dataflow engines like Spark, Flink, and Tez avoid writing intermediate state to a distributed filesystem, they tolerate faults by recomputing lost state from a prior stage or the original input rather than restarting from durable files, which requires tracking how each piece of data was computed (Spark's resilient distributed dataset ancestry, Flink's operator-state checkpoints).

Recomputing lost data requires operators to be deterministic, because if a recomputed value differs from the lost one already sent downstream the downstream operators must be killed and rerun, so remove sources of nondeterminism such as hash-table iteration order, random numbers, the system clock, and external data (for example by seeding a pseudorandom generator with a fixed value).

Recovering from faults by recomputing data is not always best: if the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.
condition: the intermediate data is small relative to the source or the computation is expensive

statement: Dataflow engines execute in a pipelined manner, incrementally passing an operator's output to the next without waiting for its input to complete, but any operation that requires sorting must consume its entire input before producing output (since the last record could hold the lowest key) and therefore accumulates state; the job's final output still goes to durable storage, with inputs immutable and previous output fully replaced.

Batch processing an entire graph (for example PageRank) is different from a dataflow engine's operator DAG (where the data flow is a graph but the data is relational tuples, versus graph processing where the data itself is a graph), and many graph algorithms traverse one edge at a time propagating information until convergence (a transitive closure), which plain MapReduce cannot express because it makes a single pass, so it is done in an inefficient iterative style that rereads the whole dataset each round.

The Pregel (bulk synchronous parallel) model optimizes batch graph processing by having each vertex send messages to other vertices along edges and calling a function per vertex each iteration with its incoming messages; unlike MapReduce the vertex remembers its state across iterations so it only processes new messages and idle parts of the graph do no work, much like the actor model but with fault-tolerant durable state and fixed communication rounds.

Pregel guarantees each message is processed exactly once at its destination vertex in the next iteration despite an unreliable network, achieving fault tolerance by periodically checkpointing all vertex state to durable storage so a failure can roll the computation back to the last checkpoint, or selectively recover only the lost partition if the algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged.

Pregel partitions the graph by vertex ID and routes messages so a vertex need not know its physical machine, but because co-locating communicating vertices is hard the graph is usually partitioned arbitrarily, causing heavy cross-machine communication where the messages can exceed the size of the original graph, so if the graph fits in memory or even on disk on a single machine a single-machine algorithm often outperforms a distributed one.

High-level dataflow APIs such as Hive, Pig, Spark, and Flink express computations with relational building blocks (joining, grouping, filtering, aggregating), which require less code, enable interactive incremental development in a shell that is great for exploring data, and also improve execution efficiency at the machine level.

Specifying joins declaratively lets a cost-based query optimizer choose the most suitable join algorithm and reorder joins to minimize intermediate state, so the application states only which joins are needed and need not understand or remember the various join algorithms.

MapReduce and its dataflow successors differ from fully declarative SQL by being built on function callbacks where user code can call arbitrary libraries (for parsing, natural language analysis, image analysis, or statistics), and this freedom to run arbitrary code, well integrated with normal package managers, is what has long distinguished them from MPP databases whose user-defined functions are cumbersome and poorly integrated.

Incorporating declarative features beyond joins lets a batch framework's optimizer exploit column-oriented storage (reading only the required columns) and vectorized execution (tight cache-friendly inner loops with generated native code or bytecode) for simple filters and projections, so batch frameworks come to resemble MPP databases in performance while keeping the flexibility of running arbitrary code over arbitrary formats.

The deliberately restricted batch programming model, in which callback functions are stateless and have no externally visible side effects beyond their designated output, lets the framework hide hard distributed-systems problems by safely retrying tasks, discarding the output of failed tasks, and making only one successful task's output visible, so it can guarantee the job's final output is the same as if no faults had occurred, which is much stronger than the semantics of online services that write to databases as a side effect.

The distinguishing feature of a batch job is that it reads bounded input of a known, fixed size and derives output without modifying the input, so it knows when it has read everything and eventually completes, in contrast to stream processing whose input is an unbounded never-ending stream so the job never completes.

Combining load balancing with message redelivery in a traditional broker inevitably reorders messages, because a message left unacknowledged by a crashed consumer is redelivered to another consumer after later messages have already been processed; you can avoid this with a separate queue per consumer, and reordering is harmless for independent messages but matters when messages have causal dependencies.

AMQP and JMS style messaging is transient and destructive, because acknowledging a message deletes it from the broker (so you cannot rerun a consumer and get the same result) and a newly added consumer only receives messages sent after it registered, unlike files and databases where a new client can read data written arbitrarily far in the past.

A log-based message broker combines database durability with messaging's low-latency notification by having producers append to an append-only log and consumers read it sequentially (waiting at the end like tail -f); the log is partitioned across machines for throughput, and within each partition every message gets a monotonically increasing offset that totally orders it, with no ordering guarantee across partitions.

Log-based brokers trivially support fan-out (multiple consumers read independently because reading does not delete) and load-balance by assigning whole partitions to consumer-group nodes, but this caps parallelism at the number of partitions and lets one slow message block its partition (head-of-line blocking), so the JMS/AMQP style suits expensive-to-process messages needing per-message parallelism with unimportant ordering while the log style suits high-throughput, fast-to-process, order-sensitive messages.

Sequential consumption of a partition lets the broker track progress by periodically recording just the consumer's offset rather than acknowledging every message (reducing bookkeeping and enabling batching for higher throughput), making the broker behave like a leader database and the consumer like a follower; if a consumer fails, another resumes at the last recorded offset, so messages processed but not yet recorded are processed twice.

A log is a bounded circular buffer on disk whose old segments are deleted or archived, so a consumer that falls behind a deleted segment misses messages, but the on-disk buffer can hold days or weeks of messages and the log's throughput stays roughly constant regardless of retention because every message is written to disk anyway, unlike in-memory brokers that slow down sharply once they start spilling to disk.

With a log-based broker you should monitor how far each consumer lags the head of the log and alert before it falls behind the retained buffer, since the large buffer gives an operator time to fix a slow consumer, and a slow or crashed consumer affects only itself, so you can experimentally consume a production log for development, testing, or debugging without disrupting other consumers.

Because consuming a log is a read-only operation that only advances the consumer's own offset, you can replay old messages by starting a consumer at an earlier offset and reprocess them repeatedly with varying code, which makes log-based messaging behave like a batch process (derived data separated from input by a repeatable transformation) and supports experimentation and recovery from errors and bugs.

A write to a database is itself an event that can be captured and processed, and a replication log is a stream of database write events, so the state-machine-replication principle (every replica applying the same events in the same deterministic order ends in the same state) is just a case of event streams.

When the same data lives in several systems (an OLTP database, cache, search index, and data warehouse) it must be kept in sync, and the dual-writes approach of having the application write to each system has serious problems: concurrent writes can be ordered differently in each system and leave them permanently and silently inconsistent, and one write can succeed while another fails, which is an expensive atomic-commit problem.

Change data capture observes all changes written to a database and extracts them as an ordered stream that other systems consume, effectively making the source database the leader and the derived data systems (search indexes, caches, warehouses) followers that hold accurate copies; a log-based message broker is well suited to transport the change events because it preserves their order.

Change data capture can be implemented with database triggers (which tend to be fragile and impose significant performance overhead) or by parsing the replication log (more robust but must handle schema changes), and it is usually asynchronous, so the source database does not wait for consumers, which makes adding a slow consumer cheap but means all the issues of replication lag apply.

To add a new derived data system you generally need a consistent snapshot of the source database corresponding to a known offset in the change log, because a log of only recent changes would miss items that were not recently updated, and you then apply changes from that offset onward after loading the snapshot.

Log compaction keeps only the most recent value for each key (with tombstones removing deleted keys), so the compacted log's size depends on the database's current contents rather than the total number of writes, which lets a new consumer scan a log-compacted topic from the beginning to obtain a full copy of the database without taking a fresh snapshot, allowing the broker (for example Kafka) to serve as durable storage.

Event sourcing stores all changes to application state as a log of immutable, append-only application-level events that express the intent of a user action (such as a student cancelling an enrollment) rather than the low-level state changes it causes, which is more meaningful for data modeling, eases evolving the application over time, helps debugging by recording why something happened, and lets new side effects be chained off existing events.

Log compaction works for change data capture but not for event sourcing in the same way, because a CDC update event contains the whole new record so the latest event for a key fully determines its value and older events can be discarded, whereas event-sourcing events express intent and do not override prior events, so the full history is needed to reconstruct the final state.

An event log alone is not useful because users want the current state rather than the history, so an event-sourcing application transforms the event log into readable application state using deterministic logic that can be rerun to derive the same state, and it stores periodic snapshots only as a performance optimization for reads and recovery while intending to keep all raw events and reprocess them when required.

Event sourcing distinguishes a command (an incoming user request that may still fail validation) from an event (a durable, immutable fact created once the command is validated and accepted), and because a consumer cannot reject an event already in the log, validation must happen synchronously before the event is generated (for example via a serializable transaction that atomically validates and publishes) or be split into a tentative event plus a later confirmation event for asynchronous validation.

Mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events are two sides of the same coin, because any state is the result of the sequence of events that mutated it over time and the changelog represents the evolution of state, so treating the event log as the system of record and mutable state as a derived cache of the log (the truth is the log, the database is a cache of it) makes the flow of data through a system easier to reason about.

Immutable events bring auditability like an accounting ledger, where a mistake is corrected by adding a compensating transaction rather than erasing the incorrect one so the original remains for auditing, which also makes it much easier to diagnose and recover from buggy code that wrote bad data than when code can destructively overwrite data.

Immutable events capture more information than the current state alone, for example recording that a customer added an item to their cart and later removed it, which is useful for analytics even though order fulfillment cancels it out, whereas a database that deletes items on removal would lose that information.

Separating the immutable event log from mutable state lets you derive several read-oriented views from the same log (command query responsibility segregation), which eases evolving the application because you can build a new read-optimized view alongside existing systems and shut the old one down later instead of doing a complicated schema migration, and makes normalization debates largely irrelevant since read views can be freely denormalized while kept consistent with the log.

The biggest downside of event sourcing and change data capture is that log consumers are usually asynchronous, so a user can append a write and then read a log-derived view that does not yet reflect it; this can be addressed by updating the read view synchronously with the append (requiring a transaction or the same storage system) or by total-order-broadcast techniques.

Deriving state from an event log simplifies concurrency control: much of the need for multi-object transactions comes from one user action changing data in several places, but if each event is a self-contained description of a user action then the action is a single atomic append, and if the log and application state are partitioned the same way a single-threaded log consumer needs no write concurrency control because the log defines a serial order of events.

Keeping an immutable history forever is feasible for workloads that mostly add data but problematic for workloads with a high rate of updates and deletes on a small dataset, where the history can grow prohibitively large and compaction and garbage-collection performance become crucial; and administrative or privacy requirements may force you to truly delete data by rewriting history, which is hard because copies persist in storage engines, SSDs, and backups, making deletion more about making data harder to retrieve than impossible.

There are three things you can do with a stream: write its events into a storage system (keeping a database in sync, the streaming equivalent of batch output), push the events to users as alerts, notifications, or a dashboard, or process one or more input streams into derived output streams; a stream-processing operator consumes input streams read-only and writes output append-only, like a Unix process or MapReduce job.

The crucial difference from batch processing is that a stream never ends, which means sorting (and therefore sort-merge joins) does not apply to an unbounded dataset and fault-tolerance must differ, because a stream job running for years cannot simply be restarted from the beginning after a crash the way a short batch job can.

Complex event processing and stream search reverse the usual database relationship between queries and data: instead of storing data and treating queries as transient, they store queries long-term and let events or documents continuously flow past them in search of matches, which is the model used by CEP engines and by stream-search tools like Elasticsearch's percolator.

Stream analytics computes aggregations and statistical metrics over time windows of events (such as rates, rolling averages, and comparisons to prior periods) and may use probabilistic algorithms like Bloom filters and HyperLogLog that use far less memory in exchange for approximate results, but stream processing is not inherently lossy or inexact; those approximations are merely an optimization.

Keeping derived data systems (caches, search indexes, data warehouses) up to date from a stream of database changes, and maintaining application state in event sourcing, are both cases of maintaining a materialized view, but unlike windowed stream analytics they generally require all events back to the beginning of time (apart from those discarded by log compaction) rather than only events within a recent time window.

A stream processor that windows by time should use the event time embedded in each event rather than the processing machine's system clock, because using processing time breaks down when there is processing lag from queueing, network faults, restarts, or reprocessing, and message delays can reorder events, so windowing by processing time produces artifacts such as a redeploy's backlog appearing as a request spike when the real rate was steady; event-time processing is also deterministic and rerunnable.
exception: the delay between event creation and processing is negligibly short

statement: With event-time windows you can never be certain all events for a window have arrived, so you must handle straggler events that arrive after the window was declared complete by either ignoring them (tracking the dropped count as a metric and alerting if it grows) or publishing a correction that includes the stragglers and retracts the previous output.

Assigning event timestamps is hard when events are buffered (for example a mobile app offline for days) because the device clock is meaningful but untrustworthy while the server-receipt clock is trustworthy but less meaningful; one fix is to log three timestamps (event time and send time by the device clock, receive time by the server clock) and use the send-versus-receive difference to estimate the device clock's offset and correct the event timestamp.

Common window types for stream aggregation are the tumbling window (fixed length, each event in exactly one window), the hopping window (fixed length but overlapping for smoothing), the sliding window (all events within an interval of each other, with no fixed boundaries), and the session window (no fixed duration, grouping a user's events that occur close together and ending after a period of inactivity).

Stream joins come in three types (stream-stream, stream-table, and table-table) and are harder than batch joins because new events can appear at any time, but all three require the stream processor to maintain state derived from one join input and query that state when messages arrive on the other input.

A stream-stream (window) join matches related events that occur within a chosen time window (such as a search and a later click sharing a session ID) by maintaining state of recent events indexed by the join key and emitting a result on a match or on window expiry without one; note that embedding one event's details into another is not equivalent to a join because it misses the cases where no matching event occurred.

A stream-table join enriches each activity event by looking up its key in a database, and rather than querying a remote database per event (which is slow and risks overloading it) you keep a local copy queried without a network round-trip (like a hash join) and keep that copy up to date via change data capture by subscribing to the database's changelog; this is like a stream-stream join where the table-changelog side uses an effectively infinite window with newer records overwriting older ones.

A table-table join maintains a materialized view from two changelog streams, for example keeping a per-user Twitter timeline cache up to date from streams of tweet and follow events, which corresponds to maintaining the materialized result of a join query that is updated every time either underlying table changes.

Joins on streams are time-dependent because the order of state-changing events matters yet a partitioned log preserves order only within a partition, so when joining with changing state you must decide which point-in-time version to use (for example the tax rate at the time of sale, not the current rate, when reprocessing history); undetermined cross-stream ordering makes the join nondeterministic, and the slowly-changing-dimension fix of giving each version a unique identifier restores determinism but prevents log compaction because all versions must be retained.

Exactly-once (more precisely effectively-once) semantics means the visible output is as if each record were processed exactly once despite retries, and it is harder to achieve in stream processing than in batch processing because you cannot wait for an unbounded stream to finish before making its output visible.

Microbatching (as in Spark Streaming, breaking the stream into roughly one-second mini-batches, where smaller batches add overhead and larger ones add delay) and rolling checkpoints to durable storage (as in Flink, restarting from the last checkpoint and discarding output produced since) provide exactly-once semantics within the framework, but once output leaves the processor (a database write, an external message, or an email) the framework can no longer discard a failed task's output, so a restart causes that side effect to happen twice.

To make stream output appear exactly-once despite faults, all of an event's outputs and side effects (messages to downstream operators or external systems, database writes, operator-state changes, and advancing the input offset) must take effect atomically if and only if processing succeeds, which is the exactly-once message processing problem and can be implemented efficiently in restricted single-framework environments (as in Google Cloud Dataflow, VoltDB, and Kafka) by keeping the transaction internal and amortizing its overhead across many messages.

Idempotence is an alternative to distributed transactions for safe retries, where an operation performed multiple times has the same effect as performing it once (setting a key is idempotent, incrementing a counter is not); a non-idempotent operation can often be made idempotent with extra metadata such as storing the triggering message's offset with the written value to skip already-applied updates, though relying on idempotence assumes replay in the same order, deterministic processing, and no concurrent updates, and may require fencing on failover.

A stateful stream process (windowed aggregations or join tables and indexes) must be able to recover its state after a failure, which can be done by keeping state in a remote replicated store (slow to query per message), by keeping it local and replicating it periodically (Flink snapshots to durable storage, Samza and Kafka Streams replicate via a log-compacted Kafka topic, VoltDB reprocesses on several nodes), or by rebuilding it from the input streams (replaying a short window or rebuilding a change-data-capture replica from the log-compacted change stream), with the best trade-off depending on the infrastructure's performance.

Batch processing has a functional flavor of deterministic pure functions with immutable inputs and append-only outputs, and stream processing extends this with managed fault-tolerant state; thinking of derived data as pipelines of such deterministic functions deriving one thing from another aids fault tolerance and simplifies reasoning about an organization's dataflows.

Maintain derived data systems asynchronously rather than synchronously, because asynchrony makes event-log-based systems robust by containing a fault locally, whereas synchronous distributed transactions abort if any participant fails and tend to amplify failures across the system; cross-partition secondary-index maintenance is likewise most reliable and scalable when done asynchronously.

Reprocessing existing data is a good mechanism for evolving a system to support new features, because without reprocessing schema evolution is limited to simple changes such as adding an optional field or a new record type, whereas reprocessing lets you restructure a dataset into a completely different model to better serve new requirements.

Derived views allow a gradual, reversible migration: rather than switching schemas all at once, maintain the old and new schemas side by side as two derived views onto the same underlying data, route a small fraction of users to the new view to test it, increase that fraction gradually, and finally drop the old view, so every stage is reversible with a working system to fall back to, which reduces risk and lets you move faster.

The lambda architecture records incoming data as immutable events and derives read-optimized views by running a batch system (slower but exact and correcting) and a stream system (fast but approximate) in parallel; it usefully popularized deriving views from immutable event streams and reprocessing, but its drawbacks are maintaining the same logic in two frameworks, merging the two outputs (hard for joins or sessionization), and the expense of frequent full reprocessing that pushes the batch layer toward incremental processing and reintroduces streaming complexity.

Unifying batch and stream processing in one system captures the lambda architecture's benefits without its downsides, and requires being able to replay historical events through the same engine that handles the live stream, exactly-once semantics that discard the partial output of failed tasks, and windowing by event time rather than processing time (since processing time is meaningless when reprocessing historical events).

Databases, Hadoop, and operating systems all fundamentally store and process or query data, but Unix offered low-level abstractions (byte-sequence files and pipes) while relational databases offered high-level abstractions (SQL and transactions) that hide on-disk structures, concurrency, and crash recovery, and this decades-old tension is unresolved, with the NoSQL movement applying a Unix-style low-level approach to distributed OLTP storage.

Running CREATE INDEX reprocesses the existing dataset to derive the index as a new view by scanning a consistent snapshot, building the index, processing the backlog of writes made since the snapshot, and then keeping it up to date on every subsequent write, which is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica and to bootstrapping change data capture.

The dataflow across an entire organization can be viewed as one huge database in which every batch, stream, or ETL process that moves and transforms data acts like the subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date, with the derived data systems behaving like different index types but implemented as separate software running on different machines and administered by different teams.

Because no single data model or storage format suits all access patterns, diverse storage and processing tools can be composed in two complementary ways: a federated database that unifies reads behind one query interface over many underlying engines (the relational tradition), and an unbundled database that unifies writes by reliably plugging systems together through change data capture and event logs (the Unix tradition of composable tools).

To synchronize writes across heterogeneous storage systems, prefer an asynchronous ordered event log with idempotent writes over distributed transactions, because there is no standardized cross-technology transaction protocol while an ordered log with idempotent consumers is a much simpler and more feasible abstraction, and log-based integration gives loose coupling that makes the system robust to a single component's outage (the log buffers for a slow or failed consumer, containing the fault) and lets teams develop components independently behind well-defined interfaces.

Unbundling does not replace databases, which are still needed for stream-processor state and for serving the outputs of batch and stream processing, and specialized engines such as MPP data warehouses remain important; running many pieces of infrastructure carries real operational cost and a single integrated product can give better, more predictable performance for its target workload, so building for scale you do not need is a form of premature optimization.

Unbundling is about breadth rather than depth: its goal is to combine several databases to perform well across a wider range of workloads than any single product can, so if one technology already does everything you need you should simply use it, and the advantages of unbundling and composition appear only when no single piece of software satisfies all your requirements.
condition: no single product satisfies all the application's requirements
exception: a single technology already does everything you need

statement: A missing piece for composing data systems is an unbundled-database equivalent of the Unix shell, a high-level declarative language for wiring storage and processing systems together, so that one could declare something like piping a database into a search index and have all documents indexed and all subsequent changes continually applied without writing custom application code.

A dataflow design treats a data system like a spreadsheet where changing an input automatically recalculates dependent cells, so when a record changes its indexes, cached views, and aggregations are automatically updated without the application worrying about the refresh mechanics, except that real data systems must additionally be fault-tolerant, scalable, durable, and able to integrate disparate technologies written by different teams.

Application code can be seen as a derivation function that transforms one dataset into a derived one (a secondary index picks and sorts fields, a full-text index applies language processing then builds an inverted index, a machine-learning model is derived from training data by feature extraction, and a cache is a UI-shaped aggregation); the secondary-index derivation is so common it is built in as CREATE INDEX, but non-standard derivations need custom code, which databases handle awkwardly because triggers, stored procedures, and user-defined functions have been an afterthought.

Databases are poorly suited as deployment environments for arbitrary application code because they do not fit modern needs like dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, monitoring, and integration with external systems, so it is better to specialize some parts of a system for durable storage and others (such as cluster managers like Kubernetes) for running application code, letting the two interact while remaining independent.

Most web applications keep stateless application logic separate from state management by putting no application logic in the database and no persistent state in the application, so servers can be added or removed freely while the database acts as a mutable shared variable accessed synchronously over the network.

Databases inherited a passive approach to mutable data, in which a reader usually cannot subscribe to changes and is not notified when a value changes (unlike a spreadsheet) but must poll by repeating a query periodically, with subscription to change streams only just beginning to emerge as a feature.

Thinking in terms of dataflow renegotiates the relationship between application code and state: instead of treating the database as a passive variable the application manipulates, application code responds to a state change in one place by triggering a state change in another, and unbundling the database means applying this idea (like a trigger or index update) to derived datasets outside the primary database using stream processing.

Maintaining derived data is not the same as asynchronous job execution, because the order of state changes matters (several views derived from one log must process events in the same order to stay consistent, and many brokers reorder on redelivery, so dual writes are ruled out) and fault tolerance is essential (losing a single message permanently desyncs the derived dataset); these stringent ordering and reliability demands are nonetheless cheaper and more robust than distributed transactions and let application code run as stream operators.

Composing stream operators into a dataflow system shares the microservices benefit of organizational scalability through loose coupling and independent deployment, but its communication is one-directional asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request/response, which can give better fault tolerance and performance.

For a dependency such as a currency exchange rate, the microservices approach queries a remote service synchronously per request, whereas the dataflow approach subscribes to a stream of rate updates ahead of time and records the current rate locally, replacing the synchronous network request with a local query (a stream-table join) that is faster and more robust to the other service failing, though the join is time-dependent so reprocessing needs the historical rate at the original time.

Data travels a write path (work done eagerly when data is written, like eager evaluation) and a read path (work done only when someone queries, like lazy evaluation) that meet at the derived dataset, and caches, indexes, and materialized views are exactly the mechanisms that shift this boundary by precomputing more on the write path to save effort on the read path.

Along the write-path versus read-path spectrum, having no index means little write work but expensive full scans on reads, precomputing the results of all possible queries means trivial reads but infinite write cost, and a cache or materialized view of only the most common queries is the practical middle ground, with uncommon queries falling back to the index.

The stateless-client and authoritative-server assumption is worth questioning, because single-page and mobile apps now hold state and storage locally, enabling offline-first applications that work from a local database and sync in the background when connected, which improves the user experience on slow or unreliable connections and lets on-device state be treated as a cache of server state.

Pushing state changes to clients extends the write path all the way to the end user: instead of polling or reloading, server-sent events and WebSockets keep an open connection so the server actively pushes changes to reduce client staleness, an offline device reconnects and catches up using offsets like a log-based consumer, and propagating a change end to end from one device through logs and processors to another user's interface requires moving from request/response to publish/subscribe dataflow.

Reads can be represented as events too: although writes normally go through an event log while reads are transient requests, you can route read events to the same stream operator as writes, performing a stream-table join between read queries and the database (a one-off read being a transient join and a subscription a persistent join with future events), and logging read events helps track causal dependencies and provenance at the cost of extra storage and I/O.

Treating queries as streams enables distributed execution of complex queries that combine data from several partitions (as in Storm's distributed RPC, or assessing fraud risk by joining a purchase against differently partitioned reputation databases), reusing the existing message-routing, partitioning, and join infrastructure, though for a single multi-partition join it is simpler to use a database that already provides the feature.

Stateful systems require more care for correctness than stateless ones, because a stateless read service can be fixed by restarting whereas a stateful system remembers things forever so a fault's effects can persist; the ACID transaction properties used for decades are weaker than they seem (witness weak-isolation confusion), it is hard to tell whether an application is safe at a given isolation or replication configuration, and Jepsen experiments reveal stark gaps between products' claimed safety and actual behavior under network problems and crashes.

Strong correctness has a cost: serializability and atomic commit are established approaches when you need strong assurances but typically work only within a single datacenter and limit achievable scale and fault tolerance, so applications that can tolerate occasional data corruption are much simpler while stronger guarantees must be paid for.

By the end-to-end argument, an application using a data system with strong safety properties such as serializable transactions is still not guaranteed free from data loss or corruption, because an application bug that writes incorrect data or deletes data is not prevented by serializability; immutable, append-only data makes recovery from such mistakes easier but is not a cure-all by itself.

To achieve exactly-once (effectively-once) semantics when a failed operation is retried, one of the most effective approaches is to make the operation idempotent so it has the same effect whether executed once or many times, but turning a naturally non-idempotent operation into an idempotent one requires effort such as maintaining extra metadata (like the set of operation IDs already applied) and ensuring fencing when failing over between nodes.

TCP's duplicate suppression via sequence numbers works only within a single connection, so a non-idempotent money-transfer transaction tied to a client connection that drops after sending COMMIT leaves the client unsure whether it committed, and retrying can transfer the money twice, which means the standard transaction-atomicity example is actually not correct and two-phase commit's coordinator reconnection does not fix it.

Database-level duplicate suppression does not cover the network between the end-user device and the application server (a timed-out HTTP POST that the user retries is a separate request and transaction), so making an operation idempotent across several network hops requires an end-to-end operation identifier, such as a client-generated UUID or a hash of the form fields, passed all the way through to the database.

End-to-end duplicate suppression can be enforced with a uniqueness constraint on the operation's request ID (inserting the request ID in the same transaction so a duplicate insert fails and aborts), which relational databases maintain correctly even at weak isolation levels, unlike an application-level check-then-insert that can fail under non-serializable isolation; the requests table also doubles as an event log.

By the end-to-end argument, a function such as duplicate suppression can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge of the application at the communication endpoints, so providing it solely in the communication system (TCP, database transactions, or a stream processor) is insufficient; the same argument means catching all data corruption needs end-to-end checksums and full protection needs end-to-end encryption, while low-level reliability features still help by reducing the probability of higher-level problems.

Because strong database safety does not by itself guarantee application correctness, the application must take its own end-to-end measures like duplicate suppression; transactions remain a useful abstraction that collapses many faults into commit-or-abort, but they are not enough and are expensive across heterogeneous storage, and refusing distributed transactions forces reimplementing fault tolerance in application code, which is hard to get right and leads to lost or corrupted data.

Enforcing a uniqueness constraint in a distributed setting requires consensus to decide which of several concurrent conflicting requests is accepted, commonly via a single leader (which works unless you mind funneling all requests through one node or it fails); it scales by partitioning on the value that must be unique, but asynchronous multi-master replication is ruled out because different masters could concurrently accept conflicting writes, so immediately rejecting violating writes requires unavoidable synchronous coordination.
