A log-based system can enforce a uniqueness constraint by partitioning the log on the value that must be unique and having a single-threaded stream processor read requests sequentially and deterministically decide which conflicting request came first (recording taken values in a local database and emitting success or rejection to an output stream that the client watches); the principle of routing all potentially conflicting writes to the same partition and processing them sequentially, with arbitrary validation logic, generalizes to many kinds of constraint.

A multi-partition operation can achieve exactly-once correctness without an atomic commit by first durably logging the request as a single atomically-written message and then having a deterministic stream processor derive the per-partition instructions (such as a debit and a credit) carrying the request ID, so that downstream processors deduplicate by request ID; a crash simply reprocesses from the last checkpoint and, being deterministic, produces the same instructions, which are then deduplicated.

The term consistency conflates two separable requirements: timeliness (users observe an up-to-date state, where violations are temporary and resolved by waiting, with linearizability a strong form and read-after-write a weaker useful one) and integrity (absence of corruption, loss, or contradictory data, where a derived view must correctly reflect its source and violations are permanent and need explicit checking and repair).

In most applications integrity is much more important than timeliness, because a violation of timeliness is merely annoying and confusing (such as a recent credit-card transaction not yet appearing on a statement) while a violation of integrity is catastrophic (such as a statement balance not equal to the sum of its transactions, or money charged to a customer but never paid to the merchant).

ACID transactions provide both timeliness and integrity, but event-based dataflow systems decouple them: asynchronous streams give no timeliness unless a consumer explicitly waits, yet integrity is central and is preserved by exactly-once or effectively-once semantics (fault-tolerant delivery plus duplicate suppression), so reliable stream processing can achieve comparable correctness to distributed transactions with better performance and operational robustness.

Integrity in a dataflow system can be achieved without distributed transactions by combining four mechanisms: representing each write as a single message that is written atomically (fitting event sourcing), deriving all other state updates from that message with deterministic functions, passing a client-generated request ID through every processing stage for end-to-end duplicate suppression and idempotence, and keeping messages immutable and reprocessable to ease recovery from bugs.

Many real applications can accept a much weaker notion of uniqueness than a linearizable constraint by temporarily violating it and fixing up afterward with a compensating transaction or apology (asking a duplicate username registrant to rechoose, reordering oversold stock with a discount, deliberately overbooking flights or hotels with compensation, or charging an overdraft fee), and whether the apology's cost is acceptable is a business decision.

When the cost of an apology is acceptable, checking every constraint before writing the data is unnecessarily restrictive and no linearizable constraint is needed, so you can write optimistically and validate the constraint after the fact (still validating before doing anything expensive to recover from); such applications require integrity, such as not losing a reservation or money, but not timeliness on enforcing the constraint.
condition: the cost of apologizing and compensating for a violated constraint is acceptable

statement: Because dataflow systems can maintain integrity guarantees on derived data without atomic commit, linearizability, or synchronous cross-partition coordination, and because many applications accept loose constraints that can be temporarily violated and fixed up later as long as integrity is preserved, coordination-avoiding data systems can provide strong integrity guarantees while achieving better performance and fault tolerance than systems that require synchronous coordination.

A coordination-avoiding system can run multi-leader across datacenters with asynchronous cross-region replication so each datacenter operates independently, giving weak timeliness (not linearizable) but strong integrity, with serializable transactions still useful at a small scope and synchronous coordination introduced only where strictly needed (such as a constraint from which recovery is impossible) so the whole system does not pay the cost of coordination for the sake of a small part that needs it.

Coordination and constraints reduce the apologies you must make for inconsistencies but also reduce performance and availability and so increase the apologies you must make for outages, so since you cannot reduce apologies to zero you should aim for the trade-off sweet spot with neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems.

A system model's fault assumptions are really matters of probability rather than binary certainties, and rare violations such as data corruption sitting untouched on disk, network corruption evading TCP checksums, and random memory bit-flips (including the rowhammer effect) do occur at sufficient scale, so they deserve attention rather than being assumed impossible.

Software bugs that lower-level checksums cannot catch occur even in mature databases (such as MySQL failing to maintain a uniqueness constraint or PostgreSQL's serializable isolation showing write skew) and far more in application code, which receives much less review and often misuses integrity features, so ACID consistency only holds if transactions are bug-free and the application uses the database correctly.

Since both hardware and software fail eventually, data corruption is inevitable in the long run, so a system should at least be able to detect corruption by auditing rather than blindly trusting promises, as large-scale storage systems like HDFS and Amazon S3 do by running background processes that continually read files back, compare them to other replicas, and move data between disks to mitigate silent corruption.

To be sure your data is still intact you have to actually read it back and check, and you should periodically test restoring from backups, otherwise you may only discover that a backup is broken when it is too late and data has already been lost.

Rather than assuming correctness guarantees are absolute, systems should adopt a trust-but-verify culture of continually auditing their own integrity, which is especially important now that weaker NoSQL consistency guarantees and less mature storage technologies are common even though the audit mechanisms to match them were never developed.

Event-based systems are more auditable than transactions that mutate several objects (whose deciding application logic is transient and not reproducible), because event sourcing records user input as a single immutable event with deterministic, repeatable derivation, so you can verify the event log with hashes and re-run or redundantly run the derivation to check that the derived state matches, and the deterministic dataflow also enables time-travel debugging.

Integrity checking is best done end to end, because the more systems a check includes the fewer opportunities corruption has to go unnoticed (an end-to-end check of a derived data pipeline implicitly covers every disk, network, service, and algorithm along the path), and continuous end-to-end integrity checks, like automated testing, find bugs quickly and give the confidence to evolve the system faster.

Cryptographic tools such as Merkle trees, which are trees of hashes that efficiently prove a record appears in a dataset, underpin integrity checking in technologies like certificate transparency and distributed ledgers and could become more widely used for auditing data systems in general, given work to keep them scalable and low-overhead.

Engineers bear ethical responsibility for both the intended and unintended consequences of the systems they build, and because many datasets are about people (their behavior, interests, and identity) such data must be treated with humanity and respect, since a technology is not good or bad in itself and what matters is how it is used and how it affects people.

Predictive analytics that make automated decisions about individuals (such as recidivism risk, loan default, insurance claims, or hiring) directly affect people's lives, and as algorithmic decision-making spreads a person labeled risky can be systematically excluded from jobs, travel, insurance, and finance with little chance of appeal, an outcome called an algorithmic prison that contrasts with a justice system's presumption of innocence.

Algorithmic decisions are not inherently fairer than human ones, because a systematic bias in an algorithm's input is learned and amplified in its output, and features correlated with legally protected traits (such as a postal code or IP address predicting race) can encode discrimination, so a predictive system that extrapolates from a discriminatory past will codify that discrimination unless humans apply moral imagination.

Automated decision-making must address responsibility and accountability, because algorithmic decisions are often opaque (especially machine-learning models using wide inputs and stereotyping based on people similar to you), errors from incorrect data are hard to appeal, and a probabilistic model that is correct on average can still be wrong in individual cases, so algorithms that affect people should be made accountable, transparent, and correctable.

When predictions affect people's lives they can create self-reinforcing feedback loops (for example using credit scores to hire, where financial trouble lowers a score, which blocks employment, which worsens the score), so designers should use systems thinking that considers the whole system including the people in it to anticipate whether it amplifies existing inequities and to watch for unintended consequences.

Storing data a user explicitly entered serves the user as the customer, but tracking activity as a side effect (especially under an advertising-funded model where advertisers are the real customers) builds detailed profiles whose interests can conflict with the user's and is better understood as surveillance; not all collection is surveillance, but the framing clarifies the relationship and shows why surveillance tied to consequential outcomes like insurance or employment, or revealing intrusive details, is far from benign.

Consent to data collection is rarely meaningful, because users have little knowledge of what data they feed in or how it is retained and processed, privacy policies obscure more than they illuminate, and one user's data often reveals information about non-users who never agreed, so the derived datasets that combine an entire user base with behavioral tracking and external sources are precisely what users cannot meaningfully understand or consent to.

Data is extracted from users through a one-way, asymmetric process with no reciprocity or negotiation, since the service sets the terms, and declining to use the service is not a free choice when the service is regarded as essential for basic social or professional participation (especially with network effects), so opting out is realistic only for the privileged.

Privacy is not the same as secrecy but is a decision right, the freedom to choose what to reveal to whom and what to keep secret; collecting data through surveillance does not necessarily erase a person's privacy but transfers that decision right from the individual to the data collector, which then exercises it to maximize its own profit.

User-facing privacy settings hand back only partial control, because the service itself retains unfettered internal access to the data and usually grants itself broad rights to process and analyze it beyond what is overtly visible to users, even when it promises not to sell the data to third parties.

With any kind of data you should expect the possibility that it is wrong, undesirable, or inappropriate and build mechanisms to handle those failures, because algorithms are oblivious to human notions of what is inappropriate unless explicitly programmed to respect human needs, so engineers must remain humble and plan for such failings.

Behavioral data is often not worthless data exhaust but a service's core asset (the application being a means to lure users into feeding the surveillance infrastructure), and because it is valuable it is wanted by companies, governments, and criminals, gets sold when a company goes bankrupt, and is leaked in frequent breaches, so it is better regarded as a toxic asset or hazardous material than a pure asset.

When collecting data you must balance its benefits against the risk of it falling into the wrong hands (criminals, hostile intelligence services, insiders, unscrupulous future management, or a future regime), considering not just today's political environment but all possible future governments, because it is poor civic hygiene to install technologies that could someday facilitate a police state.

Engineers should self-regulate data practices by treating users as humans deserving respect and agency rather than metrics to optimize, collecting data only for specified legitimate purposes, not retaining data forever but purging it as soon as it is no longer needed, educating users about how their data is used, and preferring to enforce access control through cryptographic protocols rather than by policy alone.

Because no single tool efficiently serves all use cases, applications must compose several pieces of software, and the data-integration problem is solved by letting data changes flow between systems through batch processing and event streams, designating certain systems as systems of record and deriving other data (indexes, materialized views, machine-learning models, summaries) from them through transformations.

Making derivations and transformations asynchronous and loosely coupled prevents a problem in one area from spreading to unrelated parts and so increases overall robustness and fault tolerance, and expressing dataflow as transformations from one dataset to another eases application evolution (rerun new transformation code over the whole input to rederive the output) and recovery (fix the code and reprocess).

Strong integrity guarantees can be implemented scalably with asynchronous event processing by using end-to-end operation identifiers to make operations idempotent and by checking constraints asynchronously (the client either waiting until the check passes or proceeding and risking having to apologize for a violation), which avoids most coordination and is more scalable and robust than distributed transactions while still maintaining integrity even in geographically distributed and fault-prone scenarios.
Every software system is constructed to satisfy an organization's business goals, and a system's architecture is the bridge between those abstract business goals and the concrete resulting system.
Software architectures can be designed, analyzed, and documented using known, repeatable techniques rather than being purely intuitive or ad hoc.
The central purpose of architecture is taming complexity, and because system complexity keeps rising, architectural work remains necessary rather than obsolete.
Adopting microservices does not by itself guarantee modularity; without deliberate attention to modularity a system still becomes hard to understand, change, and debug.

Most quality attributes (performance, security, availability, safety) are susceptible to weakest-link problems, and harmful emergent quality-attribute properties may appear only when independently developed systems are composed.

Selecting, instantiating, and configuring off-the-shelf tools, frameworks, and infrastructure does not remove the need for architectural knowledge, because the architect must still reason about the resulting and emergent quality attributes.
Quality attribute requirements are derived principally from business goals and are what architecture design, analysis, and documentation activities exist to satisfy.
The software architecture of a system is the set of structures needed to reason about the system; these structures comprise software elements, relations among them, and properties of both.

A software structure is architectural only if it supports reasoning about a system property that matters to some stakeholder; what counts as architectural depends on what is useful to reason about in the given context.
condition: the structure supports reasoning about a stakeholder-relevant property

statement: Architecture is an abstraction that deliberately selects some details and suppresses others; private, internal implementation details of elements are not architectural, only the public interface side is.
Architecture is design, but not all design is architecture: many design decisions are intentionally left unbound by the architecture and delegated to downstream designers and implementers.

Every software system has an architecture because it has elements and relations, but that architecture is not necessarily known or documented; the architecture exists independently of any representation of it, which is why architecture documentation matters.

An architecture can either support or hinder the achievement of a system's important requirements, so an architecture should be deliberately designed and evaluated rather than chosen by trial and error.

An element's behavior is part of the architecture insofar as that behavior helps reason about the system or influences the acceptability of the system as a whole, and such behavior should be documented.
condition: the behavior affects system-level properties or acceptability

statement: Architectural structures fall into three categories: module structures (static implementation units), component-and-connector (C&C) structures (runtime elements and interactions), and allocation structures (mapping software to non-software environments). No single structure is the architecture.

Component-and-connector (C&C) structures show how elements interact at runtime and are the primary basis for reasoning about runtime quality attributes such as performance, security, and availability.
Module structures partition the system into static implementation units with assigned functional responsibilities and are the primary tools for reasoning about a system's modifiability.
Allocation structures map software elements onto non-software structures such as hardware processors, file systems, and development teams, and let you reason about deployment-related qualities.
The module decomposition structure largely determines a system's modifiability, which depends on whether anticipated changes fall within the purview of a few preferably small modules.

In the uses structure, one unit uses another if the correctness of the first requires a correctly functioning (not stubbed) version of the second; an accurate uses relation enables engineering of subsets and incremental development.

A layer is an abstract virtual machine providing a cohesive set of services through a managed interface; in strictly layered systems a layer may use only one other layer, and the layer structure gives the system portability.
condition: in strictly layered systems for the single-layer-use rule

statement: The deployment (allocation) structure is the key structure for achieving deployability and lets the architect reason about performance, data integrity, security, and availability, and is of particular interest in distributed systems.

The work-assignment structure makes clear that who implements which module has architectural as well as management implications; on large projects, identify units of functional commonality and assign each to a single team rather than letting everyone reimplement them.
condition: on large development projects

statement: Architectural structures are not independent: elements of one structure relate to elements of others and mappings between structures are generally many-to-many, so the relations between structures must themselves be reasoned about.

Design and document an architectural structure only when doing so brings a positive return on investment, usually as decreased development or maintenance cost; smaller systems warrant fewer structures.
exception: trivial cases such as a single process or single processor, where the corresponding structure collapses and need not be represented

statement: System architecture concerns the totality of hardware, software, and human interaction and establishes constraints within which the software architecture must live; the system and software architects frequently negotiate the distribution of functionality.

A project often designates one structure as dominant (frequently the module decomposition structure, because it tends to mirror and spawn the team and project structure) and casts other structures in its terms.
An architect should choose which structures to work on and document based on how well each provides insight and leverage into the system's most important quality attributes, not document all of them.
Architectural patterns are documented, reusable compositions of architectural elements that package proven strategies for solving recurring problems across many domains.
There is no inherently good or bad architecture; an architecture is only more or less fit for a stated purpose, so architecture evaluation only makes sense in the context of specific stated goals.

Architecture rules of thumb can be applied proactively for greenfield development or as analysis heuristics for existing systems; violating one is not automatically fatal but is a warning sign that should be investigated.

A software architecture should be the product of a single architect or a small group with an identified technical leader, to give the architecture conceptual integrity and technical consistency; this holds for agile and open-source projects as well as traditional ones, and requires a strong connection between architects and the development team to avoid impractical ivory-tower designs.

The architecture should be based on a prioritized list of well-specified quality attribute requirements, which inform the tradeoffs that always occur; getting the quality attributes right matters more than functionality.

The architecture should be documented using views (each a representation of one or more structures) that address the concerns of the most important stakeholders in support of the project timeline, starting minimal and elaborated later as needed.

The architecture should be evaluated for its ability to deliver the system's important quality attributes early in the life cycle, when evaluation returns the most benefit, and re-evaluated as appropriate when the architecture or its intended environment changes.

The architecture should lend itself to incremental implementation to avoid integrating everything at once and to discover problems early; one way is to build a skeletal system that exercises the communication paths with minimal functionality and grow it incrementally, refactoring as needed.

The architecture should feature well-defined modules whose responsibilities are assigned using information hiding and separation of concerns: information-hiding modules encapsulate things likely to change behind a well-defined interface, insulating the rest of the software from those changes and letting teams work largely independently.

Unless the requirements are unprecedented, a system's quality attributes should be achieved using well-known architectural patterns and tactics specific to each attribute rather than inventing new mechanisms.
exception: when requirements are genuinely unprecedented

statement: The architecture should never depend on a particular version of a commercial product or tool; if such a dependency is unavoidable, it should be structured so that changing to a different version is straightforward and inexpensive.
exception: if a version dependency is unavoidable, isolate it so the version can be changed cheaply

statement: Modules that produce data should be kept separate from modules that consume data, which tends to increase modifiability because changes are usually confined to either the production or the consumption side and upgrades can be staged.

Do not expect a one-to-one correspondence between modules and components; with concurrency, multiple component instances may run in parallel from the same module, and one thread may use services from several components each built from a different module.

Every process should be written so that its assignment to a specific processor can be changed easily, perhaps even at runtime; this flexibility is a driving force behind virtualization and cloud deployment.

The architecture should feature a small number of simple, uniform component-interaction patterns (do the same things the same way throughout), which aids understandability, reduces development time, and increases reliability and modifiability.

The architecture should contain a small, clearly specified set of resource-contention areas whose resolution is maintained; for each area of concern the architect should produce and enforce budgets or guidelines (for example, time budgets for performance or traffic guidelines for network utilization).
A system's ability to meet its desired quality attributes is substantially determined by its architecture.

Architecture alone cannot guarantee a system's functionality or quality; poor downstream design, coding, or implementation decisions can undermine an adequate architecture, so quality depends on decisions at all life-cycle stages.

To enable a quality attribute, focus architectural attention accordingly: for performance manage time-based behavior, shared-resource use, and inter-element communication; for modifiability assign responsibilities and limit coupling so most changes touch few elements; for security protect inter-element communication and control which elements access which information; for scalability localize resource use and avoid hard-coding resource limits; for reusability restrict inter-element coupling.

Every architecture partitions possible changes into local (one element), nonlocal (multiple elements but the architectural approach intact), and architectural (changing how elements fundamentally interact); an effective architecture is one in which the most common changes are local and therefore easy to make.
Roughly 80 percent of a typical software system's total cost is incurred after initial deployment, which makes modifiability an economically dominant quality attribute.

It is possible to predict a system's qualities from an evaluation of its architecture alone, because certain architectural decisions lead to certain quality attributes; this lets architects spot potential trouble early instead of building, testing, and hoping.

Architecture is a shared abstraction that stakeholders use to build mutual understanding, negotiate, form consensus, and communicate, because different stakeholders are concerned with different architecture-affected characteristics of the system.

Presenting the architecture to stakeholders often triggers important behavioral and requirements questions and can reveal missing or unreasonable requirements, so reviews that emphasize synergy between requirements and architecture are valuable.

Software architecture is the manifestation of the earliest design decisions about a system, and these early bindings carry disproportionate weight over the system's development, deployment, and maintenance; architecture is also the earliest point at which those decisions can be scrutinized.
Changing an early architectural decision causes a ripple effect of further changes that can turn into an avalanche, so architecture refactoring or redesign should not be undertaken lightly.

For an implementation to conform to an architecture it must contain the prescribed elements, have those elements interact as prescribed, and have each element fulfill its prescribed responsibilities; each prescription is a constraint on the implementer.

An architect can decompose a transaction's performance requirement into per-unit performance budgets; if each software unit stays within its budget the overall transaction meets its requirement, even though implementers may only know their own budget.

Architects need not be experts in every algorithm or language detail, but must know enough not to design something difficult to build; they are the people responsible for establishing, analyzing, and enforcing architectural decisions and tradeoffs.

The architecture's broadest decomposition becomes engraved in the project's work-breakdown structure and often the wider organization, dictating units of planning, scheduling, budget, inter-team communication channels, configuration control, and integration and test plans (a reflection of Conway's law).

Once an architecture is agreed and responsibilities are formalized (especially contractually), it becomes very costly for managerial and business reasons to significantly modify it, which is an argument for analyzing a large system's architecture before settling on a specific choice.

An architecture enables incremental development through a skeletal (walking-skeleton) system that contains infrastructure such as element initialization, communication, data sharing, resource access, error reporting, and logging, but only minimal application functionality, then grows end-to-end; this surfaces performance and other problems early.
Build infrastructure and application functionality hand in hand: design and build a little infrastructure to support a little end-to-end functionality, and repeat until done.

Cost and schedule estimates based on a bottom-up understanding of the system's pieces are typically more accurate than purely top-down estimates, and the best estimates emerge from a consensus negotiated between the architect/manager's top-down estimates and the developers' bottom-up estimates.
The earlier in the life cycle reuse is applied, the greater the benefit, and reuse of architectures provides far greater leverage than code reuse for systems with similar requirements.

A product line is a set of systems built from shared assets, chief among them an architecture designed for the whole family that defines what is fixed and what is variable across members; product lines have shown order-of-magnitude payoffs in time to market, cost, productivity, and product quality.

Architecture-based development focuses on composing or assembling independently developed elements, which is possible because the architecture constrains acceptable replacements and additions by how they interact, receive and relinquish control, consume and produce data, access data, and use communication protocols.

An open system defines standards for how software elements behave, interact, and share data so that many suppliers can produce elements, which helps avoid vendor lock-in; open systems are enabled by an architecture that defines the elements and their interactions.

Voluntarily restricting the design vocabulary to a small number of proven solutions (tactics, patterns, and reused off-the-shelf elements) minimizes design complexity; engineering is about discipline, not unrestricted creative freedom.

Restricting the design vocabulary to proven solutions yields enhanced reuse, more regular and simpler designs that are easier to understand and communicate with more predictable outcomes, easier analysis with greater confidence, shorter selection time, and greater interoperability.
Unprecedented designs are risky, so novel solutions should be sought only when existing proven solutions are insufficient to solve the problem at hand, not invented for the sake of novelty.
exception: when existing solutions are genuinely insufficient for the problem

statement: Different architectural views serve different communication needs: module views show project structure and who builds what, C&C views explain how the system works at runtime, and allocation views show where a part fits in the development or deployment environment.
A quality attribute is a measurable or testable property of a system that indicates how well the system satisfies stakeholder needs beyond its basic function.

Functionality does not determine architecture: any required functionality can be satisfied by many different architectures, and if functionality were all that mattered a single monolithic blob would suffice; systems are structured into cooperating elements precisely to achieve quality attributes.

Functionality is achieved by assigning responsibilities to architectural elements, a process that produces the module decomposition structure; architecture constrains that allocation when other quality attributes matter.

Systems are frequently redesigned not because they are functionally deficient (replacements are often functionally identical) but because they are too hard to maintain, port, or scale, too slow, or have been compromised, which are all quality-attribute failures.

Quality attribute definitions are only meaningful relative to specific changes, faults, or conditions: no system is absolutely modifiable or robust, only modifiable or robust with respect to a stated set of changes or faults, so the context must be specified.

Quality attribute scenarios should be used to characterize quality attributes, which solves the problems of untestable attribute definitions and of arguing over which quality category an issue (such as a denial-of-service attack) belongs to.

Quality attributes divide into two categories: those describing a runtime property of the system (such as availability, performance, usability) and those describing a property of the system's development (such as modifiability, testability, deployability).

Quality attributes can never be achieved in isolation; achieving one always affects others positively or negatively, and almost every quality attribute negatively affects performance, so design is partly a matter of making appropriate tradeoffs.

All quality attribute requirements should be specified in a common, testable, unambiguous six-part scenario form, which removes sensitivity to vocabulary differences and category disputes and gives uniform treatment across quality attributes.
A quality attribute scenario has six parts: source of stimulus, stimulus, environment, artifact, response, and response measure.

The source of a stimulus can affect how the system treats it, so it must be specified; for example, a request from a trusted user need not undergo the same scrutiny as a request from an untrusted user.

A scenario's response must have a measurable response measure so the scenario is testable; for performance this might be latency or throughput, and for modifiability the labor or wall-clock time required to make, test, and deploy the modification.

Environment and artifact are often overlooked but important scenario parts: the same stimulus may be handled differently depending on system state (for example a change request arriving after code freeze, or the fifth successive failure versus the first) and on which artifact it targets, so both should be made precise.
Even when some scenario parts are omitted in early thinking, knowing that all six parts exist forces the architect to consider whether each part is relevant to the requirement.

Distinguish general (system-independent) quality attribute scenarios from concrete (system-specific) ones; provide general scenarios for elicitation, because it is much easier for a stakeholder to tailor a general scenario to their system than to generate a concrete scenario from scratch.

The software architect may not bear responsibility for every quality attribute requirement; some quality concerns are addressed outside the software (for example, security provided by physical network isolation and guards rather than by the architecture).
A tactic is a design decision that directly influences the achievement of a single quality attribute response to some stimulus.

An architectural pattern describes a recurring design problem in a specified context and a well-proven solution defined by the roles, responsibilities, relationships, and collaborations of its elements; a pattern usually affects more than one quality attribute.
Patterns typically bundle multiple tactics and therefore frequently embody tradeoffs among quality attributes; choosing a pattern thus commits the design to those tradeoffs.

Architectures often emerge and deteriorate over time as developers add features and fix bugs while focused on immediate tasks rather than architectural integrity; this death by a thousand cuts is a form of technical debt called architecture debt.

Architecture debt is reversed by refactoring, which applies to architectural elements as well as code; for example, separating modules into subsystems by security property, removing performance bottlenecks, or factoring duplicated functionality into one module to improve cohesion and reduce the number of places a change must touch.

Tactics deserve focus because no pattern may solve a problem completely (tactics systematically augment and adapt a pattern to fill gaps), because when no pattern exists tactics let the architect build a design fragment from first principles with insight into its properties, and because tactics make design and analysis more systematic.

A tactic must be refined into a concrete strategy when applied (for example schedule resources into shortest-job-first or round-robin, or use an intermediary into a layer, broker, proxy, or tier), and its applicability depends on context (for example manage sampling rate suits some real-time systems but not systems where losing a single event is unacceptable).

Some super-tactics recur across many patterns and quality attributes (for example the modifiability tactics of encapsulation, restricting dependencies, using an intermediary, and abstracting common services, plus scheduling and monitoring), so a tactic should not be expected to live in only one place for a single quality attribute.

Architecture analysis should not wait until the design is complete; tactics-based questionnaires are a lightweight technique that yields insight into an architecture's ability to provide a quality attribute at any maturity stage, with confidence scaled to the maturity of available artifacts.

For each tactic in a tactics-based questionnaire, record whether the architecture supports it, any risk in using or not using it, the specific design decisions and the code-base location that realize it (useful for auditing and architecture reconstruction), and the rationale or assumptions behind the decision.

A tactics-based questionnaire records each tactic as Supported (Y/N), Design Decisions and Location, Risk (High/Medium/Low), and Rationale; a single quality attribute questionnaire typically takes 30 to 90 minutes and forces the architect to step back and consider the bigger picture.

Functional requirements are satisfied by including an appropriate set of responsibilities in the design, whereas quality attribute requirements are satisfied by the structures and behaviors of the architecture.

Availability is the property that software is present and ready to perform its task when needed; it builds on reliability by adding recovery, that is, the system's ability to repair itself and to mask or repair faults so the cumulative outage does not exceed a required value over a specified interval.

A failure is an externally visible deviation of the system from its specification and requires an external observer; a failure's cause is a fault, and the intermediate states between a fault occurring and a failure occurring are errors. Faults can be prevented, tolerated, removed, or forecast.

If code containing a fault executes but the system recovers with no externally observable deviation from specified behavior, no failure has occurred; distinguishing faults from failures is what enables discussing repair strategies.

Steady-state availability can be computed as MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), where MTBF is mean time between failures and MTTR is mean time to repair; reasoning about availability therefore means reasoning about what makes the system fail, how likely it is, and how long repair takes.

Scheduled downtime is normally excluded from availability calculations because the system is deemed not needed then, as defined by the service level agreement; high availability typically refers to designs targeting 99.999 percent (five nines) availability or greater.
condition: as specified by the system's SLA

statement: Detected faults should be categorized before being reported and repaired, commonly by severity (critical, major, minor) and service impact (service-affecting or non-service-affecting), which gives operators timely accurate status and lets an appropriate automated or manual repair strategy be chosen.

In an availability general scenario the stimulus is a fault (omission, crash, incorrect timing, or incorrect response) from internal or external sources; desired responses include preventing the fault from becoming a failure, detecting, logging, notifying, recovering, disabling the fault source, masking or containing damage, or operating in a degraded mode; measures include availability percentage, time to detect, time to repair, degraded-mode duration, and the proportion or rate of faults handled.

Achieving a quality attribute often requires process decisions in addition to architectural ones; for example, a strong security architecture is worthless if employees fall for phishing attacks or choose weak passwords.

Availability tactics serve one of three purposes: fault detection, fault recovery, or fault prevention; their goal is to keep a fault from becoming a failure, or at least to bound the fault's effects and make repair possible.

Availability tactics are often provided by software infrastructure such as a middleware package, so the architect's job is frequently to choose, assess, and combine the right tactics rather than to implement them.

A monitor component is a fault-detection tactic that watches the health of processors, processes, I/O, memory, and shared resources, can detect failure or congestion (such as from a denial-of-service attack), and orchestrates other detection tactics like self-tests and heartbeats.

Ping/echo and heartbeat both detect component or connection failure through message exchange; the key difference is who initiates the health check (the monitor pings, whereas with heartbeat the monitored component sends), and ping/echo requires a timeout threshold after which the unresponsive component is declared failed.

Timestamps or sequence numbers detect incorrect sequences of events primarily in distributed message-passing systems, and sequence numbers are preferable where distributed clocks may be inconsistent across processors.

Condition monitoring and sanity checking validate conditions or the reasonableness of outputs (for example via checksums), typically at interfaces; the monitor itself must be simple and ideally provably correct so that it does not introduce new software errors.

Voting compares results from multiple sources that should produce the same output and decides which to use; it depends critically on having multiple sources and on simple, rigorously reviewed and tested voting logic so the probability of voter error is low.
Replication (exact clones) protects against random hardware failures but cannot protect against design or implementation errors in hardware or software, because it embeds no diversity.

Functional redundancy adds design diversity to address common-mode failures (where replicas share the same fault because they share an implementation), but it remains vulnerable to specification errors and is more expensive to develop and verify.

Analytic redundancy uses separate requirement specifications and diversity among inputs and outputs to tolerate specification errors, and its voter must be more sophisticated than simple majority or average (for example understanding which sensors are reliable and blending or smoothing values over time).

Exception detection tactics (system exceptions, parameter fence, parameter typing, and timeout) detect conditions that alter the normal flow of execution; for example a parameter fence places a known data pattern after variable-length parameters to catch memory overwrites, and timeout raises an exception when timing constraints are missed.

The redundant spare recovery tactic keeps one or more duplicate components that take over when the primary fails; its hot, warm, and cold spare variants differ primarily in how up to date the backup is at the moment of takeover.

Rollback reverts the system to a previously saved known-good checkpoint (the rollback line) when a failure is detected, so it depends on a stored checkpoint and is often combined with the transactions and redundant-spare tactics to promote a standby to active after the rollback.

On detecting an exception, a system should never simply crash; productive exception handling ranges from error return codes to exception classes that carry the exception's name, origin, and cause so software can mask or repair the fault.

In-service software upgrade tactics differ by purpose: function patch and class patch deliver bug fixes incrementally, while hitless in-service software upgrade (ISSU), which leverages the redundant spare tactic, delivers new features and capabilities without affecting service.
The retry tactic assumes the fault that caused a failure is transient and re-attempts the operation, and a limit must be placed on the number of retries before a permanent failure is declared.
condition: the fault is plausibly transient

statement: Graceful degradation maintains the most critical system functions in the presence of component failures while dropping less critical functions, so that individual failures reduce functionality rather than causing complete system failure.
Reconfiguration recovers from failures by reassigning responsibilities to the resources or components left functioning while maintaining as much functionality as possible.

Reintroduction tactics return a repaired component to service: shadow mode runs it under monitoring while it repopulates state before reactivation, state resynchronization syncs standby state via parallel inputs or checkpointing, escalating restart varies restart granularity to minimize service impact, and nonstop forwarding splits control and data planes so the data plane keeps working while the control plane recovers.

Removal from service (software rejuvenation or therapeutic reboot) temporarily takes a component out of service and resets it to scrub latent faults such as memory leaks, fragmentation, or soft errors before they accumulate to a service-affecting failure.

The transactions tactic uses ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable) semantics, commonly realized via the two-phase commit protocol, to prevent race conditions caused by two processes updating the same data item at the same time.

A predictive model combined with a monitor watches operational metrics (such as session establishment rate, resource threshold crossings, process-state statistics, and message-queue length) to predict the onset of faults and take corrective action before a critical threshold is crossed.

Exception prevention techniques such as exception classes, error-correcting codes, smart pointers (which bounds-check pointers and automatically de-allocate unreferenced resources), and wrappers prevent faults like dangling pointers, resource leaks, and semaphore access violations.

Increase competence set means designing a component to handle more states and faults as part of its normal operation (for example waiting for or deferring on a blocked shared resource rather than throwing an exception), so it raises an exception in fewer situations.
Beyond runtime tactics, producing high-quality code through code inspections, pair programming, and solid requirements reviews is itself an excellent way to prevent faults in the system being built.

The availability tactics-based questionnaire enumerates the detect, recover, and prevent tactics as yes/no questions, and the answers should focus further investigation such as documentation review, code analysis, and reverse engineering.

Active redundancy (hot spare) has all nodes in a protection group process identical inputs in parallel so a spare keeps a synchronous state and can take over from a failure in milliseconds, at the cost of being the most compute-intensive and expensive redundancy pattern.

Passive redundancy (warm spare) has only active members process traffic and periodically push state updates to loosely coupled spares, providing a balance between the more available but more expensive active redundancy and the cheaper but less available cold spare.

Cold sparing keeps redundant spares out of service until failover, then runs a power-on-reset before placing them in service; its poor recovery performance and high mean time to repair make it poorly suited to systems with high-availability requirements.

The core tradeoff among hot, warm, and cold spares is time to recover from a failure versus the runtime cost incurred to keep a spare up to date, with a hot spare carrying the highest cost but the fastest recovery.

Triple modular redundancy (TMR) implements the voting tactic with three components receiving identical inputs and forwarding outputs to voting logic that reports inconsistency and picks an output (majority or average); three components are usually a sweet spot between availability and cost because the chance of two or more failing is vanishingly small.

A circuit breaker stops an invoker from retrying endlessly by returning immediately once it deems a fault present (until reset), which removes per-component retry policy and prevents cascading failures where many callers of an unresponsive component go out of service themselves.

Timeout or retry values for a circuit breaker must be chosen carefully: too long adds unnecessary latency, while too short causes false-positive trips that lower the availability and performance of the services.

Forward error recovery escapes an undesirable state by moving forward to a safe, possibly degraded state using built-in error correction such as data redundancy, instead of rolling back to a previous state or retrying.

Continuous deployment is most valuable where just-in-time feature releases are a competitive advantage and just-in-time bug fixes are essential to safety, security, or continuous operation, but it is not desirable or even possible in all domains, such as software in complex ecosystems requiring coordinated multi-part releases, or embedded, hard-to-access, or non-networked systems.
exception: complex coupled ecosystems, embedded, hard-to-access, or non-networked systems

statement: If the deployment process from coding to production is fully automated with no human intervention it is called continuous deployment; if it is automated up to placing the system into production but a human performs that final step (for example due to regulations or policy), it is called continuous delivery.

A deployment pipeline is the sequence of tools and activities from checking code into version control to the application being deployed for users, during which tools integrate and automatically test the code for functionality and for concerns such as performance under load, security, and license compliance.

Each deployment-pipeline stage runs in an isolated environment with an expanding test scope: standalone unit tests in the development environment, build plus unit and integration tests in the integration environment, broad quality tests (performance, security, license conformance, possibly user and field testing) in the staging environment, and close usage monitoring in the production environment.

Architectural choices affect deployability; for example the microservice pattern lets each team make its own technology choices, removing the version and library incompatibilities that would otherwise surface at integration time.

A continuous deployment mindset forces earlier attention to testing infrastructure (because it requires continuous automated testing) and to rollback and disable mechanisms such as feature toggles and backward-compatible interfaces, and these architectural decisions are best taken early.

Virtualization enables environment parity, where development, integration, staging, and production environments differ in scale but not in type of hardware or fundamental structure, reducing time wasted diagnosing why a test passes in one environment and fails in another.

The quality of a deployment pipeline is measured by cycle time (pace through the pipeline, which rapid deployment requires to be free of human intervention and cross-team coordination), traceability (ability to recover every artifact, including code, dependencies, tests, and tools, that led to a problem, kept in an artifact database), and repeatability (the same action with the same artifacts yields the same result).

Repeatability is harder than it sounds and is undermined by non-deterministic build inputs such as fetching the latest version of a library, or by tests that modify shared state (for example database values) without restoring it.

DevOps is a set of practices intended to reduce the time between committing a change to a system and that change being placed into normal production while ensuring high quality, relying on cultural and organizational change together with tools and architectural design.
Automated testing is a critically important ingredient of continuous deployment and the tooling for it often represents the highest technological hurdle for DevOps.

DevSecOps is a flavor of DevOps that builds security for both the infrastructure and the applications it produces into the entire process, and is valuable wherever DevOps is useful and a security breach would be particularly costly.

Deployability is the property that software can be allocated to an execution environment within a predictable and acceptable amount of time and effort, and that a deployment failing to meet its specifications can be rolled back within a predictable and acceptable amount of time and effort.

Architects should ensure deployments are granular (deployable as whole system or finer-grained elements, since finer granularity reduces risk), controllable (deployable at varying granularity, with monitoring of deployed units and rollback of failures), and efficient (rapid deployment and rollback with reasonable effort).

In a deployability general scenario the stimulus is a new element available to deploy (such as a defect fix, security patch, or component or framework upgrade) or a need to roll back; the response is to incorporate, deploy, monitor, or roll back; and measures include effort, elapsed time, money, new defects introduced, number of failed deployments, repeatability, traceability, and cycle time.

When assessing deployment risk the architect must consider how software arrives at its host (push of unbidden updates versus pull on request), whether it can be integrated while the existing system runs, its packaging, the efficiency of the process, and its controllability.

Deployability tactics are often provided at least in part by a purchased CI/CD infrastructure, so the architect's job is often to choose, assess, and combine the right tactics rather than implement them.

The scale rollouts tactic deploys a new version gradually to controlled subsets of users while the rest stay on the old version, so effects can be monitored and rolled back; it requires an architectural routing mechanism, outside the service being deployed, to direct each user to the new or old version.

Because a deployment may involve multiple coordinated updates of multiple services and their data, the roll-back mechanism must track all of them or be able to reverse the consequences of any update, ideally in a fully automated fashion.

Deployment commands should be scripted and the scripts treated like code (documented, reviewed, tested, and version controlled) and executed automatically by a scripting engine, which saves time and minimizes opportunities for human error.

The manage service interactions tactic lets multiple versions of a service be deployed and executed simultaneously by mediating their interactions to proactively avoid version incompatibilities, avoiding the need to fully replicate resources to run old and new versions separately.

The package dependencies tactic bundles an element with its dependencies (libraries, OS versions, utility containers) so they deploy together with consistent versions as the element moves from development to production, commonly realized with containers, pods, or virtual machines.

A feature toggle (kill switch) automatically disables a newly released feature at runtime without initiating a new deployment, giving control over deployed features without the cost and risk of redeploying services.

The microservice architecture pattern structures a system as a collection of independently deployable, usually stateless services that communicate only via messages through service interfaces, with no direct linking, no direct reads of another team's data store, no shared memory, and no back doors; service dependencies are acyclic and a discovery service routes messages.

The microservice architecture pattern reduces time to market because a small independently deployable service can be deployed without coordinating with other teams, lets each team make its own technology choices (reducing integration incompatibilities), and scales more easily by adding service instances to match demand.

The microservice architecture pattern has significant tradeoffs: increased network and message overhead with heavy use of discovery services that can become a bottleneck, poor suitability for complex distributed transactions, the cost of maintaining many chosen technologies, difficulty maintaining intellectual control over a large number of services, and the formidable task of designing services with appropriate responsibilities and granularity.

A blue/green deployment stands up N new (green) instances, switches the DNS or discovery service to point at them, and removes the N old (blue) instances only after the new ones are confirmed working, allowing a quick switch-back before cutover; its peak resource utilization is 2N instances.

A rolling upgrade replaces old service instances with new ones a small fraction at a time (allocate, install and register, direct requests to the new instance, drain and destroy an old instance, repeat); its peak utilization is N+1 instances and it can reveal an error in the new version while old instances still exist, unlike blue/green where rolling back after the old instances are deleted can take considerable time.

Running two versions of a service simultaneously (as in a rolling upgrade) risks temporal inconsistency (a client's successive requests served by differently behaving versions) and interface mismatch; prevent temporal inconsistency with the manage service interactions tactic, and prevent interface mismatch by extending rather than modifying the existing interface and using a mediator to translate to it.

Canary testing, the continuous-deployment analog of beta testing, routes a new release to a small designated set of users (external power users or internal staff) in the production environment to gather real in-use data and run controlled experiments at low risk while limiting the number of users exposed to a serious defect.

A/B testing routes a small but meaningful set of users to a different version to run a marketing experiment with real users, monitoring which version yields the best business result rather than checking for defects.
Energy efficiency has become a first-class quality attribute that architects can no longer ignore, with nontrivial tradeoffs against performance, availability, modifiability, and time to market.

A system-wide architectural approach is necessary to gain control over energy efficiency; without system-wide techniques for monitoring and managing energy, developers invent ad hoc approaches that, at best, produce a system hard to maintain, measure, and evolve, and at worst fail to predictably achieve energy goals.

Energy concerns differ by context: cloud platforms rarely run out of energy but must continuously decide optimal resource allocation as they scale up and down, whereas mobile and IoT devices face daily energy constraints with no room for bulky batteries, and in cloud allocating more resources improves performance and robustness at the cost of energy and capital.

In mobile and IoT contexts where adding local resources is not an option, shifting the computational burden from the device to a cloud back-end is a way to manage energy, trading energy efficiency against performance and usability.

In an energy efficiency general scenario the stimulus is a request to conserve or manage energy, the response is one or more of disabling or deallocating services, changing service-to-server allocation, running services at a lower consumption mode, allocating or deallocating servers, or changing service levels or scheduling, and the measures concern energy saved or consumed (kilowatt load, kilowatt-hours, powered-on duration) while maintaining required functionality and acceptable other quality attributes.
Energy efficiency is fundamentally about effectively utilizing resources, and its tactics group into three categories: resource monitoring, resource allocation, and reducing resource demand.
Because you cannot manage what you cannot measure, resource monitoring is the starting point for energy management, with tactics of metering, static classification, and dynamic classification.

Metering collects near-real-time data about the energy consumption of computational resources via a sensor infrastructure (such as data-center power meters, metered rack PDUs, or a battery management system in battery-operated devices).

Static classification estimates energy consumption from cataloged resource energy characteristics (benchmarks or manufacturer specifications) when real-time metering is infeasible, such as when using an off-premises cloud, while dynamic classification estimates energy from transient conditions like workload using table lookup, a regression model on prior data, or simulation when a static model is inadequate.

The reduce-usage tactic lowers energy by deactivating or removing resources no longer demanded (spinning down drives, turning off or slowing CPUs and servers, consolidating VMs onto the minimum number of servers), and in mobile applications by offloading computation to the cloud when communication energy is lower than the computation energy saved.
condition: offloading saves energy only when communication energy is lower than computation energy

statement: Energy can be allocated by annotating service requests with energy information so a requestor chooses a provider by its (possibly dynamic) energy characteristics (via a green service directory), and by scheduling tasks to computational resources that offer better energy efficiency or lower energy cost based on monitoring data while respecting task constraints and priorities.

Reduce-resource-demand tactics (manage event arrival, limit event response, prioritize events, reduce computational overhead, bound execution times, increase resource usage efficiency) increase energy efficiency by doing less work, and are complementary to reduce usage, which instead assumes demand stays the same.

Energy patterns include sensor fusion (using cheap low-power sensor data to decide whether to consult an expensive high-power sensor, which can backfire if it frequently triggers the high-power sensor), kill abnormal tasks (monitoring and killing energy-greedy apps as a fail-safe), and power monitor (disabling devices and interfaces not actively used, at the cost of startup latency and possible startup energy).

Integrability is concerned not only with making separately developed components cooperate but with the costs and technical risks (schedule, performance, technology) of anticipated and unanticipated future integration tasks.

Integration difficulty, meaning its cost and technical risk, can be modeled as a function of size (the number of potential dependencies between the components being integrated and the system) and distance (the difficulty of resolving the differences at each of those dependencies).

Dependencies include forms not detectable by any syntactic relation: components can be coupled temporally or through shared finite resources (memory, bandwidth, CPU, a device, or timing) or semantically (sharing a protocol, file format, unit of measure, or metadata); these temporal and semantic dependencies are often not well understood, acknowledged, or documented, which is a major source of integration cost and risk.

Service and microservice orientation reduces only the syntactic aspect of dependency and does not address temporal or semantic coupling, so components that are supposedly decoupled but actually share detailed knowledge of and assumptions about each other are in fact tightly coupled and may be costly to change.

For integrability, interfaces must be understood as much more than APIs: they must characterize all of the relevant dependencies between elements, including the implicit ones not mentioned in a programming-language interface description.

Integrability requires bridging five kinds of distance between cooperating elements: syntactic (agree on the number and type of shared data), data semantic (agree on the interpretation and units of equally typed values), behavioral semantic (agree on states, modes, and control assumptions), temporal (agree on rates and timing assumptions), and resource (agree on shared-resource assumptions).

Syntactic distance such as a data-type mismatch is usually easy to detect (a compiler may catch it), but data-semantic, behavioral, temporal, and resource distances are typically difficult to observe and predict and require comparing interface documentation or metadata or scrutinizing code, so each should be consciously analyzed.
At its essence integrability is discerning and bridging the distance of each potential dependency, which is itself a form of planning for modifiability.

In an integrability general scenario the stimulus is to add a new component, integrate a new version of an existing component, or integrate existing components in a new way; an integrable system responds by completing, integrating, testing, and deploying the change with components correctly exchanging information syntactically and semantically, collaborating, and not violating resource limits; and measures include components changed, percentage or lines of code changed, effort, money, calendar time, and effects on other quality attributes.

Integrability tactics reduce the cost and risk of adding, reintegrating, or combining components either by reducing the number of potential dependencies between components or by reducing the expected distance between them.

Encapsulation is the foundation on which all other integrability tactics are built: it introduces an explicit interface through which all access to an element must pass, eliminating dependencies on the element's internals and reducing the probability and distance of change propagation.

Using an intermediary breaks dependencies between components or between components and the system: intermediaries such as a publish-subscribe bus, shared repository, or dynamic discovery remove the need for parties to know each other's identity, while data transformers and protocol translators resolve syntactic and data-semantic distance.

The restrict communication paths tactic limits the set of elements an element can communicate with, implemented through visibility restriction and authorization, as seen in service-oriented architectures that force requests through an enterprise service bus for consistent routing and preprocessing.

Adhering to standards is a primary enabler of integrability and interoperability across platforms and vendors, but a standard's benefit is limited to the dimensions of difference it actually addresses and to how likely future component suppliers are to conform to it.
condition: benefit limited to addressed dimensions and to supplier conformance

statement: Abstracting common services hides similar but not identical elements behind a single common abstraction (a shared interface or an intermediary) so future components integrate with one abstraction rather than with each element separately, and it centralizes cross-cutting concerns such as translation, security, and logging so changes occur in fewer places.

The tailor-interface tactic adds or hides capabilities of an existing interface (translation, buffering, data smoothing, hiding functions from untrusted users, or intercepting filters for input validation) without changing its API or implementation, resolving syntactic and data-semantic distance so services with syntactic differences can interoperate unmodified.

The configure-behavior tactic makes a component configurable at build, initialization, or runtime so it can interact with a range of components; offering multiple options increases the chance that the assumptions of the system and a future component will match.

The orchestrate tactic uses a control mechanism to coordinate the invocation of services so they remain unaware of each other, centralizing dependencies at the orchestration mechanism so future integration targets that mechanism instead of point-to-point integration with multiple components.

The manage-resources tactic uses a resource manager (a form of intermediary) that governs access to computing resources such as threads and memory so components request rather than directly access them, preserving invariants like avoiding resource exhaustion or concurrent use and enforcing fair access while reducing resource distance.

Wrappers, bridges, and mediators all allow access to an element without changing it or its interface: a wrapper encapsulates one specific component and transforms its data or control, a bridge translates one component's requires-assumptions to another's provides-assumptions, is independent of any particular component, must be externally invoked, and fixes its translation at construction time, and a mediator adds a runtime planning function and becomes a first-class persistent architectural component.
The more assumptions a bridge tries to address, the fewer components to which it applies.

The service-oriented architecture (SOA) pattern is a collection of distributed components that provide and consume services across heterogeneous languages and platforms and often distinct organizations, governed by SLAs and web-services standards such as WSDL and SOAP; unlike the microservice pattern (assumed to be one system managed by one organization), SOA components are heterogeneous and independently owned, which adds interoperability complexity and overhead.

Dynamic discovery applies the discovery tactic at runtime so a service consumer binds to a concrete provider at startup or runtime (chosen for example by pricing or availability), but it requires automated registration and de-registration and tools to support them.

Modifiability is about lowering the cost and risk of change, and to plan for it an architect must answer four questions: what can change, how likely the change is, when the change is made and who makes it, and what the change costs.

An architect cannot plan a system for all potential changes, because such a system would never be finished, would be far too expensive, and would likely suffer quality-attribute problems elsewhere, so the architect must make the tough decisions about which changes are likely and therefore which will be supported.

A change can be bound at different times (implementation by modifying source, compile time via switches, build via library choice, configuration setup via parameters, or runtime via parameters, plug-ins, or allocation) and made by different agents (a developer, an end user, a system administrator, or a self-adapting system), and these choices determine modifiability cost.

Making a system more modifiable involves two distinct costs, the cost of introducing the modifiability mechanism and the cost of making each modification using it, so the choice of mechanism should be justified by the expected number of similar modifications it will serve.

A modifiability mechanism is justified when N times the cost of making a change without the mechanism exceeds the cost of creating the mechanism plus N times the cost of making the change with it; because N is a prediction, an expensive mechanism may not be warranted if fewer changes than expected arrive, and opportunity cost and time-to-completion must also be weighed.
If code is modified frequently, not introducing any architectural modifiability mechanism and simply piling change on top of change typically leads to substantial technical debt.
condition: code is modified frequently

statement: Scalability is accommodating more of something: horizontal scalability (scaling out) adds resources to logical units such as another server in a cluster, vertical scalability (scaling up) adds resources to a physical unit such as more memory in one computer, the challenge in both is effectively utilizing the added resources, and cloud horizontal scalability is called elasticity.

Portability is achieved by minimizing platform dependencies in the software, isolating those dependencies to well-identified locations, and writing the software to run on a virtual machine that encapsulates the platform dependencies.

Variability is the ability of a system and its artifacts to support a preplanned set of variants, and it is especially important in a product line, where sharing engineering assets across the family sharply lowers the overall cost.

In a modifiability general scenario the source can be a developer, user, administrator, product-line owner, or the system itself; the stimulus is a directive to add, delete, or modify functionality or to change a quality attribute, capacity, platform, technology, product-line membership, or service location; the environment is design, compile, build, initiation, or runtime; and measures include affected artifacts, effort, elapsed time, money, effect on other quality attributes, new defects introduced, and adaptation time.
Modifiability tactics control the complexity, time, and cost of change by affecting one or more of four parameters: reduce module size, increase cohesion, reduce coupling, and defer binding time.

Coupling is the probability that a modification to one module will propagate to another, and high coupling is an enemy of modifiability; reducing coupling decreases the expected cost of any modification affecting either module, and coupling-reducing tactics place intermediaries between otherwise highly coupled modules.

Cohesion measures how strongly a module's responsibilities are related (its unity of purpose), defined as the probability that a change affecting one responsibility also affects others in the module; high cohesion lowers the chance a change touches multiple modules, and low cohesion is improved by removing responsibilities unaffected by anticipated changes.
All other things being equal, larger modules are more difficult and costly to change and more prone to have bugs.

Ignoring the cost of preparing the architecture, a change should be bound as late as possible, but late changes can be made quickly and cheaply only if the architecture is suitably prepared; an architecture equipped to accommodate late modifications costs less on average for those modifications.

The split-module tactic refactors a module that contains non-cohesive responsibilities into several more cohesive modules to reduce average future change cost, and the split should sensibly produce submodules that are each cohesive rather than just placing half the lines of code in each.

The redistribute-responsibilities tactic gathers similar responsibilities scattered across modules into one place; likely change scenarios help identify what to move, since scenarios that consistently affect just one part of a module suggest the other parts are separate responsibilities, and scenarios that require modifying multiple modules suggest those responsibilities should be grouped together.

The restrict-dependencies tactic limits which modules a given module can interact with or depend on, implemented through visibility restriction and authorization, as seen in layered architectures where a layer may use only lower (often only the next-lower) layers and in wrappers that expose only themselves.

Defer binding lets computers rather than people handle a change, which is usually cheaper and less error-prone; parameters are the best-known flexibility mechanism, and values should be bound as late in the life cycle as possible as long as the mechanism enabling that late binding is cost-effective.

Binding time can be deferred by phase: compile or build time (component replacement, compile-time parameterization, aspects), deployment, startup, or initialization time (configuration-time binding, resource files), and runtime (discovery, interpret parameters, shared repositories, polymorphism).

Separating the building of a modifiability mechanism from its use lets different stakeholders be involved, so that installing a mechanism enables an administrator or installer to make a change later without changing code, which is called externalizing the change.

The client-server pattern has a server providing services to multiple distributed clients with low coupling (the server has no a priori knowledge of clients and there is no coupling among clients), scales with client count up to the server's capacity, and lets clients and server evolve independently; its tradeoffs are network-induced performance unpredictability and the need for special security and integrity provisions over shared networks.

The plug-in (microkernel) pattern has a core providing base functionality and plug-ins adding functionality through a fixed set of interfaces (bound at build time or later); plug-ins can be developed by different teams or organizations and evolve independently from the core, but because plug-ins can come from different organizations they make it easier to introduce security vulnerabilities and privacy threats.

The layers pattern partitions software into layers offering cohesive services with a strictly unidirectional allowed-to-use relation (normally only the next-lower layer), so lower layers can change or be reused without affecting upper layers; its tradeoffs are that poor layering can get in the way, layering adds a performance penalty as calls traverse layers, and excessive layer bridging undermines the portability and modifiability that strict layering provides.
