The publish-subscribe pattern has components communicate through asynchronous messages (events or topics) via implicit invocation, with publishers unaware of subscribers and subscribers aware only of message types, yielding loose coupling so subscribers can be added or changed without changing the publisher.

The publish-subscribe pattern has notable tradeoffs: it can increase latency and reduce determinism, makes system performance and resource use harder to reason about, can reduce testability because a small change in event-to-component associations has wide effects, and limits end-to-end encryption because publishers and subscribers do not know each other's identity.

Performance is about a system's ability to meet timing requirements, and characterizing the events that can occur (and when) together with the system's time-based response to those events is the essence of reasoning about performance.
All systems have performance requirements even when they are not explicitly expressed, and performance remains a fundamentally important quality attribute for all software.

Architect for performance up front (for example with a scalable resource pool you can later enlarge), because fixing inadequate performance after the system is built otherwise leaves limited, mostly bad options that may involve considerable rework.

It is not useful to spend much time optimizing a portion of the system responsible for only a small percentage of total time; instrument the system by logging timing information to determine where time is actually spent and focus on the critical portions.
Concurrency improves performance when there are multiple CPUs or wait states to exploit, because a delay introduced in one thread lets the processor make progress on another thread.
condition: there are multiple CPUs or wait states to exploit

statement: Race conditions can occur whenever two threads of control share state with unguarded interleaving, so managing concurrency comes down to managing how state is shared, for example by using locks to enforce sequential access to state or by partitioning state per thread so it is not shared.

Race conditions are among the hardest bugs to discover because their occurrence is sporadic and depends on minute timing differences, so an architect using concurrency must carefully identify critical sections in the code and ensure race conditions cannot occur in them.

In a performance general scenario the stimulus is the arrival of an event that is periodic (arriving at a predictable interval), stochastic (arriving by a probability distribution), or sporadic (neither), and the response measures include latency, throughput, the number or percentage of unsatisfied requests, jitter (variation in response time), and resource utilization level.

The two basic contributors to response time and resource usage are processing time, when the system is actively working and consuming resources, and blocked time, when the system is unable to respond.

Resources behave differently as utilization approaches capacity: a CPU usually degrades fairly steadily as it is more heavily loaded, whereas running out of memory causes page swapping that makes performance crash suddenly.

A computation can be blocked by contention for a resource usable by only one client at a time (more contention grows latency), by a resource being unavailable (offline or failed), or by dependency on another computation's result (significant when the called component is across a network or heavily loaded), so the architect must identify where resource limitations significantly contribute to latency.

Performance tactics fall into two categories: control resource demand, which reduces or limits the demand placed on resources, and manage resources, which makes the available resources handle the demand more effectively.

The manage event arrival tactic uses a service level agreement specifying the maximum event arrival rate supported (the system guarantees response time Y for up to X events per unit time, and beyond X the response is not guaranteed so the client must use multiple instances), and such SLAs are a method for managing scalability of Internet-based systems.

The manage sampling rate tactic reduces the sampling frequency of stimuli (such as sensor data rate or video frames per second) to maintain predictable latency at the cost of fidelity, which is viable when a lower-fidelity but consistent data stream is good enough, and some systems adjust the sampling rate dynamically.
condition: a lower-fidelity but consistent stream is acceptable

statement: The limit event response tactic handles events arriving too rapidly by queuing them, discarding them, or processing only up to a set maximum rate for predictable processing; if no event may be lost the queues must be sized for the worst case, and if events are dropped a policy must be chosen for whether to log them and whom to notify.

The prioritize events tactic ranks events by importance so that when resources are insufficient, low-priority events can be ignored (which consumes minimal resources and increases performance); for example a life-threatening fire alarm should outrank an informational alarm.

Reducing indirection improves latency because the intermediaries that aid modifiability add computational overhead to processing an event stream, which is a classic modifiability versus performance tradeoff; clever code optimization or a broker that establishes direct client-server communication after the initial setup can keep the modifiability while eliminating costly runtime indirection.

Co-locating communicating resources reduces context-switching and inter-component communication cost, whether by hosting cooperating components on the same processor to avoid network delay, placing them in the same runtime component to avoid a subroutine call, or putting tiers of a multi-tier architecture on the same rack.

The bound execution times tactic limits how much execution time is spent responding to an event (for example by capping the number of iterations of a data-dependent algorithm) at the cost of less accurate computation, so its effect on accuracy must be assessed; it is frequently paired with the manage sampling rate tactic.

Increasing the efficiency of algorithms used in critical areas can decrease latency and improve throughput and resource consumption, but this code-tuning approach is only one of many performance tactics, not the only one.

Even when demand for resources is not controllable, the management of those resources is, and one resource can be traded for another (for example keeping intermediate data in a cache versus regenerating it, depending on whether time, space, or network bandwidth is more critical).

Increasing resources (faster or additional processors, more memory, faster networks) is in many cases the cheapest way to get immediate performance improvement, with cost being the usual consideration.

Introducing concurrency reduces blocked time when requests can be processed in parallel by running different event streams or activity sets on different threads, after which a scheduling policy can be chosen via the schedule resources tactic.

Maintaining multiple copies of a computation (such as replicated services or web servers in a pool) reduces the contention that would occur if all requests went to a single instance, with a load balancer assigning new work to an available duplicate by a scheme such as round-robin or least-busy.

Maintaining multiple copies of data is done by replication (separate copies to reduce contention, at the cost of keeping them consistent and synchronized) or caching (copies on storage of differing access speed, requiring a choice of what to cache and optionally prefetching predicted requests).

Bounding queue sizes controls the maximum number of queued arrivals and hence the resources used to process them, but requires a policy for what happens on overflow and a decision about whether failing to respond to lost events is acceptable; it is frequently paired with the limit event response tactic.

Whenever contention for a resource occurs the resource must be scheduled, and the architect's job is to understand the characteristics of each resource's use and choose a scheduling strategy compatible with it.

A scheduling policy has two parts, priority assignment and dispatching, and serves competing criteria such as optimal resource use, request importance, minimizing resources or latency, maximizing throughput, and preventing starvation for fairness, so the architect must be aware of how the chosen policy affects these possibly conflicting goals.

Common scheduling policies trade fairness against priority: FIFO treats all requests equally but can stick a request behind a slow one, fixed-priority scheduling (by semantic importance, deadline-monotonic giving shorter deadlines higher priority, or rate-monotonic giving shorter periods higher priority) serves high-priority requests better but can starve lower-priority ones, dynamic-priority strategies include round-robin, earliest-deadline-first, and least-slack-first, and static (cyclic executive) scheduling fixes preemption points and sequence offline to remove scheduler runtime overhead.

For a single processor with preemptible processes, both earliest-deadline-first and least-slack-first scheduling are optimal, meaning that if any schedule can meet all deadlines, these strategies will successfully schedule that set.
condition: single processor with preemptible processes

statement: Some patterns serve multiple quality attributes; for example the circuit breaker is an availability pattern that also benefits performance by reducing the time spent waiting on nonresponsive services.

The service mesh pattern for microservices attaches a sidecar proxy to each microservice that handles application-independent cross-cutting concerns (interservice communication, monitoring, security, service discovery, load balancing, encryption, observability) and is co-deployed (often in a pod) to cut network latency, letting developers separate business logic from those concerns; its tradeoff is that the sidecars add executing processes and overhead and include functions not needed in every service.

A load balancer is an intermediary that serves as a single point of contact and farms incoming requests out to a pool of providers (implementing the schedule resources tactic), making server failures invisible to clients and keeping latency lower and more predictable, but its algorithm must be very fast and it is a potential bottleneck or single point of failure, so it is often itself replicated.

The throttling pattern packages the manage-work-requests tactic using an intermediary throttler that decides whether incoming requests can be serviced, so services gracefully handle demand variation and stay in a performance sweet spot; its tradeoffs are that the throttling logic must be very fast, buffers must be large if demand regularly exceeds capacity or requests are lost, and it is hard to add to a system where clients and servers are tightly coupled.

The map-reduce pattern performs a distributed, parallel sort and analysis of a large data set: a map function hashes and filters input into buckets using many stateless, non-communicating map instances over data portions, the infrastructure shuffles the buckets to reduce nodes, and reduce functions perform the heavy analysis and emit a much smaller output, with map and reduce instances communicating only via key-value pairs.

The map-reduce pattern is justified only for large data sets, loses its parallelism advantage if the data set cannot be divided into similarly sized subsets, and is complex to orchestrate for operations requiring multiple reduces, though a single instance failure has only a small impact on processing.
condition: large data sets divisible into similarly sized subsets

statement: Safety is a system's ability to avoid straying into states that cause or lead to damage, injury, or loss of life to actors in its environment, and to detect and recover from such unsafe states to prevent or at least minimize the resulting harm.

Software can cause physical harm only through what it is connected to, since actuators translate a digital value into mechanical action; because a program with no externally observable effect serves no purpose, software is effectively always connected to the outside world.
A system can be unsafe merely by sending erroneous information to its human operators through a display, so a system need not directly control machinery to cause harm.

Designing safety-critical software to rely on a single sensor when redundant sensors are available, and never testing that software under sensor-failure conditions, is a dangerous design decision implicated in real fatal accidents.

Unsafe states can be caused by omission (an event fails to occur), commission (a spurious undesirable event), timing failures (events too early or too late), incorrect system values (coarse incorrect values are detectable while subtle incorrect values are typically undetectable), sequence omission or commission, and out-of-sequence events.

Once an unsafe state is detected, the responses parallel those for availability: continue after recovering or place the system in a safe mode, shut down (fail safe), or transition to manual operation; in addition the unsafe state should be reported immediately and/or logged.

Architecting for safety begins by identifying the system's safety-critical functions using techniques such as failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA, also called hazard analysis) and fault tree analysis (FTA, a top-down deductive approach), then designing mechanisms to detect and mitigate the identified faults and hazards.

You should perform your own hazard analysis or fault tree analysis once you have the architecture in hand, because the design decisions themselves may have introduced new safety vulnerabilities not accounted for during requirements analysis.

Safety tactics are categorized as unsafe-state avoidance, unsafe-state detection, and unsafe-state remediation (containment and recovery), and they overlap substantially with availability tactics because availability problems often lead to safety problems and share design solutions.

In a safety general scenario the stimulus is an omission, commission, incorrect data, or timing or sequence failure from a sensor, software component, communication channel, or clock; the response is to avoid the unsafe state, recover, continue in a degraded or safe mode, shut down, switch to manual or backup, notify, and log; and measures include the percentage of unsafe states avoided or recovered from, change in risk exposure computed as size of loss times probability of loss, and time spent in degraded, safe, or shutdown mode.

The substitution tactic replaces potentially dangerous software design features with hardware protection mechanisms such as watchdogs, monitors, and interlocks, which control their own resources and cannot be resource-starved like software versions, but it is typically beneficial only when the function being replaced is relatively simple.
condition: the replaced function is relatively simple

statement: The predictive model tactic monitors the state of health of processes, resources, or properties to give early warning of a potential problem (for example a cruise control computing the closing rate to a vehicle ahead and warning before a collision is unavoidable), and is typically combined with condition monitoring.

The timeout tactic detects late-timing and omission failures by raising an exception when a component fails to meet its timing constraints, and is particularly common in real-time, embedded, and distributed systems.

The comparison tactic detects unsafe states by comparing the outputs of synchronized or replicated elements (working with active redundancy), and with three or more replicas it can both detect an unsafe state and identify which component caused it, though differing outputs may simply trigger a shutdown rather than a vote.

In safety, redundancy lets a system keep operating where a shutdown or further degradation would be undesirable: replication protects only against random hardware failures because it embeds no diversity, functional redundancy adds design diversity to handle common-mode failures (still vulnerable to specification errors and more costly), and analytic redundancy uses separate specifications, often partitioning the system into a simple reliable high-assurance portion and a more complex, accurate, but less stable high-performance portion.

Limit-consequences containment tactics limit harm after an unsafe state is entered: abort stops an operation determined unsafe before it causes damage and is widely used for fail-safe behavior, degradation maintains the most critical functions while dropping or replacing others in a planned safe way (for example dead-reckoning navigation when GPS is lost in a tunnel), and masking compares redundant components and votes, requiring a simple and highly reliable voter.

Barrier containment tactics keep problems from propagating: the firewall tactic limits access to specified resources such as processors, memory, and network connections, and the interlock tactic protects against failures from incorrect event sequencing by controlling all access to protected components and the correct sequencing of events affecting them.

Safety recovery tactics place the system in a safe state: rollback reverts to a saved known-good state (combined with checkpointing and transactions, then retry or degradation), repair state fixes an erroneous state to enlarge the set of states a component handles competently but is inappropriate for unanticipated faults, and reconfiguration remaps the logical architecture onto the remaining functioning resources, falling back to degradation when full functionality cannot be maintained.

Condition monitoring checks conditions in a process or device or validates design assumptions (for example via assertions) to identify states that may lead to hazardous behavior, but the monitor must be simple and ideally provable so it does not introduce new errors or add significant workload, and it feeds the predictive model and sanity checking.

The redundant sensors safety pattern replicates any sensor whose data determines whether a state is safe or unsafe, with independent software monitoring each sensor (the redundant-spare tactic applied to safety-critical hardware), at the cost of added expense and more complex multi-sensor processing.

The monitor-actuator pattern separates an actuator controller, which computes the value to send to a physical actuator, from a monitor, which checks that value for reasonableness before it is sent, so the monitor is a redundant check that separates value computation from value testing and can be made as simple or as sophisticated as required.

The separated safety pattern divides a system into safety-critical and non-safety-critical portions (certifying the safety-critical portion and the separation itself) to reduce certification cost and focus effort, accepting that the separation work is expensive but that it limits the risk of bugs in the non-safety-critical portion affecting the safety-critical portion.

Design Assurance Levels (DAL), defined by DO-178C and ranked A catastrophic, B hazardous, C major, D minor, to E no effect, classify each software function by the severity of its failure condition from hazard analysis, helping allocate limited validation and testing resources to the most safety-critical functions.
Security is the system's ability to protect data and information from unauthorized access while still providing access to people and systems that are authorized.

Security is characterized by three properties, confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA): confidentiality protects data or services from unauthorized access, integrity protects them from unauthorized manipulation, and availability ensures the system is available for legitimate use.

Threat modeling uses an attack tree, similar to a fault tree, whose root is a successful attack and whose child nodes decompose its direct causes; the leaves of the attack tree are the stimulus in a security scenario, and the response is to preserve confidentiality, integrity, and availability or to deter attackers by monitoring their activity.

Privacy is about limiting access to personally identifiable information (PII) by deciding which information is access-limited and to whom access is allowed; PII is generally obscured for testing purposes, and the architect is frequently asked to verify that PII is hidden from members of the development team who do not need access to it.

In a security general scenario the stimulus is an attack (an unauthorized attempt to display, capture, change, or delete data, access services, change behavior, or reduce availability) from a human or system inside or outside the organization; the response maintains confidentiality, integrity, and availability, identifies parties with assurance, ensures non-repudiation, and tracks activity by recording access and attempts and notifying on an apparent attack; and measures include detection accuracy, time to detect, attacks resisted, recovery time, and how much data is vulnerable.
Security tactics fall into four categories that mirror physical security: detect attacks, resist attacks, react to attacks, and recover from attacks.

The detect intrusion tactic compares network traffic or service-request patterns against a database of signatures or known patterns of malicious behavior, where signatures can be based on protocol characteristics, request characteristics, payload sizes, applications, source or destination address, or port number.
The detect service denial tactic compares the pattern or signature of incoming network traffic against historical profiles of known denial-of-service attacks.

The verify message integrity tactic uses checksums or hash values to verify the integrity of messages and of resource, deployment, and configuration files, where a hash is a string for which even a slight change in the input produces a significant change in the output.

The detect message delivery anomalies tactic catches potential man-in-the-middle attacks by checking for suspicious message delivery timing, or abnormal numbers of connections and disconnections, when delivery times are normally stable.
condition: message delivery times are normally stable

statement: The identify actors tactic identifies the source of every external input to the system, with users typically identified by user IDs and other systems identified by access codes, IP addresses, protocols, or ports.

The authenticate actors tactic ensures an actor is actually who or what it claims to be using mechanisms such as passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates, two-factor authentication, biometrics, or CAPTCHA, and may require periodic reauthentication.

The authorize actors tactic ensures an authenticated actor has the rights to access and modify particular data or services, usually via access control assigned per actor, per actor class, or per role.

The limit access tactic restricts the number of access points to resources and the type of traffic allowed through them to minimize the attack surface, as in a demilitarized zone (DMZ) that sits between the Internet and an intranet protected by a pair of firewalls.

The limit exposure tactic is a passive defense that minimizes the damage from a hostile action by reducing the amount of data or services that can be accessed, and hence compromised, through a single access point.

The encrypt data tactic achieves confidentiality by applying encryption to data and communication, providing protection beyond authorization and serving as the only protection for data passing over publicly accessible communication links that lack authorization controls; encryption may be symmetric (shared key) or asymmetric (paired public and private keys).

The separate entities tactic limits the scope of an attack through physical separation on different servers and networks, virtual machines, or an air gap (no electronic connection), and sensitive data is frequently separated from nonsensitive data to reduce the risk from users with access to the nonsensitive data.

The validate input tactic cleans and checks received input through filtering, canonicalization, and sanitization (often using a security framework or validation class) and is the main defense against attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

The change credential settings tactic forces users to change the default security settings assigned at delivery (which may be publicly known) and to choose a new password after some maximum time period, preventing attackers from using publicly available default settings.

React-to-attack tactics include revoke access (severely limiting access to sensitive resources, even for normally legitimate users, when an attack is suspected), restrict login (limiting access from a computer after repeated failed attempts, sometimes with escalating lockout periods), and inform actors (notifying operators, personnel, or cooperating systems when an attack is detected).

Recovery from an attack reuses the availability recovery tactics (since a successful attack is a kind of failure) plus audit, which records user and system actions to trace and identify an attacker and improve future defenses, and nonrepudiation, which guarantees a sender cannot deny sending nor a recipient deny receiving a message, achieved through digital signatures and trusted third parties.

The intercepting validator pattern inserts a wrapper between the source and destination of messages (especially valuable when the source is external) to implement verify-message-integrity and other detect-attack tactics, at the cost of intermediary performance overhead and an obligation to keep its intrusion patterns up to date as they evolve.

An intrusion prevention system (IPS) is a standalone element that identifies and analyzes suspicious overall usage patterns, allowing acceptable activity and preventing and reporting suspicious activity, covering most detect-attack and react-to-attack tactics, but its pattern database must be constantly updated and it incurs a performance cost.

Software testability is the ease with which software reveals its faults through typically execution-based testing, formally the probability that software with at least one fault will fail on its next test execution; an architecture can also enhance testability by making it easier to replicate a bug and narrow down its root cause.

For a system to be properly testable it must be possible to control each component's inputs (and possibly manipulate its internal state) and then observe its outputs (and possibly its internal state), frequently accomplished through a test harness of specialized software designed to exercise the software under test.

A test oracle is an agent (human or computational) that decides whether a program's output is correct by comparing it to the expected result, where output includes derived quality-attribute measures such as how long it took and possibly the program's internal state.

Some systems are too complex and adaptive to be tested fully because some behaviors are emergent, so responses include injecting faults into the running system in a controlled, monitored fashion (as with Netflix's Chaos Monkey) and logging operational data for later lab analysis to reproduce faults, with more emphasis placed on finding the most severe faults.

In a testability general scenario, tests are initiated to validate system functions or qualities or to discover emerging quality threats, triggered by a completed coding increment, integration, full implementation, deployment, delivery, or schedule; the response controls the system and test infrastructure to run tests and observe results; and the response measures represent how easily the system gives up its faults, including effort to find a fault, effort to reach a coverage percentage, probability a fault is revealed by the next test, time to test, and reduction in risk exposure.
Testability tactics fall into two categories: adding controllability and observability to the system, and limiting complexity in the system's design.

Specialized testing interfaces (such as set and get methods for key variables, a method to report full state, a reset method, and methods to turn on verbose output or logging) let testers control or capture state, and should be kept separate from functional interfaces so they can be removed, though removing test code is problematic in performance-critical and safety-critical systems because the released code may not have the same behavior or timing as the tested code.
exception: in performance-critical or safety-critical systems, removing test code risks fielding different behavior than was tested

statement: The record/playback tactic captures the state crossing an interface so it can be used to play the system back and re-create a fault whose triggering state is otherwise difficult to reproduce.

Localizing state storage in a single place makes it convenient to start a system, subsystem, or component in an arbitrary state for a test (for example by externalizing state into a state machine object), whereas buried or distributed state makes this difficult or impossible.

Abstracting data sources by abstracting their interfaces lets test data be substituted easily, so the architecture can point the test system at alternate test databases or files without changing the functional code.

The sandbox tactic isolates a system instance from the real world so experiments have no permanent consequences or can be rolled back, and virtualizing resources such as the system clock, memory, battery, or network (using stubs, mocks, and dependency injection) lets the system be tested at critical conditions like time boundaries without waiting for them in real time.

Executable assertions placed where data values are referenced or modified (as pre- and post-conditions and class invariants) check that data satisfies specified constraints, increasing observability by flagging a failure, and to the extent they cover the test cases they effectively embed the test oracle in the code.

Limiting structural complexity improves testability: avoid cyclic dependencies, isolate and encapsulate dependencies on the external environment, reduce coupling, and simplify the inheritance hierarchy (limiting derivation, tree depth, children, and polymorphism); the response-of-a-class metric (a class's own methods plus the methods of others it invokes) empirically correlates to testability and should be kept low, and high cohesion, loose coupling, and separation of concerns all help.

Limiting nondeterminism improves testability because nondeterministic systems are harder to test than deterministic ones, so sources of nondeterminism such as unconstrained parallelism should be found and removed where possible, and unavoidable nondeterminism (as in multi-threaded systems responding to unpredictable events) should be managed with tactics like record/playback.

The dependency injection pattern separates a client's dependencies from its behavior using inversion of control, where an injector creates the service and injects it through an interface so the client has no knowledge of the concrete implementation, allowing test instances to be injected in place of production ones; its tradeoffs are less predictable runtime performance and added up-front complexity.

The strategy pattern lets a class's algorithm be selected and changed at runtime through an abstract method chosen by context, which is useful to replace non-test functionality with test versions and keeps classes simpler, but adds up-front complexity that is wasted when the class is simple or has few runtime choices.

The intercepting filter pattern injects pre- and post-processing (such as logging, authentication, or testing filters) between a client and a service in an arbitrary order without disturbing other processing and promotes reuse, but can be inefficient and add latency if a large amount of data passes through many filters that each scan the entire input.

Usability is concerned with how easily a user accomplishes a desired task and the user support the system provides, and a focus on usability is one of the cheapest and easiest ways to improve a system's perceived quality and end-user satisfaction.

Usability comprises learning system features, using the system efficiently, minimizing the impact of user errors, adapting the system to user needs, and increasing user confidence and satisfaction (for example through progress feedback on long-running tasks).

Usability is strongly connected to modifiability because user interface design is an iterative generate-and-test process that is highly unlikely to be right the first time, so the architecture should be designed to make UI iteration less painful.

In a usability general scenario the stimulus is the end user wanting to use the system efficiently, learn it, minimize the impact of errors, adapt it, or configure it; the response provides the needed features, anticipates the user's needs, and gives appropriate feedback; and measures include task time, number of errors, learning time, tasks accomplished, user satisfaction, and time or data lost when an error occurs.

Support-user-initiative tactics give feedback and let users respond: cancel requires a constant unblocked listener, terminating the canceled activity, freeing its resources, and informing collaborating components; undo requires maintaining enough state (snapshots or reversible operations) to restore an earlier state, recognizing that some operations cannot be reversed; pause/resume frees and reallocates resources during a long operation; and aggregate groups lower-level objects so a repetitive operation is applied once, reducing drudgery and mistakes.

Support-system-initiative usability tactics rely on encapsulated models: a task model infers what the user is attempting so the system can assist (for example type-ahead or spell correction), a user model represents the user's knowledge and behavior (for example adaptive exercises or user-interface customization), and a system model represents the system itself to predict behavior and give feedback (for example a progress bar).

The model-view-controller pattern (and its MVP and MVVM variants) separates the model (business logic) from one or more UI views with a controller interpreting user input, so changes to the UI layout often do not affect the model or controller and teams can develop and test the parts in parallel; updates use the observer pattern in one process or publish-subscribe when distributed, but MVC can be burdensome for complex UIs, unjustified for simple ones, and adds some latency.

The observer pattern links a subject to one or more registered observers that are notified when the subject's state changes (often used to implement MVC), allowing runtime change of bindings, but it is overkill without multiple views, leaks memory and wastes performance if observers fail to de-register, and wastes resources when a fine-grained subject and a coarse-grained view have an impedance mismatch.

The memento pattern implements the undo tactic with an originator, a caretaker, and a memento: before changing the originator's state the caretaker requests a memento (a state snapshot) and can pass it back to restore the state, knowing nothing about how state is managed; its tradeoff is that mementos can consume arbitrarily large memory and are hard to keep opaque in some languages.

The quality attributes covered in detail all measure either the system in operation (availability, energy efficiency, performance, security, safety, usability) or the people acting on the system while it is not running (modifiability, deployability, integrability, testability), but these only begin to cover the quality attributes a system may need.

Some quality attributes measure the architecture itself: buildability is the cost in money or time to turn the architecture into a working product, conceptual integrity is consistency that demands the same thing be done the same way throughout (providing alternatives only with a compelling reason, where less is more), and marketability reflects that the perception of an architecture can matter as much as the actual qualities it brings.

Development distributability is designing software to support distributed teams by minimizing the coordination needed among them, which requires low coupling in both the code and the data model, so that the architectural structure and the social and business structure of the project are reasonably aligned.

For software embedded in a physical system the software architecture can profoundly affect the whole system's quality attributes (weight, power consumption, battery life, size), and the architecture can enable or preclude meeting quality requirements (for example software performance is fundamentally bounded by the processor), so the architect must understand the system-level quality attributes and work with the system engineers to contribute to them.
The six-part scenario technique used for software quality attributes works equally well for system-level quality attributes.

Standard quality attribute lists such as ISO 25010 are useful as checklists and a basis for domain-specific checklists and measures, but no list is ever complete, lists generate more controversy than understanding, and quality attributes are not clean taxonomies because an issue like denial of service spans security, availability, performance, and usability.

Quality attribute names by themselves are largely useless and at best an invitation to begin a conversation, and time spent debating which qualities are subqualities of others is almost useless; instead scenarios are the best way to specify precisely what a quality attribute means, so standard lists should be used as checklists without slavishly adhering to their terminology and without treating the checklist as a substitute for deeper analysis.

To bring a new quality attribute into the fold, first capture scenarios by interviewing the stakeholders whose concerns created the need, refining the quality attribute into subattributes, crafting specific scenarios, and then generalizing the collection into a general scenario by generalizing each part (sources, stimuli, responses, measures, artifacts, environment).

To deal with a new quality attribute, find or build a conceptual model of it, meaning the bounded set of parameters the quality attribute is sensitive to and the architectural characteristics that influence those parameters (as a queuing model for performance exposes seven latency parameters: arrival rate, queuing discipline, scheduling algorithm, service time, topology, network bandwidth, and routing algorithm); the bounded parameter set is what gives the model its analytical power.

To assemble design approaches for a new quality attribute, enumerate the model's parameters and for each enumerate the architectural characteristics and mechanisms that affect it (by revisiting known mechanisms, searching for proven designs and publications, and consulting experts); the resulting list of mechanisms is finite and reasonably small because the parameters are bounded, which makes the design problem tractable.
An interface is a boundary across which elements meet, interact, communicate, and coordinate, and it controls access to an element's internals.
Interfaces are a fundamental abstraction mechanism for connecting elements and have an outsized impact on a system's modifiability, usability, testability, performance, and integrability.

All elements have interfaces because every element interacts with some actors, interfaces are two-way in that an interface includes both what an element provides and what it requires of its environment (so a missing required resource breaks the element), and a single interface can serve more than one actor at a time.

A single interface can be split into multiple interfaces, each with a related logical purpose serving a different class of actors, which provides separation of concerns and supports different access levels and rights (for example a public read-only interface for anonymous actors versus private authenticated interfaces, or separate debugging, monitoring, and administrative interfaces).

A resource has syntax (its signature, including the resource name and the names and data types of arguments) and semantics (the result of invoking it, including value assignments, changes in element state and side effects of partial operations, events or messages signaled, effects on the future behavior of other resources, observable results, and whether execution is atomic or can be interrupted).

The resources of a provided interface consist of operations (which transfer control and data and may fail, so error detection must be made clear), events (normally asynchronous incoming or outgoing notifications), and properties (interface metadata such as access rights, units of measure, or formatting assumptions that influence operation and element behavior).
Software encapsulated by an interface is free to evolve without impact to the elements that use it as long as the interface itself does not change.

An interface is a contract between an element and its actors and should be changed with care using one of three techniques: deprecation (removing it, ideally with extensive advance notice such as a warning error code), versioning (keeping the old interface and adding a new one, requiring the actor to specify which version it uses), and extension (leaving the original unchanged and adding new resources, using an internal interface plus a mediator if the extension introduces incompatibilities).

Decisions about which resources are externally visible should be driven by the needs of the actors that use them, because adding a resource commits you to maintaining it as long as the element is in use, and actors that depend on a resource will break if it is changed or removed, harming the architecture's reliability.

Interface design should follow the principle of least surprise (behave consistently with actor expectations, aided by apt names), the small interfaces principle (interacting elements exchange as little information as possible), the uniform access principle (do not leak implementation details, so a resource is accessed the same way whether its value comes from a cache, a computation, or a fresh fetch), and the don't-repeat-yourself principle (offer composable primitives rather than many redundant ways to achieve the same goal).

An architect should establish and follow consistent conventions across an architecture for how resources are named, how API parameters are ordered, and how errors are handled, and follow the underlying platform or language idioms, because consistency minimizes development errors caused by misunderstanding.
A successful interaction with an interface requires agreement on four aspects: interface scope, interaction style, the representation and structure of the exchanged data, and error handling.

A gateway (often a message gateway) constrains and mediates access to an element's resources by translating actor requests into requests to the target element and becoming an actor for it, which is useful for bridging mismatches in resource granularity, restricting actors to specific resource subsets, and providing a more stable interface when the underlying resource specifics change over time.

The interaction style should be chosen by the communication and coordination needs and element co-location: co-located elements can use efficient local shared-memory buffers, elements expected to be available simultaneously can use synchronous calls, and elements in an unreliable distributed environment should rely on asynchronous event-based interactions via message queues or data streams.

Remote Procedure Call (RPC) models a remote call as if it were a local procedure call translated into messages to and from a remote element, while Representational State Transfer (REST) is a web-services protocol defined by six constraints: a uniform interface (resources named by URIs), client-server, stateless interactions, cacheable resources, a tiered system architecture, and optional code on demand.

A general-purpose data interchange format should be selected by weighing expressiveness, interoperability (matching what actors expect, favoring a standard like JSON), performance (bandwidth, parsing complexity, and cost), implicit coupling (shared assumptions that risk decode errors), and transparency (self-describing text aids debugging but also eavesdroppers, whereas binary or encrypted formats are more secure but need special tools).

Common data representations trade verbosity and validation against performance: XML is a verbose schema-validatable textual meta-language whose validation prevents malformed-document faults but whose parsing is expensive (the document must be read completely, possibly in multiple passes), JSON is a less-verbose textual format that can be parsed as it is read with efficient serialization, and Protocol Buffers are a compact schema-defined binary format that is efficient in memory and bandwidth and is mostly used with gRPC.

A well-designed interface must handle undesired circumstances (such as invalid parameters, insufficient memory, a call that never returns, or an unresponsive sensor) and let actors know whether their interaction succeeded, through strategies such as throwing exceptions, returning status codes, error-indicating properties, error events like a timeout, or a readable error log.

The specification of which exceptions, status codes, events, and information describe erroneous outcomes is itself part of an element's interface, and the interface should gracefully handle common error sources including invalid or illegal input, the element being in the wrong state for a request, hardware or software failure, and incorrect configuration.

Indicating the source of an error guides the correction and recovery strategy: temporary errors with idempotent operations can be handled by waiting and retrying, invalid-input errors require fixing and resending the request, missing dependencies should be reinstalled, and implementation bugs should be fixed and the failure scenario added as a regression test case.

Interface documentation should expose only what actors need to know to interact with the interface, not every possible interaction; properties that a developer observes but that are not part of the documentation reflect the implementation, are subject to change, and are used at the developer's own risk.

Different stakeholders need different information about an interface (the element developer, the maintainer, a developer using the interface, a systems integrator and tester, an analyst who may need an SLA, and an architect seeking reusable assets), so interface documentation may need separate sections for these roles.

Documenting an interface is a promise that the element will fulfill the contract, so any implementation that does not violate the contract is valid; a distinction must be drawn between the interface (everything observable about the element, such as how long an operation takes) and the documentation of the interface (the subset of behavior actors are told they may depend on).

By Hyrum's law, with a sufficient number of users of an interface, all observable behaviors of the system will be depended on by somebody regardless of what the contract promises, but an actor that depends on unpublished behavior does so at its own risk.

Interface design is an architectural duty because compatible interfaces are what let an architecture's many elements work together productively, a primary purpose of an interface is to encapsulate an element's implementation so it can change without affecting others, and interfaces should be as simple as possible but no simpler.

Virtual machines and containers isolate one application from another while still sharing resources, letting developers write applications as if they alone use the computer, but the isolation is inherently limited because the applications share one physical machine with fixed resources, so one application consuming all of a resource such as CPU can prevent the others from executing.

The four resources typically shared are CPU (shared via a thread scheduler that no thread can bypass to gain a processor), memory (shared via virtual memory that pages between physical and secondary storage with hardware isolation of address spaces), disk (shared via a disk controller that sequences access plus OS tagging of threads and content by user and group), and the network (isolated by IP addresses that identify and route messages, and by ports on which services listen).

A virtual machine runs a simulated computer inside a physical host, and a hypervisor is the operating system for VMs: a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware and is typical in data centers and the cloud, whereas a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as a service on top of a host operating system and is typical on desktops and laptops for running incompatible applications or replicating a production environment.

A hypervisor requires its guest VMs to use the same instruction set as the underlying physical CPU because it does not translate or simulate instruction execution, so cross-processor execution instead requires an emulator, which reads the guest processor's binary code and simulates the execution of its instructions and often its I/O hardware.

A hypervisor performs two main functions: it manages the code in each VM (intercepting and tagging external disk and network I/O so the asynchronous interrupt responses are routed to the correct VM) and it manages the VMs themselves (creating and destroying them on instructions from a user or cloud infrastructure, monitoring their health and resource usage, sitting inside the VMs' security perimeter, and enforcing each VM's CPU, memory, disk, and network limits after first verifying sufficient physical resources).

Virtualization has two major implications for an architect: a performance cost (modest for a Type 1 hypervisor but potentially significantly larger for a Type 2 hypervisor, with around 10 percent overhead reported and more for I/O-heavy services) and separation of concerns, since virtualization lets the architect treat runtime resources as commodities and defer provisioning and deployment decisions to another party.

A VM image (the bootable disk contents holding the operating system, services, and boot loader) can be created by snapshotting a running machine, extending an existing image, or building from scratch, but running an image you or your organization did not create risks uncontrolled OS and software versions, insecure configuration, vulnerabilities, or even malware.

Because VM images are very large (slow to transfer over a network) and bundle all their dependencies, it is customary to create images containing only the operating system and essential programs and then add services after the VM boots, in a process called configuration, to avoid a proliferation of one unique image per service version that is hard to manage.

Containers keep most of the advantages of virtualization while reducing image transfer and startup time, because all containers on a host share the same operating system kernel through a container runtime engine, so the operating system need not be transferred in the container image as long as a standard runtime engine is present on the target machine.

Container images are built in layers, and the container management system transfers only the changed uppermost layer when a version is updated, making deployment of a new container version far faster than a VM (milliseconds rather than minutes); however, this fast partial update applies only to the uppermost layer, so changing a lower layer requires rebuilding every layer above it.
condition: only the uppermost changed layer is moved; a lower-layer change forces rebuilding the layers above it

statement: The steps to build a container image should be scripted into a version-controlled specification file and treated as code (consciously designed, tested, configuration controlled, reviewed, documented, and shared), so that every team member can create an identical container image.

A VM virtualizes the physical hardware and runs an entire operating system, so it can run almost any OS and almost any program (important for legacy or purchased software) and can host multiple tightly coupled services that share data, whereas container instances share the host operating system, must be compatible with the container runtime engine, and typically run a single service because the runtime engine starts and monitors just one program per container and the container ends when that program exits.

Other differences between VMs and containers are that a VM can run any operating system while containers are limited to Linux, Windows, or iOS, VM services are managed through operating-system functions while container services are managed through container runtime engine functions, VMs persist beyond the termination of their services while containers do not, and containers have some port-usage restrictions that VMs lack.

Because the interface between a container and a container runtime engine has been standardized by the Open Container Initiative, a container built with one vendor's package can run on another vendor's runtime engine, so a container developed on a development computer can be deployed to production, and specifying all resources as configuration parameters simplifies that move even though differing available resources keep deployment non-trivial.

A Kubernetes Pod is a group of related containers that are allocated and deallocated together and share an IP address and port space, interprocess communication mechanisms, and ephemeral storage; its purpose is to reduce communication cost between closely related containers by co-locating them on the same VM so they can use faster mechanisms than message passing.

In a serverless (function-as-a-service) architecture, a fresh short-lived container is allocated per request and the responsibility for allocation and deallocation moves to the cloud infrastructure, which forces the containers to be stateless, so any state needed for coordination must be stored in a cloud-provider infrastructure service or passed as parameters.

Function-as-a-service has practical limitations: cloud providers offer a limited selection of base container images that restrict programming language and library options (to keep load time low), the cold-start time on first allocation can be several seconds while subsequent cached requests are near-instant, and the execution time per request is capped so a service must process and exit within the provider's time limit.

Cloud computing is the on-demand availability of resources stored on someone else's computers, accessible over the Internet, paid for by use, elastic so it can grow or shrink with need, and self-provisioned.

Clouds are deployed as public (owned by a provider and accessible over the public Internet), private (owned and operated by an organization for internal use, chosen for control, security, or cost), or hybrid (some workloads private and some public, used for migration or for data legally requiring greater control), and from the architect's technical perspective there is little difference between private and public clouds.

A cloud provider organizes data centers into regions, and choosing the region a service runs in is an important design decision because it keeps the service physically close to its users (reducing network delay) and helps comply with data-residency regulations such as GDPR; within a region, data centers are grouped into availability zones such that the probability of two different zones failing at the same time is extremely low, making the zone choice a key availability and business-continuity decision.

To allocate a cloud VM, an architect sends the management gateway a request specifying the region, instance type, and VM image ID; the gateway finds a hypervisor with enough unallocated CPU and memory, has it create the VM, and returns the VM's IP address and a DNS hostname; the management gateway also collects billing information and provides the ability to monitor and destroy the VM, and is accessed through a scriptable API or a web application.

In a data center with tens of thousands of physical computers it is almost certain that some will fail every day (for example roughly 5 computers and 17 disks per day per about 64,000 computers), and switches, overheating, or disasters can also cause failures, so even though the provider has few total outages the physical host of a specific VM may fail, and a service for which availability matters must deliberately decide its target availability and how to achieve it.

In distributed systems a timeout is commonly used to detect failure but cannot distinguish a real failure from a reply that is merely slower than the timeout, cannot localize where the failure occurred, and can falsely suggest failure when a chain of barely-slow responses accumulates; because recovery actions carry a cost such as latency or starting a new VM, concluding there was a failure on a temporary delay can incur unnecessary cost.

Timeout-based failure detection should be parameterized by a timeout interval and a number of missed responses over a window (for example a 200 ms timeout triggering recovery after 3 missed messages in 1 second) and tuned to context: parameters can be aggressive for single-data-center systems with minimal network delay but should be relaxed for wide-area, cellular, or satellite networks with intermittent longer delays to avoid triggering unnecessary recovery.

Most distributed systems do not trigger failure recovery after a single missed response but instead wait for some number of missed responses over a longer time interval, because reacting to one missed message risks unnecessary recovery from a transient delay.

Cloud service requests exhibit long tail latency, where a reasonable fraction of requests take 2 to 10 times longer than the average (the 95th percentile can be far above the mean), caused by congestion or failure somewhere in the request path that is out of the developer's control, so monitoring and performance and availability strategies must reflect this long-tail distribution.
When characterizing a latency measurement set you must be careful which statistic you use, because under a long-tail distribution the mean, median, and high percentiles differ substantially.

Two techniques to handle long tail latency are hedged requests (issue more requests than needed and cancel or ignore the extras once enough responses arrive) and alternative requests (issue the needed number, then issue a few more once most have completed, and cancel the remaining stragglers once enough responses are received).

Vertical scaling (scaling up) runs the same service on a larger instance type providing more of the needed resource without changing the service design, but is limited by the largest available instance, whereas horizontal scaling (scaling out) runs multiple copies of the service behind a load balancer, corresponding to the maintain-multiple-copies tactic and the load balancer pattern.

A load balancer must be very efficient because it sits in the path of every message from a client to a service, and from a client's perspective the service's IP address is actually the load balancer's, so the client need not know how many service instances exist or their addresses, making the client resilient to that information changing (an example of using an intermediary).

A round-robin load-balancing algorithm balances load uniformly across service instances only if every request consumes roughly the same resources to process; for requests with varying resource consumption, other distribution algorithms are needed.
condition: every request consumes roughly equal resources

statement: Load balancers can themselves become overloaded, and the solution is to balance the load of the load balancer through a hierarchy of load balancers, known as global load balancing.

Because return messages go directly from service instances to clients and bypass the load balancer, the load balancer has no inherent knowledge of whether instances are alive, so health checks (periodic pings, TCP connections, or processing messages) let it detect an unhealthy instance and stop sending it messages.

Because an instance can move from healthy to unhealthy and back (for example a transiently overloaded queue), a load balancer checks multiple times before moving an instance to the unhealthy list and then periodically re-checks that list, while failed instances restart and re-register or are replaced to maintain overall service capacity.

A load balancer with health checking improves availability by hiding instance failures from clients, and the instance pool should be sized to tolerate some simultaneous instance failures while still meeting the required request volume and latency; because an instance may start a request and never return a response, clients must be designed to resend on no timely response and services must be designed to accommodate multiple identical requests.

State is service-internal, history-dependent information that affects the response to a request, and managing it matters when a service handles concurrent requests; the three options for where to store it are in each service instance (making the service stateful), in each client, or in an external database (the latter two making the service stateless).

Common practice is to design services to be stateless, because stateful services lose their history if they fail and recovering it can be difficult, whereas statelessness lets a newly created instance process a request and produce the same response as any other instance.

When statelessness is impractical, a series of messages from a client can be routed to the same service instance through a direct client-to-instance session or a load balancer configured for sticky sessions, but these approaches should be used only under special circumstances because of the risk of that instance failing or becoming overloaded.
exception: only under special circumstances, given instance-failure and overload risk

statement: Hardware clocks drift (about one second every 12 days) and NTP synchronizes devices to roughly 1 millisecond on a LAN and 10 milliseconds on public networks (worse under congestion), so an architect should assume some clock error exists between devices and design most distributed systems so that correct application functioning does not require time synchronization among devices.

For many purposes the order of events matters more than the actual time they occurred (as in stock trading and online auctions), so for critical cross-device coordination distributed systems use mechanisms such as vector clocks (counters that trace actions as they propagate) to determine whether one event happened before another rather than comparing clock times, and the architect must decide whether real clock times or correct sequencing is what is actually required.

Coordinating shared data across distributed machines (such as a lock on a shared data item to prevent a race condition like two simultaneous deposits overwriting each other) is hard in a distributed system because the two-phase commit protocol requires multiple network messages that add delay or may fail to be delivered, and a lock holder may fail after acquiring the lock and block others.

Distributed coordination is a problem you should not try to solve yourself, because consensus algorithms like Paxos are notoriously hard to design correctly and even implementing a proven one is difficult due to language and network-interface subtleties, so using an existing package such as Apache ZooKeeper, Consul, or etcd is almost always better than rolling your own.

Autoscaling is an infrastructure service that automatically creates new service instances when needed and releases surplus instances when they are not, working with load balancing to grow and shrink the instance pool, and it exploits cloud elasticity so an organization pays only for the capacity it requisitions rather than provisioning for peak workload.

Autoscaler rules should trigger on resource metrics averaged over a reasonable time interval rather than instantaneous values, because the metrics have spikes and valleys and because starting a new VM takes minutes (loading the image, connecting the network, booting the OS), so rules typically take the form of creating a new VM when CPU utilization stays above a threshold for several minutes, and can also enforce minimum and maximum instance counts or schedule allocations from historical usage patterns.

Removing an instance requires draining rather than an abrupt shutdown: the autoscaler must first notify the load balancer to stop sending requests to the instance, then notify the instance to terminate its in-progress activities and shut down before destroying it, and the service developer is responsible for implementing the interface that receives these terminate-and-drain instructions.

Scaling containers is a two-level decision (whether an additional container or Pod is needed for the workload, and whether it fits on an existing runtime engine or requires a new VM), and keeping the container-scaling software independent of the VM-scaling software keeps container scaling portable across cloud providers, whereas integrating the two risks creating a hard-to-break dependency on a specific cloud provider.

A mobile system delivers some or all of its functionality while in motion, which makes five characteristics differ from fixed systems: energy (limited power sources), network connectivity (mobility complicates connections), sensors and actuators (more environmental interaction), resources (more constrained by size and weight), and life cycle (testing and deployment differ).
For mobile energy the architect must monitor the power source, throttle energy usage, and tolerate loss of power.

A battery manager periodically queries the battery management system to retrieve battery state so the system can inform the user, trigger battery-saving mode, and alert registered applications to imminent shutdown, and the battery manager's own CPU consumption can be controlled by adjusting the query interval.

Because a battery's maximum capacity and maximum sustained current both change as it ages, an architect must manage consumption within this changing envelope of available power so the device still performs at an acceptable level.

Mobile energy usage can be throttled by terminating or degrading energy-consuming parts of the system, such as reducing display brightness or refresh rate, reducing the number of active processor cores or their clock rate, or reducing the frequency of sensor readings like GPS sampling.

Mobile systems should gracefully tolerate power failures and restarts, which implies the runtime can be killed at any moment without corrupting the integrity of binaries, configurations, and data in permanent storage and while keeping state consistent after restart, applications need a strategy for data arriving while inoperative, and the startup time from power-on to a ready state must be under a specified limit.

Wireless networks are categorized by operating distance: Near Field Communication within about 4 centimeters, IEEE 802.15 (Bluetooth, Zigbee) within about 10 meters, IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) within about 100 meters, IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) within several kilometers, and cellular or satellite beyond that, with the technologies and standards evolving rapidly.

A mobile system should include only the strictly required communication interfaces (to optimize power, heat, and space rather than supporting every protocol), make protocol transitions during a session seamless to the user, choose dynamically among simultaneously available protocols by cost, bandwidth, and power, be designed for modifiability to support new protocols over its lifetime, maintain data integrity and resume consistently across intermittent or lost connectivity with degraded and fallback modes, and address mobile-specific threats such as spoofing, eavesdropping, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

A sensor translates physical characteristics of the environment into an electronic representation, an actuator is its reverse by taking a digital input and causing an action in the environment, and a sensor hub is a coprocessor that integrates and processes data from multiple sensors to offload that work from the main CPU, saving battery and improving performance.

The sensor stack turns raw data into interpreted environmental information through layered functions: a driver reads raw data at a period that trades processor load against accuracy, smoothing (for example a moving average or Kalman filter) reduces noise across successive readings, conversion normalizes differing sensor formats into a common form, and sensor fusion combines multiple sensors for a more accurate, complete, and dependable representation than any single sensor (for example fusing thermal imagers, radar, lidar, and cameras to detect pedestrians).

When sensors fail or become unreadable the system should enter a degraded mode (for example using dead reckoning to estimate location when GPS is unavailable in a tunnel), and the appropriate representation of the environment and approach to degraded operation are domain specific.

The choice of a mobile system resource trades the resource's contribution against its volume, weight, and cost, and because many mobile systems are manufactured by the millions and are highly price-sensitive, a small per-unit cost difference multiplied across millions of units can significantly affect profitability.

Mobile resource constraints that affect the architect include safety (safety-critical physical resources must not fail or must have backups, which add cost, weight, and space), thermal limits (heat from the system itself or the ambient environment can degrade or even fail it, so the operating environment must be understood before hardware choices), and other environmental exposure such as moisture, dust, or being dropped.

Assigning subsystems to electronic control units (ECUs) in larger mobile systems should weigh fit of ECU power to the function, criticality (reserving more powerful and reliable ECUs for critical functions like engine control), location, connectivity (functions split across ECUs must share an internal network), locality of communication (co-locating intensely communicating components on the same ECU improves performance and reduces network traffic), and cost (minimizing the number of ECUs).

Offloading functionality to the cloud splits an application between the mobile device, where the sensors are, and the cloud, where more storage and processing power are available, so the architect must judge whether the device has sufficient power for given functions, whether connectivity is adequate to offload, how to meet performance requirements when functions are split, and the local storage, update intervals, and privacy implications.

For many mobile systems the hardware is chosen before the software is designed, so the software architecture must live with the chosen hardware's constraints, and the architect should actively drive these early hardware discussions emphasizing the tradeoffs involved rather than passively awaiting the outcome, since the early stakeholders (management, sales, regulators) tend to focus on reducing risk rather than promoting quality attributes.

Mobile testing has unique demands: verifying display layouts across many sizes and aspect ratios (where automatic layout generation can produce overlapping or off-screen controls that escape detection), testing operational edge cases such as battery-exhaustion state preservation and hard-to-reproduce asynchronous user-interface timing bugs, testing resource usage (where simulators help but battery testing on a simulator is problematic), and testing seamless transitions between communication networks.

Transportation and industrial systems are tested on four levels (software component, function, device on the target ECU, and full system integration), and an issue found at the system level must be reproducible and traceable through all the test setups because the fix must pass through all four levels again.

When deploying mobile updates, consumer upgrades tend to be automatic and one-way with no rollback (which favors keeping data in the cloud), the architect must determine which system states can safely support an update (for example not updating engine control software while driving), the frequently changing portions should be architected for easy automated partial update without physical access, and long device lifetimes require planning for extendability and retrofitting.

In mobile systems, logs should be offloaded to a location accessible regardless of the accessibility of the mobile system itself, both for investigating and resolving incidents and for analyzing system usage.

Architectures exist to build systems that satisfy requirements, meaning the set of properties that would make the system a failure if unmet, and regardless of how those requirements are captured, the architect needs to know them.

An architecturally significant requirement (ASR) is a requirement that has a profound effect on the architecture, such that the architecture would be dramatically different in its absence, and you cannot design a successful architecture without knowing the ASRs.

Architecturally significant requirements often, but not always, take the form of quality attribute requirements, and the more difficult and important a quality attribute requirement is, the more likely it is to significantly affect the architecture and hence to be an ASR.

Requirements documents fail an architect in two ways: most of their content concerns features and functionality, which shape the architecture the least, while the quality attribute requirements that drive it are rarely captured adequately, and much of what drives an architecture (business goals, developmental qualities such as teaming, stakeholders, and the technical environment) never appears as a system observable in any requirements document.

Untestable, non-falsifiable quality attribute requirements such as the system shall be modular or shall exhibit high usability are not useful requirements, but they can be viewed as invitations for the architect to begin a conversation about what the requirement in that area really is.

An architect must begin work while the requirements are still in flux rather than wait until they are finished, so the quality attribute requirements are quite likely to be uncertain when the architect starts.

When mining a requirements document for ASRs (which will not be labeled as such), look in categories such as usage, time and coordination, external elements, networking, orchestration, security properties, data, resources, project management, hardware choices, flexibility and portability, and named technologies, and also consider which of these are likely to change over time, because anticipated evolution is itself architecturally significant.

Stakeholders often do not know what their quality attribute requirements actually are, so architects are called upon to help set them, and projects that recognize and encourage this collaboration are much more likely to succeed; insisting prematurely on quantitative quality attribute numbers tends to yield arbitrary values that are hard to satisfy and ultimately detract from system success.

Experienced architects have deep insight into which quality attribute responses similar systems exhibited and which are reasonable to expect, and can quickly flag which will be straightforward and which problematic or prohibitive, so they can surface tradeoffs (for example explaining the cost of 24/7 availability so stakeholders can trade availability against affordability).

Interviewing the relevant stakeholders is the surest way to learn what they know and need, and a project should capture this critical information in a systematic, clear, and repeatable way, for example using a Quality Attribute Workshop.

The Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW) is a facilitated, stakeholder-focused method to generate, prioritize, and refine quality attribute scenarios before the architecture is completed, through a business and mission presentation, an architectural plan presentation, identification of architectural drivers, scenario brainstorming (each scenario given an explicit stimulus and response), scenario consolidation, prioritization (each stakeholder gets votes equal to about 30 percent of the consolidated scenario count), and refinement of the top scenarios into the six-part scenario form.

When a stakeholder says they do not know what a requirement should be, elicit the something they do know (especially if they are experienced in the domain) rather than inventing the requirement yourself; playing dumb by proposing progressively tighter values often yields a range of acceptable values, which is typically enough to choose architectural mechanisms because a response time of 24 hours versus 10 minutes versus 10 seconds versus 100 milliseconds implies very different architectural approaches.

Business goals are the reason a system is built and frequently lead directly to architecturally significant requirements, so they should be captured explicitly because they often imply ASRs that would otherwise go undetected until it is too late or too expensive to address them.

There are three possible relationships between a business goal and the architecture: a business goal may lead to a quality attribute requirement (and knowing the goal behind a stringent requirement lets the architect meaningfully question it or marshal resources to meet it), a business goal may affect the architecture without inducing any quality attribute requirement (such as mandating a database to keep an internal database team employed), or a business goal may have no architectural influence at all (such as reducing cost by lowering the thermostat).

The PALM method holds a workshop with the architect and key business stakeholders to elicit important business goals expressed as business-goal scenarios (consolidated and prioritized) and then, for each goal, identify a quality attribute and response-measure value that would help achieve it, using a set of candidate business-goal categories as conversation starters to ensure coverage.

A utility tree is a top-down representation of the quality-attribute-related ASRs an architect believes critical to a system's success, used when primary requirement sources such as stakeholders are unavailable; it has Utility as the root, then the major quality attributes, then specific refinements of each, then the specific ASRs expressed as quality attribute scenarios at the leaves.
